stories.Headline: OpenAI releases GPT-Live-1.1 with standby billing for idle voice sessions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released GPT-Live-1.1, a full-duplex voice model for multilingual conversations, in its API under the model ID gpt-live-1.1 on November 21, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. The model can listen while it speaks and follows GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026, and has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. It accepts audio and text inputs and outputs, supports streaming and function calling, and does not support images, video, structured outputs, fine-tuning or predicted outputs. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions, and the model runs only on OpenAI's cloud through v1/live/sessions, with clients connecting over WebRTC or WebSocket.

Live sessions hold a 128,000-token default context window, and instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. Standby bills idle WebRTC time at $0.02 per minute versus $0.05 active, a 60% lower rate, or $1.20 per hour against $3.00. Standby pauses inference during silence while the connection stays open, the server emits session.paused after the timeout and session.resumed when the user speaks, and the session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower and says the microphone track should stay active during standby, and standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1.

Voice sessions are billed by duration, and the GPT-Live-1 model page says billing is per second, while backend model and tool usage are billed separately. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model, and OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks, though third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses, where responses mode uses OpenAI models and client mode connects your own backend. Switching an existing Live session requires setting the model to gpt-live-1.1 and starting a new session.

OpenAI says the model speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages, handles transcription, letters and numbers better, and completes tasks more reliably than GPT-Live-1. OpenAI published no benchmark scores for 1.1, so the quality gains are self-reported with no numbers. The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech, and OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model, handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Outbound SIP calling reached all organizations on November 2, so phone agents are supported, and GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1 have separate concurrent-session limits that each apply across inference regions, though the 1.1 page does not publish tier numbers.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics opens an AI home experience store in Singapore to test and expand its AI appliances across Southeast Asia
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics established an artificial intelligence home advance base in Singapore on November 23, 2026, to target the Southeast Asian market. The company opened this new experience store to reach a regional population of 700 million people through a strategic base. This outpost allows the company to verify the marketability of its AI home appliances before expanding into other neighboring countries. The company aims to use Singapore as a gateway to enter the broader Southeast Asian region and its premium consumers. LG Electronics intends to promote its AI home competitiveness and expand customer contacts to major countries such as Malaysia.

The company opened an AI home experience store of about 140 square meters at the Milenia Walk complex shopping mall. This space implements real residential areas including a kitchen, a living room, a laundry room, and a children's room. Customers use the LG ThinQ app to connect and control various home appliances and Internet of Things devices. The store features Fit and Max refrigerators and wash towers designed to minimize gaps between walls and home appliances. These specific products target the local residential environments of Singapore, which contains many apartments and condominiums.

Lee Gun-ho is the head of the Singapore branch of LG Electronics and is responsible for this new outpost. He stated that the company will provide an AI home experience that is differentiated by products optimized for local lifestyles. He noted that the services are specifically designed to fit the residential environment and the lifestyle of the local people. Employees at the store use dioramas implemented in transparent OLED to introduce the various AI home solutions to the customers. This approach helps the company inform visitors about the specific benefits of their differentiated AI home products and services.

Customers in Singapore are the primary people affected by the opening of this new AI home experience space. These consumers can now directly experience how to control their home appliances using the integrated LG ThinQ mobile application. Global companies also use the Singapore market to monitor consumer reactions before they enter the wider Southeast Asian market. The company targets premium consumers who live in the many apartments and condominiums found throughout the city of Singapore. This allows the company to test local reactions to its specialized home appliance products in a key market.

LG Electronics started its home appliance subscription business in Singapore last year before securing this AI home experience base this year. The company is speeding up its efforts to tap into the local market by establishing this strategic advance base. Grandview Research claims the home appliance market in five major Southeast Asian countries will grow from 21.25 billion dollars in 2024. This market is expected to reach 30.9 billion dollars by 2030 according to the global market research company. The average annual growth rate for this specific region is expected to be 6.7 percent from 2025 to 2030.

The company will now use this Singapore base to expand its business operations into other neighboring Southeast Asian countries. LG Electronics plans to increase its customer contacts in major markets like Malaysia using the data from this store. The company will continue to promote its AI home competitiveness to reach more consumers across the wider regional market. The articles leave open how the company will specifically implement its expansion into the other four major Southeast Asian countries. They also do not state the specific timeline for when the business will move into the Malaysian market.

stories.Headline: Philippe Laffont buys over $1 million each in Salesforce, Microsoft, Meta and Shopify in Q3
stories.Summary:
Philippe Laffont of Coatue Management rebalanced his portfolio in Q3, and four of his biggest buys, each more than $1 million in the quarter, were in the application layer space rather than hardware. His largest purchase in the quarter was Salesforce, followed by Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Shopify. Geoffrey Seiler wrote about the buys for The Motley Fool on November 22, 2026. The article appeared on Yahoo Finance and on fool.com. The article said Laffont seemed particularly bullish on AI agents.

Salesforce created its Data 360 solution, which used zero-copy technology to retrieve data from within an organization and from outside storage places like cloud providers and data warehouses without the time and cost of moving it. Salesforce then acquired Informatica to clean and organize this data. Since then it has acquired Fin, Qualified, Cresta and Braze to improve its front- and back-end for AI agents. Microsoft's Copilot saw an eightfold increase in customers to more than 50,000 users last quarter. Microsoft shifted to a hybrid seat plus consumption model for Copilot and GitHub, and it said agentic AI consumption features at GitHub have more than doubled since the pricing change.

Microsoft said the pricing strategy shift is boosting average revenue per user growth and increasing its total addressable market. Meta's Muse AI agents could be a game-changer for the social media company and its stock. AI is already driving strong ad revenue at Meta's social media sites by feeding users more content and ads they are interested in, leading to a higher ad load and stronger ad prices. Meta's growth driver will be facilitating e-commerce purchases, with revenue from affiliate or transaction fees. Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol with Alphabet and others and uses that protocol for its AI-ready database called Shopify Catalog.

Catalog-based searches at Shopify converted to sales at double the rate of ordinary searches last quarter. Shopify's Sidekick AI assistant saw daily active users soar 3.7 times year over year last quarter. Shopify recently launched a new online store builder to help merchants personalize their digital stores and build them more quickly. The article said Salesforce has worked diligently to build the foundation to become a leading agentic AI company in the enterprise space. The article said AI agents are only as good as the data to which they have access.

The article said Microsoft looks set to be a big AI software-as-a-service winner given how ingrained it is with enterprise productivity tools. The article said Meta's massive user base puts it at a big advantage to capture a nice chunk of the agentic AI commerce market. The article said Shopify looks positioned to be one of the biggest winners for agentic commerce. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include Salesforce among the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now. Geoffrey Seiler has positions in Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Salesforce, and The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Salesforce and Shopify.

The article said Salesforce's buy of Salesforce makes a lot of sense if Laffont is bullish on AI agents. The article said Microsoft's growth is being driven by its cloud computing unit, Azure. The article said Meta has been one of the best companies at employing AI to drive growth in its core business. The article said Shopify's e-commerce software company is one of the best ways to play the agentic commerce theme. The article said Meta's consumer AI agents can help individuals perform a lot of different tasks.

The article did not give the size of any individual purchase beyond saying each was more than $1 million. The article did not give the exact date in Q3 when the buys were made. The article did not say what Laffont or Coatue said about the purchases. The article did not give the size of Laffont's stakes after the buys. The article did not say whether Laffont still held the shares at the time of writing.

stories.Headline: US Senate passes permitting reform bill to accelerate energy construction for AI power demand
stories.Summary:
Financial markets suffered major losses this week as concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble grew. The US Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday to speed up energy construction. Confusion is also growing over new Medicaid work requirement rules that are set to begin in January. Investors feared the AI boom could bust despite a record initial public offering from Anthropic on Thursday. The entire stock market was pummeled on Friday during one of the worst weeks in years.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 passed the Senate with a 62-33 vote. It rewrites the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act. The bill changes the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 and shortens timelines for getting most permits. It requires data centers to pay for energy usage and exempts some projects from environmental review. These changes aim to lower energy costs and speed up oil, gas, solar, and hydropower projects.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Ruben Gallego supported the bill to bring down carbon emissions. Senator Martin Heinrich said the legislation provides a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito stated that Americans deserve bipartisan solutions that make life more affordable. These authors argued that cutting red tape allows more energy production and lowers prices for the public. They believe working people cannot afford to wait years for these necessary infrastructure improvements to happen.

The Sierra Club and Natural Resource Defense Council opposed the bill because it weakens bedrock environmental protections. Executive Director Loren Blackford said the bill is deeply flawed and threatens endangered species and tribal sovereignty. Nearly a dozen tribal organizations warned that the changes limit Indigenous input on sites with important cultural significance. Labor unions, oil and gas companies, and most clean energy industry groups expressed their support for the measure. Many voters in recent elections prioritized cost of living and affordability issues over these environmental concerns.

The NASDAQ dropped 10 percent this week, marking its worst performance since the pandemic year of 2020. The S&P and Dow Jones indices both ended the week in a correction after dropping 10 percent. In September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years, increasing borrowing costs. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang resigned this month following suspicions of an affair with a woman spying for China. Democrats are set to take over Congress and many state governments in January and promise to slow AI.

The permitting bill must now clear the House before it reaches the desk of President Donald Trump. The House is out of session next week for Thanksgiving and must extend government funding by December 11. Republicans may need Democratic votes in a narrowly divided chamber to pass the bill before January. It remains unclear if the House will pass the bill or if Democrats will wait until January. The articles leave open whether the AI market is a bubble or just a temporary readjustment.

stories.Headline: Preparing the U.S. economy for the age of AI
stories.Summary:
The Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research held its Fall Policy Forum on AI's economic and political effects on Nov. 12, 2026, gathering leaders in business, government and academia. The forum, titled "Economic Policy in the Age of AI," focused on what is happening today and how policies can handle the expected and the unexpected. Mary C. Daly, president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, delivered the opening keynote. Neale Mahoney, the Trione Director at SIEPR and the TG Wijaya Professor of Economics at Stanford, kicked off the event and moderated a Q&A with Daly. Speakers included Anton Korinek of the Anthropic Institute, Jennifer Duff of Mesa, Ariz.'s city council, Scott Strand of Google, David Deming of Harvard College, Josh Zoffer of CIV, Erika McEntarfer of SIEPR, Ioana Marinescu of the University of Pennsylvania, Ben Hyman of UCLA's California Policy Lab, Elena Patel of the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center and Ezra Kagan of RAISE US.

Prompted to estimate AI's contribution to U.S. economic growth in the next three years, economists' predictions ranged from 1.5% to 30%, Korinek said. Strand said AI adoption is "broad yet shallow," with automating tasks accounting for just 10% of current usage. Deming described three potential outcomes: a white-collar jobs apocalypse, a broken career ladder for young workers, and AI as "a normal technology" akin to the internet or personal computer. Patel noted that individual incomes make up 85% of federal tax revenues, and she said there is talk of imposing an AI usage tax and a "windfall" tax on companies profiting from AI. Duff said Mesa, a city of 530,000, now has rules around water and power use and restrictions on the location and height of data centers.

Mahoney said, "We do too much predicting, and not enough planning, around AI," and said policymakers face pressure to act and need evidence-based advice. Daly said she is "extremely bullish" about what AI will ultimately mean for the economy but is keenly aware of the need for policymakers to be proactive. "The transition dynamic matters," Daly said, and if the AI economy hasn't worked as wanted in 10 years, "it won't be the technology's fault. This is ours to decide." Korinek said the range of predictions "tells you how large the span of uncertainty is." Zoffer said "the right has said, 'We want reindustrialization' and the left has said, 'We want electrification,'" and said he would love to see trillions of dollars expected to pour into data-center development used to create jobs in the United States, finance clean energy infrastructure and help the U.S. reindustrialize.

McEntarfer said "Our social safety net here in the U.S. is pretty rickety," and said an obvious place to start is unemployment benefit programs run by states. Marinescu and Hyman suggested "wage insurance" to subsidize workers transitioning to lower-paying jobs, and said employers could be given tax breaks to train workers for new roles or to allow job sharing to minimize layoffs. Hyman said that if there are a lot of correlated layoffs across many different firms, that kind of minimizes the crowd-out across job seekers when they are searching for fewer and fewer jobs. Kagan said it is imperative, in getting ready for this disruption, to start building the muscle at the state level, within educational institutions and within the federal government to deliver new programs and new policies if a policy window opens. Duff said she would like to see a policy framework that smaller municipalities, which don't always have the money to hire outside advisers, could use to broker more advantageous deals with developers.

Mahoney said in kicking off the event that in a labor market meltdown, workers wouldn't be the only ones to suffer, because a falloff in income tax revenues could cripple government programs like Medicare and Social Security. The articles say the widespread layoffs many anticipated would strike fast haven't happened, and the same goes for the widely expected productivity surge key to economic growth and improved living standards. The articles say AI isn't infiltrating white-collar work with zero impact on blue-collar jobs, and that mechanics are using the technology to inspect worn engine parts and farmers to plant crops. Duff said Mesa is learning from mistakes made when data-center developers demanded non-disclosure agreements preventing local officials from talking publicly about the terms of proposed projects while also expecting hefty tax subsidies. Duff said, "We went from one extreme and not even knowing what a data center is to it affecting an entire election in our nation in just five years."

Duff said she wants data-center developers to disclose publicly their emissions and to commit to sustainable practices, and said Mesa is trying now to be ahead of this and to anticipate what it needs to prepare for and negotiate instead of being empty-handed and just stumbling. McEntarfer recounted her own brief but agonizing attempt to apply for unemployment after she lost her BLS job in what has been widely viewed as a political move by President Trump. Zoffer recently authored a SIEPR Policy Brief examining job growth at U.S. factories given the demand for data-center components. The articles leave open which, if any, of the discussed policies, including wage insurance, tax breaks, an AI usage tax, a windfall tax, a consumption tax or a value-added tax, will be adopted. The articles also leave open what the forum's discussions will lead to and whether a policy window will open.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers urge parents to choose low-tech toys over AI toys this holiday season
stories.Summary:
Kathy Hirsh-Pasek, Jennifer M. Zosh and Sweta Shah wrote a Brookings commentary published on November 20, 2026, arguing that AI toys should not make holiday lists. They said many AI toys had been pulled from shelves this holiday season, but the ones that remain can still pose risks. They wrote that last year Santa packed his bag with many toys that violated the rule that a good toy is 90% kid and 10% toy. They named plushy dolls advertised to become a child's friend, robots like Miko advertised as "Safe AI for everyday learning," and Wuffy the robot dog, designed to teach kids love and responsibility. They noted the battery-powered dog did not have to eat or even go for a walk, suggesting few lessons in responsibility.

The authors said AI toys often suggest what the child should do and need less imagination or human interaction. They said Public Interest Research Group's "Trouble in Toyland" piece sparked concerns that plushy friends would help a child find a match when asked and would even help the child light it. They said Common Sense Media gives AI toys an "unacceptable risk" designation, citing a child who said she "liked to jump from high places" to Miko, which recommended a tree, a bench, a roof or a window and said to be safe. They said California passed legislation instituting a four-year moratorium on "the sale and manufacturing of toys with artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot capabilities for children under 16." They said the New York Assembly and House recently passed similar legislation.

The authors said you can still find the toys if you specifically search for them, and some toys from last year have been reshelved. They said PIRG retested these toys and noted that they still have unacceptable risks. They said toy companies appear to be pushing back against screen-based and AI-infused toys, and that even marketing for AI toys this year has emphasized that they are often screenless, even if not yet ready for prime time. They said the top toy lists for the 2026 holiday season host many more old favorites that stick by the 90% child rule. They named the 2026 Good Housekeeping Winners, Amazon's Top 100+ Toy List, Target's Bullseye's Top 50 Must-Have Toys, The Toy Foundation's Toy of the Year Finalist Lists and Walmart's Top Toy List as including familiar manipulatives, pretend play, block building and artistic creation toys.

The authors said the toy industry is at an inflection point, and that today's toy lists offer opportunities for children to play together and practice human-to-human skills necessary to thrive in school and beyond. They said that when children build forts and castles together with blocks, practice taking turns and being a good winner or loser, pretend to bake brownies in a plastic oven, or imagine a plush cat is real and pretend to take care of it, they build key developmental skills like spatial skills and story creation. They said these skills help drive early literacy. They said a 2026 Common Sense Media report finds that 49% of parents have either bought or are interested in buying an AI toy for their children, with 19% being at least somewhat interested in having that toy serve as a companion for their child. They said parents also report worries about these toys collecting personal information, their own difficulty in setting limits, cybersecurity risks, toys providing inappropriate content, and a fear of these toys displacing playtime with family and friends.

The authors said this is not to say that AI-enhanced toys cannot be good for young children, but at the moment the science cautions, let the buyer beware. They said future AI-embedded toys can be designed to prompt children to work together on problems or excite families with challenges and games, but these toys are just not available yet. They said perhaps future toy designers can work with scientists and educators to help use tech as a tool for building imagination and human connection rather than dampening it. They said it seems that, in response, Santa left many of the AI toys at the North Pole this year.

They said they look forward to seeing what developers can create in the coming years that centers play and human engagement. The authors said kids and their parents will benefit most from the magnetic tiles, blocks and low-tech toys of old, the ones that are 90% child and 10% toy. The article carries a photograph of a person looking at a teddy bear equipped with AI in Singapore on November 27, 2025, credited to Roslan RAHMAN / AFP via Getty Images. The article lists related content, including "What happens when the toy talks back?

Calling for caution and guardrails on AI toys" by Karyn Allee, Elias Blinkoff and Kathy Hirsh-Pasek from December 19, 2025. It lists "What we still don't know about AI and children's relationships" by Sweta Shah and Brinleigh Murphy-Reuter from August 27, 2026, and "Generation AI starts early: A guide to technologies already shaping young children's lives" by Sweta Shah from April 1, 2026. The disclosures say Zero to Three has made a contribution toward the forthcoming Brookings Center for Universal Education task force on AI and young children, and Kathy Hirsh-Pasek is on the board of Zero to Three. The article says future AI-embedded toys can be designed to prompt children to work together on problems or excite families with challenges and games, and that these toys are just not available yet.

It says future toy designers could work with scientists and educators to use tech as a tool for building imagination and human connection rather than dampening it. It says the authors look forward to seeing what developers can create in the coming years that centers play and human engagement. It says that until then, kids and their parents will benefit most from the magnetic tiles, blocks and low-tech toys of old. It leaves open what developers will create in the coming years and when AI-enhanced toys that meet the 90% child rule might become available.

stories.Headline: European Commission confirms AI-assisted cyberattack disrupted its services
stories.Summary:
The European Commission detected a cyberattack on October 22 and confirmed the incident on October 26 after an initial investigation. This event marked the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack that utilized an artificial intelligence tool. The attack targeted the headquarters of the executive branch of the European Union located in the city of Brussels. A spokesperson for the Commission spoke to the press about the event on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Investigators have been dealing with this AI-generated attack for almost a month since it was first detected.

The Commission temporarily took several applications offline, and most of these digital tools have since been restored by the authorities. Politico reported the attack lasted ten days and affected reimbursement tools, translation tools, and databases for timesheets and salaries. The EU agency CERT-EU oversees digital security for institutions that employ about 40,000 people just in the city of Brussels. The European Commission informed the departments concerned and remains in contact with the European Data Protection Supervisor and CERT-EU. No similar incidents were reported by the European Parliament or the European Council, the other two main EU institutions.

Thomas Regnier, a spokesperson for the European Commission, stated that AI-assisted tools can be misused to detect vulnerabilities in digital systems. He confirmed that AI tools were used in this case and noted that no one is immune to global cyberattacks. Regnier said that investigators found no evidence of a data breach affecting the Commission staff as a whole. He declined to identify the specific AI tool used or say who was behind the campaign against the bloc. The spokesperson also stated that he was unaware of any ransom demand and that many campaign elements were contained.

Politico first reported the incidents, though Thomas Regnier declined to confirm the specific reports regarding the affected databases and tools. The attack affected the executive body of the 27-nation EU, but other main institutions did not report similar cyber incidents. Staff members of the European Commission were the primary group mentioned in the context of potential data breach investigations. Cybersecurity experts have been working to manage the fallout and restore the digital tools that were taken offline. The reports indicate that the attack targeted key systems used for administrative tasks like salaries and reimbursement.

The EU agency CERT-EU posted a blog on November 4 warning about threats from a specific AI tool called ARTEX. This tool was designed to use artificial intelligence to identify vulnerabilities in digital systems across various global networks. The agency assessed that the public availability of ARTEX would likely accelerate adoption by threat actors for automated attacks. Such attacks are expected to be more frequent, faster, and more scalable with a higher success rate for attackers. This background explains the nature of the AI tools that can be misused to target institutions like the EU.

The European Commission continues its investigation into the attack, but Regnier declined to confirm if the campaign has fully ended. He also declined to assess the total scale of the attack while the official investigation remains ongoing at this time. The articles leave open the identity of the attackers and the specific AI tool used in the October cyberattack. It remains unclear which specific applications are still offline or when all digital tools will be fully restored to service. No final conclusion has been reached regarding the total impact of the breach on the European Union executive branch.

stories.Headline: Analysts favor Nebius over SoundHound as the better AI stock for 2027
stories.Summary:
On November 20, 2026, The Motley Fool published a comparison of Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) and SoundHound AI (NASDAQ: SOUN) for 2027, written by Brendan Coffey. On November 21, 2026, the Foreign Policy Journal published its own comparison by senior reporter David Prior. On November 19, 2026, Seeking Alpha published a piece on Nebius titled with a 65% crash reference. The Fool article listed Nebius at $81.31, down 16.11% or $15.61, and SoundHound at $2.61, down 10.31% or $0.30. The Fool's page showed the NASDAQ at 22,617.73, down 5.3% or 1,261.47, and Nvidia at $125.53, down 14.0% or $20.45.

Nebius has a market capitalization of $28 billion and SoundHound $1.4 billion, per both articles. Nebius revenue was about $2.2 billion for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, growth of approximately 535.8%. SoundHound revenue was roughly $223.6 million over the same period, growth of about 50.7%. Nebius net income was roughly $124.5 million at a net margin of approximately 5.7%, while SoundHound posted a net loss of around $74.2 million at a negative net margin of roughly 33.2%. Nebius debt-to-equity was approximately 1.1x with a current ratio of 3.1x as of its December 2025 balance sheet, and SoundHound debt-to-equity was roughly 0.0x with a current ratio of 4.6x.

In the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, Nebius free cash flow was nearly negative $3.7 billion and SoundHound's approximately negative $103.1 million. SoundHound trades at a price-to-sales ratio of 5.9x versus Nebius at 10.6x, and Nebius carries a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 43.3x while SoundHound has none because it is not projected to turn a profit. The Fool listed Nebius gross margin at 30.01%, P/E ratio 157.95 and EPS of $0.22, and SoundHound gross margin at 30.55%, P/E ratio of -6.50 and EPS of -$0.45. Nebius's 52-week range was $73.52 to $299.86 and SoundHound's $2.60 to $13.12. Stock-based compensation was roughly 21.6% of Nebius operating cash flow in the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025.

Prior wrote that Nebius is still the smarter AI bet for 2027, and Coffey wrote that for 2027 he would go with Nebius Group. Coffey said the choice depends on a preference for cloud scale or specialized voice interfaces. Prior said the lesson of the AI boom so far is that scale compounds advantage and Nebius holds a structural edge. Coffey said the lessons of AI so far are that size matters and SoundHound's lack of profit for the foreseeable future is a red flag. Prior said SoundHound's persistent losses and uncertain path to profitability tip the balance toward Nebius for those willing to accept its richer valuation.

Prior wrote that four of the five largest automakers, four of the five biggest airlines and 12 of the world's 15 largest banks count SoundHound as a technology partner. Coffey named LG and Ultraviolette Automotive as major SoundHound partners. Prior wrote that SoundHound could face Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOG) and Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL), which command enormous user bases and resources to replicate its core functionality. Coffey wrote it is not beyond the realm of possibility that Alphabet or Apple could take over the speech recognition space using their war chests. Prior wrote that Nebius faces capital intensity and competition from global hyperscalers with far larger financial reserves.

Coffey wrote that SoundHound faces integration challenges and potential asset impairment risks after the LivePerson and Amelia acquisitions. Prior wrote that Nebius traces back to Yandex, the Russian internet giant, from which it was carved out to separate its non-Russian operations. Prior wrote that Nebius used a substantial cash reserve from that separation to buy thousands of top-tier chips from Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ: NVDA) and reposition as a full-stack AI cloud hyperscaler almost overnight. Coffey wrote that Nebius was split from Yandex to separate the Russian parts from the non-Russian parts, leaving it with a lot of cash and a few unconnected businesses. Coffey wrote that just last year Nebius went all-in on AI, and annual sales hit about $530 million last year, versus less than a fifth of that the year prior.

Prior wrote that the $530 million in the prior fiscal year was more than five times what the business generated before its pivot. Prior wrote that SoundHound was founded in 2005 and has a two-decade head start in conversational AI, and that its LivePerson acquisition, along with the earlier purchase of Amelia, introduces execution risk and has contributed to ongoing losses. Prior wrote that Nebius operates a platform from raw data processing through model training to production deployment, targeting physical AI, life sciences, media entertainment and robotics with over 1,300 employees. Coffey wrote that Nebius's full-stack approach serves specialized markets like physical AI and media entertainment to carve out space against the largest cloud providers.

Coffey wrote that SoundHound provides platforms for voice-enabled agents for cars, TVs and restaurants, and that the LivePerson acquisition strengthens its digital engagement and messaging for high-volume enterprise clients. Prior wrote that SoundHound's voice recognition business serves speech-enabled interfaces for automobiles, televisions and restaurants. Coffey wrote that SoundHound faces competition from established big tech firms and specialized AI vendors and needs constant product innovation to avoid obsolescence. The articles leave open whether SoundHound will reach profitability and whether Nebius can justify its richer valuation against larger cloud rivals.

stories.Headline: Nebius shares drop as the company raises projected investment to 27 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Nebius shares fell 16 percent on Friday during a broad selloff of artificial intelligence equities. This retreat affected infrastructure providers and headline names in the sector. The decline followed a sharp rally tied to NVIDIA earnings and the Anthropic initial public offering. Investors began reassessing whether huge sums spent on infrastructure can earn adequate returns. This market shift occurred as S&P 500 futures dropped 0.9 percent.

The company reported third quarter 2026 revenue of 980.8 million dollars, which is up 571 percent. Nebius narrowed its 2026 revenue outlook to the low end of 3.0 billion to 3.4 billion dollars. Projected investment rose from a 20 billion to 25 billion dollar range to roughly 27 billion dollars. Third party data center capacity is arriving later than planned, shifting some revenue into 2027. These changes occurred while the stock traded at 91.52 dollars on Friday.

Nebius reported that delays from third party providers caused the narrowed revenue outlook for 2026. Evercore senior managing director Amit Daryanani said neocloud providers face constraints around financing and capacity. He stated that NVIDIA described the demand environment as extraordinarily strong for these providers. Daryanani noted that neoclouds need more funding and infrastructure to serve this high demand. He also mentioned that NVIDIA neocloud financing totals roughly 32 billion dollars.

Analysts are affected by the tension between long term confidence and cautious valuations for the company. Baird analyst Rob Oliver kept an Outperform rating but cut his price target to 200 dollars. Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson reaffirmed a neutral rating and halved his target to 125 dollars. Tyler Radke of Citi stayed bullish but lowered his target to 215 dollars on November 16. Two other houses set targets between 200 and 245 dollars on November 13.

The market grew more critical of the case for the build out and sector spending. Anthropic priced its initial public offering at 83 dollars per share, above the 70 to 78 range. NVIDIA reported quarterly results that were above expectations, which reinforced optimism about infrastructure demand. CoreWeave discussed revenue of 11 million dollars per megawatt, compared to 20 million for long term contracts. Restrictions on Chinese companies accessing cloud infrastructure in Asia may increase Western capacity.

Nebius is pressing ahead by giving compute credits worth 150,000 dollars to Physical AI Awards winners. These winners include Chef Robotics and Archetype AI, who also receive mentoring and technical support. The company must now align its investment needs with available infrastructure and growth. Articles leave open whether current demand conditions will persist over the longer term. It remains uncertain if the business model can convert growth into an economically viable business.

stories.Headline: xAI asks 9th Circuit to block California AI training data disclosure law
stories.Summary:
A three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco heard arguments on Wednesday in a challenge by Elon Musk’s xAI to a California law that requires artificial intelligence companies to publish summaries of the datasets used to train their models. The law was signed by Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom in September 2024 and took effect on January 1 as part of the state’s broader effort to set transparency requirements for the rapidly expanding AI industry. xAI sued California last year, arguing that the disclosure rules violate its rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and could force it to reveal trade secrets about how its models are developed, and the company is seeking to block enforcement of the law while its challenge proceeds. US District Judge Jesus Bernal rejected its request for a preliminary injunction in March, finding that xAI had not shown at that early stage that it was likely to prove the law unconstitutional.

The judges appeared skeptical of xAI’s argument that the law violates constitutional free-speech protections, but they also questioned whether California had placed clear limits on how much information it could compel AI companies to reveal. US Circuit Judge Johnnie Rawlinson challenged xAI’s position, telling xAI attorney James Xi of Clement & Murphy that to say the law violates the First Amendment you have to show it is not a reasonable request from the government, and asking whether it is not reasonable for the government to want citizens to know up front what information is being input into the AI instrument. US Circuit Judge Danielle Forrest asked California attorney Joe Meeker where the limit would be if the state could require companies to disclose information about their training datasets. The hearing did not produce a ruling, and the court has yet to determine whether the law can remain in force as xAI’s constitutional challenge continues.

The case, x.AI LLC v. Bonta, is before the 9th Circuit under docket number 26-1591, and legal experts expect its outcome to help define the limits of state authority over AI development at a time when governments are seeking greater oversight of systems that influence public and commercial life. Because California’s law applies to generative AI companies more broadly, a decision limiting the state’s authority could constrain how regulators require AI developers to explain the data behind their systems, while a ruling in California’s favor could strengthen the legal basis for similar transparency measures. The dispute also highlights the difficulty of regulating technology whose development depends on large-scale data collection and processing, with governments under pressure to improve accountability while companies argue that requirements must not expose proprietary information or impose obligations that are too broad to meet.

stories.Headline: Google employees petition to keep AI-free Search in schools as parents protest
stories.Summary:
More than 550 Google employees signed a petition on November 21, 2026, to allow schools access to Search without artificial intelligence. During the previous week, parents and educators held protests outside Google offices in six different cities to support this same request. These actions followed a November 3 announcement that students using classroom software would lose access to Google Search if administrators opted out of AI tools. This conflict emerged after Google activated its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students in August.

The new policy requires school administrators to individually enable or disable tools like Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search. While these features are now off by default, schools that reject AI will also lose access to Google Search through student accounts. This change affects approximately 150 million students and teachers worldwide who use Google Classroom and school-issued Chromebooks. The policy specifically impacts districts across southwest Missouri, southeast Kansas, northeast Oklahoma, and northwest Arkansas.

Google Vice President and General Manager of Education Chris Phillips stated that schools should have control over how this technology is used. The company claimed that updating Search to provide step-by-step guidance would better support learning than providing quick answers. However, former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan argued that Google is using its influence to encourage AI adoption. Josh Golin of the advocacy group Fairplay suggested that schools should seek privacy-protective alternatives to Google.

Senators Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal sent a letter to CEO Sundar Pichai with a November 2 deadline for answers. They asked nine questions regarding the effects of AI on the mental well-being of children and the ability of students to think critically. Google's November 3 announcement changed settings for administrators but did not directly answer the senators' specific questions. School systems nationwide continue to navigate how to incorporate emerging technology while preserving the authority of educators.

stories.Headline: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. finalizes a HIPAA rule that cuts patient record response time to 15 days
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights finalized a 363-page HIPAA Privacy Rule overhaul, released late Monday, November 16, 2026, and slated for Federal Register publication Thursday, November 19, 2026. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the final rule, which cuts patient record response time to 15 days. The rule is titled HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens. HHS OCR issued the proposed modifications in January 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term. The proposal remained on the back burner during the Biden administration.

The rule becomes effective 60 days after publication, on January 18, 2027, and HIPAA-regulated organizations must comply 180 days after the effective date, or July 17, 2027. Business associate agreements must be updated by January 18, 2028, at the latest, and existing BAAs not renewed or modified before the compliance date are deemed compliant until renewed or modified, subject to transition provisions. The rule cuts the response deadline for patient access requests from 30 calendar days to 15 days, with a one-time extension of up to 30 additional days under specific circumstances. It clarifies patients' rights to obtain electronic health information through personal health apps, including consumer apps not subject to HIPAA, and prohibits refusing transmission solely because an app lacks encryption at rest. It bars unreasonable identity verification measures, stating organizations in the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement generally should not refuse requests through personal health apps when conditions are met, including a cryptographically signed token from a credential service provider certified consistent with NIST Identity Assurance Level 2 and Authentication Assurance Level 2, and matching demographic information.

Kennedy said Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records. He said the rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and helps providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy. HHS OCR dropped a proposal that would have relaxed the minimum necessary standard for certain disclosures of sensitive health information. The rule clarifies that health plans may use and disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management, and expressly permits disclosures to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management. HHS retained the minimum necessary standard for applicable healthcare operations disclosures rather than adopting a proposed exception for certain care-coordination activities.

Privacy attorney Adam Greene of Davis Wright Tremaine said he appreciated deletion of the requirement to obtain acknowledgments of receipt of the notice of privacy practices, which he said was founded on good intentions but led to administrative burden and confusion with minimal corresponding benefit. Privacy attorney Kirk Nahra of WilmerHale said he would have liked an additional stage to obtain new comments on issues that changed significantly since the proposal five years ago. Nahra said HHS chose coordination over individual privacy, a complicated decision that essentially allows disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer. Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve administrative burdens, including the 15-day access deadline, which she called a very short amount of time. Several healthcare industry groups, including the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives, signed a letter to HHS last week warning that loosening identity verification for third-party apps could expose providers to security threats and regulatory scrutiny.

The final rule eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers to make a good-faith effort to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices. It abandons a requirement that would have obligated covered organizations to exercise individuals' right of access on their behalf by requesting designated record sets from other covered entities. Greene said that proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate taxing covered entities' already limited resources. Greene said the final rule includes helpful changes but nothing earth-shattering, and he does not expect compliance to be difficult, though changes to notices and right-of-access policies will take significant time and resources. Peters said organizations must still update, redistribute and post their notices, update websites with required fee information and revise applicable business associate agreements.

Greene said the most significant gains for patients will likely come in quicker access to their protected health information and fewer obstacles to exercising this access. Nahra said companies should remain cautious about these disclosures even if permitted, and should be cognizant of security risks and ensure appropriate steps beyond the identity confirmation limitations. The signatories of the letter did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the final rule. The rule also defines electronic health record and revises permissible access fees, specifying which fees apply. The articles leave open how covered entities will implement the shortened deadline and what further guidance HHS may issue.

stories.Headline: New York attorney general Letitia James creates an AI enforcement unit before the RAISE Act takes effect
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on November 17, 2026, the creation of a new unit to enforce the state’s artificial intelligence laws. The unit is called the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit, known as the ASSET Unit. James announced it six weeks before the Responsible AI Safety and Education Act takes effect on January 1, 2027. The announcement was reported by Bushwick Daily on November 22, 2026, and by Regulatory Oversight on November 20, 2026. WRGB reported the announcement on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 6:13 AM.

The ASSET Unit will lead the attorney general’s enforcement of the RAISE Act and other AI safety laws, develop new policy proposals, and lend technical expertise to investigations across the office. The RAISE Act requires large AI developers to publicly disclose their safety measures and swiftly report security and safety incidents. Developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue must register with New York regulators before the January deadline, according to Bloomberg Law. The law applies to any company with $500 million or more in annual revenue, and developers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta are expected to register. The unit’s stated focus includes data privacy, digital scams, cybersecurity, and online safety.

James said her office has always stepped up to enforce the law to protect New Yorkers when big tech companies try to take advantage of them. She said promising new technologies like artificial intelligence should never come at the expense of New Yorkers’ safety and privacy. She said the ASSET Unit will lead the way in ensuring AI and other emerging technology are developed safely and for the benefit of all New Yorkers. The unit does not add legal duties on its own and will enforce duties already in place and those arriving in 2027. The attorney general’s office has invited AI industry employees to file whistleblower complaints.

State Sen. Andrew Gounardes has introduced a follow-on bill called “RAISE 2.0,” which would require quarterly reports from large developers. The bill would require developers to report significant gains in a model’s capability or computing power within 72 hours and give third-party auditors “employee-level access.” It would also let a new state office order a developer to slow its computing power, a power that would sit with the Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust, not the ASSET Unit. Companies that build, deploy, or advertise with AI in New York should know which of the unit’s laws could reach them. Chatbot, AI-in-advertising, and data security laws may reach companies that deploy AI or hold New Yorkers’ personal data.

The attorney general’s office points to New York’s Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security Act, which requires reasonable data security to prevent breaches. It also points to S.9051B/A.10379C, which bans unsafe chatbot features for children and takes effect in June 2027. General Business Law, Article 47 requires AI chatbots to try to detect and address suicidal ideation and to tell users they are not talking to a human. Penal Law § 245.15 criminalizes sharing intimate images with intent to harm, including AI-generated or AI-altered images, and the Synthetic Performer Disclosure Act requires disclosure when ads use AI in place of humans. The office also has broad authority to act on privacy violations, unfair or deceptive business practices, and hacking, including under the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

The legislative session begins in early January, so the ASSET Unit will start work while lawmakers consider more AI bills. How the two offices would divide enforcement is an open question. Companies should decide what counts as a reportable incident, who decides, and how fast they can report. Companies should watch the unit’s first moves, including new hires, guidance before January 1, and whether early inquiries focus on disclosures, incident reporting, or data security. The articles leave open how the ASSET Unit and the proposed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust would divide enforcement.

stories.Headline: Jay Clayton links NSA outage to AI-assisted PHP patching as experts debate change risk
stories.Summary:
A series of major technology outages hit the United States, disrupting email, air travel, banking and government operations, according to SecurityWeek. The incidents included a nearly day-long Microsoft 365 outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that slowed transactions at other banks, and an outage affecting the NSA's classified internal network. United Airlines and Apple also experienced disruptions. Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a link between the incidents. Microsoft traced its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA blamed a newly installed router, and the NSA cited routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton linked the NSA disruption to patching for a PHP vulnerability found with the help of AI. Sen. Mark Warner said AI-driven vulnerability discovery is pushing organizations to patch many systems at once, putting strain on infrastructure that wasn't built for that pace of change. Industry professionals commented on whether AI-accelerated patching played a role, the need for tested rollback plans, and the fragility of interconnected systems. One professional said there is strong reason to believe AI-accelerated patch velocity is already causing major operational incidents, based on direct experience with customers deploying large OpenJDK updates. That person said the Java community has had to absorb four update events in the past four weeks, including three separate critical vulnerability events, and that security-only updates minimize risk by limiting change to what is necessary.

Another professional said AI plays a part but should not be made the whole story, and that the outages look less like an AI problem than a change problem, with updates pushed onto systems that can't take much change. That person said a fix that takes the service down is a security failure too, and asked who owns the choice between leaving a flaw open a few more days and risking the service by closing it tonight. A third professional said AI is finding vulnerabilities faster than many remediation processes were built to handle, noting that Microsoft fixed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities in its October security release, a monthly record, and 1,094 in November. That person said nothing published so far links this pressure to the recent Microsoft 365 outage, but Microsoft's own explanation shows how easily planned work can take a service down.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the head of Nvidia on Thursday, November 14, 2026. He stepped down after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, a Singaporean executive. This woman is believed to be a spy for the government of China. A New York Times report also linked him to a second affair. This subordinate worked at the microchip company where Huang served as chief executive.

The scandal triggered federal investigations and a sell-off of Nvidia stock in Santa Clara, California. Huang lobbied Donald Trump to ease chip export controls established under President Joe Biden. The Commerce Department stopped investigating if Alice Huang smuggled chips after an Nvidia lawyer called. Nvidia is a major investor in a 1.4 trillion dollar IPO for Anthropic. This AI company warns that its technology poses catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped there was no problem with Huang. He called the former executive an amazing, honorable, and very high quality guy. Trump believes that the microchip leader will eventually end up in good shape. He previously decided that AI companies should self police after meeting with tech executives. The president has facilitated the goals of a man potentially tied to China.

Stephen Witt told the New Yorker that sleeping with spies is generally regarded as bad. The New York Times reported that Trump was warned about the relationship last year. He received another warning in May before joining Huang on a trip to Beijing. The company board is populated by early investors and longtime associates of the cofounder. This board had no succession plan or clear replacement before the chief executive resigned.

Huang argued that the United States must sell more chips to maintain a chipmaking advantage. He served as the closest adviser to the president on artificial intelligence technology. The articles describe him as a leather swathed man who flattered the president for favors. The AI industry had previously issued warnings about the destructive potential of its own technology. These warnings failed to prevent the current mess involving the world's most valuable AI company.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will lead Nvidia while the search for a replacement begins. The new Congress includes members who promised to rein in data centers and AI. Some of these elected officials have a history of regulating various aspects of technology. The articles leave open whether the president will change his current laissez faire AI policy. It remains unclear if the new Congress will successfully implement these promised AI regulations.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike schedules virtual event on fighting AI-powered threats with AI
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced a virtual event titled "The Next Era of Cyber Defense: Fighting AI-Powered Threats with AI," dated November 20, 2026, on its website. The event is scheduled for the Americas on December 9 and for JAPAC and Europe on December 10. CrowdStrike leaders will give a special update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness, and the shift to the agentic SOC. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike Senior Vice President of Counter Adversary Operations, will give a special AI threat briefing on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The briefing includes real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work.

The event covers AI detection and response, which secures AI adoption and development from agents to models to prompts across endpoints, cloud, and SaaS. It also covers AI observability, which evaluates agents pre-deployment and then observes their behavior and enforces accountability in production. CrowdStrike offers a Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience Service to reduce exploitable risk with ongoing scans, expert prioritization, and guided remediation. It also offers a Shadow AI Visibility Service to discover hidden AI tools, activity, and agents across endpoint, cloud, and SaaS. Project QuiltWorks is described as an industry coalition mobilizing to close the frontier AI vulnerability gap at scale.

CrowdStrike states that AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and that defenders need to keep pace. The company says the event will feature CrowdStrike leaders and a briefing from Adam Meyers on AI-enabled adversary activity. CrowdStrike describes its Falcon Complete as elite 24/7 managed detection and response across the entire attack surface. It describes Charlotte AI as autonomous intelligence fueled by world-class expertise that accelerates outcomes. CrowdStrike says its Next-Gen SIEM is the world's only AI-native SOC platform.

CrowdStrike says its Agentic SOAR orchestrates agents, workflows, and automation across a security ecosystem. It says its Agentic SOC Transformation unlocks machine-speed responses with unified data and agentic workflows. CrowdStrike says its Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience service addresses risk as the time between patch and exploit continues to collapse. It says its Agentic Adversary Emulation red teams an environment to simulate real-world attacks and validate defenses. CrowdStrike lists customers by industry including small business, federal government, Department of War, state and local government, financial services, healthcare, election security, education, retail, and manufacturing.

CrowdStrike's resources include the 2026 Global Threat Report, the 2026 Threat Hunting Report, a New Adversary Hub, and an AI Security Hub. Its training and education offerings include CrowdStrike University, Cybersecurity 101, and Hands-On Workshops. Its events include Fal.Con Europe, Fal.Con Las Vegas, and CrowdTour. CrowdStrike's pricing tiers are Falcon Go, Falcon Pro, and Falcon Enterprise. CrowdStrike advertises a Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale from November 23 to December 4 on Falcon Go, Pro, or Enterprise.

CrowdStrike's site promotes guidance on Java4Shell and NGINX2Root to find exposures, monitor post-exploit activity, and remediate faster. It invites those who experienced a breach to contact the company. The article text ends mid-sentence at "Cyber Superintell," leaving the full description of the Cyber Superintelligence Lab incomplete. The articles give no further details on the event's speakers beyond Adam Meyers or on registration terms. More to follow.

stories.Headline: mEinstein outlines Human Context Contracts to define revocable human authorization for AI agents
stories.Summary:
mEinstein is outlining a framework called Human Context Contracts, which the company says is meant to address how human authorization can be represented and applied when AI agents interact with personal information and external systems, according to an article published by aithority.com on November 23, 2026. The company describes the framework as a way to translate human consent into defined, enforceable and revocable authority over autonomous actions. The article says existing consent mechanisms were largely developed for websites and digital services, while autonomous agents introduce requirements involving delegated authority, task limitations and accountability. Prithwi Thakuria, Founder and CEO of mEinstein, said a checkbox records consent but an autonomous system needs permission it can actually execute.

The framework is designed to represent distinctions between kinds of permission through structured requests that specify the purpose, required information and permitted action, and its architecture includes authorization conditions covering the requesting entity, scope, duration, value, revocation and audit records. The article gives the example of a request to find a flight, which may authorize an AI assistant to search and compare available options, while purchasing a ticket, selecting a payment method, accepting a connecting flight or disclosing travel information to external services may require separate authorization. It also says a healthcare system may be authorized to assess clinical-trial eligibility without automatically receiving permission to disclose patient information to a research sponsor, and a financial assistant may evaluate mortgage readiness without having authority to share an individual's complete financial information or submit an application. Thakuria said permission to know something is not permission to share it, and permission to share it is not permission to act on it. The framework forms part of the company's broader Human Intelligence Infrastructure concept, which addresses the relationship between enterprise AI systems and an individual's private, user-controlled information, and the company summarizes the operating principle as AI interprets, rules govern, device executes.

The article says the issue is receiving attention across the AI industry, noting that the National Institute of Standards and Technology has been examining AI-agent identity and authorization, including how agents establish authority, operate under delegated permissions and maintain evidence connecting their actions to human authorization. It also says Microsoft has outlined a Dynamic Permissions approach in which AI agents receive permissions appropriate to specific tasks rather than relying on unrestricted standing access, with permissions limited by task and duration and additional verification for actions requiring human approval. OpenAI's computer-use guidance similarly distinguishes direct user instructions from information encountered by an agent during operation and recommends confirmation before certain consequential actions, including financial transactions and the transmission of sensitive information. The article says Mastercard's Verifiable Intent initiative focuses on establishing evidence of consumer authorization when AI agents conduct purchases, and its Agent Pay Trust Framework incorporates identity, intent, controls, execution and intelligence into the management of agent-led transactions.

The article says the framework also addresses the operational limitations of repeated approval requests, because rather than requiring confirmation for every individual action, permission boundaries can define which activities an agent may perform independently and which require renewed authorization, and changes in circumstances or actions outside the approved scope may trigger additional verification. It says that as AI agents take on more responsibilities across digital services and commercial transactions, the distinction between consent, delegated authority and executable permission is becoming an important consideration for system developers and organizations. The article describes Human Context Contracts as mEinstein's approach to structuring that authorization layer, with the aim of maintaining defined human authority as autonomous systems perform increasingly complex tasks. The article does not say when the framework will be available or how it will be adopted.

stories.Headline: Cumberland schools board advances AI policy limiting tools to approved apps
stories.Summary:
Cumberland County Schools is looking to update its technology responsible use policy, including provisions governing generative artificial intelligence, which is AI that creates text, images, video, audio and other content. The Board of Education approved a first reading of the policy update at its Nov. 17 meeting. Board Attorney Nick Sjoka told board members at a Nov. 3 policy committee meeting that the district has had a policy on the books for a number of years. Sjoka said that policy incorporates federal laws involving student confidentiality and protecting students from harmful material along with state statutes and expectations for responsible use. Sjoka said the update is more extensive and detailed, specifying, for example, prohibited uses of internet file sharing, and addressing increased use of generative artificial intelligence.

The updates include recommendations from the North Carolina Schools Boards Association and the district's technology director, Sjoka said. The updated policy will apply to all district employees and students, Sjoka said, and the policy states it also applies to former employees, visitors, contractors and other authorized users who use the district's technology. The updated policy states that it applies to use of all school system computer networks, connections, resources, tools and learning environments made available through those networks, and all devices that connect to them. School system technological resources include desktop and laptop computers, tablets, Chromebooks, mobile devices, internet services, cloud-based applications, communication and collaboration platforms and AI tools authorized by the district. The policy states that the school system reserves the right to monitor, filter, log, inspect, and review the use of all school system technological resources to ensure compliance with Board policy, protect district resources, maintain system security, and comply with applicable law.

The policy states that the use of generative AI tools shall be limited to district-approved applications and must comply with Board policies, student privacy requirements, copyright laws, and instructional guidelines. The policy states that plagiarism of internet resources will be treated in the same manner as any other incidents of plagiarism, as stated in the Code of Student Conduct. The policy states that Cumberland County Schools fosters a dynamic learning environment that integrates cutting-edge technology, including generative AI, to empower students. The policy states that the district holds integrity at the forefront, demonstrating a firm commitment to academic honesty, responsible AI use, copyright respect, and data privacy. The policy further states the district believes it is important to promote courteous technology use that prevents cyberbullying and harmful creation or sharing of deepfake images.

Deepfakes use AI to create or alter photos, videos or audio recordings to make them appear real. The policy states that only pre-approved software and AI tools are permitted on school devices. The policy states that users must take responsibility for the content they create or store using school resources, and be aware that misuse of equipment or failure to adhere to policy guidelines may result in financial liabilities or other consequences. The policy states that school employees shall not disclose, post, upload, transmit or otherwise make available personally identifiable, private or confidential student information through school system websites, social media, cloud services, digital applications, AI tools, electronic communications or any other online service concerning students, such as their name, address or photos, without written permission from a parent or guardian.

Technology users are also not allowed to install, create, modify or introduce unauthorized software, applications, AI tools, games, communication applications or more on school system devices without permission from the technology director or designee. Staff writer Rachael Riley can be reached at rriley@fayobserver.com or 910-486-3528. The article originally appeared on The Fayetteville Observer. stories.Headline: Congressional researchers propose marijuana tax rules as model for taxing AI data centers
stories.Summary:
A report from the Congressional Research Service released on November 18 identifies the federal tax treatment of marijuana businesses under Section 280E as a possible model for taxing artificial intelligence companies and data centers, according to The Marijuana Herald. The report, titled Taxing AI: Alternative Approaches, examines several methods Congress could use to tax the growing artificial intelligence industry. Among the options discussed is applying restrictions similar to those that have long prevented marijuana businesses from deducting ordinary operating expenses on their federal tax returns. Under Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code, businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II controlled substances are generally prohibited from deducting standard business expenses, even when operating legally under state law. They can subtract the cost of goods sold from their revenue when calculating gross income, but generally cannot deduct expenses such as rent, employee wages, utilities and depreciation.

The CRS report dedicates an entire section to marijuana tax treatment, explaining that the restrictions make the resulting tax resemble a value-added tax. Researchers discuss whether comparable limitations on business expense deductions could be applied to participants in the artificial intelligence market, although they acknowledge uncertainty about the feasibility of such an approach. The report returns to marijuana taxation in a separate discussion of potential gross receipts taxes on AI data centers, describing an alternative that would apply the same general tax treatment as marijuana businesses. Under this approach, companies would be taxed on receipts minus the cost of goods sold, without the full range of ordinary operating expense deductions available to most businesses. CRS notes that because data centers generally do not manufacture or sell physical inventory, applying this approach would effectively function as a gross receipts tax, subjecting nearly all their revenue to taxation rather than just their profits.

The analysis comes as members of Congress consider multiple proposals to increase taxes on AI-related businesses. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), for example, has separately proposed a gross receipts tax on data centers, along with restrictions on depreciation deductions and other tax benefits. CRS identifies the marijuana-style tax treatment as a closely related alternative to the gross receipts approach. Other proposals discussed in the report include taxes on electricity consumption, computer processing power, digital advertising revenue and AI-related services.

The report also examines arguments against additional AI taxes, including concerns about reduced investment, economic productivity and international competition. The comparison comes as Section 280E remains a major financial issue for marijuana companies. An April federal order moved certain qualifying medical marijuana activities to Schedule III, generally removing those activities from Section 280E's restrictions. However, marijuana activities that remain classified under Schedule I continue to face the deduction limitations, and federal tax guidance addressing businesses with multiple activities remains pending.

stories.Headline: Manufacturers face a data gap that blocks physical AI rollout on factory floors
stories.Summary:
Robotics and physical AI companies raised nearly 48 billion dollars so far in 2026. These companies want to roll out fully autonomous machines in industrial settings. Robots need real world data to move beyond controlled environments onto manufacturing floors. Most production facilities are not currently set up to provide this necessary information. This data gap may prevent manufacturers from achieving expected efficiency and quality improvements.

Manufacturers must capture complex interactions between process parameters and quality outcomes to help systems make reliable adjustments. They need to connect equipment and quality management systems that were not designed to communicate. This requires creating a digital thread connecting production conditions with inspection results and finished part quality. In medical device manufacturing, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent quality. This limits how freely AI systems can modify production parameters in those specific environments.

Michael Kenworthy, chief technology officer at VulcanForms, says manufacturers must understand what information robotic systems will rely on. He suggests identifying production conditions that systems need to recognize and respond to early. Kenworthy believes manufacturers should focus investments where they will have the greatest impact. He states that a system cannot make independent decisions if it cannot evaluate resulting quality. He advises linking existing process records to inspection results rather than just collecting more data.

Lior Susan of Eclipse says a physical asset is a dead asset if it does not generate real time operational data. The Manufacturing Leadership Council conducted a 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey. This survey found that 37 percent of manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock. This figure is an increase from 22 percent in 2025. These silos affect manufacturers who want to implement smart factory strategies.

Technicians develop understanding of welding angles, travel speed, and workpiece position through years of hands on experience. Much of this knowledge is not captured in a form robotics partners can use. Operational data is often collected but never reviewed or structured for autonomous learning. Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems, such as quality management systems. In metal additive manufacturing, powder characteristics and processing temperatures can influence a component's final properties.

Manufacturers should now identify the specific data needed for a targeted robotic application. They must work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers. Companies need to define acceptable operating limits and establish how systems verify results. They must also develop clear criteria for when an unexpected outcome requires engineering review. The articles leave open how long it will take to overhaul existing production infrastructure.
