stories.Headline: India's chief justice says clear AI rules beat a ban for legal education
stories.Summary:
The Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant, said on Saturday, November 21, 2026, that setting clear rules to regulate the use of AI tools would be a better option than a total ban for legal students and the legal profession. He made the statement while delivering the inaugural address at the first annual international conference on legal education, which was convened by the Commonwealth Legal Education Association in Hyderabad. The Chief Justice observed that generative artificial intelligence had unsettled the assumption that an answer sheet reflects the knowledge of a student. He also said that assessment methods should be improved so that written works are supported by oral explanations, and that a law school must ultimately be able to certify with confidence what the students it had produced had learnt.

On legal education in the country, the Chief Justice noted that practical training can strengthen doctrinal teaching only if it is genuine, and that a student learns the strength of law in a supervised moot trial better than in an examination. He said Indian regulations already require clinical courses and a legal aid clinic in every law school, and that such clinical teaching requires trained supervisors, meaningful assessment and clear ethical safeguards. Justice P.S. Narasimha of the Supreme Court said students develop their legal reasoning through repeated drafting of petitions, analysing facts and finding legal solutions on their own. He warned that students who depend on AI tools for legal solutions without undergoing this rigorous training in drafting and legal reasoning might lose the capacity to analyse and fail to distinguish between right and wrong.

Attorney General R. Venkataramani said legal education must respond to the challenges brought about by globalisation, technology and artificial intelligence, and that law schools should evolve into centres of research and innovation while AI tools are used to assist them. He said AI should not be the master but an assistant. P. Sam Koshy, the Acting Chief Justice of the Telangana High Court, said it was high time everyone examined whether the next generation of legal professionals was being prepared merely to understand the law as it existed or was being equipped to shape the laws the future demands. He said the present legal professional cannot be confined to the legal framework of one jurisdiction, and that while learning a domestic law governing a dispute, one should also be aware of its international dimensions. He added that the future of the Commonwealth's legal tradition will not be secured by merely preserving its past, but by its capacity to learn, adapt and evolve without losing its foundational principles.

stories.Headline: EU law gives citizens no way to influence public-sector AI design, a study finds
stories.Summary:
A doctrinal legal investigation published in Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examined whether public participation can serve as an operational mechanism to reduce risks in public-sector artificial intelligence across the European Union. The study found that the legal architecture of the European Union currently provides no functional avenues for natural or legal persons to influence the design and development of public-sector algorithmic tools. Public administrations across thirty European countries documented nine hundred and forty cases of artificial intelligence deployment in 2024, an increase of nearly thirty percent compared to figures reported at the end of 2022. Citizen involvement in those deployments remains nonexistent, the study found. The disconnect leaves the general public detached from decisions governing algorithmic systems used in traffic offense enforcement, tax collection, welfare benefit processing, crime risk forecasting, and asylum procedures.

In administrative rulemaking, public participation does not constitute a legally enforceable individual right, the study found. The European Commission conducts open consultations, as observed during revisions of public procurement directives, stakeholder hearings on the Artificial Intelligence Act, and drafting of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice involving more than one thousand participants. These mechanisms remain informal and non-compulsory under established European Union case law, and they target structured representative associations and civil society groups rather than individual citizens. The fundamental right to be heard cannot function in system development because it requires a strict bilateral legal relationship between an authority and an individual addressee directly and negatively affected. Even under the expanded doctrinal scope established in the Al-Jubail jurisprudence concerning hybrid regulations, acts performed during algorithmic development produce effects too indirect and preliminary to confer standing.

The right of access to documents allows any natural or legal person residing within the Union to inspect files held by European Union institutions without demonstrating a direct legal or economic interest. This right is strictly limited by the commercial interest exception, which protects proprietary algorithms, commercial data, and corporate trade secrets when authorities contract out technology development to private software companies. It is also limited by the internal documents exception, which shields in-house administrative deliberations whenever disclosure risks impairing bureaucratic decision-making. Even where non-confidential records can be obtained, the right functions merely as a passive mechanism for information retrieval, with no obligation compelling administrative bodies to incorporate, evaluate, or respond to citizens' critiques. Existing European procurement directives and financial regulations applicable to European Union institutions do not accommodate public or civil society intervention within procurement operations or contract performance phases.

European procurement law defines participation exclusively as the right of economic operators to compete for contracts, having been constructed around interaction between contracting authorities and bidding economic operators to safeguard equal treatment, market efficiency, and non-distortion of competition. Member states maintain limited administrative discretion during statutory transposition to require transparency, publish procurement contracts, or expand preliminary market consultations to include technical experts and civic organizations, but such avenues remain entirely indirect. The Artificial Intelligence Act introduces explicit mentions of stakeholder participation across multiple lifecycle stages, but participatory provisions are concentrated heavily in preliminary phases prior to actual system development. These processes are legally restricted to structured, qualified entities including small and medium enterprises, consumer groups, accredited social stakeholders, industry actors, academia, and trade unions, excluding ordinary lay individuals lacking formal institutional representation or technical credentials. In fundamental rights impact assessments, which public entities and designated private bodies delivering public services must conduct prior to deploying standalone high-risk systems, inclusion of affected populations is not mandated in statutory text and is merely outlined in non-binding recitals.

The study establishes that the core rationale behind citizen engagement stems from documented evidence of widespread societal harms generated by artificial intelligence deployments, which frequently exacerbate historical biases, generate discriminatory outcomes, and disproportionately affect disadvantaged and marginalized groups. Legal and administrative scholars have long argued that consulting the public before public bodies deploy automated systems could prevent administrations from pursuing projects bound to fail from lack of societal acceptance. Such consultation could also incorporate varied communal values into public service technologies and identify sensitive vulnerabilities early during the development phase. Direct engagement during early design stages has been theorized to confer democratic legitimacy, preserve public trust, prevent the corporate takeover of public infrastructures when private vendors build public software, and ensure algorithmic systems reflect public interest rather than narrow bureaucratic or commercial imperatives. Legal scholarship had previously left the practical, doctrinal avenues governing such participation unexamined, leaving a substantial gap between theoretical aspirations and existing statutory administrative law.

The study critically appraised whether participatory frameworks from environmental law, widely regarded as the most mature administrative domain for public involvement, could be transposed to public-sector artificial intelligence. Both fields involve administrative decisions guided by specialized technical experts, both suffer from severe democratic deficits, and both manage long-term activities capable of generating widespread negative externalities that accumulate across time and transcend national borders. By the time an administrative agency takes an individual adverse measure against an individual using an algorithmic system, the underlying architecture has already been locked in, rendering the right to be heard entirely ineffective for shaping the software itself. The study demonstrates that the legal architecture of the European Union currently provides no functional avenues for natural or legal persons to influence the design and development of public-sector algorithmic tools. The articles do not state what steps, if any, European Union institutions or member states plan to take in response to the study's findings.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Business Guide: ai vs corporate lawyer egypt in 2026
stories.Summary:
The articles do not report an event with a date, place, actors or outcome, so there is no news story to write. They are a business guide, dated November 23, 2026, on the question of ai vs corporate lawyer egypt, published by Global Advisory Experts. The guide names Muhammad Al-Bedeawi of Al-Bedeawi and Partners LLP in Egypt as its featured expert on the matter. It states that generative AI can now draft, review and summarise commercial documents faster than any person. It states that Egyptian practice brings formalities around notarisation and registration, sector-specific approvals and the Personal Data Protection Law that general-purpose software does not understand.

The guide's stated position is that AI is a valuable assistant for routine, low-risk corporate work but cannot replace an Egyptian-qualified lawyer wherever enforceability, regulatory approval, negotiation or liability is in play. It says AI can take over first-pass drafting of standard documents, clause libraries, playbook-based redlining, scoping of due diligence and document summaries. It says AI cannot take over interpreting regulation, planning negotiations, company formation and registry filings, notarised instruments, litigation and arbitration strategy, and anything carrying professional liability. It recommends a hybrid model with compulsory human sign-off points, a data protection impact assessment for each AI vendor and a documented audit trail before any document becomes binding. It cites the World Bank as saying AI adoption in developing economies can lift productivity but can also widen the gap between organisations that govern the technology well and those that do not.

The guide states that in-house teams at multinationals in Cairo and Alexandria are among the early adopters, using AI for contract triage, knowledge management and diligence preparation. It states that foreign investors assessing Egyptian targets increasingly use it to read hundreds of data room documents in hours rather than days. It states that Egyptian corporate teams typically encounter three kinds of AI legal tool in 2026: contract automation platforms, LLM-based drafting and review assistants, and due-diligence scoping tools. It states that models are trained mostly on common-law and English-language material and often miss Egyptian civil-law formalities, Arabic-language statutory requirements and sector approval regimes. It cites the OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence as resting AI governance on human oversight, transparency and responsibility.

The guide states that AI will not replace corporate lawyers in Egypt, though it will change how lawyers spend their time, and that the technology displaces tasks, not roles. It states that lawyers who work with AI will tend to outperform those who ignore it, and that businesses relying on AI alone for high-stakes matters may later pay for the shortfall in enforceability or compliance. It states that an AI-drafted agreement is not automatically invalid but is only as enforceable as its compliance with Egyptian formation and formality rules, which the model does not check for itself. It states that Egyptian law recognises electronic transactions and electronic signatures for many commercial dealings, so an AI-drafted document signed electronically can be valid for many standard business-to-business arrangements. It states that documents that must be notarised or registered, including various corporate filings and transactions under the companies legislation, need execution and authentication steps that no automation can supply.

The guide states that whether a draft came from a person or a machine does not by itself decide admissibility, and that what matters is whether the executed document meets Egyptian evidentiary standards and whether signatures and authentication can be proven. It states that an AI-generated draft reviewed, finalised and properly executed by the parties generally stands on the same footing as any other written contract. It states that the weak point is the audit trail rather than the authorship, and that a documented chain showing human review and deliberate execution considerably strengthens a party's position if authenticity or intent is later disputed. It states that the exact formality depends on document type and sector, and that counsel should verify execution requirements for anything beyond routine agreements. It states that only a lawyer admitted before the Egyptian courts can represent a company and shape its dispute strategy.

The guide ends mid-sentence at the heading "Three ways to reduce the risk," so the measures it promises are not given. It gives no figures, no case, no party and no outcome, and it reports no decision by any regulator, court or company. It leaves open what the three risk-reduction steps are, which vendors or tools it means and what any of them cost. It leaves open how Egyptian authorities treat AI-drafted instruments in practice, since it gives no ruling or example. It leaves open what Al-Bedeawi himself said, since the guide offers only his profile and contact details. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Israel introduces AI into courtrooms to ease judges caseloads
stories.Summary:
Israel has begun introducing artificial intelligence into its courtrooms in a country that sanctifies innovation, according to a Haaretz report published on November 21, 2026, by Shay Aspril. The article describes the technology as a means to ease the caseloads that judges currently carry. It raises the prospect that such systems could ultimately replace judges altogether. The report frames the change as one that has already entered the judicial system rather than one that remains only a proposal.

The article sets out what a trial conducted by a machine would involve, describing a process in which the pleadings are input into a system. That system would also analyze the evidence and determine the verdict in the case. No judge would sit across from the person on trial, and there would be no expression to read and no silence to interpret. No one would have to bear the cost of what is decided under such an arrangement.

The report does not name the officials or courts responsible for the introduction, and it records no statement from any judge, ministry or developer about the systems. It presents the shift as one that eases the work of judges while carrying the possibility that they could be replaced. The article offers no date for when an algorithm might deliver verdicts. It gives no figures on how many courts or judges are involved.

The context the article supplies is the country's attitude toward innovation, which it describes as sanctifying, and the pressure of judges' caseloads that the technology is meant to relieve. Beyond that, the report does not say what happens next, and it names no pilot program, budget or timetable for further adoption. It leaves open whether an algorithm will soon deliver verdicts, which its headline poses as a question. No further steps are described in the article.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal contractors to clear congressional requests with the White House
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump on Friday ordered every company holding a federal contract to notify the White House and its contracting agency immediately of any pending or future congressional request about its communications or work with the executive branch, and to withhold material the administration determines is protected by executive privilege. Executive Order 14438, titled "Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting," was posted on the White House website late on Nov. 20. The requirements extend to subcontractors, and prime contractors are made responsible for ensuring their subcontractors comply. Each agency must promptly inform its contractors and subcontractors of the new obligations and require compliance, and the Office of Management and Budget is to write guidance on how agencies check that contractors are complying. Agencies are directed to coordinate with the White House and contractors on responses to congressional requests, including the assertion of privileges.

If a contractor or subcontractor fails to comply, contracting agencies shall consider all appropriate actions consistent with applicable law, including the potential termination or cancellation of contracts and the potential debarment or suspension of contractors. The order cites the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act and the common law as its legal basis, and it states that it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law against the United States and must be implemented consistent with applicable law. It does not mention existing federal whistleblower protections for contractor employees. The White House defended the order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including on national security, and said contractors answering congressional requests on their own could expose privileged information and force the administration into costly legal disputes, according to a Reuters report published by CNBC. The order itself frames the rule as an efficiency measure, saying separate litigation strategies by contractors and the government over the same requests waste taxpayer money.

The move follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Democrats, who won both chambers in this month's midterm elections, have vowed to investigate the administration, the Trump family's business dealings and its relationships with private companies. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump's allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct. The offices of Garcia, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren did not respond to requests for comment on Friday night, Reuters reported. The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas, according to the Reuters report, which notes that executive privilege lets presidents protect certain confidential communications but courts can step in when Congress and the White House dispute access to information.

stories.Headline: OpenAI updates security to block unauthorized reasoning extraction from its latest AI models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI strengthened the security safeguards for its latest artificial intelligence models, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, on November 22, 2026. These updates were designed to stop unauthorized reasoning extraction, which is a machine learning technique known as distillation. This process allows attackers to reproduce advanced capabilities without the original safety restrictions. The company implemented these changes after detecting multiple distillation campaigns that increased significantly over the summer.

The new defenses drastically reduced attack success rates for GPT-6.2 Astra, dropping from 54 percent to 0.2 percent for earlier interactions. For reasoning generated during current interactions, the success rate fell from 22.9 percent to 0.9 percent. The anti-distillation strategy utilizes a combination of model training, automated classifiers, and API-level restrictions. Reasoning is now tied to the specific conversation that generated it, meaning that rewriting an earlier message removes all subsequent reasoning.

OpenAI officials stated that unauthorized distillation poses significant risks in dual-use fields like biological research and cybersecurity. They warned that distilled models might provide dangerous assistance that the original systems would refuse under safety policies. The company reported disrupting an extraction campaign involving individuals from Moonshot AI in September. Additionally, OpenAI briefed the US Congress in February regarding activity that indicated DeepSeek was attempting to distill US frontier models.

The company took weekly enforcement actions affecting thousands to tens of thousands of accounts to protect national security. Internal studies showed that student models trained on exact reasoning traces performed better than those trained on summaries. These models retained an advantage across two cybersecurity benchmarks, proving that exact traces help models develop skills beyond original tasks. OpenAI continues to use input and output classifiers to identify suspicious requests and prevent potential leaks.

Articles.Title: OpenAI strengthens AI safeguards, cuts reasoning extraction attack rates

stories.headline_source: OpenAI strengthens AI safeguards, cuts reasoning extraction attack rates

stories.Headline: Hickenlooper urges Senate Democratic leader candidates to create a select committee on AI
stories.Summary:
Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper said this week that Senate Democrats are debating how to quickly establish guardrails around artificial intelligence in the next Congress. He urged the two candidates for Senate majority leader to create a new committee on the issue. Hickenlooper has so far withheld an endorsement in the race between Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen. He said the person leading their majority next year should have a day one plan for responsible regulation on AI. Hickenlooper made the proposal in letters to both Schumer and Van Hollen.

Hickenlooper said he proposed a select committee on artificial intelligence to consolidate the conversation. He wrote that with the presidential election two years away, there is a two-year audition to show Americans they can deliver on affordability, accountability and AI safety. He said his priorities are robust third-party evaluation requirements, mitigation of national security challenges and clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable. Democrats take the majority in January, and top policy proposals could include regulating data centers, safety standards and stepping up monitoring and research. Schumer is favored to win reelection in the closed-door Dec. 1 caucus leadership vote.

A spokeswoman for Schumer, Allison Biasotti, said he has been working closely with the incoming heads of committees to develop an ambitious AI agenda and hit the ground running in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority. She said they are working to deliver comprehensive legislation that addresses the serious risks AI poses to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Hickenlooper said there has not been enough progress in Congress since Democrats formed a working group on AI three years ago and convened tech leaders from across the country. He said there is a perception that Congress has not done anything.

Van Hollen said he supports the idea and that he does think a joint committee is needed because AI covers so many different areas impacting lives. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the incoming chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, said he would want to see the specifics and what topics would be covered. Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, expected to become chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, did not immediately endorse the idea and said Democrats have to make it a priority no matter what particular way they approach it. Sanders said Congress has been way behind where it should be in protecting the American people. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, the current Republican chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, said a plan to take the issue out of his committee and others makes no sense.

President Joe Biden's administration called on lawmakers to develop policies after a 2023 executive order on AI oversight, which President Donald Trump rescinded soon after returning to office. The bipartisan working group on artificial intelligence formed by Schumer released a report in 2024 recommending the U.S. spend at least $32 billion over the next three years to develop artificial intelligence and implement safeguards around it. Republicans who have led the House and Senate for the last two years have said AI should be a priority but have focused mostly on innovation, with no major push to establish safeguards or increase monitoring. Trump, who will hold the power of the veto, has repeatedly maintained that little regulation is needed. House Democrats have also been discussing a way forward on AI and have proposed a robust package of proposals.

Cruz said there were already bipartisan conversations about the issue looking forward to next year and that he hopes the next Congress can see Republicans and Democrats finding common ground on addressing catastrophic risk. This week, three Democrats announced the launch of the House AI Safety and Innovation caucus to address security risks. It is unclear if other Democrats, especially the heads of committees already working on AI proposals, will support Hickenlooper's select committee. Wyden said he would want to see the specifics. Sanders did not immediately endorse the idea.

stories.Headline: Huawei introduces new architecture and scaling law to build 1.4nm chips without EUV lithography
stories.Summary:
Huawei introduced the Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture on May 26, 2026, to develop semiconductor chips. The Chinese technology company aims to produce 1.4nm-class chips by the year 2031 without using EUV lithography from ASML. This new approach focuses on reorganizing chip architecture to increase computing density and reduce signal propagation time. The company plans to debut this technology in a Kirin processor for the Mate 90 series this autumn.

The LogicFolding architecture reportedly provides a 55 percent increase in transistor density without relying on expensive Western machinery. Tau Scaling moves away from traditional Moore's Law by focusing on smarter engineering to manage heat and distribute power. These changes are designed to help China reduce its dependence on foreign chip technologies amid ongoing geopolitical tensions. Such innovations could lead to faster AI processing and lower energy consumption for massive cloud infrastructure.

Huawei believes that smarter coordination between hardware and software is more important than simply shrinking transistors. The company suggests that these methods can bypass the manufacturing barriers created by current global semiconductor export restrictions. By focusing on efficient designs, they intend to create more competitive AI hardware that does not depend on a few Western firms. This strategy represents a major shift in how the company approaches the future of high performance computing.

The semiconductor industry is now exploring 3D stacking and chiplet-based designs to improve flexibility and overall performance. Experts remain cautious because managing heat and maintaining yield consistency at 1.4nm is extremely difficult. If these concepts succeed, they may influence global chip design and create alternative ecosystems across Asian markets. Future innovation will likely depend on smarter architecture to support the growing demands of large language models.

stories.Headline: US education unions condemn Google for tying school search access to AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Google announced earlier this month that it plans to turn off search engine access as soon as next year for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools, claiming the decision is necessary based on the technologies' recent fusion. Education unions in the United States strongly criticized Google's reported decision to require schools to adopt its AI tools if they wish to continue using the company's search and education services. The American Federation of Teachers condemned the move, arguing that schools should not be presented with an all-or-nothing choice. The National Education Association echoed those concerns, stressing that schools must remain free to decide whether and how AI technologies are used. The criticism follows reports that Google is pressuring schools to choose between access to its search and education ecosystem and the adoption of its AI products.

Google disclosed that it would turn off its Gemini AI program and search engine for schools until schools decide which services to enable. Google has only offered school districts more ways to interact with AI, such as AI Mode and AI Overview, which provides users with chatbot search functions and summarized results. Potential options include DuckDuckGo and Microsoft's Bing, both of which offer users the option to disable AI-generated answers. Some of the country's largest school districts, including in Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago, are considering doing away with Google altogether. A January report by the Brookings Institution's Center for Universal Education found that AI can undermine children's foundational development.

Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement that if Google doesn't reconsider their position, they will explore other search options. Samuels said they refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out. Google told the Times in a statement Wednesday that it is actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure its products support students and teachers. The AFT said it is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of children. The AFT said that instead of working with educators and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, Google throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to its tools altogether.

The NEA said educators, school districts, and parents should have the freedom to decide which AI tools are right for their students. The NEA said they deserve the time and opportunity to make sure these tools are useful, safe, fair, accessible, protect student privacy, and keep educators involved in how they are used. Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report's authors, told NPR in January that when kids use generative AI that tells them what the answer is, they are not thinking for themselves. Winthrop said they are not learning to parse truth from fiction and are not learning to understand what makes a good argument. Winthrop said they are not learning about different perspectives in the world because they are actually not engaging in the material.

Education International has consistently argued that the adoption of artificial intelligence in education must be guided by pedagogical needs and democratic governance, not by commercial profit making. EI General Secretary David Edwards said no technological product or platform can replace the trust, care, and professional judgement at the heart of teaching and the lifeblood of our societies. Edwards said we demand transparency, accountability, meaningful teacher consultation, and the right to say no to technologies that undermine professional judgement, educational quality, equity, or student privacy. The reported decision by Google also raises concerns about vendor lock-in and the growing dependence of schools on a small number of technology companies. The Google announcement comes at a time when schools around the world are grappling with how to harness new technologies while safeguarding students' rights.

The AFT has called on Google to engage constructively with educators and families and to demonstrate its commitment to protecting students by adopting stronger safeguards for privacy and data protection. Education International emphasizes that education is not a site for technological innovation and product testing. Clear public regulatory frameworks are needed to ensure transparency, accountability, data protection, human oversight, and respect for educators' professional judgement. As governments and education systems develop policies governing artificial intelligence, education unions continue to advocate for transparent regulation, meaningful consultation with education workers, strong privacy protections, and the right of schools to determine whether AI tools serve their educational mission. Studies conducted over the last several months have indicated that the risks attached to the use of AI in schools outweigh the potential benefits.

stories.Headline: Tech stocks plunge as Anthropic loses 109 billion dollars in value
stories.Summary:
Wall Street suffered its worst tech selloff in years during the week of November 22, 2026. The S&P 500 fell 8.6 percent, marking its biggest weekly drop since April 2025. The Dow lost 8 percent, its worst week since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 10 percent, also its worst week since March 2020. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged about 17 percent, its worst week since September 2001.

Anthropic hit the market this week and lost 109 billion dollars in value on Friday. The stock finished Thursday with a market cap of 1.28 trillion dollars. President Donald Trump says his administration will ban U.S. companies from building data centers overseas. Companies that build these centers will face a tremendous tax. Meta and Alphabet signed agreements worth billions of dollars to build overseas data centers.

Attorney General Rob Bonta said California is examining potential criminal violations of state law. He stated the legal framework involves prohibitions against misleading investors and the public. Analyst Michael James McDonald says extreme bearish sentiment supports a near-term rally. He noted long-term indicators suggest the correction could last three to four months. Dividend Value Investor called HP revenue growth spectacular due to AI PC demand.

Hyperscalers are worrying about data center opposition and increased costs after the Democratic midterm sweep. Nvidia is being probed for unlawfully selling advanced chips to China and misleading investors. Gen Z is expected to lead a rebound in in-store Black Friday shopping. A CivicScience survey found 41 percent of shoppers plan to shop in stores. This is the highest share of in-store shoppers since 2014.

The Nasdaq is in the red for the year. The S&P and Dow are in correction territory for the first time since Liberation Day. An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Two independent groups verified the proof, but formal recognition is still pending. HP operates on thin margins, and rising memory prices threaten its profitability recovery.

HP and Dell report earnings on Tuesday, while Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Zoom report Monday. The October core PCE price index is expected to rise 3.2 percent on Wednesday. Hyatt Hotels goes ex-dividend Monday, and Johnson and Johnson goes ex-dividend Tuesday. Newmont and S&P Global go ex-dividend Wednesday. The articles leave open whether the current market correction will end soon.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop AI framework to integrate urban building energy modeling across life cycles
stories.Summary:
Researchers Chao Wang, Xin Wang, Francesco Causone, and Xing Shi detailed an artificial intelligence framework for urban building energy modeling. This comprehensive review examined how AI transforms city-scale simulations into an integrated system. The work was published on November 23, 2026. It focuses on decarbonization across urban design, building renewal, and multi-building operations. The researchers formalized this extended paradigm as UBEM plus.

The UBEM plus framework requires distinct workflows for three specific stages of the built environment lifecycle. In the design phase, it optimizes urban form and building layouts to reduce energy demand. The renewal phase evaluates retrofit options and renewable resource availability across existing building stocks. For the operational phase, the system integrates diagnosis and control optimization to coordinate energy demand. These processes occur across urban districts to foster low-carbon and thermally comfortable environments.

The authors are responsible for identifying three core structural barriers hindering the implementation of this framework. They stated that the interdisciplinary nature of urban modeling requires fusing heterogeneous data from various fields. They noted that scaling from individual properties to districts creates high-dimensional modeling obstacles. The researchers explained that urban environments are dynamic cyber-physical-social systems with longitudinal interdependencies. They argued that detailed simulations capture physical heterogeneity only at a substantial computational expense.

The review affects urban planners and those managing city-scale energy simulations to address the global climate crisis. Urban areas are critical because they account for approximately seventy percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. These regions have also experienced a roughly seventy-four percent increase in heat-related mortality over three decades. The researchers used a corpus of 473 publications to evaluate how others addressed these challenges. This corpus included studies from China, the United States, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Canada, and Italy.

The background involves a systematic literature retrieval from Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect databases. The search covered English-language publications from 2020 through a cutoff date of July 24, 2026. Initial searches retrieved 3,499 records before removing duplicates and ineligible document types. The authors analyzed top-down methodologies using historical statistics and bottom-up methodologies using physics-based or data-driven modeling. They also examined hybrid surrogate modeling to solve scalability bottlenecks where high-fidelity simulations collapse.

Next, the framework integrates advanced AI like transformer architectures, diffusion models, and foundation large language models. Vision transformers enhance footprint extraction and facade material identification for better urban modeling. Diffusion models are used in generative design to avoid training instabilities found in generative adversarial networks. Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning coordinates decentralized devices like heat pumps and battery storage. The articles leave open how to tailor general foundation models to specialized building domains.

stories.Headline: Researchers review atomic-scale imaging and AI methods for materials science
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive academic review published in the Journal of Materials Science: Composites evaluates recent technical milestones in atomic-scale characterization, establishing how modern microscopy, spectroscopy, and artificial intelligence workflows are reshaping materials science. Authored by Obinna Onyebuchi Barah, Mushabe David, and Malisaba Joseph, the study highlights how examining matter at sub-nanometer and sub-angstrom scales has become essential for unlocking structure-property relationships in energy storage systems, quantum materials, and macromolecular biological structures. The authors emphasize that static observations are increasingly replaced by multimodal platforms operating under in situ and operando conditions. By combining aberration-corrected imaging, localized chemical spectroscopies, and automated data pipelines, researchers can now interrogate transient atomic rearrangements that dictate macroscopic device behavior. The review demonstrates that atomic-scale insights directly resolve critical engineering challenges, including efficiency losses in solar cells, battery degradation mechanisms, and structural variations in additive manufacturing.

The development of modern atomic-scale microscopy traces an evolutionary path from early optical tools to twentieth-century electron and scanning probe systems that bypassed fundamental diffraction limits. The introduction of transmission electron microscopy during the nineteen thirties enabled direct nanoscale visualization, which was later complemented by scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy in the nineteen eighties. Over the past two decades, innovations in electron optics, notably spherical aberration correctors, monochromators, and direct electron detectors, have dramatically elevated spatial, temporal, and energy resolutions. These refinements allow modern transmission instruments to resolve individual atomic columns in complex crystal lattices with sub-angstrom precision. Furthermore, environmental transmission electron microscopy has extended atomic-scale imaging into dynamic gaseous and liquid settings, permitting operando observations of catalytic reactions and battery electrodes.

For example, aberration-corrected environmental cells have visualized lattice distortions and ion migration pathways in hybrid perovskite films, directly linking dynamic defect propagation to operational degradation under simulated working conditions. Scanning transmission electron microscopy enhances structural analysis by focusing an electron probe to scan specimens while collecting simultaneous signals across complementary imaging detectors and spectroscopic channels. High-angle annular dark-field detectors provide atomic number contrast, known as Z-contrast, which offers heightened chemical sensitivity for resolving atomic species across heterostructures, quantum dots, and engineered interfaces. Modern developments in four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy collect complete two-dimensional convergent beam electron diffraction patterns at every individual probe position across a raster grid. This high-density multidimensional acquisition enables quantitative mapping of local strain tensors, crystallographic orientations, and three-dimensional atomic configurations with spatial precision reaching approximately three tenths of a nanometer in battery cathodes.

Although scanning transmission electron microscopy delivers superior chemical and structural sensitivity compared to conventional scanning probe techniques, the review notes that the methodology requires significantly more elaborate specimen preparation protocols to achieve electron transparency without altering fragile native phases. Surface-sensitive and cryogenic imaging modalities complement transmission electron techniques by analyzing specimens under specialized ambient, liquid, or low-temperature environments without destructive specimen processing. Scanning tunneling microscopy precisely maps local electronic states and densities on conductive surfaces, whereas atomic force microscopy operates across both conductive and insulating substrates in varied operational modes. High-speed atomic force microscopy captures real-time conformational transitions of dynamic biomolecules under physiological buffer conditions, bridging static structural models with functional kinetic behaviors. In parallel, helium ion microscopy utilizes a focused beam of helium ions to deliver sub-nanometer surface imaging with approximately half-nanometer resolution, elevated secondary electron yields, and minimal sample charging on delicate polymers.

Meanwhile, cryogenic electron microscopy has transformed structural biology through rapid plunge vitrification, dose fractionation, and direct electron detection that preserves macromolecular assemblies in vitreous ice without chemical staining, resolving structures such as the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein at resolutions finer than two angstroms. Spectroscopic techniques provide essential chemical, vibrational, and electronic information that contextualizes structural images obtained from atomic-scale microscopy platforms. Electron energy loss spectroscopy integrated within scanning transmission electron microscopes utilizes monochromated electron sources to achieve energy resolutions below ten millielectronvolts, facilitating nanoscale vibrational spectroscopy and phonon mapping in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. Complementary energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy leverages advanced silicon drift detectors to record high-count elemental maps across alloys and nanoparticles. For surface investigations, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy resolves quantitative chemical bonding states, particularly through near-ambient pressure instrumentation applied to heterogeneous catalysis.

Tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy couples metallic probe tips with optical excitation, circumventing conventional optical diffraction barriers to provide molecular vibrational fingerprints at spatial resolutions down to ten nanometers. Additionally, atom probe tomography applies controlled laser-assisted field evaporation to generate three-dimensional compositional reconstructions with near-atomic spatial precision around three tenths of a nanometer, exposing subtle elemental clustering and phase separation phenomena. The rapid proliferation of complex, high-dimensional datasets generated by advanced analytical instrumentation has elevated artificial intelligence from an auxiliary computational tool to a central analytical engine. Supervised machine learning algorithms, including convolutional neural networks, support vector machines, and random forests, are widely deployed to automate image segmentation, map grain boundary networks, and identify atomic vacancies with higher consistency than manual inspection. Generative adversarial networks assist training workflows by synthesizing realistic image patches and spectroscopic profiles, effectively mitigating data scarcity in resource-intensive experimental settings.

Simultaneously, unsupervised clustering algorithms, such as k-means, density-based spatial clustering, and manifold projection algorithms including t-SNE and UMAP, identify hidden correlations across high-dimensional spectral images without prior manual labeling. To counteract model vulnerabilities related to dataset noise and annotation bias, researchers increasingly incorporate Bayesian inference and Monte Carlo dropout for rigorous uncertainty quantification, ensuring algorithmic inferences remain reproducible and physically grounded against synthetic benchmarks. Multimodal data fusion and correlative workflows address the growing challenge of interpreting heterogeneous datasets that frequently encompass terabytes of raw experimental output. Modern characterization studies integrate structurally and chemically diverse information from transmission electron microscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to capture complete material behaviors. Advanced computational frameworks apply joint non-negative matrix factorization, canonical correlation analysis, and deep learning image registration to align disparate modalities with nanometer and sub-nanometer spatial fidelity.

These correlative workflows allow simultaneous evaluation of topographic features, vibrational modes, and elemental oxidation states across complex interfaces that appear ambiguous in isolated measurements. Furthermore, experimental observations are increasingly coupled with high-performance computing simulations, including density functional theory, molecular dynamics, and finite element analysis. These first-principles computational models establish quantitative reference benchmarks for interpreting observed spectral signatures, generating predictive surrogate frameworks that accelerate the rational exploration of advanced composition spaces. Autonomous experimentation and real-time data processing represent a transformative shift toward closed-loop laboratory ecosystems where analytical instruments function as active research collaborators. Integrated computational pipelines perform on-the-fly image denoising, pattern recognition, and feature extraction, enabling dynamic acquisition steering toward emergent defects, grain boundaries, or unexpected phase transitions.

Autonomous artificial intelligence agents guided by reinforcement learning algorithms and Bayesian optimization dynamically calibrate microscope operating parameters, optimize detector dwell times, and adapt electron dosages based on real-time feedback. In automated cryogenic electron microscopy, intelligent algorithms detect properly preserved macromolecular assemblies to trigger acquisition autonomously, while self-driving scanning transmission electron systems navigate complex specimen landscapes to capture high-value structural details while minimizing beam-induced specimen damage. This closed-loop responsiveness proves particularly vital during in situ and operando experiments, where transient electrochemical transformations and catalytic reaction pathways unfold rapidly, requiring immediate parameter adjustments to record non-equilibrium physical phenomena before structural degradation occurs. Targeted case studies documented throughout the review underscore how atomic-scale characterization directly guides performance breakthroughs in commercial energy technologies and specialized manufacturing. In photovoltaic research, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy identified lead iodide segregation along grain boundaries in methylammonium lead iodide films, guiding chemical passivation strategies that elevated single-junction perovskite solar cell ef More to follow.

stories.Headline: Futurist Silvia Leal warns quantum computing threatens current encryption methods
stories.Summary:
Silvia Leal, a futurist who has advised the European Commission for 15 years, gave a new interview on the series Tomorrow in which she warned that quantum computing poses a fundamental threat to current cybersecurity practices. In the interview she described how modern cyberattacks work, saying attackers get into a company, stay there, wait, spy and gather information, data, projects and knowledge of everything. Leal, who has also presented a technology series on RTVE, Spain's public broadcaster, said current encryption methods could become obsolete and that existing security protocols are vulnerable to attacks using the processing power of quantum computers. She explained that the speed at which quantum computers can break current encryption standards requires proactive adaptation rather than reactive damage control.

Leal's 15-year collaboration with the European Commission has recently focused on the intersection of artificial intelligence and industries such as retail, food and automotive. She argued that trust is the central issue for AI adoption, because many organizations moved quickly without putting IT governance, controls and reliable data in place. She also called for continuous professional development, noting that skills require refreshing every 15 to 18 months and that experienced professionals should embrace learning from younger colleagues. Shekhar Natarajan, host of Tomorrow, echoed that sentiment, saying life is about lifelong learning and that you never stop it.

Leal detailed how successful cyberattacks are no longer immediate extractions of data but prolonged, insidious infiltrations that let attackers accumulate comprehensive intelligence before any disruptive action. She said the threat demands a new generation of cybersecurity specialists who can adapt as the technological landscape rapidly evolves. The emphasis on adaptability is important for a workforce that must navigate constant change and secure systems against emerging quantum threats. The articles do not say what the European Commission or any other body plans to do next in response to her advice.

stories.Headline: Researchers find phone accelerometer models detect quakes best at higher sampling rates and tight false alarm budgets
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a comparative evaluation showing that deep learning models running directly on smartphones can detect earthquake signals from built-in accelerometers, but how well they perform depends heavily on sensor sampling rates and the allowed number of false alarms. The team tested five neural network architectures to tackle long-standing problems in crowd-sourced earthquake early warning, including severe data imbalance, limited computing power on phones, and the difficulty of modeling signals over time. Crowd-sourced warning systems use accelerometers inside everyday smartphones to widen seismic monitoring across earthquake-prone regions, yet deployment has been held back by the huge imbalance between constant human vibration and rare earthquakes. To benchmark the architectures rigorously, the investigators built a unified dataset of 35.4 million two-second windows drawn from roughly 186,000 recordings, covering broadband seismometer traces, shake-table smartphone experiments and human-activity data in a 60-gigabyte archive.

The team handled training difficulties with a stratified majority-class under-sampling approach based on a sampling index, which kept the original 60-gigabyte archive while balancing the test-set positive-to-negative ratio from 79.74 to 1 down to 1 to 1. The same method cut the number of training windows per epoch by a factor of 8.6, making training more practical. Model comparisons showed contrasting strengths: an attention-augmented network combining convolutional layers, bidirectional recurrent units and Bahdanau attention reached an area under the curve of 0.9617 with the smallest generalization gap, an absolute difference of 0.004. A dilated temporal convolutional network reached a higher overall area under the curve of 0.9688, but because broadband seismometers made up 99.99 percent of positive test windows, the researchers stratified validation by sensor provenance.

Discrimination stayed robust at 0.944 to 0.962 when seismic and non-seismic classes shared the same instrument type, but accuracy dropped to between 0.86 and 0.92 for earthquakes recorded on 50-hertz smartphones. Performance fell to chance levels on devices sampling at 25 hertz, where the crucial 0.5 to 20 hertz seismic band is only partly observable. On the deployment side, 8-bit quantized models occupied between 44 and 138 kilobytes, while built-in operator variants on Android devices needed 239 to 486 kilobytes and ran inferences in 3.2 to 6.4 milliseconds per window. Under a budget allowing 100 false alarms per device-day, the Bahdanau attention architecture detected 76 percent of seismometer-recorded events and 61 percent of smartphone-recorded events, while the dilated temporal convolutional network detected 53 percent and 33 percent respectively.

The evaluation was carried out by Şara, Almaqtari, Eken, Koç, Arslan, Kahveci and Atay, and their paper, Real-time seismic detection with edge-AI: a balanced comparison, appears in Cluster Computing, volume 30, issue 1, Article 47, with DOI 10.1007/s10586-026-06833-z. The findings show that the ranking of models by unconstrained receiver operating metrics can reverse once realistic false alarm budgets are applied, which matters for anyone choosing an architecture for a phone-based warning system. The results also indicate that sensor bandwidth sets a hard limit, since phones sampling at 25 hertz cannot reliably capture the seismic frequencies the models depend on. The articles do not say what deployment or follow-up work comes next.

stories.Headline: Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Framework Calibrates Urban Traffic Fundamental Diagrams in Jordan
stories.Summary:
Transportation engineers developed and tested a hybrid calibration framework combining video trajectory analytics, mobile smartphone telemetry, and machine learning optimization to measure how vehicles move along congested urban roadways. Researcher Laith D. Alomari conducted the study, published in the Journal of King Saud University ,  Engineering Sciences, evaluating macroscopic traffic fundamental diagrams across thirty heterogeneous road segments in Irbid, Jordan. The experimental campaign gathered empirical field observations across thirty distinct locations throughout Irbid, including major arterials, intersection approaches, roundabouts, and mid-block road segments. Each site was monitored for thirty to sixty minutes during multiple weekdays, covering both peak and off-peak travel periods. In total, the field deployments produced approximately 3,000 validated observation points.

The investigation treated each monitored road segment and intersection approach as an independent link-level traffic system rather than merging all data points into a single city-wide diagram. Data collection relied on thirty high-definition video cameras recording at 1080p resolution and thirty frames per second, processed using YOLOv8 with Deep SORT. The team also gathered mobile sensor telemetry from volunteer drivers operating approximately twenty participating vehicles, logging GPS coordinates and accelerometer signals at 1 Hz. The validated microscopic trajectory records were aggregated into macroscopic traffic variables using fifteen-second observation intervals. Speed curves declined sharply once traffic density reached approximately 35 to 40 vehicles per kilometer, while flow-density plots peaked within a critical density boundary of 30 to 35 vehicles per kilometer.

The researchers implemented a sequential, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization routine pairing a Genetic Algorithm with Bayesian Optimization to refine model parameters while maintaining physical interpretability. The Genetic Algorithm conducted a global parameter search, capping free-flow speed between 40 and 120 kilometers per hour and jam density between 80 and 250 vehicles per kilometer. Bayesian Optimization then applied a Gaussian process surrogate model with exploration-exploitation acquisition functions to locate optimal basins of convergence with high numerical stability. The two-stage routine yielded parameter variance of less than 8 percent across test iterations and showed smooth convergence within fifteen to twenty-five generations. The authors emphasized that reported numerical parameters characterize link-level performance across specific road sections and roundabouts rather than serving as network-wide macroscopic fundamental diagrams or universal engineering standards.

Baseline formulations yielded free-flow speeds generally estimated between 62 and 68 kilometers per hour and jam densities clustering around 130 to 160 vehicles per kilometer. At Site S02, the baseline Underwood model achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.93 and a root mean square error of 4.9 kilometers per hour, outperforming the linear and logarithmic alternatives. The refinement process reduced root mean square errors by approximately 15 to 25 percent across the evaluated sites compared with standard baseline regression, while lifting the coefficient of determination for the Underwood formulation up to 0.96. A Support Vector Regression model with a radial basis function kernel, evaluated on a 70 percent training, 15 percent validation, and 15 percent testing split, achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.97 and a root mean square error of 3.9 kilometers per hour. The authors noted its functional black-box nature, which prevents direct physical interpretation of structural roadway indicators such as roadway carrying capacity or spatial vehicle packing thresholds.

Classical analytical expressions, originally introduced decades ago under assumptions of uniform vehicular streams and strict lane compliance, often diverge from empirical observations in rapidly growing developing cities. In these environments, mixed fleets, weak lane discipline, and volatile flow transitions complicate standard theoretical assumptions, creating an operational need for low-cost, localized calibration methods. The investigators initially fitted four canonical analytical formulations using standard nonlinear least-squares regression: the linear model proposed by Greenshields, Greenberg’s logarithmic formulation, Underwood’s exponential decay structure, and the multi-regime exponential-polynomial model introduced by Drake and colleagues. The vehicular mix mirrored standard developing urban streams, comprising passenger automobiles, minibuses, motorcycles, and light commercial vehicles. Data collection relied on a dual-modality sensing strategy designed to bypass expensive fixed roadway detectors such as inductive loops or radar systems.

The framework integrated the calibrated models into a physics-guided hybrid architecture, with the evolutionary-optimized analytical equations defining the base physical trajectory and the Support Vector Regression component acting as an adaptive residual corrector predicting localized deviations. When aggregated across all field study locations using observation-weighted metrics, the resulting empirical dataset yielded an average free-flow speed of approximately 65 kilometers per hour, a critical density of approximately 32 vehicles per kilometer, and a jam density of approximately 145 vehicles per kilometer. The field empirical trials were confined to thirty locations within a single city, excluding broader environmental variables such as inclement weather, variable geometric grades, and dynamic traffic signal splits. Because traffic density was derived through flow and speed calculations, comparative evaluations measured relative mathematical fit rather than causal transport mechanisms. The research team identified the low-cost sensing workflow and hybrid algorithmic framework as scalable and transferable tools for developing metropolitan regions, while cautioning that direct operational deployments require localized parameter recalibration.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose AI-assisted roadmap to overcome SuperDEM-CFD bottlenecks in gas-solid reactor simulation
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a peer-reviewed review in ENGINEERING Chemical Engineering on November 21, 2026, examining the state of SuperDEM-CFD technology for simulating gas-solid reactors, according to a report by Blake Davidson on Scienmag. The work focuses on systems where gas-solid multiphase flows govern operations, including fluidized bed reactors, packed bed catalytic units, and facilities conducting thermochemical conversion of biomass and plastics. Because most actual particles feature non-spherical geometries rather than ideal spheres, capturing their complex multi-scale behavior remains fundamentally challenging for engineers seeking process intensification and reliable scale-up. The discrete element method coupled with computational fluid dynamics, commonly designated as DEM-CFD, serves as an established technique for resolving particle-level collisions, hydrodynamics, heat transfer, and mass exchange, but extending it to non-spherical particles through the superquadric equation, an approach known as SuperDEM, introduces severe mathematical and computational complications. The review identified four critical bottlenecks restricting industrial deployment of SuperDEM-CFD technology, the first being anisotropic contact hydrodynamics and persistent numerical singularities that arise at sharp particle edges.

The remaining three obstacles encompass incomplete frameworks for modeling heat transfer, immature reaction models tailored to non-spherical surfaces, and exceptionally heavy computational expenses when simulating systems containing massive particle counts. To overcome contact mechanics failures, the researchers proposed adopting a reduced-space Newton iteration method designed to circumvent numerical singularities at sharp edges, and for thermal modeling they recommend developing generalized shape-factor Nusselt correlations. Modeling chemical transformations in irregularly shaped particles also requires specialized formulations, so the authors put forward a shrinking core reaction model adapted directly to superquadric coordinates to accurately capture progressing reaction fronts. To tackle the prohibitive computational burden of simulating large-scale particulate systems, the roadmap outlines a strategy combining coarse-grained particle models with graphics processing unit acceleration to drastically expand accessible system sizes. The roadmap emphasizes the transformative role of artificial intelligence, noting that deep learning algorithms can construct universal drag and heat transfer correlations by training on detailed direct numerical simulation datasets.

Furthermore, AI techniques can generate interpretable chemical reaction kinetics while accelerating stiff numerical solvers to significantly reduce computational overhead during intensive calculations, and machine learning workflows can assist engineers in analyzing numerical convergence and optimizing mathematical stability when formulating new computational solvers. Together, these mathematical formulations and computational strategies provide a clear development roadmap for next-generation SuperDEM-CFD modeling platforms. By resolving longstanding physical and numerical bottlenecks, the researchers aim to advance predictive reactor design and establish real-time digital twins for industrial gas-solid reactors, supporting more sustainable and efficient chemical processing systems. The review states that modern chemical engineering faces significant hurdles in scaling up reactors and supporting carbon neutrality, particularly in systems where gas-solid multiphase flows govern operations. The articles give no further details on the authors, their institutions, or a publication date beyond the November 21, 2026 report, and they do not say what happens next beyond the stated aims of the roadmap.

stories.Headline: Lenovo and Microsoft expand Hybrid AI Factory to help small businesses run AI locally
stories.Summary:
Lenovo has enhanced its Hybrid AI Factory portfolio in collaboration with Microsoft, according to an article published by Small Business Trends on November 22, 2026. The offering combines Lenovo’s integrated infrastructure solutions, specifically the ThinkAgile series, with Microsoft’s Azure Local and Foundry Local. This partnership is intended to let businesses use AI closer to their operational data, which the article says supports faster insights and improved decision-making without compromising security and sovereignty. The article frames the announcement around small businesses seeking to deploy artificial intelligence while keeping control over their data and workloads.

The Hybrid AI Factory supports local inference, conversational RAG, agentic AI, and vision AI in environments businesses operate and trust, a Lenovo representative said, according to the article. The infrastructure includes the Lenovo ThinkAgile MX650a V4 systems, which feature NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and the article says NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 GPUs are included for those with different capacity needs to balance performance and cost. Lenovo Top Choice Express and Lenovo AI Express are named as programs meant to provide quicker access to necessary infrastructure and accelerate the move from AI pilot projects to full production. The article says the offering lets small businesses use familiar Azure tools to manage workloads across hybrid cloud environments.

Data protection is another focal point, and the article says businesses can choose from various hyperconverged or disaggregated architectures so they can scale compute and storage needs independently. Lenovo’s introduction of confidential computing with Azure Local is described as protecting sensitive data during processing, and a Lenovo spokesperson said confidential VMs and confidential GPUs give organizations greater confidence to bring AI models into environments where privacy, resiliency, regulation, and operational control matter most. The article notes that implementing a sovereign AI framework requires careful planning and governance as organizational needs, regulatory landscapes, and technology requirements evolve, and it says Lenovo’s advisory services offer tailored assessments and roadmaps for aligning AI initiatives with business goals. It adds that the offering extends to broader business IT needs through Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid features, which the article says may appeal to businesses with remote or decentralized operations.

The article says small business owners should consider potential challenges, including the planning and governance that a sovereign AI framework requires. It directs interested businesses to Lenovo’s Premier Solutions and ThinkAgile series and to the original press release for more information. The article presents the Hybrid AI Factory as setting the stage for a controlled and efficient deployment of technology capable of driving growth. It does not say when the offering becomes available or what it costs.

stories.Headline: Amazon sells second generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $284
stories.Summary:
Meta and Ray-Ban released the second generation of their camera-equipped Wayfarer smart glasses, and on November 22, 2026, Gizmodo reported that Amazon was selling the Matte Black model with clear lenses for $284 instead of $379, the lowest price the second generation had reached. The glasses carry a 12 MP camera in the corner of the frame that captures photos and records video in 3K Ultra HD, and recording starts with a tap on the frame or a voice command. Meta AI is built in, so wearers can ask about what is in front of them or have a conversation translated while traveling without reaching for a phone. Open-ear speakers sit near the ears without blocking them, and five microphones in the frame pick up the voice for calls and Meta AI requests, even outdoors in the wind.

Battery life is rated at up to 8 hours of moderate use, and the charging case holds another 48 hours, so a long weekend away does not require a separate charger for the glasses. Meta and Ray-Ban offer the Gen 2 with a wide range of lenses, including Transitions lenses that darken outdoors and clear up inside, along with Standard and Large frame sizes to fit different faces. A separate Fox News deals article from November 19, 2026, said shoppers could save up to 25 percent on select styles from Ray-Ban and Oakley, with Meta glasses starting at $249 for up to 15 percent off and Ray-Ban Meta glasses starting at $379 for up to 25 percent off. That article said buyers could save up to $115 on Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 glasses, including Wayfarers with matte-black frames and clear, transition or tinted graphite lenses, and that the Oakley Meta line started at $399 with up to 25 percent off, including the Vanguard model in lens colors such as pink, blue, red and yellow.

Ray-Ban Meta is the best-selling line of AI glasses on the market, according to IDC sales data cited by Gizmodo, and the Gen 2 refines what made the first pair popular. Gizmodo described the translation feature as the most impressive part, because it makes the glasses genuinely helpful on a trip abroad rather than just fun to wear, and said the open-ear speakers let you hear your playlist and the traffic around you at the same time, which feels safer on a bike or a city sidewalk. The Fox News article said the glasses let people take calls, snap photos and more, all hands-free, and that the Oakley Meta glasses can connect with Garmin smartwatches to provide real-time insights and alerts while you move. The Fox News piece was written by Caitlyn Martyn, an editor who primarily writes and edits commerce content for the Deals section, and both articles state that the publishers may earn a commission when readers buy through links on their sites.

Gizmodo framed the appeal around moments like filming a child's first bike ride without training wheels, since pulling out a phone usually means watching through a screen instead of with your own eyes, while the glasses put the camera on your face. It said the 12 MP camera changes the kind of footage you get, whether it is a cooking session filmed while both hands are busy or a concert where you would rather not hold your phone above the crowd. The Fox News article presented the glasses as a gift idea for the tech lover on a list, noting that the Adventurer model has a classic tortoiseshell frame, brown lenses and standard or high-bridge fit options. Neither article says what happens next beyond the current deals, which the articles describe as available now at the prices given.

stories.Headline: Apple develops an autonomous AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta
stories.Summary:
Apple is reportedly developing an advanced autonomous AI agent to rival OpenAI, Anthropic, and Grok. This news emerged on Thursday, November 20, 2026, following a report by Bloomberg. The company aims to create a tool that can autonomously control devices and use apps. It will also be capable of browsing the web and writing code. This project is intended to compete with Meta's Muse, ChatGPT's Dots, and Claude Code.

The agent will run on Apple operating systems and navigate between browsers, terminals, and services. It must be able to write and debug code while deciding which tools to use. Apple is hiring a senior engineering manager for this proactive, agentic AI assistant. Meanwhile, macOS 27.3 will increase authorization steps from four to 14 for other AI agents. This change is intended to improve security on the Apple devices.

Mark Gurman, the executive editor of Bloomberg, said the agent is far beyond today's Siri. He noted that the job listing describes an AI that uses computers like a person. The listing claims the agent will work privately with the polish people expect from Apple. It aims to move fluidly between tools just as human workers currently do. Apple has not yet confirmed the development of this specific AI agent.

Some users view the new macOS authorization requirements as a sign of anti-competitiveness. These changes affect users who enable agents from ChatGPT and other apps on their devices. The project targets competitors like OpenAI, which is currently involved in a trade secrets lawsuit. Apple claims that over 400 former employees now work for the company called OpenAI. This legal battle involves allegations of stolen circuit schematics and internal engineering applications.

The reports are based on fresh job postings for a senior engineering manager. These listings describe an agent that can navigate devices on a user's behalf. Apple currently allows third party AI apps to carry out functions on its macOS. The company is focusing on privacy and its strong iPhone ecosystem for this project. This development follows a record breaking Wall Street debut for the AI firm Anthropic.

Apple will continue developing the agent to handle complex tasks and run commands. The company seeks to build a tool that can call various services autonomously. It remains unclear when the autonomous AI agent will be released to the public. The articles do not state the specific timeline for the project's completion. They also leave open whether Apple will officially confirm these reported development plans.

stories.Headline: Pat Gelsinger says AI needs a 10,000-fold efficiency gain beyond incremental chip upgrades
stories.Summary:
Former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger used a fireside chat called “Reality Check: Beyond Chips” at the COSM Technology Summit 2026 in Scottsdale, Arizona, to argue that small generational chip upgrades cannot meet the demands of artificial intelligence, which he said needs a 10,000-fold gain in computing efficiency. He appeared alongside technology theorist George Gilder and Heritage Foundation director Bret Swanson. After the event he wrote on X that Moore’s Law should be woken up rather than declared dead. He said the revival depends on fundamental breakthroughs across five engineering fronts.

Gelsinger said the needed advances span light, power, cooling, composition and packaging, and that turning one gigawatt of electricity into ten gigawatts of AI token output requires far more than shrinking transistors. He pointed to U.S. energy capacity growing only in the low single digits over the past decade, gas turbine supply backlogs of eight years and nuclear projects that take a decade to build. He cited NVIDIA’s Kyber racks built on the Blackwell NVL72 architecture, which push power needs to 600kW, enough to supply 500 homes, and a Harvard study finding U.S. data centers consume as much electricity as Chile. He also noted that major AI foundation models now ship roughly every four weeks.

Since joining the venture firm Playground Global as a general partner in March 2025, Gelsinger has backed startups aimed at these hardware bottlenecks, including the government-supported lithography venture xLight, which seeks to move past ASML’s 13.5nm extreme ultraviolet wavelength barrier, and the nuclear capacity firm Alva Energy. His roadmap also points to optical interconnects and silicon photonics to carry data with light instead of copper. He said that after more than 40 years in semiconductors he believes the greatest innovations are still ahead. On an earlier occasion he called HBM a hideous memory while conceding it is the best technology the industry has now, and he proposed Z2RAM as an alternative with potentially better density, performance and power draw.
