stories.Headline: Viola Fintech's Noam Inbar says distribution is now the real moat in enterprise AI, vertical AI and fintech
stories.Summary:
Noam Inbar, General Partner at Viola Fintech, made the statement in an interview with CTech for its 2027 VC Survey, published on 23.11.26 at 10:17. The interview was conducted by Elihay Vidal and Zachy Hennessey. Inbar said Israel has always won on deep technical moats, but in enterprise AI, vertical AI and fintech the real moat is now distribution. Inbar said Israel has never excelled at distribution. Inbar said developing that commercial muscle is the big challenge and opportunity for the next generation of Israeli companies.

Viola Fintech has $210 million in total assets under management. Its partners and managers are Daniel Tsiddon and Noam Inbar. Its notable portfolio companies are Planck, Rewire, Quinn, Advance, Insurify, Cowbell and True Accord. Its notable exits are Planck and Rewire. Inbar said the fund's strategy is to go earlier than it used to and look for defensible niches, markets that are not purely winner-takes-all.

Inbar said AI has lowered the barrier to building a convincing story or an impressive early product, which forces the fund to be much sharper in its underwriting. Inbar said technical execution is becoming more commoditized, so the fund cares far less about what specific tech unit someone came out of in the army and much more about raw leadership, grit, stamina, risk appetite and integrity. Inbar said heavy capital concentration has made things trickier for a smaller fund like Viola Fintech. Inbar said the fund is not built to compete in hyper-rounds at inflated valuations and does not want to back underfunded copycats or tiny companies destined for a quick acqui-hire. Inbar said cyber is not Inbar's focus and left it to others, though Inbar believes the ecosystem needs to diversify its core strengths.

Inbar said defense tech is too exposed to shifting geopolitics and global attitudes toward Israel to be a pillar to bet everything on. Inbar said foreign appetite is split, with Tier-1 global funds still very active in Israel while mid-tier funds that used to be important syndicate partners are largely sitting out due to inflated valuations and mega-rounds. Inbar said depending solely on a handful of top-tier funds is a fragile position. Inbar said domestic political instability and growing global alienation are real risks to the ability to scale companies from Israel. Inbar said the concentration in startup funding reflects concentration among VCs themselves, with a small handful of massive funds holding a huge share of the capital and funneling it into a small number of companies.

Inbar said those mega-funds have become true market makers, which makes it tough for smaller funds to compete on traditional terms. Inbar said the market is moving way too fast for 12-year fund cycles to make sense anymore. Inbar said locking up capital for over a decade with little to no liquidity is not worth the uncertain upside. Inbar said startups can build and scale with far less capital today, so outside the mega-rounds a growing number of good companies are choosing to bypass VC altogether. Inbar said in the mid-market there will likely be some convergence between VC and private equity, with faster paths to liquidity, different ownership structures and more flexible capital.

Inbar said the exact blueprint is not yet clear because the industry is still figuring out what the next step should look like. Inbar named Quinn, Livez and Advance as startups worth watching this year. Inbar said Quinn lets financial institutions give customers an agentic experience built on each customer's unique financial DNA and a judgement layer. Inbar said Quinn is the only company in its space that is SEC certified, giving it a significant edge, and that it already works with top brands with larger ones underway. Inbar said Livez lets employers and insurers turn every mobile phone into an AI-powered screening tool that spots risk early and acts on it automatically, booking care and navigating benefits for each person.

Inbar said Advance is the financial platform built for how insurance moves money, automating collection, reconciliation and payments and giving agencies and brokers real-time visibility. Inbar said Advance turns premium money from a passive liability into an asset that works for agencies and brokers. Inbar said the US healthcare system is built to treat illness, not to prevent it. Inbar said that when prevention finally happens at scale, employees, employers and insurers all win. Inbar said insurance runs on money that never stops moving, with premiums coming in, carriers getting paid and commissions being split, yet most of the industry still handles that money with spreadsheets, disconnected systems and generic bank accounts where errors stay hidden and balances sit idle.

stories.Headline: Nio CEO says AI boom drives memory chip prices up fivefold
stories.Summary:
Nio Founder and Chief Executive Officer William Li spoke at a user event in Changzhou on Saturday. He stated that the artificial intelligence boom pushed memory chip prices up fivefold. This cost shock occurred between the first and second quarters of the year. Li likened this event to the lithium price surge of 2022. He noted that nobody saw this coming at the end of last year.

The cost of each car rose by 14,000 yuan, which is about 2,100 dollars. Li said costs would rise another 2,000 to 3,000 yuan in the second half. This brings the total increase to 16,000 or 17,000 yuan, or 2,400 to 2,500 dollars. Memory accounted for 10,000 yuan of that increase. These figures were first mentioned at a media briefing on September 3.

William Li said AI data centers are taking all the demand and supply. He claimed the industry has taken several blows from AI, starting with memory. Li stated that carmakers cannot outbid data centers that invest without counting costs. He said that if suppliers provide chips at all, they are doing a favor. Li noted that the auto industry is the biggest application industry for AI.

The cost shock falls hardest on the most intelligent cars using the most memory. Li said that those using little memory are hit less. Other affected components include copper, aluminum, circuit boards, and some basic chips. Some buyers paid five to eight times the price for printed circuit boards. The auto industry also lost capital and talent to AI startups and companies.

In 2022, battery-grade lithium carbonate in China briefly topped 600,000 yuan a ton. Nio added 10,000 yuan to three models in May of that year. Lithium prices spiked from the first quarter to the second quarter in 2022. That surge cost carmakers about 30,000 to 40,000 yuan, or 4,500 to 6,000 dollars, per car. This historical context explains why Li compared the current memory crisis to lithium.

Nio will report third-quarter results on December 1. The company plans to unveil NWM 3.0 at a technology day on November 25. Li said memory and bulk material prices should fall somewhat by 2028. He claimed revenue this year would definitely exceed 100 billion yuan, or 15 billion dollars. The articles leave open how Nio will manage its current net losses.

stories.Headline: Northwestern students use AI to prepare for internships as employers expect faster work
stories.Summary:
Simon Benigeri, a French fourth-year artificial intelligence Ph.D. candidate at Northwestern, said he brought hidden efficiency to his internships in the U.S. by making tasks seem to take longer than they did, giving him more time to “chill.” He realized soon after starting an internship with Apple’s Siri Speech and Innovation team that he could no longer pull this off. Benigeri quickly saw how fast AI was changing the culture and pace in the office. He said the team had a big budget for AI and that expectations changed so that people should be getting work done really fast. His experience reflects a broader shift in which students turn to AI to land internships and employers increasingly expect them to know how to use it.

Northwestern Career Advancement encourages students to use AI as a supplementary tool in their job searches, leaving many students to decide for themselves where AI fits as they apply for and complete internships. Benigeri said he has noticed a change in companies’ hiring practices, with many more interviews where candidates are expected to use AI to code during the interview. He said there are also many more interviews where companies set programming aside and try to see how a person thinks and tackles problems. McCormick junior Benjamin Runde secured a job this summer as an investment banking summer analyst at Morgan Stanley and used AI to prepare for technical questions and practice speaking with recruiters. Runde said he would put ChatGPT or Claude on voice mode, give it the 400 questions and a test bank of appropriate answers, and have it grade his responses for precision.

Runde said practicing mock interviews at any time and place ended up being a useful asset in his preparation, though he said he did not know how good the AI actually was at grading and that it just got him to do it all the time. Weinberg sophomore Victoria Wang interned at Concannon Business Consulting this past summer and, like Runde, used AI to prepare for interviews by practicing case interviews, the problem-solving exercises consulting firms use to evaluate candidates. Wang said that as a younger student she found AI helpful when she could not find a “case buddy” or felt too embarrassed to case with people. She said she has learned to match different tools to different parts of the process, preferring Claude for technical case preparation because she said it has a better grasp of the frameworks consulting interviews require. For behavioral interviews and networking, Wang said she would ask ChatGPT to generate a possible scenario of how a behavioral interview would go or how she should lead a coffee chat to get to the questions she wants to ask.

Runde said AI use is not the same in every field, and while he leaned heavily on AI for investment banking recruitment, he rarely used it during engineering internships at companies including Procter & Gamble and L3Harris Technologies. He said that was especially true in defense, largely because the industry is heavily regulated and much of the work his team handled was confidential, and that AI is not as pervasive in defense or consumer goods as it is on a college campus. Medill senior Laura Garcia, an editorial intern at Sunset Magazine, said she built her resume without AI and was thankful because Medill is super extensive in the whole resume process. Garcia used AI as an editing tool for cover letters in her internship applications, asking ChatGPT to identify the main points she should keep and build around after her original draft ran long.

Wang said LinkedIn is a good tool to find and apply for jobs and that AI has been helpful in tightening the bullet points under her experience section, but she drew the line at editing the headshot for her profile picture because she felt the photoshop made it not look like her anymore. Wang said combining LinkedIn and AI use has helped her land coffee chats with current employees to boost her odds in consulting recruitment, and in crafting emails she uses a standard prompt that tells ChatGPT to introduce her, explain how she found the person and mention something specific such as their office location or past projects before closing with a request for a short phone call. She said she puts people’s LinkedIn or a screenshot of their information to AI, has the AI write the email, double checks, and then sends them out. Runde said most of his emails are either written or heavily edited by ChatGPT, and following the release of the AI agent Grok Bot in August, which now acts as his personal assistant, he has it look at his Canvas twice a day and go through every assignment page and calendar page and put everything on his Google Calendar.

Runde said he also has it check his email and organize his day, and he expects tools like the Grok Bot that handle monotonous tasks to become the standard of AI use going forward. Garcia said her editors at Sunset have told her they find it strange that Medill does not teach students how to use AI given its capabilities and potential, and she said she thinks students have to learn as much from it as they can rather than hide it and put it in a box. Benigeri, who once stretched out the time it took to complete tasks, now urges students to do the opposite and said he thinks students should do the work to really understand what they are doing. He said students can use AI later, that it is going to be great and they absolutely should use it, and that it is good not to take shortcuts so they can give themselves the best chance to understand things.

The article also lists other Daily Northwestern pieces, including one on the Northwestern Network for Collaborative Intelligence’s five strategic leaders aiming to expand interdisciplinary AI across campus and one asking who Sharath Narayan is, a former “Jeopardy!” champion continuing cancer research and quizbowl competitions at Northwestern. Other listed pieces cover how an international exchange student lives on $1,000 a month in Evanston and how Evanston artist Val Zee reshapes “her-story” through bold colors. The page carries a 2026 Daily Northwestern copyright notice and credits a FLEX Pro WordPress theme by SNO.

stories.Headline: Newton police chief Timothy Cohoon backs AI surveillance cameras with privacy safeguards
stories.Summary:
Newton’s Public Safety & Transportation Committee discussed the City Council’s potential role in regulating AI surveillance technology at a meeting on Wednesday. Ward 5 Councilor-at-Large Brittany Hume Charm said the key question was whether the City Council should have a seat at the table if a surveillance technology proposal came before the city. Charm said the matter was certainly not about inviting surveillance technology into Newton and that she wanted to be very clear about that. Newton Police Chief Timothy Cohoon, who was sworn in last March, worked with surveillance technologies in the past and expressed support for bringing them to Newton, Charm explained. Charm said initial conversations with Cohoon showed he had used some of these technologies in his previous cities and roles.

Charm said Cohoon remains supportive of the technologies with safeguards and discussions about the right use of them to balance interest in privacy. In September, after a request from The Heights, the Newton Police Department stated in a notice on its public records portal that it did not have plans to install Flock cameras. Cohoon has now expressed a willingness to implement AI surveillance technologies such as Flock Safety cameras and automated license plate readers. Cohoon said his job is to make sure police give their folks the most modern equipment, systems and investigative capabilities. Cohoon said police should embrace responsible innovation while protecting individual privacy and civility.

Residents of Newton have taken an interest in opposing Flock cameras, and several members of the public were present at Wednesday night’s committee meeting holding up signs reading “No Mass Surveillance.” Charm explained that repeated instances of misuse and threats to public safety involving Flock cameras played a significant role in generating the high level of community concern. Charm cited Texas tracking a woman across state lines who was seeking an abortion, and examples of misuse by police for former romantic partners. Charm said there are examples of this locally across Massachusetts as well. According to Charm, these technologies could be brought to Newton without any notification to or say from the City Council.

Charm said cameras have been installed in many cities without the City Council or even the public being made aware, and that kind of lack of transparency and discussion is quite concerning. Charm said the council would not have to be notified if the police department wanted to implement this currently. Ward 7 Councilor-at-Large Brian Golden said cameras proliferating around a community do cause a sense of anxiety because of the potential for invasions of privacy and sharing information. Golden said he wants to be really sure that the council needs to be involved in that. Ward 8 Councilor-at-Large Jacob Silber said he is no more afraid of this technology than of his cell phone in his pocket because he does not really feel he has an expectation of privacy anymore in this society.

Ward 1 Councilor Maria Scibelli Greenberg said Newton is 43 percent below the national average in crimes, so she wondered how necessary this is. Greenberg said increasing staffing, professional development and developing a crisis intervention program would seem to be better funding than having this type of surveillance in a city that does not have that kind of crime. Several council members believe the risks posed by Flock cameras demonstrate the need for the City Council to take a stand on the issue. Ward 6 Councilor-at-Large Sean Roche said this is a very scary set of technologies and that we should be very careful.

Roche said it is in good judgment for the council to say “Let’s not implement these” and that we should just draw a line in the sand. Roche proposed a moratorium to temporarily prevent AI surveillance technologies from being brought to Newton. Roche asserted that the City Council has the ability to regulate the use of these devices. Roche said a moratorium says that, right now, we are not going to implement that.

Although Cohoon reaffirmed his support for automated license plate readers, he stated that there are no current plans to bring any AI surveillance technologies to Newton. Cohoon said the automatic license plate readers have been a game changer for policing and that there has been abuse, but to throw the baby out with the bathwater is a step too far. Cohoon said he does not have any plans right now to bring this technology to the city. The committee discussed the City Council’s potential role in regulating AI surveillance technology at the Wednesday meeting.

Charm said the key question before the committee that night was whether the City Council should have a seat at the table if a proposal for surveillance technology came in front of the city. Cohoon was sworn in last March. The Newton Police Department’s September notice on its public records portal stated it did not have plans to install Flock cameras. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI tools raise team output but leaders risk burnout by raising workloads
stories.Summary:
Companies that begin using AI tools are definitely seeing a productivity boost, but as team production increases, team performance dips, according to an article published by Entrepreneur on November 22, 2026. The cause is that AI helps to make task completion faster, which at face value sounds beneficial since human workers don’t need to spend as much time getting their work done. But organizations are responding by increasing workloads and expectations, so teams are getting more work accomplished while individual employees aren’t getting any kind of a break. Instead, they’re expected to multiply their workloads, which the article calls a surefire road to capacity strain and burnout.

The article says leaders should teach team members how to think more clearly in disruptive, fast-moving environments, helping them create enough cognitive space to apply judgment, adaptability and emotional intelligence they already possess. It cites human performance company Q Studio, which takes this approach through organization-wide Mind Skills Training, and corporate agile training company Agile Seekers, which teaches team members to show curiosity and skepticism about AI rather than simply accepting what it recommends. It also says leaders should make human connection an expectation, because Thomson Reuters research shows that when employees are given the okay to just turn in AI work, they lose a sense of connection with that work and eventually with each other. The article adds that encouraging team members to role play difficult conversations with each other can be a stronger way to build bonds than using chatbots trained for that purpose.

The article says leaders around the world are laying off team members in the name of AI, though some giants aren’t, and it calls that a tricky move that should be reconsidered even if AI has improved productivity. When people are let go because AI took their jobs, the article says, everyone who remains gets a mixed signal that productivity matters more to the organization than performance. As a result, those employees may stop trying to hand in stellar work and just try to be as busy as possible. The article concludes that productivity will always matter and AI can let employees do more work in less time, but leaders should not concentrate so hard on getting more done that they forget to celebrate the human characteristics and acumen only their team members can provide.

stories.Headline: Ottero CEO Nadav Eyal unveils Skip robot to carry hospital waste and linens
stories.Summary:
Nadav Eyal, co-founder and CEO of Ottero, introduced a robot named Skip at Tel Aviv University during AI Week, which ran November 9 to 11, 2026, alongside Cyber Week. Eyal built Skip to make a trip that hospital staff make repeatedly, from a patient's room to the waste chute. A nurse calls Skip and loads it with used linens and garbage when it arrives, and the robot can find the chute on its own, Eyal said. Eyal expects Skip to start work within weeks at Rambam Medical Center in Haifa. The Media Line spoke with four Israeli startups at the event, including Ottero, Orion AI Pro, Cyvore and AgentZero.

Ottero combines maps from its machines into a digital model of the hospital so its software can coordinate their movements, Eyal said. He gave the example of a corridor that gets busy at certain times of day, saying that if there is a rush hour the robots will know and go around it. The system can also prioritize more urgent jobs, and the software can call in another robot while the first one recharges, he said. Eyal said Ottero would expand in Israel first, then look to the United States and parts of Europe. He said hospitals adding robots for cleaning and deliveries would need someone to take charge of all the robots inside the building and see that they meet procedures and protocols.

Dikla Zakay, founder and CEO of Orion AI Pro, refers to her robot as "she," and Orion is designed for older adults, particularly those who live alone. It can go through a calendar, play a radio station, or give someone a medication reminder, and Zakay said the device senses when a person enters the room or sits nearby and can decide when to speak up. Zakay gave the example of someone who usually gets up at 8 a.m., saying that if an hour or two goes by and the person is still out of sight, Orion could check on them. If they fail to respond, she said, the device could call an emergency contact, and Zakay said Orion takes images and stores them on the robot. Zakay said the team has paid for development so far, that Orion is starting to look for funding, and that she expects the robot to be available for purchase in about six months.

Ori Segal, co-founder and CEO of Cyvore, used a fake Microsoft login page to explain what his company looks for, saying an attacker might change the shading on a page that otherwise looks familiar enough for someone to type in a password. Cyvore's software examines the page for visual signs of a forgery and looks for connections across the apps employees use, including email, Slack, Teams and Zoom. Segal told The Media Line the company's focus is to "track the chain of events" as an attack moves from one system to another. In one investigation, the starting point was a text message impersonating a postal service, and in the attackers' database his team found other campaigns impersonating postal services in Dubai and Greece. Segal said one Cyvore customer had asked for help with Zendesk, the platform it used for customer support, and that it took Cyvore two weeks to connect the platform.

Yoav Shechter, co-founder and CEO of AgentZero, gave the example of an employee photographing a balance sheet on a work computer and sending the picture to a personal AI assistant for analysis, which he said is something chief information security officers do not have visibility into today. Shechter said AgentZero's software would check the image on the phone itself and that if an employee shares business data with his personal agent, it will block it. He said the company already has an MVP and design partners in just four months, and that he was also looking at the permissions people grant when they connect an AI assistant to their personal email or photo gallery. He brought up family photos, medical information and financial records as examples of what people keep on their phones and can give an assistant permission to access. Shechter said the software can block users from sharing sensitive personal information, naming Social Security numbers and health information as examples.

Erez Askal, head of the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office, said his concern was whether the government could count on having the computing infrastructure and models it needs. Askal told The Media Line he believes that some years from now all the critical infrastructure is going to work based on AI, and that if you have no access you have a problem. Asked what the government should prioritize, Askal brought up worker retraining and health care, and he also mentioned loneliness among older adults, a problem Zakay had in mind when she designed Orion. Askal referred to AI that people would use in their day-to-day lives as "lived AI," and before the interview ended he said you must first be sure that you have the infrastructures and the sovereignty. Sanjaya Poudel of the Nepal delegation told The Media Line he wanted to speak with people in government and business and find out what might work back home, saying "We can take back a lot of things from this ecosystem."

Isaac Ben-Israel, who founded AI Week and directs Tel Aviv University's Blavatnik Interdisciplinary Cyber Research Center, told The Media Line he works in the field every day and still struggles to keep up with the new applications. Ben-Israel said he is very satisfied with the progress but that it is going so fast that we may ignore also the risks that come with it. He pointed to the effect on jobs and warned against the temptation to first do the application and then think how to avoid the risk. Zakay said Orion uses outside AI services for conversation, while contact lists and details of a person's routine can stay on the device. Eyal said getting the robot ready meant working through each situation it might encounter in a hospital, one by one, and that the aim was to have it actually work reliably.

stories.Headline: Zurich and St Gallen study finds AI risks could exceed private insurance capacity
stories.Summary:
A joint study by Zurich Insurance Group and the University of St. Gallen, developed as part of the Zurich AI Lab and published on 23 November 2026, concludes that artificial intelligence can create new risks and significantly amplify existing dangers, and that in the extreme case losses could exceed the capacity of the private insurance market. The report, titled "The AI Resilience Challenge," is based on interviews with 50 experts, including 36 Zurich executives and specialists and 14 external experts, conducted between July and September 2026. The authors see a key challenge in the growing concentration among a few technology providers, since companies using different AI applications can still depend on the same underlying models, cloud infrastructures or data sources. As an example of the consequences of technological dependencies, the study points to the global IT outage in 2024, when a faulty software update from a cybersecurity provider disabled around 8.5 million devices and affected banks, airlines and hospitals, although the incident was not directly related to AI.

The study distinguishes four categories of AI risk, ranging from limited and understandable losses that existing insurance products can in principle cover, through risks with identifiable causes that can hit numerous companies at once, to difficult-to-understand errors where liability or decision pathways remain unclear, and finally systemic risks whose scale and causes can hardly be determined in advance. It notes that matters become especially critical when AI systems independently conclude contracts, purchase services or execute transactions, because there is still insufficient experience regarding the frequency and extent of possible losses in such autonomous applications. Insurance works especially well when risks are measurable, losses are limited and individual events are largely independent of one another, and AI can undermine these conditions at the same time, so that risks can no longer be spread as effectively across a large portfolio when many policyholders depend on the same technologies or similar errors occur. As possible early warning signs the study cites rising premiums, lower coverage limits, additional exclusions and higher requirements for risk documentation, which it describes as possible developments rather than already proven general changes in insurance terms.

Zurich CEO Mario Greco and HSG professor Karolin Frankenberger emphasize in the foreword that AI risks cannot be completely ruled out, and that what matters is to identify errors in time, limit their spread and keep the consequences manageable. The study recommends that companies more closely track their AI applications and technological dependencies, clearly define responsibilities, and create ways to shut down critical systems in the event of malfunctions or switch to alternatives. Insurers, for their part, should increasingly examine how companies actually use AI and what shared risks are building up in their portfolios as a result. In the case of especially large systemic losses, the authors believe public-private solutions may be required, citing existing models for covering natural catastrophes and terrorism risks as general examples.

stories.Headline: Google launches AI Max to expand Search ads beyond keywords
stories.Summary:
Google announced AI Max, an enhancement setting for existing Search campaigns rather than a new campaign type, in a post dated 22 November 2026 aimed at advertisers in the UK and wider EMEA region. The feature combines three tools: keywordless Search Term Matching, which uses AI to expand reach beyond manual keyword lists, Text Customization, which uses Gemini models to rewrite headlines and descriptions in real time to match a user's query, and Final URL Expansion, which crawls a site and routes users to the landing page that best answers the query. Google said the setup can capture 15% more conversions by unlocking net-new Search queries and deliver up to 27% more conversions at a similar CPA or ROAS. The post cited over 5 trillion Google searches a year and said habits are shifting through AI Overviews, Lens and AI Mode, with users asking longer and more complex questions.

Advertisers enable AI Max by toggling on "Optimize your campaign with AI Max" in campaign settings or by setting up an AI Max A/B experiment, and Google recommended picking an always-on Search campaign using Smart Bidding with enough budget headroom. Google advised implementing enhanced conversions for leads or Google Tag Gateway in Data Manager, locking in bidding goals such as target CPA or target ROAS, and turning on all three settings together for what it described as a compound effect. It also recommended keeping budgets uncapped or leaving sufficient headroom so campaigns can scale into newly discovered demand. Controls include brand inclusions and exclusions at ad group level, negative keyword lists, and URL inclusions and exclusions to protect sensitive pages, with transparency through search terms and landing page reports.

The announcement was presented by Pauline and Zeina of Google, who said manual keyword lists leave high-intent demand on the table as consumer search behaviour evolves. They described endless manual restructures, duplicating match groups, building dozens of ad variants and mapping landing pages by hand, as hours of weekly work that should go to strategy, and warned that rigid keywords hand valuable customers to competitors. They stressed that advertisers keep total control through the brand and URL settings, and that AI Max is not a campaign type to build from scratch. Google directed advertisers to input brand and URL exclusions and negative keywords before going live and to follow a testing timeline over the following couple of weeks, and pointed readers to Accelerate with Google for announcements, reports, recommendations and training.

stories.Headline: Amazon puts an AI agent ahead of manual Brand Store page building
stories.Summary:
Amazon placed an AI agent in front of the manual page builder for its Brand Stores, according to an Amazon Ads Support Center page updated on November 11, 2026. Clicking Add page in the Store builder opens a new window with the Brand Store Builder Agent, a tool that drafts Store pages from typed instructions or from one of six prewritten prompts. A companion page on page templates, updated on November 21, 2026, describes the manual route as the exit from that window. The two pages belong to a set of ten Amazon Ads help articles on Stores, plus Amazon's Brand Registry sales page. Their update dates run from May 1, 2024 to November 21, 2026.

The agent generates content and layouts based on prompts, and brands can choose from six prewritten prompts or write their own custom prompts. Chat can happen in any language, but Brand Store content generates in the marketplace's primary language. A note gives two exits: click Add page without AI Assistance in the upper-right corner or click X in the left-side corner. A separate All Deals tab, updated on November 21, is built and filled by Amazon inside eligible Stores unless a brand switches it off. It uses three named themes with up to 30 discounted products by default, and brands can switch it off or replace it with their own deals page.

Amazon states that the Brand Store Builder Agent is an AI tool that helps create and manage Brand Store pages. Amazon lists three benefits: adding new pages and editing existing pages while following brand store design guidelines, editing any generated content or layout elements to match specific needs, and chatting with the AI agent in any language while content generates in the marketplace's primary language. The page uses three names for one tool: Brand Store Builder Agent in the title, the AI agent in the steps, and the AI Assistant in the single worked example. The Support Center header above all of it now reads Amazon Ads Agent. The page sets one prerequisite: review if Amazon Brand Registry status is Approved in the Store builder.

It describes five steps: click Add page, choose one of six prewritten prompts or write your own instructions in the text bar, review the AI-generated page and request adjustments, click Save and Continue to edit in Store builder, and customize design elements and click Publish. The prompt guide, updated on October 13, 2025, sets out four best practices, each with an example. The Stores moderation guide, last updated on October 9, 2025, states that all assets in a Store go through moderation and must be in the primary language of the locale in which they are delivered. A separate page, Supported primary language per country, updated on September 2, 2025, lists one language for each of 23 countries. By PPC Land's count, English is the primary language in nine of the 23 countries, Arabic, French and Spanish in two each, and eight other languages in one each.

The table names no second language anywhere, so a Belgian Store is assessed in French, not Dutch, and a Canadian Store in English, not French. The table omits Colombia, Chile and Nigeria, which Amazon's own Product Selector guide lists among the 25 marketplaces where that Store module runs. The template page documents three ways to reach the manual templates, and it does not explain why accounts see different controls. The September 29, 2026 renaming of Amazon's advertising platform around Ads Agent was examined by PPC Land in October. The companion prompt guide carries an update date of October 13, 2025, four weeks before Amazon's unBoxed conference on November 11, 2025, where it announced Ads Agent for campaign building and extended Creative Agent to Streaming TV and Sponsored TV formats.

Neither Store page gives a launch date, a list of marketplaces where the agent is available, or a record of what changed in the November 11 update. The Create your Store guide, last updated on July 22, 2026, mentions the agent only as a tip after its template step. The agent page lists editing existing pages as a benefit but gives no steps for it, and step 5 ends at Publish while other guides end at Submit for publishing followed by a moderation review the agent page does not mention. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Travis Tritt warns fans that AI videos of him commenting on the CMA Awards are fake
stories.Summary:
Travis Tritt posted a warning on social media on the morning of November 22, 2026, after a video that claimed to show his thoughts on that week's CMA Awards went viral and drew hundreds of thousands of views. The video was made with artificial intelligence and carried a watermark disclosing that fact, though the mark was partly cut off in some of the versions that circulated online. In the fake clip, an AI-generated Tritt called the people running the CMA "idiots" for sidelining Ella Langley while celebrating Taylor Swift, who he said did not win a damn thing. The video also claimed that Ella Langley got almost no camera time, which the article calls a dead giveaway that the clip was fake, because she spent much of the show on stage accepting awards for "Choosin' Texas."

Tritt told fans that any recent videos of him supposedly commenting on the latest CMA Awards show are obviously fake and were created using AI, and he asked people to disregard them completely. The article says the fake Tritt video is not even good AI and is clearly fake, yet plenty of people in the replies still fell for it, some supporting the supposed comments and others disagreeing with them. A second AI video is also going around that claims to feature Jason Aldean sharing much the same opinion, bashing the CMA Awards and Taylor Swift, and it has been shared dozens of times and drawn nearly 100 replies from people on both sides of the debate. The article notes that the AI in both the Tritt and Aldean videos is not very good, but that as the technology advances it is getting harder to spot fake content, and people are falling for it regardless.

Tennessee is one of the few states so far that have tried to protect artists from AI-generated uses of their likeness and voice, through a law called the ELVIS Act, which stands for Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security. That law prohibits AI creators from using a person's name, image, likeness, photograph, or voice without consent, and it allows artists and others to sue creators who use their likeness or voice without permission. The article says lawmakers have been slow to respond to the rise in AI, and it calls the problem one that will no doubt get worse before it gets better. Until there are laws not only on the books but actually enforced against the people who make this fake content claiming to be from others, the article says, it is a reminder to verify anything you see online these days.

stories.Headline: IT leaders prioritize data streaming over AI to feed real-time systems, Confluent survey finds
stories.Summary:
IT leaders are now prioritizing the infrastructure that feeds artificial intelligence over the technology itself, according to a report released on November 22, 2026. This shift indicates that enterprises are focusing on data streaming platforms to ensure information moves continuously rather than remaining locked in disconnected systems. The trend suggests that organizations are becoming more realistic about the foundational work required to make advanced technology successful. The 2026 Data Streaming Report from Confluent surveyed 4,625 IT leaders across 14 countries to identify these changing strategic priorities. In Singapore, 51 percent of respondents ranked data streaming as a top priority for 2026, while only 31 percent chose AI and machine learning solutions.

Security remains the highest overall category at 96 percent, and combined data management, protection, and governance priorities reached 90 percent. Furthermore, 78 percent of leaders reported that insufficient infrastructure for real-time processing is a major challenge, an increase from 62 percent in 2025. Greg Taylor, the senior vice president and general manager for Asia Pacific at Confluent, stated that investing in data infrastructure is essentially investing in AI outcomes. He noted that 81 percent of respondents struggle with data silos and 76 percent face inconsistent data sources. Taylor suggested that framing infrastructure as a prerequisite for performance is more persuasive than treating it as a separate expense.

He emphasized that the real value of data is realized when it is used as and when it is needed. The report highlights that 97 percent of leaders believe data streaming increases the impact of AI investments. Many organizations are seeing significant returns, with 47 percent of Singaporean firms anticipating at least five times return on investment. Beyond AI, 96 percent of respondents expect benefits in customer experience and 95 percent see a reduced time to market for new services. These findings suggest that real-time data infrastructure supports broader business goals while improving the reliability of live operational decisions.

stories.Headline: NSPCC campaign addresses how under-16s are protected from and prepared for AI
stories.Summary:
The Times published a report on 22 November 2026 asking what school children hope and fear about artificial intelligence, framed around questions of cheating and deepfakes. The article describes how the question of protecting under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it is being addressed through an NSPCC campaign. Alice Thomson, writing for the paper, saw how students reacted to that campaign. The piece sets out the tension between guarding young people against harm and equipping them to work with the tools.

The report presents the issue as a choice between protection and preparation, asking how under-16s should be shielded from new technology and helped to use it at the same time. It names cheating and deepfakes as among the concerns the discussion covers. The NSPCC campaign is described as the vehicle for addressing the issue, and the article follows Thomson as she observes students responding to it. No further figures, dates or names appear in the available text.

Responsibility for the issue is placed with the NSPCC, whose campaign the article says hopes to address it, and with the wider question of how under-16s should be protected and helped. The article does not record what the students themselves said, so their views are not set out in the text available. Thomson's role is limited to seeing how the students reacted to the campaign. The paper frames the matter as one of balancing protection against preparation.

The context given is the arrival of new technology, with cheating and deepfakes cited as the specific worries in view. The article does not say what happens next, beyond the campaign's stated hope of addressing the issue. It offers no timetable, no figures and no further named individuals. More to follow.

He noted that free chatbot options became more restrictive throughout 2026, including the October 2026 move by Google to shift free Gemini app accounts to Flash-Lite. Additionally, the free sign-in options for Gemini CLI and Qwen Code were ended entirely during this period. Users can access Gemini 4 Hydrogen, released on November 12, 2026, for free through Google AI Studio without providing a credit card. GitHub Copilot Free offers 2,000 monthly inline code completions and uses Copilot Fusion to route tasks to models like GPT-6 Luna.

OpenRouter provides 11 free models as of November 22, 2026, allowing 50 free requests per day for users who skip the payment method. Eligible United States college students aged 18 or older can claim 12 months of Google AI Pro, worth 19.99 dollars monthly, if they redeem the offer by December 31, 2026. Yasir explained that while these routes work, they each have specific drawbacks that users should consider before relying on them. He warned that Google AI Studio may use prompts for training purposes, and OpenRouter models can disappear without notice as promotions end. For the student offer, he advised setting a reminder because Google will charge the monthly fee after the free year expires.

He suggested that AI Studio is best for general prompts, while Copilot Free is the strongest choice for coding tasks. The author noted that free access is now primarily found through developer tools and student promotions rather than standard chatbot applications. He mentioned that GitHub Education provides free Copilot access for verified students, though sign-ups were paused from April until June 2026. He also clarified that a previous offer for four months of free ChatGPT Plus for students ended on October 31. stories.Headline: Google blocks 41 AI crawlers from accessing Google Maps pages
stories.Summary:
Google updated its robots.txt file on google.com to block 41 AI crawlers from accessing Google Maps pages. This change occurred between November 17 and November 22, 2026, according to an analysis of archived files. The company placed these bots under a shared AI training opt-out token. Google's own AI control, Google-Extended, remains in the default group to keep Maps open.

The new rules apply to 41 named crawlers, including OpenAI's GPTBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, and ByteDance's Bytespider. These bots are now shut out of every Google Maps page on the domain. The group uses the __usage_ai-training token, which Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic committed to honor on October 30, 2026. The list includes Japanese bots Cotoyogi and SBIntuitionsBot, as well as Applebot-Extended and img2dataset.

Japanese SEO specialist Masahiro Tsuji first flagged the update in a post on X at 14:03 UTC on November 22. He initially claimed Google blocked search results and goto pages, but later revised this claim. Tsuji noted that the update makes the stance of refusing scraping clear in the robots.txt file. He expressed surprise at seeing a crawler from Japanese academic institutions on the list.

Barry Schwartz of Search Engine Roundtable replied that some of these rules were added back in July. The change affects various model builders, including Amazonbot, Meta's FacebookBot, and developers from China like DeepSeekBot and QwenBot. Other affected entities include Mistral, Cohere, the Allen Institute for AI, and the Common Crawl archive. These crawlers now lose access to business listings, directions, and contributor profiles on Maps.

The robots.txt file uses a protocol where crawlers follow the most specific user agent group that matches them. Google rewrote an internal comment to ensure new named groups are paired with either the default or AI training group. This design prevents the default group's longer allow rules from overriding the training group's single disallow for maps. Most other pages, like search results, were already off limits to every crawler.

Microsoft will begin honoring these training preferences on February 1, 2027, based on the shared token. Google plans to support the token in early 2027, though private agreements may override these rules. The draft specification states that the policy token is not a directive for crawling behavior. The articles leave open why Google split its own Gemini control from the other 41 bots.

stories.Headline: IndexBox reports edge AI drives embedded smart camera market growth to 2035
stories.Summary:
IndexBox released a report on November 22, 2026, regarding the global embedded smart cameras market. This market is entering a phase of structural expansion through 2035. Growth is fueled by the migration of artificial intelligence from cloud to edge devices. These compact modules perform inference locally to reduce latency and bandwidth. They are used in industrial automation, automotive, retail analytics, and smart infrastructure.

The market index is projected to reach 245 by 2035, with 2025 as the base of 100. A compound annual growth rate of 9.4 percent is envisioned from 2026 to 2035. Industrial automation holds a 35 percent share, while automotive and transportation hold 25 percent. Retail and commercial applications account for 20 percent of the market. These changes are supported by 5G connectivity and declining costs of vision SoCs.

IndexBox reports that the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals and disciplined procurement. They state that a more regionally diversified supply architecture is now in place. The report says competitive advantage hinges on the integrated performance of optics and vision SoCs. It notes that value is migrating toward software stacks and AI model lifecycle management. The firm claims that industrial automation will remain the largest end-use sector.

Retailers are affected by demand for people counting, heat mapping, and frictionless checkout. Healthcare and smart infrastructure users adopt embedded vision for patient monitoring and traffic management. Automotive users face long qualification cycles for driver monitoring and advanced driver-assistance systems. Privacy regulations like GDPR affect the retail sector, requiring on-device anonymization. Some regions face stringent regulations due to data privacy and security concerns.

The market uses a hardware-software co-design paradigm with fragmented demand across various segments. Design and IP are concentrated in innovation hubs, while manufacturing is in electronics regions. In September 2026, U.S. communications equipment output rose 15.2 percent year over year. Computer and electronic product manufacturing producer prices rose 12.9 percent in the same month. U.S. import prices for electrical machinery and equipment rose 3.8 percent in September 2026.

Future growth depends on the integration of NPUs into vision SoCs for complex models. The market may be tempered by semiconductor fabrication bottlenecks and a shortage of AI talent. High non-recurring engineering charges and SDK licenses will continue to impact total ownership costs. Geopolitical factors and trade policies could disrupt multi-jurisdictional supply chains. The report leaves open how competition will evolve between software capabilities and factory integration.

stories.Headline: Visa Crypto Labs lets US cardholders run up to 25 AI agents that earn OUSD for paid tasks
stories.Summary:
Cuy Sheffield, the head of Visa Crypto Labs, announced an experimental wallet upgrade on Sunday, November 22, 2026. This new system allows artificial intelligence agents to earn income rather than just spending money. The project expands upon the Visa CLI command line tool that the company first released in March. Users can now connect their agents to marketplaces like Taskmarket to perform paid work. These agents earn payments in the form of OUSD, which is a dollar stablecoin.

The pilot program is currently invite only and limited to personal Visa card holders residing in the United States. Eligible users must hold cards from US banks, as corporate and prepaid cards are not permitted. Each single account is allowed to run up to 25 agents, and every agent has its own spending limit and signing key. To verify ownership, a user provides card details and a one time code to register the agent in the Trusted Agent Protocol directory. Payouts are handled through the Bridge firm, which issues the OUSD stablecoin backed by cash and US Treasuries.

Cuy Sheffield stated that Visa Crypto Labs believes ordinary people should be able to earn income from the AI economy. Visa clarified that the card verification process is not a sanctions screening or a formal know your customer procedure. The company uses Turnkey for non custodial storage to ensure that the human owner maintains control over all funds and approvals. During an October contest on Taskmarket, ten winners earned 1 OUSD each, with the final settlement occurring in 76 minutes. This specific test involved creative tasks such as the production of 15 second video advertisements.

The system integrates several different layers, including the identity directory from Visa and the stablecoin infrastructure from a Stripe company. This setup allows agents to perform tasks like market research, gaming projects, and surveys on the Taskmarket platform. Taskmarket typically covers the network transaction costs for users and does not charge a platform fee on Tempo. Visa has not yet announced if this pilot will expand to other countries or different types of cards. The company has not provided details regarding who is liable if an agent submits plagiarized work or breaks marketplace rules.

stories.Headline: Hitachi Digital launches HARC Compose to govern agentic AI engineering
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Digital Inc. launched HARC Compose on November 18, 2026, in Santa Clara, California, according to a release dated November 22, 2026. Hitachi Digital is the global digital services company recently unveiled by Hitachi, Ltd. The product combines technology and services to govern the lifecycle of agentic engineering across complex, AI-driven systems. It does so through enterprise specific context, guardrails and intent. The release says it helps companies orchestrate AI from development to deployment through to operations and continuous improvement in a closed loop.

HARC Compose builds on Hitachi's experience and uses standardized, failure-conscious engineering. Hitachi Digital FDEs, forward deployed engineers, use it to build trustworthy AI-native applications faster and to maintain and improve AI agent performance once deployed. It strengthens Hitachi Digital's recurring service model, giving FDEs end-to-end support from ideas to outcomes. It is compatible across multi-vendor environments, and enterprises can use it entirely or opt for individual capabilities. It strengthens HMAX by Hitachi and augments HMAX Foundry solutions including HMAX Data Fabric, HMAX AI Operations, and HMAX Cyber.

Hitachi Digital is the unified brand of GlobalLogic, Inc. and Hitachi Digital Services LLC, and its legal entity is scheduled to be established on April 1, 2027. A press release on September 3, 2026 covered Hitachi expanding HMAX to accelerate deployment of Physical AI. Anand Birje, CEO and Chairman of Hitachi Digital, said HARC Compose is Hitachi Digital in action. He said the true promise of AI is not just writing code faster but shifting human ingenuity toward composing resilient, mission-critical systems. He said eliminating the divide between build and run closes the feedback loop and delivers governance and trust.

Premkumar Balasubramanian, Chief Technology Officer of Hitachi Digital, said speed is expected and trust has to be earned in an era of AI-generated software. He said customers need clarity on what a change is meant to improve, proof that it worked, and confidence in the process behind it. He said forward deployed engineers direct AI agents to build, test, and coordinate changes while maintaining strict human oversight over what goes live. He said live production evidence verifies outcomes. The release says AI has made code development faster and more productive but not necessarily trustworthy across enterprise systems.

The release says that without the right context, enterprise knowledge, company goals, policies, systems, and risk requirements, fast code becomes fast failure. HARC Compose carries enterprise intent from planning through production while keeping human experts in control of critical decisions. It includes CAKE, the Context-Aware Knowledge Engine, which connects enterprise intent, domain knowledge, systems, policies, risks, security, decision and production history and flags gaps and contradictions before agents act. An Orchestration Engine coordinates multiple agents across build, deploy and operate as one system and supports various AI agents and tools selected by customers. Failure-conscious Engineering uses failure mode and effects analysis to identify how a proposed change could fail and to decide what to test before release.

Universal capabilities include Responsible AI, which guards against system deviations such as agent drift, and guided and autonomous work that maintain human engagement. HARC Compose is built on OFE, outcome-forward engineering, a methodology used by Hitachi Digital's own FDE teams, which treats Define, Build, Deploy and Operate as one continuous system. Delivery is considered complete only when a system yields intended business outcomes in the real world, not at system release. The release lists principles including Fidelity, which establishes intent, constraints, failure risks and guardrails before work begins, and Throughput, which uses coding agents to turn clear intent into operable change. HARC Compose is available to enterprises worldwide, and deployments supported by Hitachi Digital FDEs are already underway in the finance, healthcare, and technology industries.

Hitachi Digital is a wholly owned subsidiary of Hitachi, Ltd. with approximately 35,000 professionals in 27 countries. Hitachi revenues for FY2025, ended March 31, 2026, totaled 10,586.7 billion yen, with 606 consolidated subsidiaries and approximately 290,000 employees worldwide. The release says HARC Compose capabilities are expected to expand as Hitachi Digital grows its technical talent base and ecosystem alliances. The release does not give pricing, customer names, or a general availability date beyond saying deployments are underway. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu and FamilyMart pilot causal AI to analyze purchases of decarbonized innerwear and build a demand creation model
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited announced on November 22, 2026, that it has launched a pilot study with FamilyMart Co., Ltd. to analyze consumer purchasing behavior and establish a demand creation model for decarbonized products. The study combines Fujitsu Causal AI, a core technology of the Fujitsu Kozuchi AI platform, with LLM causal technology. The initiative is part of the Model Project for Creating Demand for Decarbonized Products, a program publicly solicited by Japan's Ministry of the Environment. The two companies will focus the pilot on environmentally friendly innerwear sold by FamilyMart. The study will analyze sales data and survey results collected through FamilyMart's Famipay app to clarify how information and consumer touchpoints help customers understand a product's environmental value and lead to a purchase.

The companies will then implement in-store initiatives to verify their effectiveness and aim to establish a robust demand creation model. The insights and analytical methods gained are expected to be applied to other categories beyond apparel, including food, daily necessities, and household goods. The Ministry of the Environment's model project aims to promote investment and innovation in decarbonization and to encourage consumer selection of these products, thereby fostering market formation. The featured items are made with recycled polyester fibers that reduce CO2 emissions compared with conventional synthetic fibers, by 15% for inner T-shirts and 8% for REHEAT products. The Ministry of the Environment describes the project as one that appropriately displays the decarbonization value of products and services and develops an environment where consumers and procurement entities can understand and evaluate such value, assessing tolerance for price premiums and impacts on purchasing behavior.

LLM causal technology is described as a technology that discovers intervention points by having an LLM complement intermediate factors not present in the quantitative data, based on causal relationships estimated from the data. Fujitsu reported consolidated revenues of 3.5 trillion yen, or US$23 billion, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The companies will continue to discuss methods for effectively communicating environmental value and optimizing retail environments, and they will explore applying Fujitsu Causal AI to other product categories. By doing so, the partners aim to contribute to the creation of demand for decarbonized products and enhance customer value in the retail sector through advanced, data-driven marketing. Fujitsu states that its purpose is to make the world more sustainable by building trust in society through innovation, with 100,000 employees working to resolve challenges facing humanity.

stories.Headline: Graham Dumpleton builds Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps
stories.Summary:
Graham Dumpleton, who created mod_wsgi twenty years ago, has started a new project called Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for running Python web applications, and Simon Willison linked to it on 21st November 2026. Dumpleton has spent two decades thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web apps in production since he began mod_wsgi. Muru aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps in both development and production. As he did with an earlier project called wrapture, Dumpleton is publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the work as part of his development process.

The project is written in Rust and relies heavily on AI assistance, though Dumpleton says deciding what is not good enough yet remains his job. He credits twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi as useful experience for that judgment. He says he is prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something he would trust and something users would trust too. The articles give no release date, version number or availability details for Muru.

Dumpleton is the person responsible for the project, and his stated position is that the AI may do a lot of the work on the surface but the standard-setting stays with him. He frames the twenty years of mod_wsgi mistakes as an asset rather than a liability for judging the new server. He commits to continuing the polishing work until the server meets a bar he would trust himself. The articles do not say who else, if anyone, is involved in the project.

The context is that Muru follows the same open, detailed development write-up approach Dumpleton used for wrapture. Willison's link post appeared on 21st November 2026, and the article carries a timestamp of 22nd November 2026. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Dumpleton's stated intention to keep polishing Muru. No timeline, funding or adoption information is given.

stories.Headline: Jony Ive and Joey Flynn discuss whether taste can shield design from AI
stories.Summary:
The New York Times published a story by Jonah Weiner on Silicon Valley's fixation with "taste," which the article describes as a sense of discernment that some in the industry treat as a defense against AI-generated content. The piece features Jony Ive, the former Apple design chief, and Joey Flynn, a former OpenAI product designer, among the people discussing the topic. Techmeme linked to the Times story on November 22, 2026, under a headline naming Ive and Flynn. The article frames taste as something the industry is obsessed with and asks whether AI can learn it.

The discussion centers on whether taste can serve as a moat, meaning a lasting advantage that protects a company's work from being matched by machine-made output. The people quoted in the story include Ive and Flynn, and the article presents their views on taste as a quality that matters in product design. The piece also raises the question of whether AI systems can acquire taste, a question the article leaves open. The Times story is the source for the claims attributed to the people it names.

Ive is identified in the headline as the former design leader at Apple, and Flynn is identified as a former product designer at OpenAI. The article attributes to them and to others the view that taste is a moat against what the headline calls AI slop. The story does not, in the material available, give specific statements from Ive or Flynn beyond their participation in the discussion. Responsibility for the reporting rests with Weiner and the Times, and Techmeme credited the Times when it linked to the piece.

The context the articles provide is the industry's broader concern with AI-generated content and the value placed on human judgment in design. The story asks whether AI can learn taste, and it does not report an answer. What happens next is not described in the available material, which consists of the Techmeme link and the Times byline. stories.Headline: AI panel brief says countries can build AI capacity through varied paths beyond frontier models
stories.Summary:
The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence published a new Thematic Brief on AI Capacity-Building on November 23, 2026, examining the capabilities countries need to benefit from artificial intelligence. The brief finds that there is more than one pathway to AI capacity and that developing frontier models is not the only route available to countries. It says countries can pursue different approaches according to their needs, resources and national priorities. In health and agriculture, the brief notes, AI applications designed for specific tasks have already delivered documented benefits.

The brief states that access to AI does not in itself ensure that countries can benefit from it, because evidence shows substantial performance gaps in many underrepresented languages. It adds that in some low-resource languages safety protections can be bypassed more easily, so systems that perform well in English may not serve all populations equally. Evaluation sets developed with native speakers allow countries to assess how systems perform in their own languages and contexts. The brief also says compute, models and training numbers tell only part of the story, since expertise, relevant data, effective institutions and the capacity to evaluate and govern AI systems also determine whether countries can use AI to advance their own development objectives.

Drawing on evidence and practical examples from different regions, the brief showcases how countries are building these capabilities, from national training programmes and shared computing to locally developed language resources. The brief is intended to inform Member States and other stakeholders as they assess their own AI capacity and decide which pathways best suit their priorities. The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence is the body that issued the brief. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the brief's stated purpose of informing Member States and other stakeholders.

stories.Headline: INSEAD professor says human-centric design turns AI concerns into opportunities
stories.Summary:
Phanish Puranam, the Roland Berger Chaired Professor of Strategy and Organisation Design at INSEAD, said the impact of AI on organisations is a design problem rather than a forecasting problem, delivering a keynote address at the Indian School of Business, according to The Hindu. Drawing on research from INSEAD's Organisations and Algorithms Program, he examined four concerns about AI and the future of work and said evidence showed that thoughtful organisational design could turn them into opportunities. He called for a human-centric approach to organisational design in the age of algorithms. The address took place at the fourth edition of the ISB Insights Forum, held on November 20, which brought together researchers, business leaders, policymakers and philanthropists to explore practical solutions to economic and social challenges.

Puranam said people would remain valuable because they could be held accountable and could identify errors that machines might miss, and that organisations which test, learn and adapt could use AI to help employees build skills, collaborate and take greater ownership of their work. Karthik Balakrishnan, Deputy Dean for Faculty and Research at ISB, said the strength of a research ecosystem lies in the quality of research rather than its volume, and that this quality depends on how research is discussed. He said research is only relevant if it is rigorous enough to be acted upon, and that relevance should be judged over time rather than over the next quarter. The annual research platform discussed research across business, market and public policy.

Sessions at the forum examined the geopolitics of AI and AI and financial innovation, including access, competition and trust, looking at how cross-border technology regulations, market competition and governance were influencing enterprise strategy and financial inclusion. A session titled Business for good: Building livelihoods explored how commercial models could create stable incomes at the grassroots, while Policymaking during economic crises examined policy tools for responding to macroeconomic shocks. Another session, What helps women advance at work?, drew on survey data from women professionals in India to compare workplace and domestic career dynamics in the country with findings largely based on western workplaces. The final sessions examined operational models to maximise the population health impact of community health workers, looking at approaches to improving the reach and effectiveness of frontline healthcare delivery.

stories.Headline: Los Alamos runs three OpenAI models on Venado-GPT for three national labs
stories.Summary:
Los Alamos National Laboratory marked one year of its partnership with OpenAI, bringing three experimental models to its secure computing environment through a service called Venado-GPT. Weekly token use across three national laboratories rose 20-fold to more than 3 billion, according to the account published on Nov. 21, 2026. The service runs the three OpenAI models entirely on Venado's local graphics processing units, which are linked by the Ethernet-based HPE Slingshot interconnect. Venado entered service in 2024 and was designed for scientific workflows, and the source does not specify latency or cost per request. Staff at Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore and Sandia use the service, and researchers there have applied it to streamlining workflow handoffs between scientists and engineers.

They have also used it to automate translation of simulation models and to identify kernel and driver changes during network maintenance. Measured growth in Venado-GPT token throughput and usage began in mid-February 2026 and ended in late August 2026. The three laboratories sit within the Department of Energy's national laboratory system, and the partnership places them in a shared effort to deploy frontier AI on secure supercomputing hardware. The partnership is described as showing how frontier AI models can run inside secure, on-premises high-performance computing environments used for sensitive national security science. Its growth across the three laboratories is said to suggest broader adoption of AI tools in U.S. national laboratory research.

Secure, on-premises deployment lets sensitive research teams adopt frontier AI tools without sending data to outside cloud services, and the growth in use suggests the model may be replicated at other scientific institutions. Researchers across the three laboratories can now use the same OpenAI models for workflow tasks such as translating simulation models and tracing network changes. Year two of the partnership will bring enhancements to file attachment reading and application programming interface reliability, and planned enhancements to Venado-GPT are expected. The account extends the laboratories' longstanding role in high-performance computing into large language model use. The article includes information reported by Los Alamos Reporter.

stories.Headline: Elon Musk warns AI industry faces severe cash crunch by 2027 due to infrastructure delays
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk warned that the artificial intelligence industry could face a severe cash crunch in 2027 on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The xAI chief executive posted his concerns on the social media platform X regarding the race to expand computing capacity. He stated that delays in getting data centres operational could leave companies scrambling for hundreds of billions of dollars in capital. This financial challenge arises because companies must pay for infrastructure before those facilities can reliably serve customers and generate income. Musk believes that even a few months of cumulative industry delays would create a massive need for additional working capital.

The crisis involves spending on chips, servers, data centres, cooling systems, and electricity in places like the United States and Canada. IDC reported global AI infrastructure spending reached 121.4 billion dollars in the second quarter of 2026, a 53 percent increase. IDC raised its full year 2026 forecast to 521 billion dollars, while five major tech companies spent 400 billion in 2025. US and Canadian net new data centre IT capacity is projected to rise from 8 gigawatts in 2026 to 20 gigawatts. The IEA estimates global data centre electricity consumption could rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030.

Elon Musk is responsible for these warnings and said that getting this amount of compute turned on and cooled is hard. He asked where the money will come from if companies need hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital. He noted that the cash shortage is going to be nuts next year due to the difficulty of reliable operations. Musk responded to a user who argued that AI stocks remained undervalued despite the rising costs of various key components. He highlighted a problem with the economics of the boom, specifically the gap between massive spending and actual revenue generation.

Other users argued that inference is becoming increasingly profitable and that demand for AI research and model development is growing. Companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are affected as they spend massive sums to secure compute for chatbots and tools. Investors are also affected, as some speculate the AI bubble popped after the S&P 500 and Dow entered correction. Financial regulators in Taiwan responded to market volatility by limiting short selling, similar to actions taken during the 2008 housing crisis. Data centre operators are also at risk if their multibillion-dollar investments fail to generate the anticipated revenue from customers.

The IEA noted that the capacity of specialised AI data centres had more than tripled over the previous 18 months of expansion. S&P Global reported in November 20 that power shortages, grid connection delays, and local community opposition are complicating data centre expansion. The industry faces obstacles in securing electricity, connecting facilities to power grids, and obtaining necessary approvals from various local government authorities. Some investors appear bearish on chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits, suggesting that data centre construction faces serious headwinds. Recent setbacks include a blue midterm wave and backlash from the communities where these large data centres are being built.

Intercontinental Exchange launched a tool on November 17 to assess the risk of US data centre projects being delayed or halted. This tool considers local economic conditions, permitting records, and the costs of water and electricity to evaluate potential project risks. The articles leave open whether companies can secure the hundreds of billions of dollars in working capital that Musk says they need. It remains unclear if the industry can overcome the electricity shortages and grid connection delays mentioned by the S&P Global report. The reports do not state if the projected capacity increases for 2027 will be achieved despite these significant financial hurdles.
