stories.Headline: Meghan Markle's As Ever brand promotes holiday sale with an AI-generated image
stories.Summary:
Meghan Markle's lifestyle brand As Ever drew scrutiny after a holiday sale promotion reportedly used an AI-generated image, according to the Daily Mail. The image was shared on the brand's Instagram account on Thursday, November 19. It advertised the brand's holiday sale with the words "As Ever Holiday Sale: 25% off sitewide." The graphic reportedly contained SynthID, a digital watermark developed by Google to identify AI-generated content. The outlet claimed the graphic was created or edited using technology developed by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

The promotion also included a separate photograph of the Duchess wearing cream-colored clothes beside a Christmas-decorated fireplace. The brand announced a 25% reduction across its website, but the Daily Mail reported that its $148 Holiday Advent Calendar was excluded. The limited-edition product contains 24 chocolates produced with Los Angeles chocolatier Compartés. It features a sketch of the California mansion where Meghan and Harry have lived, along with countdown numbers based on the Duchess's handwriting. Other products, including the brand's fruit spreads and gift baskets, were included in the holiday promotion.

The discovery does not establish who created the graphic or whether the Duchess personally used AI. Meghan previously said on Bloomberg's The Circuit with Emily Chang in August 2025, "Aren't you a little bit scared for, by AI?" She said someone had recently introduced her to ChatGPT, which she had not previously experienced. She admitted, "I'm a little bit vintage in many ways," and said she prefers handwritten notes and traditional ways of communicating. She also revealed that Siri was not enabled on her phone and that she did not use location services.

In August 2026, Meghan and Harry publicly criticized technology companies over the dangers of AI-generated sexual images. In a statement on their official website, the Sussexes supported efforts to stop AI tools from creating nonconsensual intimate images, especially those involving women and children. They criticized companies that challenged stronger safeguards and asked, "Can AI make our world better while it enables the worst in humans?" The statement argued that technology companies were investing enormous sums in artificial intelligence while resisting measures to protect vulnerable users. During his September 2026 appearance at the Clinton Global Initiative in New York, Harry warned that AI companion applications could pose a greater threat to young people than conventional social media.

According to remarks published on the Sussexes' official website, Harry described AI companion apps as the "ultimate sycophant." He warned, "It doesn't just want your attention, it wants your attachment." He expressed concern that children could confide in artificial intelligence instead of developing relationships with real people. The Duke also called for greater accountability from technology companies, arguing that rapid AI development should not come at the expense of public safety. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Atlassian's Sherif Mansour says PMs should steer AI work rather than code
stories.Summary:
Sherif Mansour, who leads AI and product craft at Atlassian and has spent 17 years at the company according to The Futurist account of the conversation, told Lenny's Podcast that the product manager job did not disappear when AI coding arrived but narrowed to direction. He said an early experiment that turned PMs and designers into full-time AI builders fell apart after a month, and that throughput was not the problem because direction was. That failed experiment is why Mansour argues PMs own decision making velocity rather than the decisions themselves, and why the best PMs build a shared brain, a common understanding of customer, product and business context that lets engineers and designers act without waiting for a spec. He names three contexts to fill, customer context, product and market context, and the business you operate in, and said trust breaks once a group grows past 20 or 30 people unless someone maintains that shared base. The workflow change he describes is concrete, since Mansour said he tries never to do a customer interview without engineers in the room.

He cited PMs who send every engineer to test AI tools and report back, plus engineers staffing booths with him at customer events. He pointed to a 2010 Confluence interview where customers used red and green stars to mark unfinished work, and said an engineer in the room proposed the checkbox in the page, an idea he said did not exist on the web at the time. Hiring is where he gets prescriptive, and Mansour uses a triangle credited to Geoff Redfern with general manager, scientist and artist as the three corners describing how a PM naturally does discovery, from TAM and revenue math to hypothesis testing to vision-led taste. He said few people do all three well, so leaders should stop throwing PM bodies at a problem and match the archetype to the work, with all-rounders reserved for zero-to-one teams. He admitted the model is aimed at medium to large organizations rather than startups, and he joked that he is a strong artist and a terrible general manager.

Mansour said on Lenny's Podcast that the idea you no longer need to hire juniors is a misconception, in part because they bring new working norms. His example was his 12-year-old son, who he said went straight to vibe coding games without learning syntax and treats that as normal. The article closes by telling teams to watch for groups that hire for a spike, state the weakness plainly, and pair opposites, as Mansour said he does with his colleague Jamille, rather than asking every PM to ship code. The piece was written by the StartupHub.ai staff and reviewed by editor Daniel Singer, and it draws on Lenny's Podcast as its source.

stories.Headline: Analysts see over 100% upside for Ciena, Tower Semiconductor and Lumentum after steep AI stock declines
stories.Summary:
The AI boom has rewarded early investors handsomely, but the opportunity now looks considerably less straightforward, according to an article by Faheem Tahir published on Yahoo Finance on Sunday, November 22, 2026. After months of enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence, investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending behind the technology can generate adequate returns. According to Reuters on November 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had lost nearly 30% since early October, even as estimates for major technology companies' capital expenditure remained largely unchanged. Barclays strategists noted that hyperscaler spending forecasts for next year had yet to be revised downward, suggesting that the market's retreat has outpaced changes in investment expectations. Rising financing costs, regulatory uncertainty, and potential restrictions on data center construction have complicated the outlook.

The article screened U.S.-listed companies with exposure to AI through chips, cloud computing, software, or supporting infrastructure, using data as of November 20, 2026. It selected stocks that had declined by at least 25% over the preceding month and offered at least 50% upside to their median analyst price targets. The final ten are presented in ascending order of analyst upside potential, and the top five are presented in the article. Hedge fund interest was considered as of the third quarter of 2026, using Insider Monkey's hedge fund database, which tracked 994 hedge funds during the quarter. Ciena Corporation had a 27.95% one-month decline and 104.30% upside potential, with 83 hedge fund holders.

Reuters reported on November 18 that 83% of analyst ratings on key AI stocks were Strong Buy recommendations, despite mounting concerns over profitability and debt. Bank of America's November fund manager survey revealed that nearly 40% of respondents believed companies were overinvesting, while more than half anticipated at least one hyperscaler cutting capital expenditure within six months. On November 16, TD Cowen retained its Buy rating on Ciena while reducing its target to $375 from $400, arguing that strong demand made substantial near-term earnings estimate cuts difficult to justify. On November 3, Craig-Hallum maintained its Buy rating on Tower Semiconductor while cutting its target to $250 from $325, highlighting strong photonics demand and capacity expansion running ahead of schedule. UBS maintained Neutral on Lumentum on November 10, noting accelerating optical demand but identifying the acquisition as the principal near-term share-price driver.

Tower Semiconductor shares fell 39.38% over the past month, while the median analyst price target implied 111.30% upside as of November 20, and it had 49 hedge fund holders. Lumentum Holdings had a 40.75% monthly decline, with its median analyst target implying 111.60% upside, and 122 hedge fund holders. Marvell Technology had a 45.29% monthly decline, with 118.80% upside to its median analyst target, and 108 hedge fund holders. Sandisk Corporation had a 49.87% monthly decline, with 164.80% upside to its median analyst target, and 122 hedge fund holders. On November 11, Evercore maintained Outperform on Sandisk, arguing that supply discipline and long-term customer agreements could make earnings more predictable.

Ciena's fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 37% to $1.67 billion, while adjusted operating margin reached 22.5%, compared with 10.7% a year earlier, and management expected fiscal year-end backlog to exceed $10 billion. Tower Semiconductor generated approximately $240 million in silicon photonics revenue during the third quarter, nearly half its total, overall revenue increased 33% to $526 million, net income reached $120 million, and fourth-quarter revenue guidance was $600 million. Lumentum reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $1.26 billion and a 42.3% adjusted operating margin, and management secured purchase commitments exceeding $5 billion for a second major win in optics positioned near or alongside chips. Marvell generated $2.17 billion in fiscal second-quarter data-center revenue, up 46% year-over-year, and in November preliminary third-quarter revenue remained consistent with its earlier guidance. Sandisk reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $11.03 billion, up 23% sequentially, and data-center revenue increased 61% sequentially to approximately $4.8 billion.

Under the proposed transaction, Lumentum shareholders would receive 4.5 Marvell shares per share owned, and completion remains subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, with expected completion in the first half of 2028. Ciena's Hyper-Rail optical platform, designed to support distributed AI training, should begin contributing meaningful revenue during fiscal 2027, and Ciena trades at approximately 22.1 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, with consensus anticipating roughly 66% EPS growth. Tower Semiconductor trades at approximately 18.2 times estimated 2027 earnings, against projected EPS growth of roughly 72%, and has approximately $1.47 billion in cash against $154 million in debt. Lumentum trades at approximately 21.5 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, and short interest stood at 8.97% of float on October 30, before the deal announcement. Marvell trades at approximately 32.8 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings and 18.8 times fiscal 2028 earnings, and Stifel retained Buy on November 20 while reducing its target to $280 from $370.

Management expected silicon photonics manufacturing capacity at year-end to approximately double the level supporting third-quarter shipments, and Lumentum's next-quarter revenue guidance was $1.575, $1.625 billion. Management attributed roughly 60% of Sandisk's total sequential revenue growth to volume and 40% to pricing, indicating that the expansion was not solely a pricing story. The article states that the announced $1,132 equivalent for Lumentum is not a guaranteed cash payout, and that the consideration fluctuates with Marvell's stock. The article leaves open which companies' growth prospects remain intact and which valuations have further to fall, and it notes that additional production capacity takes time to become recognized revenue. The article also leaves open how the proposed Lumentum acquisition will affect customer conflicts and regulatory uncertainty for Marvell.

stories.Headline: Army works with OpenAI to automate software accreditation for vendors
stories.Summary:
The Army is collaborating with OpenAI to streamline the accreditation process for commercial software vendors seeking to provide products to the military, according to a report by DefenseScoop. The initiative, known as Project Gatekeeper, aims to automate the authority to operate process, which historically takes months to complete. By allowing vendors to submit code to an Army development, security and operations platform for rapid validation, the service intends to lower barriers for industry partners. Acting Army Chief Information Officer Gabe Chiulli stated that the project provides an initial vetting process, granting successful applicants access to secure Army enclaves. The Army plans to integrate artificial intelligence models into this pipeline within the next quarter, starting with a phased approach using OpenAI tools.

This strategy focuses on strategic validation to avoid redundant checks, according to the report. Future phases will likely incorporate additional open source and commercial providers beyond the initial OpenAI tools. To maintain security and privacy, the Army will encourage companies to utilize their own application programming interface keys during the scanning process. This approach ensures that vendors retain control over their vulnerability logs while benefiting from the automated vetting system. Chiulli said the project offers an initial vetting process that gives successful applicants access to secure Army enclaves, and officials are also working to expand access to the platform beyond current Common Access Card holders by integrating Login.gov.

The service intends to lower barriers for industry partners through the rapid validation of submitted code. The phased approach using OpenAI tools is meant to focus on strategic validation and avoid redundant checks. Vendors keep control of their vulnerability logs by using their own application programming interface keys during scanning. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ireland's Data Protection Commission blocks or delays nine AI launches over five years
stories.Summary:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission published a report on September 25, 2026, regarding its reviews of artificial intelligence. The regulator examined roughly 180 AI products and services between 2021 and 2025. Most of these reviews occurred before the products reached users in Europe. Nine of these launches were delayed or cancelled because of interventions by the regulator. These reviews were conducted by the Technology Multinational Supervision Unit.

The report, titled Responsible Artificial Intelligence Innovation, covers companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, TikTok, and X. It includes other firms like Airbnb, Apple, Deepseek, LinkedIn, and Pinterest. The DPC noted that 59 percent of AI products launched in 2024 and 2025 received recommendations. Transparency problems appeared in 72 percent of those recommendations. The regulator requires a minimum lead time of 8 weeks for substantive engagement.

The Technology Multinational Supervision Unit is responsible for engaging with large multinational tech companies based in Ireland. This unit operates separately from other regulatory functions like complaints or inquiries. The DPC stated that this voluntary process acts as a quasi-regulatory sandbox. The regulator noted that recommendations are non-binding in nature. However, the DPC may use other regulatory powers if redline issues are not addressed.

The report affects large platforms that sell advertising in Europe because the DPC is their lead regulator. Some companies, such as X, refused to stop training AI models when requested. The DPC applied to the Irish High Court on August 8, 2024, regarding X. Eurostat data shows 52.7 percent of EU firms avoiding AI due to privacy concerns. AI use among EU enterprises rose from 13.5 percent to 20 percent in 2025.

Generative AI drove most growth, accounting for 79 percent of all engagements. The DPC counted 25 generative AI engagements in 2023, 36 in 2024, and 82 in 2025. Non-generative AI engagements totaled 37 over the whole period. AI engagements with large technology controllers grew tenfold from 2021 to 2025. This activity included technologies like facial recognition, age assurance, and large language models.

The DPC now says training AI on private messages faces a very difficult legal threshold. The regulator believes training new AI models will likely require a Data Protection Impact Assessment. Future monitoring will include how mitigations, such as objection forms, work in practice. The report does not name most companies involved in the specific case studies. It remains open whether companies can justify training AI on private messages under legitimate interests.

stories.Headline: Civil Guard arrests four for using AI to spread jihadist content and radicalize youth
stories.Summary:
The Civil Guard has arrested four people in three provinces and in the autonomous city of Melilla for spreading jihadist content on social networks with the aim of indoctrinating people in terrorism, in an investigation that also detected the use of artificial intelligence to improve radicalization processes. In a first action, officers arrested three people in San Sebastián in Guipúzcoa, Vilanova i la Geltrú in Barcelona and Fuengirola in Málaga, after confirming that they had become radicalized over recent years, especially because of greater access to terrorist propaganda spread on the internet. A parallel operation in Melilla led to the arrest of a young man for his active work in spreading jihadist ideology, and he is attributed with large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially content used by young people. The detainees also recorded videos in which they expressed their jihadist affiliation and displayed bladed weapons, according to material seized during the investigation.

Among the analyzed materials are content related to Daesh and Hamas, used with the aim of indoctrinating for terrorist purposes, and the investigation has also located material that justifies violence and the carrying out of attacks. The Civil Guard considers this terrorist propaganda material to be of special danger because of the intrinsic risk of fostering jihadist radicalization, especially among a young and vulnerable group. The operations were carried out with the cooperation of the National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States, within an investigation focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for the recruitment and radicalization of users on social networks. The report was published on November 22, 2026, and the arrests were made in San Sebastián, Vilanova i la Geltrú, Fuengirola and Melilla.

The General Directorate of the Civil Guard provided the information on the analyzed materials, and the force described the propaganda as especially dangerous because it can foster radicalization among young and vulnerable people. The investigation attributes to the Melilla detainee large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially material used by young people, and the seized material shows that the detainees recorded videos expressing their jihadist affiliation and displaying bladed weapons. The National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States cooperated in the operations, which focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for recruitment and radicalization. The articles do not say what charges the four detainees face or what happens to them next.

stories.Headline: Review finds only two of fourteen tuberculosis studies directly integrate GIS with AI modelling
stories.Summary:
A systematic literature review published by Nur Adibah Mohidem and Sharifah Norkhadijah Syed Ismail in the International Journal of Health Geographics found that only two of fourteen eligible studies directly embedded spatial structures within artificial intelligence modelling frameworks for tuberculosis research. The authors searched Scopus, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and Taylor & Francis for literature published up to July 7, 2025, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. After systematic screening, eligibility checks, and quality appraisal using the MI-CLAIM framework, fourteen primary studies met all criteria for final analysis. The review examined how geographic information systems and artificial intelligence currently converge in tuberculosis research, a field marked by persistent spatial heterogeneity in incidence, mortality, and healthcare access.

Most of the included studies concentrated on tuberculosis incidence and case counts, while others examined diagnostic procedures, medical treatment, mortality patterns, community-based public health applications, and the geographic distribution of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains. Researchers used geographic information systems for spatial mapping, spatial autocorrelation, hotspot analysis, spatial clustering, spatial regression, general spatial modelling, and spatial accessibility assessments including network analysis of healthcare access. The artificial intelligence methods spanned neural networks, deep learning architectures, tree-based and ensemble machine learning, kernel-based machine learning, Bayesian modelling, time-series and regression-based frameworks, and explainable artificial intelligence. However, twelve of the fourteen studies applied the two approaches independently, in parallel, or through sequential pipelines rather than integrating them into unified structures.

The authors concluded that combining geographic information systems and artificial intelligence in tuberculosis investigations is an emerging field with limited technical integration. They said future research must prioritize standardized spatially incorporated artificial intelligence frameworks to translate analytical outputs into operational real-time disease surveillance. The review emphasizes the need for high-resolution geocoded data, spatially sensitive validation protocols, and emerging concepts such as GeoAI, digital twins, explainable artificial intelligence, and tailored implementation strategies. The article was published on November 22, 2026, with a DOI of 10.1186/s12942-026-00506-1.

stories.Headline: GE Vernova's Ateret says AI can handle seven of ten software vulnerability types
stories.Summary:
Suspected Iran-linked hackers forced a small British power generator offline for four days in July, according to Ynetnews. Around the same time, water treatment and supply systems across at least 12 U.S. states were targeted in a wave of cyberattacks. British authorities said the attack affected only a small generator and posed no threat to the country's wider electricity supply. The incidents showed attackers increasingly targeting physical infrastructure, not merely stealing information or disrupting websites. Lior Ateret heads global cybersecurity research and GE Vernova's cybersecurity center in Israel.

Ateret leads a team of dozens of researchers, software developers and ethical hackers from GE Vernova's offices in Ramat Gan, near Tel Aviv. GE Vernova says its equipment helps generate approximately 25% of the world's electricity. Ateret told Yenergya that products do not go live without passing through Israel, whether power plants or distribution systems. GE Vernova was spun off as an independent publicly traded company in April 2024. Its order backlog reached approximately $197 billion in its latest quarterly report.

Ateret said there is not a moment when someone isn't attacking power plants, and that nothing is 100% secure. He said the standard in Israel is very high and the situation is definitely above average in terms of protection. He said attacking one power station might generate publicity, but countries are built to deal with that and the system balances itself within minutes. He said what is truly frightening is a sophisticated attack by a major power against many stations simultaneously. He said AI is replacing the hacker, not completely, but it can perform tasks that previously required a human.

Ateret said an AI model given access to software code can handle approximately seven of the 10 traditional categories of software vulnerabilities. He said results that would take a human hacker a week can be achieved in just a few hours. He warned the technology can transform one person into an entire army of hackers. He said no operational technology system is managed by AI, describing them as deterministic real-time systems. He said the red button that stops electricity generation isn't in AI's hands.

Ateret began in Jerusalem, where as a high school student he enrolled in a gifted students' program at the Hebrew University. After earning his bachelor's degree through an academic program linked to military service, he joined the Israel Defense Forces' Communications and Cyber Defense Directorate. He began testing military systems in the evenings, and the initiative developed into the IDF General Staff's red team, which he established and led. His work earned him recognition from the head of the Shin Bet. In 2012, Ateret left the military with the rank of major and received an approach from General Electric the same day.

Ateret attributes Israel's relative strength to centralized cybersecurity monitoring by a security operations center in Be'er Sheva, jointly operated by Israel's National Cyber Directorate and Energy Ministry. He also cites strict regulation and one-way communication technology, sometimes called a data diode, some supplied by Israeli company Waterfall Security using fiber-optic technology. He said in most recent incidents controllers were connected directly to the internet, and that is how the attack was carried out. GE Vernova's gas turbines are used in converting the Orot Rabin power station in Hadera from coal to natural gas. GE Vernova is also involved at the Eshkol and Alon Tavor power stations, the Tzafit private power facility and the Kochav Hayarden pumped-storage project.

stories.Headline: Researchers teach a 12,000-pound John Deere loader to balance and spin autonomously
stories.Summary:
Researchers affiliated with ETH Zurich, Blue River Technology, Gravis Robotics and Intel used reinforcement learning and computer simulation to teach a John Deere skid-steer loader to perform autonomous acrobatic manoeuvres. The machine is a 12,000-pound John Deere 332G skid-steer loader, an industrial machine designed primarily for moving materials and performing construction work. The team trained it to lift itself onto two wheels, maintain balance, navigate uneven surfaces and execute controlled spins without assistance. The training relied on reinforcement learning, a machine learning approach in which an artificial agent improves its decisions through rewards and penalties.

They first trained the control system inside a simulated environment before transferring its learned instructions to the physical construction machine. The work changes how such a machine is controlled, because the researchers developed an artificial intelligence system that learned suitable movements through repeated training and feedback instead of relying on conventional programming. The loader can spin while maintaining balance on uneven terrain, and it now balances on two wheels without an operator. The researchers trained the construction machine in simulation before real-world demonstrations, and the machine learned movements normally associated with stunt driving rather than human operators.

The demonstrations showed the machine lifting itself onto two wheels, holding its balance and executing controlled spins on its own. The researchers affiliated with ETH Zurich, Blue River Technology, Gravis Robotics and Intel are responsible for the work, and the articles do not give further statements from them beyond describing the training method and the demonstrations. The articles describe the machine as a John Deere 332G skid-steer loader and say the researchers taught it using reinforcement learning and computer simulation. They report that the control system was trained in a simulated environment first, with the learned instructions then transferred to the physical machine.

The articles do not name individual researchers or quote any of them directly. The context is that the machine is an industrial loader built for moving materials and construction work, and the researchers taught it movements previously associated with highly skilled human operators. The articles say the training happened in simulation before real-world demonstrations, and they describe the resulting abilities as autonomous acrobatic manoeuvres. The articles do not say what happens next, whether the system will be deployed commercially, or when further demonstrations might take place.

stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge publishes a purported AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
stories.Summary:
On November 20, Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge published on his website a purported proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem unsolved since Bernhard Riemann formulated it in 1859, according to The Wall Street Journal. Alpöge said he reached the key result late in the evening of November 15 after several months of collaboration with the artificial intelligence Claude, and he contacted company chief Dario Amodei to coordinate the publication. He announced the discovery the day after Anthropic's stock market debut. He presented the proof as software code in the Lean programming language, which lets a computer verify the logical correctness of mathematical reasoning step by step. Alpöge himself admits the proof rests on a vast amount of complex mathematics that he is still working to fully understand, and that an attempt to generate a standard text version with AI produced an almost unreadable document of over 250,000 pages.

The Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers, those divisible without a remainder only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. Mathematicians have long known roughly how the number of primes changes among increasingly large natural numbers, but describing deviations from this pattern with precision is far more difficult, and the hypothesis concerns the properties of a special mathematical function. If proven, it would significantly refine such calculations and confirm a number of other mathematical statements. In 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute included it among its seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a one-million-dollar reward. Under the Clay Institute's rules, to claim the prize a solution must be published and achieve widespread acceptance within the scientific community no sooner than two years after publication.

Alpöge plans to prepare a more accessible explanation of his work. His claim has yet to be verified by independent mathematicians, and even if a computer confirms the logical validity of the proof, it is still necessary to ensure that it genuinely solves the problem posed. The announcement came amid rapid progress in artificial intelligence within mathematics: in September OpenAI reported an alleged solution to another Millennium Prize Problem, the Navier, Stokes problem concerning the motion of fluids and gases, and in October the company presented hundreds of new mathematical proofs, among them findings from research into the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a relaxed version of the famous problem. Terence Tao, a recipient of the Fields Medal, hailed the progress in this direction as the most significant in the last 50 years, while suggesting that humans working alongside artificial intelligence might only manage to find a complete proof of the Riemann hypothesis by 2050.

stories.Headline: Northwestern opens undergraduate AI major with 28 students declared
stories.Summary:
In spring 2022, McCormick Prof. Sara Owsley Sood began noticing that employers hiring computer science majors struggled to find people with the specific skills they needed. Companies have begun seeking students with knowledge of AI technologies as artificial intelligence has risen, signaling a need to distinguish the subject from concentrations under the computer science major. According to McCormick Prof. Samir Khuller, the Peter and Adrienne Barris Chair of Computer Science, Northwestern began creating a new undergraduate AI major in spring 2023. The major opened for enrollment in the McCormick School of Engineering and the Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences this fall. Khuller said students and professors are happy with its results so far.

Students pursuing the AI major as a primary major in McCormick, a second major in McCormick or a second major outside McCormick must all take courses in specific areas of study. “Breadth” courses require students to explore topics in AI such as symbolic AI and theoretical foundations, Sood said. Technical electives focus on the foundations of programming and computer science, and Sood said they ensure students can pivot into software engineering if they choose. Students must also take one societal impact course, which engages them in discussions about the effects of AI and the tools they create. Sood said 28 students have declared a major in AI so far, including 20 McCormick and non-McCormick students taking it as a second major.

Sood, the program’s director of undergraduate studies, said “It’s going well” and “This is a long time coming.” She said the number of declarations surprised her, especially given the program’s heavy course load, and that students feel the need to augment their studies with deeper knowledge in AI. Khuller said allowing AI as a secondary major makes the program more accessible to students in other fields. Sood said breadth requirements give students a broader understanding beyond generative AI, and that ethics are “not as an afterthought” in design. She said it is important for people building these systems to have a strong ethical framework to evaluate them.

Khuller said the interaction between AI systems and people is vital when looking at societal effects, and he wants students to think about the impact on different people. Weinberg sophomore Charlotte Morton said the AI program pairs well with her primary major in cognitive science, and that understanding human cognition helps her understand how AI models reason and use logic. Morton said she hopes the program will require more ethics courses, since of the 22 major-specific units required for primary or secondary majors and the 19 units for non-McCormick second majors, students need only one societal impact course. McCormick Prof. Kristian Hammond said programs like ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini are “damaging” because they decrease cognitive skills instead of enhancing them. Hammond said the major helps students develop systems that augment what humans do well rather than replace them.

Northwestern launched its Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence in fall 2018, and Kellogg School of Management and McCormick launched their MBAi program in fall 2021 to integrate AI into business. McCormick launched the undergraduate AI minor in fall 2024. Before the curriculum was announced, Sood said she saw confusion from people who thought the major would teach students to use AI rather than create it. Hammond said he could make his teachings accessible to thousands with AI, and that he encourages students to explore AI’s positive impacts rather than run from it. Morton said the most important thing will be integrating AI into companies and professions ethically, in a way that assists humans and genuinely adds to society.

Sood said she hopes the program takes students beyond generative AI models and explores areas supporting a longer career in AI, and that students have broad knowledge in AI, “Not just the thing that’s hot right now.” Hammond said the world is changing and “we have to help direct it,” and that students can build systems that expand their impact to a larger audience. Morton said increasing the number of societal impact courses required will help students understand AI’s potential positive and negative impacts. Faculty of the undergraduate AI major remain hopeful that students will use AI systems to be leaders within their communities. The articles do not say what the program will require next or when any changes will be decided.

stories.Headline: Machine learning and pharmacology screen finds five approved drugs targeting endometrial infertility subtypes
stories.Summary:
A computational framework combining machine learning and systems pharmacology has identified five approved medications capable of targeting distinct molecular abnormalities underlying non-timing endometrial infertility, according to findings published in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology. The work was reported on November 23, 2026, in an article whose authors include Parraga-Leo, Sebastian-Leon, Sanchez-Reyes, Sanz, Vidal, Sanchez-Ribas, Quiñonero, Wells, Pellicer, Sirota and Diaz-Gimeno. The condition is described as an idiopathic form of endometrial failure that impairs reproductive success during assisted reproduction regardless of embryo quality. The findings offer a targeted strategy to address this non-timing endometrial failure, the article states.

Investigators conducted a multicentre prospective study evaluating 192 endometrial biopsies collected during the mid-secretory phase from female patients undergoing in vitro fertilization. The research team applied machine learning algorithms to transcriptomic data and clinical outcomes to categorize tissue specimens into distinct good-prognosis and poor-prognosis endotypes, which were then partitioned into discrete molecular subendotypes based on shared gene expression alterations and reproductive trajectories. The poor-prognosis endotype, comprising 43 patients, showed a pregnancy rate of 26.3 percent compared to 66.0 percent in the good-prognosis cohort, with a statistically significant difference evaluated at p = 1.99 × 10⁻⁵. Live birth rates were likewise depressed among poor-prognosis patients at 40.0 percent compared to 87.1 percent in good-prognosis controls, at p = 0.0013. The poor-prognosis group also experienced elevated biochemical miscarriage rates of 30.3 percent versus 7.2 percent, at p = 0.0372, alongside heightened clinical miscarriage rates of 42.9 percent versus 6.2 percent, at p = 0.0159.

Deeper algorithmic partitioning divided the poor-prognosis cohort into two distinct molecular subendotypes distinguished by different failure modes and underlying cellular pathology. The first subendotype, encompassing 16 patients, was characterized by an increased biochemical miscarriage rate of 66.7 percent compared to 14.3 percent observed in the alternative poor-prognosis group, at p = 0.0022. The second subendotype, comprising 27 patients, was associated with an elevated clinical miscarriage rate of 50.0 percent compared to 0.0 percent in the first group, at p = 0.0001. In addition to impaired decidualization, the biochemical miscarriage subendotype displayed prominent immune dysregulation, identifying local immune pathway disturbances as a primary biological mechanism contributing to early embryonic loss.

To establish therapeutic countermeasures against these identified transcriptomic dysfunctions, the authors deployed systems pharmacology approaches to evaluate approved pharmaceuticals capable of inverting the abnormal molecular signatures. This in silico screening prioritized five approved compounds possessing target profiles aligned with the dysregulated subendotypes: genistein, pioglitazone, alprostadil, flunisolide and tenoxicam. The therapeutic potential of the computationally selected drugs was subsequently validated through functional biological assays in human endometrial stromal cell lines using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, F-actin cellular staining and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Concurrently, alprostadil, flunisolide and tenoxicam demonstrated clear anti-inflammatory properties by inhibiting well-established biomarkers of endometrial immune response. Although these laboratory observations confirm that repurposed compounds can modulate specific cellular pathways in human endometrial cells, the authors emphasized that formal clinical trials in patient cohorts remain necessary to validate therapeutic efficacy and advance these personalized interventions into routine reproductive medicine.

Articles.Title: Machine Learning Identifies Potential Drug Candidates for Non-Timing Endometrial Infertility

stories.Headline: AI disagreement makes a simulated doctor seem lazier and raises patient uncertainty, study finds
stories.Summary:
In an online experiment, participants interacted with an LLM-simulated doctor called “Dr. Alex” during a stress-management therapy session, and the study was reported by 2 Minute Medicine on November 22, 2026. The research team developed an LLM-powered chatbot to simulate a human doctor providing mental health support, and participants were unaware that the provider was actually AI. At the end of the consultation, Dr. Alex offered to consult an AI assistant for a second opinion and indicated whether the AI agreed or disagreed with the initial recommendation. The experiment found that AI disagreement increased perceived doctor laziness and medical uncertainty, while AI agreement enhanced perceived recommendation credibility. The study was published in the International Journal of Human-Computer Studies in June 2026, volume 213, article 103824, with an Epub date of April 21, 2026.

A total of 135 participants completed a three-step process: filling out a pre-questionnaire, participating with Dr. Alex for a mental health consultation, and filling out a post-questionnaire. The pre-questionnaire focused on demographics and control variables, while the post-questionnaire assessed “perceived recommendation credibility”, “perceived doctor laziness”, and “perceived medical uncertainty”, each gauged on a 7-point scale. Participants were also asked to indicate their perceptions of the provider’s level of anthropomorphism by assessing the provider on four sets of adjectives: artificial/natural, synthetic/real, inanimate/living, and machinelike/humanlike. The results showed that disagreement with CareBot increased perceived doctor laziness, which was then associated with lower cognitive, affective, and behavioral trust in the doctor. Disagreement with CareBot also led to increased perceived medical uncertainty, while agreement with CareBot’s recommendations led to increased perceived credibility of the provider.

The research team developed the AI chatbot that served as a proxy for a human provider, and the participants were unaware that Dr. Alex was actually AI. The study authors are Chen C, Sun Y, Liao M, and Sundar SS, and the work was cited as “When AI Disagrees: The Effect of Second Opinion on Patients' Trust in Doctors”. The article was written by Christian Shannon, MD, MSc, MPAff and Marc Succi, MD for 2 Minute Medicine. The study received an Evidence Rating Level of 3, described as Average. The researchers had participants interact with Dr. Alex during a stress-management therapy session, and Dr. Alex offered to consult an AI assistant for a second opinion at the end of the consultation.

When participants perceived Dr. Alex as more human-like, AI disagreement increased perceived medical uncertainty and doctor laziness, while AI agreement enhanced perceived recommendation credibility. All of these results were stronger among participants who perceived Dr. Alex as more human-like. The article notes that the study was novel and used a large language model-powered chatbot developed by the research team. The relevant reading cited was “Who is Trusted for a Second Opinion?

Comparing Collective Advice from a Medical AI and Physicians in Biopsy Decisions After Mammography Screening”. The article was tagged under AI disagrees, doctors, and physician trust. The study was published in the International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, with the citation Chen C, Sun Y, Liao M, Sundar SS, Int J Hum Comput Stud, 2026 Jun;213:103824, doi: 10.1016/j.ijhcs.2026.103824, Epub 2026 Apr 21. The article is copyrighted by 2 Minute Medicine, Inc. in 2026, and the content is for informational and educational purposes only.

The article states it is not medical advice and does not replace the judgment of a qualified healthcare professional. The image was credited to 2 Minute Medicine. The article was reported by Christian Shannon, MD, MSc, MPAff and Marc Succi, MD on November 22, 2026. The article leaves open no further planned steps beyond the published findings, and it does not state what happens next.

The study’s results were demonstrated in the experiment, and the article does not give any follow-up actions or future research plans. The article does not state any additional dates, places, or names beyond those given. The article does not say whether the chatbot will be used further or whether the findings will be applied in practice. The article does not give any response from the study authors beyond the published citation and findings.

stories.Headline: A YouTuber adopts AI music after losing copyright disputes over licensed tracks
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Fstoppers on 22 November 2026, is a first-person account by the site's owner of using AI-generated music in a YouTube video for the first time. He says he was pushed into it by copyright claims on YouTube, where people claim to own music creators have every legal right to use or have paid for. He describes himself as completely conflicted about the switch. He has been making YouTube videos for more than 15 years. He says AI is reshaping one creative industry after another and he thinks music is next.

He says that in the beginning nobody really knew what was legal, so everybody used popular copyrighted songs. YouTube then built an automated system that listens for copyrighted music and asks the copyright holder whether to pull the video or collect all of its ad revenue. About 12 or 13 years ago he decided the risk was not worth it and stopped using popular music entirely. He built a library of royalty-free tracks bought outright with the right to use them in any video, and he believes he has spent more than $10,000 on it over the years. He says none of those songs were incredible but they were good enough for YouTube.

He says a few years ago he made a video giving his dad a classic Camaro, the most expensive and most popular video he has ever made. As it gained views he got a copyright claim from someone saying they owned one of its songs, a track he had bought from a royalty-free music site. He disputed it and the reply was one sentence: the dispute was rejected and the claimant would get the revenue. By then the video had something like a million views, and he left it up rather than take it down, re-edit it or strip the music out. It kept growing and earning and he never saw a cent of it.

He assumed the first claim was a fluke, deleted that song from the library and kept going, then woke up to another claim on a years-old video using a song he knows he bought from PremiumBeat. He disputed it and lost again, and after that claims came in by the hundreds on videos more than a decade old with music he had legally licensed. He says some of those songs are on practically every royalty-free music site on the internet, and others used to be until they were pulled. He says it is worse for creators who talk about music for a living, citing Rick Beato, who sits down with musicians to break down their own songs and says he has had roughly 4,000 claims over nine years. He also cites Davie504, who picked up his bass in an anechoic chamber to play "The Sound of Silence" as a joke and muted the audio, played nothing at all, and says he still got a claim for that song.

He says the same thing is happening in photography, where Fstoppers has bought thousands of royalty-free images and every so often gets an email demanding a thousand dollars, or tens of thousands, for "stealing" an image available on every stock photo site for something like 50 cents. He says they licensed it legally 12 years ago and now someone shows up asking for five, 10, 20 or 30 thousand dollars. He went to court over one of these, won, and still lost $27,000 in legal fees. For the last few years that is why he stopped using music in his videos at all.

He tried Suno, thinks he paid $10 or $20 for the month, and generated songs from text prompts that he says sound incredible and better than any song he has legally purchased in the last 15 years. He says nobody ever asked what the licensed songs were because they were never that good, but on his last video the top comment asked what the songs were, saying the commenter tried Shazam and could not find them. He says on a site like PremiumBeat he would pay around $80 for a song that would show up in thousands of other videos and could still get claimed later, while each Suno song costs a fraction of that and is unique to him. He can make it instrumental or with vocals, write his own lyrics or let the AI write them, and have a song in about a minute, and he notes Suno's paid plans are the ones that include commercial use, so terms should be read before a track goes in a monetized video.

He answers people who say they will never listen to AI music because it is soulless by noting he has always heard people say they hate computerized music and only want real instruments, while much of what has been popular for the last 20 years is synthesized and built on a computer. He says he does not like most of the top charts on Spotify or know most of those artists, so generating music that sounds like what he actually likes is better for him. He says he almost went to Full Sail University for its music production program after college and chose photography at the last minute, and now the two things he cared about most have both been overtaken by AI at the same moment. He says AI can generate an image better than anything he has ever taken, instantly and for free, and now the same is true of music.

He thinks nearly every YouTube video will soon use AI-generated music because of the copyright trolls, and that Spotify will start generating songs tailored to each listener that people will love because they were built around their own taste. He says plenty of people will fight it and insist they want only human-made music while listening to chart hits produced on computers anyway. He calls this the most exciting technology he has ever seen and, on the other hand, incredibly sad. He asks readers whether they have started using AI music in their videos or are holding out, and invites them to comment.

stories.Headline: Nvidia loses three trillion dollars as an AI market crash deepens
stories.Summary:
Matt Stoller reported on an ongoing artificial intelligence crash on November 23, 2026. This financial downturn followed the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang several weeks prior. The crash also involved a failed initial public offering for the company Anthropic. On Friday, the NASDAQ fell by more than five percent into a correction. Other markets and commodities also dropped during this period of volatility.

The crash involves Nvidia losing three trillion dollars in market value. Neocloud stock prices fell by more than half, and their debt reached junk levels. Oracle reached a 52-week low and issued a denial of insolvency on November 20, 2026. This company claimed it secured all funding needed for its OpenAI contract. The 10-year Treasury bond rose from 4 percent in February to 5.27 percent.

Matt Stoller claims the AI trade is over and financial systems may blow up. He suggests the market is likely in a bear market rather than a temporary pullback. Stoller believes Nvidia's board may have fired Jensen Huang for committing fraud. He argues that the company claimed chip sales that were not actually happening. He notes that the current crash is prompted by high borrowing costs.

Steve Eisman claims that many medium-sized AI companies known as neoclouds are going to zero. Michael Burry has reportedly made similar statements about the AI trade. Senator Adam Schiff wrote in the Wall Street Journal that there will be no bailout. Hedge funds like Situational Awareness were affected, selling portfolios in July. The crash affects superrich managers, Wall Street bankers, and Silicon Valley monopolists.

The bubble grew as corporations used financial models that did not cover debt service costs. Leverage in the hedge fund sector increased after the Silicon Valley Bank bailout. The gross asset value of hedge funds reached 13 trillion dollars against 4 trillion net. This leverage grew since late 2022 and early 2023 when ChatGPT launched. Borrowing costs rose due to the war in Iran and Federal Reserve rate hikes.

The market may experience a bear market bounce before resuming its slide. Stoller suggests the Federal Reserve would need radical action to prevent a bear market. The articles leave open whether the technology will ever be profitable. It remains unclear if the current volatility will affect the real economy. The full extent of balance sheet risks remains unknown to the public.

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off pulls S&P 500 down 3.7 percent and Nasdaq down 5.3 percent
stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks occurred on Friday, November 20, 2026, causing major market declines. This event pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 percent and knocked the Nasdaq composite into the red. The Nasdaq composite slumped 5.3 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 1.9 percent. Chip stocks and other companies connected to the AI buildout bore the brunt of this heavy selling. The sell-off also spread globally, hitting European indexes and Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi by over 5 percent.

The S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39, while the Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33. The Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73, falling more than 10 percent from its October 6 high. Nvidia fell 13.8 percent, Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3 percent, Micron Technology slid 13.9 percent, and Broadcom fell 12.1 percent. Corning slid 10.9 percent, Bloom Energy gave up 15.3 percent, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7 percent. Anthropic fell 9.1 percent to 88.30 dollars, while MARA Holdings fell 18.6 percent and Hut 8 fell 17.7 percent.

Michael Antonelli, a market strategist at Baird, said the idea that AI can spend unlimited money is ending. He believes this shift is what the market is currently pricing, though the bull market from October 2022 remains. Hut 8 reported 949 MW of IT load and 1.75 billion dollars in expected average annual net operating income. This includes a 9.8 billion dollar lease at its Beacon Point campus in Texas for 352 MW over 15 years. The company claims every dollar is leased or backstopped by investment-grade counterparties for its various AI data projects.

Bitcoin miners were hit as the coin broke below 60,000 dollars on Friday and touched 55,100 dollars on Saturday. Core Scientific, CleanSpark, and Bitdeer each lost more than 13 percent, while IREN was down about 11 percent. Investors are worried that high market values and heavy spending in the AI sector are not justified. Midterm election results added fear, as candidates winning at federal and state levels want to slow data center construction. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas proposed a moratorium on new data center approvals until the legislature writes new rules.

The S&P 500 had its worst weekly loss since April 2025 and its longest losing streak since 2020. A previous correction occurred in March 2025 when the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Nvidia's stock dropped over 25 percent since the scandal involving former CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang erupted this month. Anthropic's IPO was the biggest ever, once surpassing 2 trillion dollars, but its price fell from a peak of 115.10. Listed miners sold nearly half their bitcoin since January to fund AI buildouts, increasing their exposure to infrastructure bets.

Hut 8 expects its first data halls at River Bend and Beacon Point to open in Q2 and Q3 2027. stories.Headline: Rialto opens an $82 million police headquarters with an AI-assisted real-time crime center
stories.Summary:
Hundreds of Rialto residents, police officers and city and county officials gathered at 128 N. Willow Ave. on Wednesday, Oct. 21 for the official opening of the city’s new police headquarters, a facility of roughly $82 million that includes expanded dispatch capacity, an AI-assisted real-time crime center and a lobby open around the clock. The station marks a broader expansion of the Rialto Police Department and its use of AI-assisted technology, which the city says is meant to improve officer working conditions and field results through faster dispatching and aerial support while increasing residents’ access to department services. The opening also arrives amid a national debate over surveillance, privacy, accountability and the role of artificial intelligence in policing. The department has 140 sworn officers and about 85 staff members, according to Chief of Police Mark Kling, who said the building was designed to accommodate an expanding department and the needs of a growing city.

Mayor Pro Tem Ed Scott said he once asked Kling at a lunch meeting what he needed, and Kling answered that he needed people, equipment and something done about the old building, a promise Scott said the city has now kept. Scott said the project saved the city about $8 million, and San Bernardino County Supervisor Joe Baca Jr. said the county contributed $1.4 million toward the station. Kling selected Lieutenant Jonathan Serring Palmer as project manager, and the chief worked with colleagues including City Manager Tanya Williams to hold down costs while keeping to schedule. Mayor Joe Baca Sr. told attendees it was a great day for Rialto, and council members including Andy Carrizales, Karla Perez, Edward Montoya Jr. and Scott each offered praise or recounted their work to upgrade the headquarters. Kling, who first retired in December 2011 and returned as chief in December 2017, said the new building provides the technology, working conditions and service that officers and residents deserve, and that the lobby stays open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays, because when people need the police, the police should not be closed.

He said the headquarters is not the finish line but simply a foundation for the next chapter of the department. The department adopted body-worn cameras in 2012, one of the first in the country to do so, and in November 2025 it signed a nine-year, $14.3 million contract with Axon for an Officer Safety Program that includes a Drone-as-first-Responder program through Axon Air, body-worn and in-car cameras, digital evidence platforms, automated video analysis and automatic license plate readers. Nationally, the use of artificial intelligence in policing has drawn concerns about privacy, discrimination and oversight, and the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warned in a May 2024 letter to the Department of Justice that AI-assisted systems can amplify existing biases and urged independent testing, transparency and ongoing monitoring. A 2019 National Institute of Standards and Technology study also documented differences in facial recognition accuracy across racial groups, with performance varying by algorithm and image data.

stories.Headline: Hartford council weighs AI governance principles and traffic camera authority
stories.Summary:
The Hartford City Council is scheduled to meet virtually on Monday, Nov. 23, at 7 p.m., and its agenda includes a resolution establishing a Hartford Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Governance Initiative with principles for the city's use of AI, which its sponsors' memo says does not buy any technology or spend money. Two ordinances on the same agenda would give the Hartford Parking Authority the power to run the city's automated traffic enforcement camera program. The agenda also lists a Lots to Homes lease for 175 Mather St., the sale of 144 and 148 Mather St., 151 Brook St. and 65 Pliny St. to the San Juan Center for redevelopment, an ordinance creating a Puerto Rican and Hispanic History and Culture Commission and a crossing guards' contract through June 2030. The meeting will be broadcast on hpatv.org and Channel 96 on Comcast, and City Hall at 550 Main St. is closed Monday, Nov. 23, with limited access Friday, Nov. 20, so an emergency heating pipe can be repaired, with reopening expected Tuesday, Nov. 24, and residents able to call Hartford 311 at 860-757-9311. The Planning and Zoning Commission will hold public hearings on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 6 p.m.

in a virtual WebEx meeting on rezoning Hartford Hospital property at 216 and 224 Washington St., part of 210 Washington St., and 142 and 146 Jefferson St. from MX-1 to MX-2 and adding it to the Campus Overlay, and on converting a billboard at 408 Market St. along Interstate 91 to a dynamic display, according to the draft agenda. Also scheduled are a continued hearing on a drinking place at 719-725 Wethersfield Ave., live entertainment at 339 Franklin Ave., a cannabis retailer at 1500 Albany Ave. and signage at 475 Flatbush Ave., and the Planning Division is at 260 Constitution Plaza. Separately, crews collect curbside leaves twice between Nov. 7 and Dec. 20 by zone, and residents should rake leaves to the curb, not the street, by the Sunday before their collection week, according to the city's yard waste page, which has a street-by-street map. Paper leaf bags are picked up during collection weeks, plastic bags are not, and residents with a free green permit can drop off bags year-round at the Waste & Recycling Center, 180 Leibert Road.

Hartford families can register children now for the city's 2026 Christmas Toy Drive, run with local businesses and community centers, according to the city's homepage, with registration under the "Hartford Holiday Toy Pickup 2026" tab in the city's recreation catalog. stories.Headline: Hyderabad municipal corporation commissions Osmania University to draft AI traffic management plan for 429 signals
stories.Summary:
The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation has begun work on an artificial intelligence-powered traffic management system covering 429 traffic signal locations across the Greater Hyderabad, Cyberabad and Malkajgiri municipal corporations, according to The New Indian Express. The corporation has entrusted the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University College of Engineering, Osmania University, with preparing the Detailed Project Report for the project. The GHMC Standing Committee has approved 2.83 crore rupees for the purpose, the newspaper reported on 23 November 2026. The proposed system, called CURE-ITMS, will integrate all 429 signal locations within the CURE limits on a common AI-enabled platform, with plans to extend the network beyond the Outer Ring Road. The system is expected to regulate traffic dynamically based on real-time conditions, improve traffic flow during peak hours and heavy rainfall, facilitate the movement of emergency vehicles and enhance road safety.

It is also aimed at replacing the fragmented approach to traffic signal maintenance and regulation with an integrated, technology-driven network. GHMC officials said that at recent review meetings chaired by Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy and the MAUD Special Chief Secretary, officials were directed to modernise all 429 signalised junctions within CURE limits and extend the network beyond the Outer Ring Road. The directions also included developing an Integrated Traffic Data Platform, identifying accident-prone locations and emergency vehicle routes, and testing AI-based traffic management technologies through pilot projects. The state government has also proposed setting up a dedicated institutional mechanism, Traffic Management and Road Safety, known as TG-TMARS, to oversee traffic management and road safety initiatives. The government has already accorded administrative sanction of 77.31 crore rupees for maintaining existing traffic signals, upgrading and rewiring old ones, and installing and maintaining 50 new traffic signals and 15 Pelican signals.

The latest proposal envisages a broader approach, covering the operation and maintenance of existing signals across CURE limits, installation of additional signals and AI-based road safety measures, including traffic signage and allied infrastructure. Identification and installation of additional signals are planned for December 2026. The Osmania University team has been given four weeks to prepare the DPR, detailing the technological requirements, implementation framework and other aspects of the project. The proposed AI-based traffic regulation and road safety technologies will initially be tested through pilot projects before wider implementation, according to the report.

stories.Headline: Brampton students pitch AI fixes for local businesses at first hackathon
stories.Summary:
The Brampton Venture Zone held its first student hackathon over the weekend of November 21 and 22, 2026, according to CBC News. The event, called the Brampton AI Innovator Hackathon, took place at the Brampton Venture Zone, an incubator run with Toronto Metropolitan University. It was the first stage of a year-long program that will partner post-secondary students with Brampton-based businesses to use artificial intelligence to address day-to-day challenges. About 120 students worked in groups of three to four over the two days on challenges from 13 participating Brampton businesses. The businesses want to adapt to AI but lack the teams or resources to do it, said Dione Almedia, the lead of marketing and partnerships for the Venture Zone.

Students worked with mentors, judges and the businesses that supplied the challenges so they could understand each problem and how to solve it, Almedia said. Bilawal Bhullar, the CEO and founder of Sigma Security Services, one of the participating businesses, asked students to draft solutions to last-minute customer requests, such as a jump in the number of security personnel needed for an event. He said this is a frequent problem in his industry and that it is important for business owners to empower the next generation with opportunities to learn about the real world outside the classroom. About a third of the participating students were selected as finalists. Those finalists will compete to work with the 13 local businesses in the first eight months of 2027 to develop their pitches into solutions.

Tomi Tijani was selected as a finalist alongside his teammates Shayan Khan, Ibrahim Mohamud and Isaiah Ozekhome, and their pitch focused on pharmacology. Tijani said the team wanted to show that the health sector is not something that can be played with and how AI can make it a better place. He said the hackathon gave him a chance to demonstrate his knowledge and skillset and to network with industry professionals. He said his LinkedIn connections rose from about 250 to 373 and that he worked not just with his team but with business professionals and entrepreneurs. The article gives no further details on what happens after the finalists work with the businesses in 2027.

stories.Headline: Australian AI committee is expected to publish report on copyright and data-centre policy on Monday
stories.Summary:
Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is expected to publish its report on Monday, November 23, 2026, according to the Guardian’s Josh Butler. The report concerns copyright and data-centre policy. The expected release falls at the start of parliament’s final four sitting days of 2026. The Guardian says the report could show whether Labor’s tentative cross-party cooperation on AI can hold. It is also a step toward legislation Labor is expected to bring forward on data centres, energy use and copyright.

The report may clarify Labor’s approach to data centres and energy use as well as copyright. Labor’s anticipated legislation on data centres, energy use and copyright is a next step the report could inform. The release comes just before parliament’s holiday break, after only four sitting days remain. Butler describes the report as a step toward that anticipated legislation. The report’s recommendations arrive during the final four parliamentary sitting days of 2026.

Senior figures Richard Marles, Tim Ayres and Michelle Rowland have increasingly argued that existing copyright law has shortcomings, Butler writes. Their rejection of the status quo contrasts with major rightsholder groups, which dispute the need to change the law. Shadow attorney general Michaelia Cash called the potential music carveout a “ham-fisted tactic” and said property should not be “stolen”. Liberal MP Garth Hamilton described AI as “just good old-fashioned theft” and proposed a levy on companies. Former Nationals leader David Littleproud said Anthropic could afford to pay everyone for copyright and warned against allowing large AI companies to bully Australia.

Creative industries reacted with dismay last week to reports that Labor was considering a music carveout within a permit system for AI companies. Those reports landed the morning after the Aria awards, where prominent musicians backed the Not AI’s To Take campaign. The music carveout proposal remains uncertain. Duniam and Violi made their appeal for a less partisan approach about a fortnight before the expected report. Major rightsholder groups reject the case for changing existing copyright law.

Butler reports that the report could show whether Labor’s tentative cross-party cooperation on AI can hold. The Guardian says the report may reveal Labor’s approach to data centres and copyright, amid competing calls for cooperation and stronger protection for creators. The report arrives amid a visible change in Labor’s public language on copyright. The debate is not only about changing rules, as some politicians argue directly for payment. The immediate constraint is time, with the recommendations arriving just before parliament’s holiday break.

The report is expected Monday, November 23, and may clarify Labor’s approach to data centres and energy use as well as copyright. Labor’s anticipated legislation on data centres, energy use and copyright is a next step the report could inform. Reports of a music carveout drew creative-industry criticism after the ARIA Awards and musicians’ backing of the Not AI’s To Take campaign. The proposal remains uncertain. The articles do not state what the report will recommend or whether Labor will adopt its recommendations.

stories.Headline: Connecticut police use AI with few statewide rules as lawmakers plan updates
stories.Summary:
Connecticut police departments are using artificial intelligence with few statewide rules, according to a report published by CT Insider on Nov. 23, 2026. The report was written by staff writer Jordan Nathaniel Fenster. It says artificial intelligence is entering almost every professional sector, including policing. It says Connecticut has no common set of rules, state-level tracking or guardrails on how police departments are using artificial intelligence. The report says state officials have moved to track and disclose AI use among utilities and in the job market.

Earlier this year, Connecticut prosecutors announced a moratorium on AI programs that draft, author or narrate criminal reports, the report says. That pause addresses one use case of AI and is, at present, the only statewide guidance on AI use for police, according to the report. Beyond automated license plate readers, which are a specific exception with separate state rules and public reporting requirements, there is no general statewide inventory showing which AI systems local police use, how they use them or what safeguards apply, the report says. The state's Responsible AI Framework was created in 2023 and calls for agencies to consider accuracy, privacy, fairness, transparency and human oversight, according to the report. The report says the document applies to state agencies and their contractors, while local governments are "encouraged to adopt" it, leaving cities and towns to decide whether to create separate rules for their police departments.

Mike Lawlor, an educator and former legislator who serves on the state Police Officer Standards and Training Council, said AI can be very useful as an administrative and investigatory tool, the report says. Lawlor said there is a role for this to play and that it is inevitable it will be a major part of everything, including law enforcement. He said it is a question, since it is new, of how you test it, how you figure out what the potential problems are and how you protect against those things happening. State Sen. James Maroney, D-Milford, said he was planning on going back and updating the government use of AI bill this year because of learnings since 2023. Maroney said lawmakers will likely look at it and ask the judiciary branch to do so as well.

Vahid Behzadan, an associate professor at the University of New Haven who researches AI safety and security, said AI is not a single technology, according to the report. Behzadan said police uses can range from transcription and translation to report writing, facial recognition and predictive systems that forecast where crime might occur. With report-writing tools, Behzadan said the model might end up excluding relevant facts, including potentially exculpatory information. He said software could theoretically turn an unclear or ambiguous account into a smoother, more confident-sounding narrative, changing how events appear to have happened. Behzadan said an officer's review remains essential but does not by itself show which parts of the report came from the software or what the software left out.

The report says few municipal police departments in Connecticut have any guidelines for officers' AI use, or publicly disclose how and if police officers are using it. It says academics and advocates have raised concerns that artificial intelligence may create errors in police reports, that AI used for facial recognition can create false matches and that predictive systems might create disproportionate surveillance in communities of color. An NAACP issue brief on predictive policing warns that systems trained on historical crime and policing data can reproduce unequal patterns in surveillance and enforcement, the report says. The report says the brief calls for oversight and public disclosure and is a statement of risks and recommendations, not evidence that a Connecticut police department uses predictive policing. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, facial recognition can produce false matches, and the error rates of tested systems can vary across demographic groups, producing higher error rates when examining Black persons' faces, the report says.

A presentation last year by the Connecticut Criminal Justice Information System governing board included a bullet point explaining how the agency was planning to use AI to "do a lot more with less," the report says. The presentation said the agency is automating more of its testing of new code to reduce costs, exploring possibilities of adding AI for Connecticut Information Sharing System Analytics and renegotiating maintenance agreements or instead leveraging time and materials contracts. The report says lawmakers admit that the 2023 law that created the AI framework is already outdated, and it notes that ChatGPT became available in public previews on Nov. 30, 2022. Prior to the moratorium, New Haven had a 2024 contract with Axon that included Draft One, which can use body-camera audio to generate a draft police report, according to the report. The report says there are no reports of this technology being used in Connecticut.

More to follow.
