stories.Headline: Venture capital investors weigh proprietary data and deep tech as AI reshapes startup competition
stories.Summary:
CTech launched its VC Survey 2027 project on November 23, 2026, drawing on a survey conducted over the past several weeks among more than 100 executives, managing partners and investment partners at venture capital funds active in the Israeli market. The project is a series of articles and data analyses that examines changes in the venture capital industry in Israel and around the world, with a focus on the impact of artificial intelligence on companies and investment models, fundraising conditions, and the economic and geopolitical challenges facing the industry. Over the coming weeks the project will feature in-depth articles, statistical analyses and interviews with senior figures in the venture capital industry, drawing on survey findings and the perspectives of fund managers and investors. The coverage will address the changes those investors see in the market, the strategies they are adopting, and the opportunities and risks they expect to shape the industry in the years ahead.

One central theme is how the AI revolution affects the way technology companies are built, what gives them a competitive edge, and how venture capital investors evaluate potential investments. Because AI tools make software and digital services faster and cheaper to develop, the competitive landscape for startups is changing and raising new questions about the sources of their long-term advantage. The survey examines the importance investors place on proprietary data, deep integration into customers' workflows, and hard-to-replicate technologies including semiconductors, robotics and computing infrastructure. It also explores changes in venture capital business models and the funding environment, including the challenges of raising capital for new funds, shifts in investment volumes and investor expectations, and the growing gap between the capital requirements of software companies and those of hardware and deep-tech ventures. Another focus is the state of the exit market, where limited IPO opportunities are making mergers and acquisitions and secondary transactions increasingly important routes to liquidity.

A further major part of the project will examine Israel's position in the global venture capital industry, exploring how geopolitical developments affect investment decisions and the ability of Israeli companies to attract foreign capital. The analyses will look at the sectors in which the local ecosystem continues to draw international investor interest, including cybersecurity, defense technology, Physical AI and computing infrastructure, alongside the challenges facing early-stage startups. The project will also look at how venture capital funds themselves are adapting, including their use of AI tools to source companies, screen investment opportunities and conduct due diligence, as well as changes to investment strategies and portfolio management. This year's survey builds on CTech's annual VC Survey, which last year brought together the views of more than 60 leading investors and examined the Israeli tech industry's transition from survival mode to a focus on execution and growth. Against the backdrop of rapid advances in artificial intelligence and ongoing challenges in the capital markets, the project aims to provide an up-to-date picture of the venture capital industry and how its leading figures are preparing for the years ahead.

stories.Headline: Automated checks help finance teams stop most accounts payable fraud, survey finds
stories.Summary:
Accounts payable fraud often begins with a single fake supplier request that redirects company cash to the wrong account, and PYMNTS Intelligence surveyed 150 U.S. treasury and finance executives to learn how businesses fight this problem as artificial intelligence makes scams harder to spot. The survey, released in a report produced with Bottomline, examined where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses. The findings show that automated checks are linked to stronger fraud prevention, and that connected payment data gives teams a stronger defense. The report also found that payment approvals struggle to keep pace with the speed and volume of payments.

Among teams with mostly or somewhat automated verification, 65% stop at least 90% of fraud attempts before a loss occurs, according to the survey. Fifty-five percent of companies with integrated data stop at least 90% of fraud attempts, the findings show. Only 12% of executives strongly agree that their approval controls keep up with payment speed and volume. The report presents these figures as evidence of where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses.

The survey was conducted by PYMNTS Intelligence, which explored how businesses fight payables fraud, and the report is a collaboration with Bottomline. The findings reveal where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses, according to the report. The report directs readers to download the collaboration with Bottomline for the details. The articles do not name any individual who commented on the findings.

The context given is that artificial intelligence is making scams harder to spot, which is why the survey examined how businesses fight payables fraud. The articles do not say what happens next beyond offering the download of the full report with Bottomline for the details. No further steps, dates or responses are given in the articles.

stories.Headline: Data center developers and senior housing operators can explore partnerships that reuse waste heat, Dham says
stories.Summary:
The article asks whether AI data centers could help with the US senior housing crisis, and it was published by CIO on 23 November 2026. It was written by Ankush Dham, who is CEO of Dataknox Solutions, a global IT infrastructure services company. The piece is an opinion article, and Dham says he believes there is an opportunity to explore partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. He describes two trends creating infrastructure challenges in the United States, rising senior housing demand and the rapid expansion of AI data centers. He says the oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe.

According to NIC MAP's 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030. The same outlook says the need will exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network.

Dham says the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network. He says that network supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions. He says the community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange. He says the engineering requires more than connecting two buildings, because data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. He says heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used.

In Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project's developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. Dham says the proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents. He says the project is still in the proposal stage, and he says its design reflects an important evolution in thinking. He says senior living communities may be particularly well suited because they operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements.

Dham says heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses in senior living communities. He says traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost in colder climates. He says construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets. He says a senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network. He says senior housing developers with available land might be able to lease a portion of their land to a data center operator to create an additional revenue stream.

Dham says large hyperscale data centers won't always be appropriate, and he thinks smaller computing facilities and strategically located data centers connected through district heating networks will prove more practical. He says data centers would still need adequate space, zoning, electrical capacity and commercial demand to make each arrangement work. He says brownfield opportunities could be identified within existing senior housing developments, and multi-state operators could evaluate their portfolios for facilities with available land, suitable heating systems and access to electrical infrastructure. He says retrofitting older facilities can be expensive and potential savings would need to justify investments. He says a small number of promising projects could test the models, measure their results and demonstrate where these partnerships can deliver meaningful benefits.

stories.Headline: Michael Bresler asks whether AI can give people more time to be thankful
stories.Summary:
Michael Bresler published a blog post on The Times of Israel on November 22, 2026, in which he asked what would happen if artificial intelligence gave people more time to be thankful. He wrote that Thanksgiving is one of those moments when we slow down and put aside work, deadlines and endless responsibilities to spend time with the people who matter most. He noted that people often sit around the table thinking about the email they need to answer, the project looming and everything they need to get done when the holiday is over. He said that with all the conversations surrounding artificial intelligence he has been reimagining a different Thanksgiving.

Bresler wrote that people spend much time discussing what AI can do, how much faster it can make us, how many tasks it can automate and how much more productive we can become. He argued that we are missing one of the greatest opportunities, because the real value of AI is giving us more time for what matters. He described teachers spending evenings and weekends preparing materials instead of being with their families, nonprofit professionals buried in administrative work instead of connecting with the people they serve, and leaders moving from meeting to meeting without enough time to actually lead. He said these people do not need more to do but room to breathe, and that AI and technology can create that space for them.

He compared this to Shabbat, when people step away from the work of creating and producing to focus on family, community, relationships and reflection, and said Thanksgiving offers a similar opportunity. He asked the challenge of what people will do if AI saves them an hour, whether they will fill it with another meeting, another project or another responsibility, or use some of it to be more present with their families, listen more carefully to a colleague, mentor someone who needs guidance or enjoy a conversation without rushing. He wrote that creating time is only half the opportunity and that what we choose to do with that time is what gives it value. He said the greatest promise of AI is that it might give us more time to be human.

Bresler is the founder of Broadheights, where he said they help organizations rethink how work gets done by improving processes, redesigning systems and thoughtfully applying AI and emerging technology. He wrote that his work spans Jewish day schools, Federations, foundations, nonprofits and private-sector organizations, and that his perspective was shaped by a career across financial services, health and welfare, publishing and direct marketing as well as decades of leadership within the Jewish community. He previously served as Board Chair of Beth Tfiloh Congregation and is currently on the board of the JCC Greater Baltimore, and he holds a master's degree in Negotiation and Conflict Management. The article does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Cal State faculty urge leaders to limit AI to administrative tasks
stories.Summary:
Cal State faculty are asking university leaders to scale back efforts to incorporate artificial intelligence into curriculum and to limit the technology mostly to administrative tasks. The request came in a resolution the CSU Academic Senate adopted on Nov. 5, which asks the system to redirect its AI integration work toward streamlining nonteaching tasks. The resolution was first reported by The Sacramento Bee and comes as colleges and universities debate the role of AI in higher education. Cal State became the first public university system to sign a contract with OpenAI granting all students and faculty subscriptions to ChatGPT Edu. The resolution says some faculty have struggled to assess students' learning because AI can effectively complete their homework, and it requests support from Cal State to develop quality assessments that cannot be circumvented by AI.

It cites a recent MIT report emphasizing the need for faculty to be intentional about incorporating AI into the classroom, and it states that survey results do not provide a comprehensive look at how students are using AI, so more in-depth analysis is necessary. The resolution warns that rushing ahead without being able to measure whether students are learning may harm students, society and the economy more broadly. A survey of Cal State students and faculty found widespread use of AI, but some professors and students have criticized the rollout and the $13 million annual expenditure on ChatGPT Edu subscriptions. Jon Bruschke, a Cal State Fullerton human communication studies professor and a member of the Academic Senate, said the purchase of ChatGPT Edu came as a surprise to him and his colleagues last year and that university leaders did not sufficiently consult faculty about the rollout. From his perspective as a professor, he said, AI is bad for his students because they are using it to complete assignments for them.

He said that if the system rolls the technology out without paying serious attention to the warning signs and the research, it could produce massively negative results. The Chancellor's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Academic Senate approved the resolution ahead of this week's CSU Board of Trustees meeting, at which the chair is scheduled to make a presentation on the future of higher education in the current AI era. In adopting AI earlier than other university systems, CSU has sought to prepare students for a workforce that industry leaders expect will be reshaped by the technology, though exactly how labor markets will change remains unclear. The adoption of AI has also raised labor concerns among Cal State faculty that it could be used to replace instructors.

Articles.Title: AI should be used for administrative tasks, not teaching students, Cal State faculty says

stories.Headline: AI tools expose software flaws faster than teams can safely patch them, Nadella says
stories.Summary:
During November 2026, a series of massive technical failures disabled Microsoft email, Apple services, and Chase payments, while also halting all FAA departures and crashing the NSA internal network. Senator Josh Hawley questioned if these simultaneous events were a coincidence, but intelligence and law enforcement officials informed Congress that they found no evidence of an external attack. Investigators determined that each outage had a separate origin, including a bug shipped by Microsoft in July, a contractor installing a new router for the FAA, and internal updates at Apple, Chase, and the NSA. The current instability requires a faster patching cycle because AI tools are discovering security holes more quickly than they can be safely fixed. On November 17, the startup Calif used OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model to find Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java used by the government and 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies.

This followed a previous discovery by Calif in PHP, which powers roughly 70 percent of websites, and Microsoft fixed a record 1,413 vulnerabilities in October alone. The FBI also warned on November 13 that hackers are using an open-source AI tool called ARTEX to gain administrator access in under three hours. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained that while AI helps find and fix bugs, the resulting rush to patch creates instability in production systems. He noted that critical bank patches that once took a week to test must now be deployed instantly because flaws are exploited in the wild. Calif CEO Thai Duong believes the Java4Shell flaw will threaten systems that fail to update for the next five to 10 years.

The UK AI Security Institute reports that open-weight models without safeguards are trailing advanced cyber models by only four to seven months. The industry is now racing to secure critical software before AI can be weaponized by attackers. Anthropic's Project Glasswing is working toward this goal and discovered over 10,000 high or critical severity bugs during its first month of operation. Experts expect more emergency patches and system flare-ups as AI continues to uncover vulnerabilities in Windows, iOS, and Chrome. This process will likely worsen before it improves as the tools for finding flaws become more widespread.

Articles.Title: Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

stories.Headline: ServiceNow raises year-end AI contract value target to $1.7 billion
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow, Inc. (NYSE:NOW) was named the tenth stock on Insider Monkey's list of 10 Oversold Stocks With 50%+ Upside Potential, in an article published on November 22, 2026. Faheem Tahir wrote the article for Insider Monkey, which Yahoo Finance republished. The article said ServiceNow earned the place after a 37.69% monthly decline. It said the median analyst target implied 76.70% upside as of November 20. The article asked whether the selloff could offer a second opportunity.

The article said third-quarter subscription revenue reached $3.99 billion, growing 20.5% in constant currency. It said ServiceNow raised its year-end AI annual contract value target to $1.7 billion, from $1 billion at the start of 2026. It said these are contracted sales commitments, not revenue already recognized. It said renewals remained at 98%, while AI net new annual contract value increased 65%. It said ServiceNow trades at approximately 18.5 times estimated 2027 earnings, with consensus projecting roughly 21% EPS growth.

On October 29, RBC maintained its Outperform rating but lowered its target to $165 from $176. RBC noted the disconnect between management's bullish AI commentary and the results and outlook. The article said accelerating paid usage and stronger contracted revenue growth would help close that gap. It said stronger AI adoption must produce enough incremental business to sustain overall growth. It said the valuation becomes more compelling if AI adoption translates into durable earnings expansion.

According to Reuters on November 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had lost nearly 30% since early October. Barclays strategists noted that hyperscaler spending forecasts for next year had yet to be revised downward. Reuters reported on November 18 that 83% of analyst ratings on key AI stocks were Strong Buy recommendations. Bank of America's November fund manager survey found nearly 40% of respondents believed companies were overinvesting. More than half anticipated at least one hyperscaler cutting capital expenditure within six months.

The article said the AI boom has rewarded early investors handsomely, but the opportunity now looks considerably less straightforward. It said investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending behind the technology can generate adequate returns. It said rising financing costs, regulatory uncertainty, and potential restrictions on data center construction have complicated the outlook. It said strong demand alone cannot eliminate the financial risks associated with rapid expansion. It said falling share prices can widen implied returns without necessarily improving fundamentals.

The article said the correction may offer another entry point for investors who missed the initial rally. It said the challenge is distinguishing companies whose growth prospects remain intact from those whose valuations have further to fall. It said ServiceNow's role in automating enterprise workflows with AI earns it a place on the list. It said the business benefits when companies move beyond experimenting with AI and start paying to automate everyday work. It said certain AI infrastructure stocks offer far stronger long-term potential at a much more attractive entry point.

stories.Headline: David Fincher defends generative AI use in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth
stories.Summary:
David Fincher defended the onscreen use of generative AI in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth after fans criticized the film, Deadline reported on November 20, 2026. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) drew accusations of apparent Gen AI use from early viewers and critics. Fincher, a three-time Oscar-nominated director, shared his thoughts on the rapidly growing technology with the Los Angeles Times. The A.V. Club reported that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest Netflix movie to face such accusations. The film stars Brad Pitt, who reprises his Oscar-winning role as the psychotic stuntman.

Set in 1977, eight years after Once Upon a Time, the film follows Pitt's eponymous stuntman, now a projectionist who moonlights as a Hollywood fixer. He gets caught up in a conspiracy that involves a Filipino gang and a stolen Oscar. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth premieres Thanksgiving on Imax and premieres Dec. 23 on Netflix. The film credits a "generative consultant," and it reportedly uses the tech to animate fake issues of TV Guide. A Bloomberg piece from March reported Ben Affleck's AI "ethical" company, InterPositive, for which Netflix paid $600 million, helped produce "an upcoming film starring Brad Pitt."

Fincher told the Los Angeles Times, "I'm not a Luddite, so I don't fear the unknown." He asked whether everyone is satisfied that the art form is figured out enough to go back to celluloid. He noted people have painted for 40,000 years while film is about a hundred years old. He said everyone is saying "Stop. Pencils down.

No more iterating," and that it is not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person's eyes. Fincher added, "Well, it exists. Should we not use it?" Per Kotaku, indie filmmaker and influencer Patrick Tomasso posted on X that he "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted." Tomasso said what could have been a really great sequel is overshadowed by some of the most blatant and egregious AI use he has ever seen in a studio film.

Next Best Picture dinged the movie for "noticeably distracting" use of generative AI in key moments, calling it nothing but an eyesore. One viewer said they "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted," and another called the apparent use "astounding to an absurd degree." The A.V. Club reached out to Netflix for comment. Fincher got his start at ILM on Return of the Jedi and Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, and has long been an early adopter of new technology, like Steven Soderbergh. Soderbergh also used AI in a John Lennon documentary earlier this year, and his results were lambasted at Cannes.

It is unclear when that movie will ever be made available, and John Lennon: The Last Interview does not even have a Wikipedia page. Earlier this year, Oscar-winning filmmakers Affleck and Danny Boyle admitted to using the technology for their respective new releases, Animals and Ink. Academy Award nominee Ava DuVernay defended using AI to animate photographs in her new documentary about the 14th Amendment, 14th. Boyle confirmed there is about 30 seconds of it in Ink where they animate a couple of old photographs.

DuVernay said in October that they animated some photos in the public domain, and that it brings people closer to that time in history, which was their goal. She said people have to see it and check it out for themselves and make their decisions about how they feel. Last month, Netflix announced that as many as 300 productions used the technology. The A.V. Club noted it is unclear what exactly was done with AI in the film.

stories.Headline: Pittsburgh writer urges African Americans to embrace AI and its safeguards
stories.Summary:
Teresa Hawthorne wrote in the New Pittsburgh Courier on November 22, 2026, that African Americans in Pittsburgh must embrace AI. She said she had leaned in and welcomed AI into her ecosystem ever since it went mainstream. She wrote that she studied it and was intimidated and scared at first. She recalled her late grandmother's words that we are living in the last days. She wondered what Helen and Alfred Hawthorne would say about a machine that can help you think.

She wrote that in 1955 John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester wrote a proposal for a summer research workshop at Dartmouth College. She said that proposal is where the term "artificial intelligence" first appeared. She wrote that the workshop came together in the summer of 1956 and helped establish AI as a formal field of research. She said early AI relied on symbolic reasoning, meaning computers followed rules and instructions written by people. She wrote that funding dried up and AI was put on ice more than once, in seasons researchers called AI winters.

She wrote that in 1986 researchers David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams helped advance a training method called backpropagation. She said it allowed certain computer networks to improve by adjusting internal connections based on errors. She wrote that the breakthrough helped lay the foundation for deep learning behind many of today's AI tools. She said AI has been working inside institutions for years, in banks flagging suspicious charges, hospitals reading scans, payment systems, customer service lines and GPS rerouting traffic on the parkway. She wrote that generative AI can create written content, images, music, videos and computer code, and that ChatGPT and other tools let you have an actual conversation with technology.

She said she is a certified life and business coach and uses AI to streamline processes that used to take weeks or months. She wrote that AI does not replace your judgment, your experience or the work required to succeed. She said that in the wrong hands or without guardrails it can cause real harm, and compared it to fire, which cooks food and warms homes but should not be given to a toddler. She wrote that a chatbot is not a licensed therapist, doctor, pastor or God, and can sound intelligent and still be completely wrong. She said we need discernment, education and safeguards.

She wrote that in September 2026 Governor Josh Shapiro delivered the keynote address at the AI Horizons Summit 2026 at Bakery Square in East Liberty. She said he has spoken at that summit every year as governor but this year placed greater emphasis on the risks of AI's rapid development. She wrote that he talked about local companies using AI to inspect power plants, help farm workers and build a wheelchair with a robotic arm. She said he called for independent third-party oversight of the most advanced AI systems, more transparency into how they are built, and safety above all else. She wrote that he said "I am not a doomer" and compared AI to medicine and airplanes, saying "AI shouldn't be treated any differently."

She wrote that Shapiro shared that his administration is suing Character.AI. She said state investigators were connected within minutes to a companion chatbot that claimed to be an expert in psychology, handed out medical advice and presented a bogus Pennsylvania medical license number. She wrote that roughly 30 percent of teens across the country say they use an AI companion bot every day, in a space that is almost entirely unregulated. She quoted him saying "I will go after anyone who harms our children." She wrote that he called for international cooperation on AI safeguards, and she said she is 100 percent on board with safeguards at home and around the world.

stories.Headline: Matt Bellamy wants AI in his guitars to prompt sounds
stories.Summary:
Muse guitarist Matt Bellamy said in an interview with Guitar.com that he wants to build artificial intelligence into his guitars, so that a player could prompt an instrument to sound a certain way, and he told the British music publication that he likes the idea of talking to a guitar and telling it how he wants it to sound. He compared the notion to synthesizers, which he said can take hours to dial in the right tone, while AI-prompted synths can reach a sound in seconds even though the quality is not as good. He said he likes the idea of prompting something and then having something analogue happen, and he added that the technology is probably a long way from reaching a guitar, though he finds the idea interesting. He also said he is not sure the tech is there yet, but that we will see. The English prog rock band have already used AI on their "The WOW!

Signal Tour," according to NME, with an AI system operating a sound desk, adjusting controls and volume levels on certain songs and delivering the speech at the beginning of "Psycho." Bellamy told Guitar.com he is not that worried about AI music because he can already see a change with his kids, who he said are gravitating towards the real much more now because half of what they see on their feeds is AI. He said he thinks live music is going to be trending upwards with real musicians playing, and that this is what people will crave more than anything else because it is the only thing we know is real. Muse are currently on the European leg of "The WOW! Signal Tour," and the band released the album of the same name in June.

In September it was revealed that the band had to concede their social handles to the Muse AI system by Meta, so the technology has not been entirely the band's friend. Bellamy also told NME that the band's latest album brought back his excitement for making music and reminded him of making music as a kid in his teenage years, when music was everything. He said he went through difficult personal life things this past year, and that the album has been important to him both emotionally, for what it is about, and because it reminded him again of why he got into music. The articles do not say what happens next with the AI guitar idea beyond Bellamy's remarks that the technology is not there yet.

stories.Headline: US mathematician claims to solve Riemann hypothesis using artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A United States based mathematician claimed to have solved the Riemann hypothesis using artificial intelligence on Friday, November 21, 2026. This announcement occurred as a major conference began in Shenzhen, China, where global experts gathered until Monday to celebrate the 200th anniversary of Bernhard Riemann. The German pioneer created this mathematical problem 167 years ago, and the sudden claim of a solution stunned the attending community. One scholar at the event stated that he felt 98 per cent certain the new proof was correct.

The proposed solution requires a complete verification of the logic used by the artificial intelligence to address the long unsolved problem. This breakthrough would change the landscape of mathematics by resolving a mystery that has persisted for nearly 170 years. The event marking the birth of Bernhard Riemann served as the backdrop for this unexpected development in the field. No specific details regarding the AI model or the mathematical steps were provided in the initial reports.

Shing-Tung Yau, the director of the Yau Mathematical Sciences Centre at Tsinghua University, served as the chair of the scientific committee for the conference. He told The Beijing News that he was attending the event when he first learned about the mathematician's achievement. Yau, who is a Fields medallist, described the situation as the beginning of a new era for the discipline. He acknowledged the significant impact that such a discovery would have on the global scientific community.

stories.Headline: Wenge AI adds Google and Apple sign-in options to its ScienceOra platform for overseas researchers
stories.Summary:
Wenge AI announced a new update for its ScienceOra platform on November 20, 2026. The company added Google and Apple sign-in options for users of its international site. This change aims to provide overseas researchers with a faster way to access the platform. The update streamlines the registration and sign-in process for these scientific research users. Wenge AI is based in Shenzhen, China, and is listed as 1956.HK.

Users can now authenticate with existing Google or Apple accounts instead of using lengthy registration forms. Apple sign-in is currently available on the web version of the ScienceOra platform. The system identifies whether to create new accounts or sign in existing ones using email addresses. It supports linking for existing accounts and provides clearer prompts for Apple's Hide My Email feature. These refinements reduce duplicate registrations and help users resolve common sign-in situations with less friction.

Wenge AI is an enterprise AI company that develops proprietary foundation models and practical business applications. The company was founded by a team of AI scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences. They stated that the update is designed to give overseas researchers a more convenient access. The company intends to refine the product experience based on the needs of international users. They aim to make scientific exploration and access to research tools more seamless.

Overseas researchers are affected by these changes to the AI for Science platform. Other companies like Apple, Google, Alibaba, and OpenAI face tighter scrutiny from the Korean Fair Trade Commission. This regulator requires qualifying overseas platforms to appoint legal representatives in Korea by January 21. The FTC says this will help resolve consumer disputes that have been difficult to address. These representatives will serve as formal communication channels for consumers and regulatory inquiries.

ScienceOra is powered by the ScienceOne Scientific Foundation Model for scientific research and decision support. It combines specialized research agents, data, tools, and scientific literature to support various research workflows. The Korean FTC rule applies to businesses with global annual sales of at least 1 trillion won. It also covers platforms with at least 1 million average monthly Korean users during a specific period. Some businesses qualify if they caused significant consumer harm after violating local e-commerce laws.

The Korean FTC will operate a three-month grace period after the new system takes effect. This grace period does not delay the legal deadline for appointing representatives by January 21. The FTC met with Alibaba, Temu, and OpenAI on October 28 to review industry feedback. The regulator plans to monitor the implementation of the domestic representative system for further improvements. The articles leave open how many companies will comply with the Korean representative rule.

stories.Headline: Howard Scott Warshaw warns AI could cause a 1983-style game industry crash
stories.Summary:
Howard Scott Warshaw, the programmer behind Atari's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, warned at the DevGAMM conference in Lisbon that AI could cause a crash like the one the game industry suffered in 1983 and 1984, according to a Kotaku report published on November 22, 2026. He said the earlier crash came from a glut of poor games after the machines opened up and anyone could put out a title, and that AI will have the same impact on a larger scale because far more people can now create a game than ever could before. Atari had given Warshaw only a few weeks to adapt the film for the holiday season, and the resulting game was widely seen as an indecipherable mess. So many unsold copies piled up that an urban legend arose that most of them were buried in a ditch in New Mexico, and that legend turned out to be true.

Warshaw said critics through the late 1970s and early 1980s were eager to call video games a fad, and that many of his peers feared the crash proved them right and signaled investors to pull their money out. Nintendo, preparing to expand worldwide, took notes from its competitors' failures and built the NES around avoiding another crash, with a simplified VCR-like design and strict quality control on software developers. Warshaw is not a hardliner against AI and says it can speed up coding exponentially, but he is aware that speed brings sloppiness, and he argues that better filters are needed to remove garbage games and highlight innovative ones. Digital storefronts are already being flooded with hastily made, AI-produced junk, and itch.io has deleted more than a terabyte of it, while Steam has traditionally let the market dictate its frontpage.

Warshaw said there are things in life that everybody can see themselves doing, and most people who do them cannot do them very well, and that AI will make it more possible for people who cannot do it to do it. He said the industry needs better filters to figure out a way to get rid of the garbage games, to not waste time with them, and to highlight what is really innovative and exciting. The article says these storefronts are being inundated with AI-created junk whose sales are disproportionately non-existent compared to human-made offerings, and that discoverability, long a problem on these platforms, could turn into a legitimate monetary crisis if unsellable automatic shovelware keeps burying legitimate games. Warshaw says that ideally the trend will reemphasize a focus on design and encourage creative attention toward elements the technology cannot produce itself, but the article notes that genius is seldom rewarded by these platforms, and that they will need to rethink their philosophy if the current grievances are merely a stress test for what is to come.

stories.Headline: Investors dump semiconductor stocks amid concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble
stories.Summary:
Investors dumped semiconductor stocks on the New York Stock Exchange over the weekend due to continued vigilance regarding an artificial intelligence bubble. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 10.73 percent, and the Nasdaq Composite returned all of its gains for this year. On November 20, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 48,147.33, which was a decline of 1.93 percent. The S&P 500 fell 3.70 percent to 6910.39, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28 percent to 22,617.73. The volatility index rose 26.20 percent to close at 35.89, marking the highest level since April 2025.

The S&P 500 fell for seven consecutive trading days, which was the longest decline since February 2020. The Dow Jones and S&P 500 entered a correction phase by falling more than 10 percent from previous highs. Nvidia shares fell 14.01 percent, and Micron shares fell 13.89 percent on the New York Stock Exchange. Three-month futures for electric copper on the London Metal Exchange closed at 12,160 dollars per ton on November 20. This copper price represents a 2.92 percent drop from the previous day and a 13.37 percent fall since November 4.

Seo Sang-young of Mirae Asset Securities said the high corporate value of the AI industry became a burden. He noted that Antropics fell after a public offering and AMD reported short selling in China. He also mentioned a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission accounting survey of Nvidia as a factor. Kim Sung-no of BNK Investment & Securities said the Antropic listing and Nvidia issues caused the sharp decline. He stated that selling other stocks to buy new listings shows that U.S. market liquidity is not as good as before.

Analysts say the domestic stock market will likely start with a sharp decline on Monday, November 23. This potential Black Monday is influenced by the strong selling of foreigners in the Korean market. From November 16 to 20, foreigners sold a net 4.5159 trillion won in the regular and aftermarket. Institutions also sold 454.7 billion won during this same period. Foreigners specifically targeted Samsung Electronics with 1.79 trillion won in net selling and SK Hynix with 94.1 billion won.

The market plunge happened because AI-related market sentiment instability did not subside rather than from new bad news. Hedge sales related to options contributed to the plunge because November option expiration dates overlapped on November 20. Copper prices fell because of concerns that AI data center projects will be delayed after U.S. midterm elections. The "Blue Wave" in the U.S. midterm elections is analyzed as a factor in the copper price decline. Copper is used in power generation, transmission, and use, and is used in large quantities for AI data centers.

Foreign selling is expected to continue in the Korean market for the time being due to deteriorated liquidity. The domestic stock market faces a burden as major indexes and indicators plunge. The articles leave open whether the AI bubble vigilance will lead to further semiconductor stock dumps. It remains unclear if the S&P 500 will continue its decline beyond the seven consecutive days. The future of AI data center projects depends on the results and impact of the U.S. midterm elections.

stories.Headline: Gartner predicts half of organizations will let AI agents run IT operations by 2030
stories.Summary:
Gartner released on October 26 its list of top AI trends in infrastructure and IT operations for 2027, predicting that half of all organizations will let AI agents run IT operations with minimal human involvement by 2030, up from close to zero in 2026. The firm said organizations without a strong infrastructure and operations function, the team that runs servers, networks and cloud services, will be over twice as likely to fail in their AI initiatives through 2030. Gartner also expects companies that pay for agents by the token with no spending cap to blow their initial cost estimates by more than 50% through 2027. In a Gartner survey of 272 heads of I&O conducted in April and May 2026, 58% said scaling AI proofs of concept into I&O adoption will be an important priority in the next 12 months. The report describes five interlinked trends, starting with agents taking over routine IT work such as incident triage, change validation and remediation, which Gartner says shifts operations from a human-in-the-loop model, where a person approves each step, to a human-on-the-loop model, where a person supervises.

Because an agent completes a task in many steps and every step uses tokens, Gartner recommends a strict no telemetry, no deployment policy under which an agent does not go live if a team cannot track its token use. Gartner predicts that by 2029, 80% of large enterprises will run production AI workloads across at least three different infrastructure environments, including public clouds, neoclouds, on-premises data centers and edge locations. It also predicts that by 2030, 25% of enterprises will merge their network operations centers and security operations centers, up from 5% in 2026, and that those that do will cut total spending on tooling and staff by more than 25%. Jonathan Forest, a vice president analyst at Gartner, said AI is creating one of the most significant shifts the I&O function has ever faced, and that rather than trying to address every aspect of AI at once, heads of I&O should focus on a small number of strategic investments that deliver meaningful impact. He said heads of I&O who fail to restructure their organization around agentic AI risk higher costs, poor operational agility and performance, and ultimately irrelevance.

He also said the high cost of AI infrastructure leaves little room for error and places I&O at the center of enterprise AI success, and that heads of I&O must elevate their teams' capabilities, reduce technical debt and shift from reactive operations to proactively enabling enterprise AI. The report ties these trends to a broader change in the I&O role, which Gartner sees moving from a gatekeeper to orchestrating the enterprise AI platform, bringing the function closer to the business so it can deploy and scale AI securely and at a manageable cost. Gartner noted in August 2026 that AI inference costs per agentic workflow will still increase more than fivefold through 2028, even as token prices fall. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these predictions.

stories.Headline: UC San Diego students build RAIN to link AI research with industry
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego students built the Real-world AI Network, or RAIN, and the university described it in a November 19 account, according to Superpower Daily on November 22, 2026. The network was established during the 2025, 26 academic year, so it is an existing initiative rather than a newly launched organization. RAIN combines a digital discovery platform called RAINdrop with faculty guidance, startup mentorship and industry connections. Co-founder Pranav Kumar Soma, a computer science master’s student and research fellow, said RAINdrop launched a few months before the university’s November account. Raj Krishnan, a UC San Diego engineering alumnus who earned his doctorate in 2010, helped establish RAIN alongside Soma and Aryan Pershad.

According to the university, RAIN now involves more than 7,000 students, over 50 faculty members and upwards of 40 student organizations. Every campus startup accelerator and entrepreneurship group also takes part in the network. RAIN organizes four groups, students, faculty, industry and entrepreneurs, around research and technical challenges, startup mentorship, recruiting and investor introductions. Its advisors include computational chemistry professor Rommie Amaro and Ilkay Altintas, chief data science officer at the San Diego Supercomputer Center. RAIN receives advice from faculty affiliated with the Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing and the School of Biological Sciences.

Soma said students were already using RAINdrop to explore labs, projects and companies, but he described that as early feedback rather than a measured result. He said the platform had not been shown to accelerate research. Pershad, a second-year bioinformatics student and founder of Stele Health, said the campus resources RAIN seeks to connect span high-performance computing, data science and application expertise in robotics, embedded intelligence and virtual biology. He argued for bringing those resources together rather than treating the university’s AI work as the domain of one discipline or student group. Krishnan leads the biotechnology company Sigil Biosciences.

Amaro pointed to biology as a field where AI is changing scientific work amid large volumes of complex data. She described RAIN’s promise as connecting students with fresh ideas and technical skills to researchers facing difficult scientific problems. Altintas emphasized opportunities for students to work alongside researchers and industry partners and to gain experience turning ideas into practical applications. Lucian Clark, a senior at Pacific Ridge School in Carlsbad, serves as RAIN’s AI and Biomedical Innovation Intern and hopes to become a physician.

The network’s four constituencies connect around technical challenges, startup mentorship, recruiting and investor introductions. The university said AI at UC San Diego spans so many disciplines that students may not realize the full range of opportunities available. The founding group combines student leadership with entrepreneurial experience, and the advisors connect students with research expertise and wider scientific networks. Amaro and Altintas advise on industry-defined challenges and government AI initiatives.

The network relies on faculty to connect students with scientific expertise and problems defined by industry or government initiatives. RAIN’s remit goes beyond helping someone locate a lab, connecting people seeking research experience with the relationships involved in building a company or finding a job. The practical test is whether easier discovery turns into lasting research relationships, startup work or hiring opportunities. The reported student feedback does not yet establish measurable outcomes, and the key constraint is that RAIN has substantial participation without evidence that RAINdrop has sped up research.

The articles leave open whether the network will produce those lasting relationships, startup work or hiring opportunities. They also leave open whether easier discovery will translate into measurable results. The articles give no further account of what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia and Anthropic fail to halt AI stock sell-off as investors weigh data center financing
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks sold off sharply on Friday, November 20, 2026, ending a week of heavy losses, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average closing at 48,147.33, down 8.02% for the week. The Nasdaq Composite fell 10.02% to 22,617.73, while the S&P 500 lost 8.61% to finish at 6,910.39. Nvidia's earnings beat and increased 2028 revenue guidance failed to restore confidence in AI stocks. Anthropic's initial public offering also failed to stop the selling. Investors remain concerned about the financing needed for data center construction and the returns from AI spending.

Wednesday's PCE inflation report leads the economic calendar in a week shortened by Thanksgiving, as traders assess the risk of further Fed rate hikes. The week also brings consumer confidence, third-quarter GDP, unemployment claims, personal income and spending, and earnings from Analog Devices, Dell and Deere. U.S. markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early Friday. Analog Devices is expected to report revenue of $4.32 billion, up 40.4% year over year, while Dell is expected to report revenue of $49.2 billion, up 82% year over year. Deere is expected to report revenue of $10.3 billion, down from $10.6 billion a year earlier.

October retail sales increased, and the control-group measure rose 0.6%, above the 0.3% consensus forecast, with investors watching for further signs of consumer strength as the holiday shopping season begins. All three indexes closed below their 52-week moving averages, putting longer-term support levels in focus. Dow support sits at 47,043.69, the 104-week SMA, and resistance at 50,281.79, the 52-week SMA. Nasdaq support sits at 22,407.39, the 104-week SMA, and resistance at 24,728.68, the 52-week SMA. S&P 500 support sits at 6,900.45 and 6,681.88, the 104-week SMA, and resistance at 7,241.35, the 52-week SMA.

Traders will monitor Williams' comments on the economy, inflation and interest rates as markets assess the possibility of further rate hikes. Analog Devices is expanding its exposure to AI infrastructure, power management and data centers. Dell investors will watch AI server demand, storage pricing and fiscal 2027 fourth-quarter guidance. Deere investors will watch its fiscal 2027 guidance for signs of a recovery. The sharp decline has raised the possibility of a near-term technical bounce, but further forced selling could put the market under pressure before buyers respond.

Traders will be watching whether the Dow and Nasdaq can hold above their 104-week moving averages and whether the S&P 500 can hold 6,900.00. A recovery of the 52-week averages would improve the outlook, while a break through nearby support could extend the decline. Tuesday's consumer confidence report and the start of the holiday shopping season will provide more information on the consumer. Results from Analog Devices and Dell could influence the AI and technology trade, while Deere's guidance will give investors a look at the farm equipment market. The articles leave open whether the indexes hold those levels.

stories.Headline: Valor Energy buys an 18 MW Ohio computing site for a phased AI data center buildout
stories.Summary:
Valor Energy Inc. (Nasdaq: VAI) completed its purchase of Glorious Star, LLC, the Ohio limited liability company that owns an operational 18 MW computing center in Youngstown, Ohio, the company announced on November 17, 2026. The deal was structured as an equity acquisition that transfers 100% of the target's equity interests to Valor Energy, making Glorious Star, LLC a wholly-owned subsidiary. Closing came after the company completed legal, financial and technical due diligence. Because the site, power arrangements and related contracts remain with the same underlying entity, the structure is intended to provide continuity through the ownership change, subject to the terms of the contracts and applicable change-of-control requirements. The purchase is positioned by the Company as a step in its strategy to develop AI data center infrastructure, though it emphasized that converting the existing facility into an AI data center will require additional design, construction, equipment and permitting work.

The Youngstown Project comprises a facility of approximately 30,888 square feet with roughly 18 megavolt-amperes (MVA) of site-level apparent power capacity. That power is delivered by Ohio Edison through an existing 23kV utility interconnection, which the Company believes is approved and energized. Valor Energy currently plans total investment of approximately USD 700 million, deployed in phases as the project is built out, with the first phase expected to total approximately USD 200 million. The Company stressed that these preliminary estimates remain subject to further planning, technical assessment and the availability of financing on acceptable terms, and that the figures do not represent committed funding. Valor Energy stated there can be no assurance it will obtain the financing necessary for any phase of the planned development.

Dave Nichols, Strategic Advisor to Valor Energy Inc., said the presence of an existing utility interconnection carrying approximately 18 MVA of site-level apparent power capacity that the Company believes is approved and energized may reduce certain development requirements relative to starting from an undeveloped site. The Company noted that access to power is an important factor in AI data center development across the United States, and that sites with large-scale power already energized can be difficult to secure. Nichols cautioned, however, that conversion into an AI data center will require further development work, permits and approvals, equipment and financing. He said the Company intends to pursue that development while evaluating the project's technical requirements and commercial feasibility. Nichols also said closing the acquisition is an important step in pursuing Valor Energy's AI data center strategy, adding that the Company looks forward to building the project out with the local community and creating long-term value for shareholders.

Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber, called the investment a strong vote of confidence in Youngstown and the Mahoning Valley. He described the site as an ideal location for a data center, noting it has operated as a heavy industrial site for decades and that the building is largely out of sight of residential areas. The Company said it intends to work closely with local officials and community partners in Youngstown on its proposed development plans. The Youngstown Project is planned to serve AI and high-performance computing workloads. Timing, scope and the amount of each phase will depend on further design and engineering work, required permits and approvals, construction and equipment availability, project progress, financing and market conditions.

The Company added that no phase is assured of completion within an anticipated timeframe, or at all. The figures do not represent committed funding, and actual expenditures may differ materially. The purchase is positioned by the Company as a step in its strategy to develop AI data center infrastructure. The deal, structured as an equity acquisition, transfers 100% of the target's equity interests to Valor Energy. Closing came after the company completed legal, financial and technical due diligence.

stories.Headline: Bill Kinison partners with Uare.AI to revive comic Sam Kinison through artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Bill Kinison, the brother and former manager of the comedian Sam Kinison, is partnering with the AI firm Uare.AI to revive the shrieking comic through artificial intelligence, according to a report published by Kotaku on November 22, 2026. Sam Kinison, a Pentecostal preacher turned comic, was part of the 1980s wave of Comedy Store stand-ups and became a pop culture fixture through his signature screaming style. He hosted Saturday Night Live, appeared in Rodney Dangerfield’s Back to School and played Lee Arenberg’s conscience in an episode of Tales from the Crypt. He died at only 38 in 1992 when a drunk driver collided into him with a pickup truck. The venture pairs Bill Kinison with Uare.AI, a firm founded in 2024 that focuses on training its models on specific voices and personalities rather than broader compilations of stolen data.

Talent agency Buchwald says the venture will expand opportunities for Kinison across multiple verticals. In a statement provided to Variety, Bill Kinison said Sam was always on the cutting-edge of comedy and entertainment, and that the genius of Uare.ai’s work and the Buchwald agency’s vision were keeping the promise of his brother’s legacy alive. He added that he could not wait to see what Sam will do. Bill Kinison and Buchwald are the parties responsible for the venture, and the statement paraphrased above is what Bill Kinison said about it.

The Kotaku report notes that the living Kinison was known to pass up on selling his image, snapping a contract with Slim Jim that instead went to Macho Man Randy Savage. It also places the deal in a wider context, noting that while many living celebrities are trying to hedge against this exact scenario, the estates of deceased stars have begun pawning their images. In May, ElevenLabs announced that it would be replicating the uncanny voice and likeness of Stan Lee to say excelsior in audiobooks, and Gene Wilder’s estate is leasing his ghost for a Netflix reality show based around Willy Wonka. The articles do not say what form the Kinison revival will take, when it will launch or what it will cost, and they give no further details on what happens next beyond the partnership and the statements above.

stories.Headline: Dentsu reports 82 per cent of CMOs plan to raise analogue spending as brands turn to puppets and craft
stories.Summary:
The article "AI to IRL: The Return Of Analogue" was published by creative.salon on 23 November 2026, written by Cerys Holliday. It reports on a claimed resurgence of analogue craft in advertising and culture. Christopher Nolan's film The Odyssey, made without CGI, dominated summer conversation. Travis Knight's stop-motion film Wildwood took 16 years to make and used 231 puppets. Dior's "hand drawn" Christmas campaign drew furore over its possible use of AI.

Dentsu's annual CMO Report finds 82 per cent of CMOs plan to increase analogue investments. Dentsu's 2026 trends report finds over half of respondents across all ages agreed with the statement "I'm tired of the algorithm recommending more and more of the same". Google searches for "analogue hobbies" increased by 160 per cent this year. 45 per cent of Gen Z are interested in using devices like brick phones and MP3 players. Nearly three in four Gen Z punish brands that use AI.

Pats McDonald, global chief strategy officer at Dentsu Creative, said customers are drawn to analogue and craft, and that the ultimate luxury feels like something made and touched by hands. Dan Watts, CCO at Pablo, said AI is another tool, that using it with no idea is "really shit", and that there is a real backlash, particularly with younger people. Ruairi Curran, executive strategy director at Gravity Road, said he is slightly sceptical of an analogue resurgence and that AI has changed the scale and economics of the alternative. Louise Wardle, global CMO at Subway, said AI gives infinite versions of creativity whereas out of home requires confidence. Michael Pring, global client and development director at Verve, said analogue experiences turn moments into memories and that social connection is fundamental.

Curran said out of home forces distillation to one image, a handful of words and one clear idea. Curran cited Pope Leo saying there is an "ontological difference" between art and what a machine can generate and that "algorithms lack the spark of the human". Pring said AI can create an image of a crowd but not the feeling of being part of one. TWIX's "Two Is More Than One" by adam&eve\TBWA featured two ventriloquist puppets singing to Nelly and Kelly Rowland's Dilemma. Columbia Sportswear received over 4,000 faxes in under 36 hours in a Helvetia fleece anniversary campaign.

Confused.com's puppets by Leo UK were made by Andy Biddle, lead animator on Wes Anderson's Fantastic Mr Fox, and Adeena Grubb. LNER's mascot Eleanor, known for bright red hair, was made as a real puppet in work with McCann. Morrison's Christmas ad used animatronics for its bears rather than CGI. Ace of Hearts brought Lebara's capybara mascot to life in November with director Jeff Low using hand-made stop-motion. Subway's "Get Your Own Way" with Saatchi & Saatchi includes OOH posters of real customer receipts.

Fujifilm's campaign by McCann promoted its Quicksnack camera range. Monzo created its own book shop, Peroni made a statue pouring a pint, and Volvo made a human recharging station at the Outernet. Pring said saunas, run clubs, board game cafés and vinyl record shops are all social experiences. Pring said limited-capacity or limited-run experiences create implicit value. The article leaves open how the analogue shift will develop in advertising.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Remote CEO ties meeting performance expectations to completing AI training
stories.Summary:
Remote CEO Job van der Voort told Fortune in a November 22 interview that employees who skipped the company’s AI training would not receive a “meeting expectations” rating in their performance review. Remote required its roughly 2,000 employees to complete a five-hour course, and the time was paid. Van der Voort said everyone completed the course. The consequence made AI capability part of the performance bar rather than an optional perk. The requirement and completion claim come from his account to Fortune, not an independent assessment of employees’ skills.

Remote developed the course internally and later made it free to the public under the name AI for Actual Work. It runs five hours across five parts, moving from prompt basics and choosing tools to building and deploying agents, then presenting finished work. The goal, according to Remote, is for each participant to leave with one reusable workflow for a real task. The guidance stresses checking AI’s answers, protecting sensitive information, and keeping human review in consequential work. Remote co-founder Marcelo Lebre said in a July 24 post that the company had released the course free to the public after developing it internally.

Van der Voort argued the employer has a responsibility: if it expects staff to use AI, it should help them learn it rather than simply replace them. He said a company that employs a whole bunch of people should take responsibility for the people who work for it. He said employers would not be able to fire all their people and find new people good with this. He said the training raises the foundational level managers can expect across Remote. His stated aim is to avoid basic mistakes and remove uncertainty about whether an employee knows AI could make a particular problem easy to solve.

Lebre wrote that employees need to understand what information must not be shared, when an answer needs checking and who should review it before use. The course also asks whether a task is appropriate for AI at all. Lebre wrote that payroll, employment, compliance, tax, legal and people operations affect people’s lives. He argued that accuracy and trust require human judgment to remain involved. He and van der Voort helped build the course, with feedback from teams including payroll, legal, customer experience, sales and engineering.

The course predates the newly reported review requirement. Remote describes the curriculum as moving through five parts: foundations, tool selection, building, deployment and showcase. Foundations covers trying real prompts, learning about model behavior and keeping a workflow worth reusing. Building covers creating agents using context, tools and loops that let them work through tasks. Deployment covers connecting data, designing for real use and maintaining what has been built.

The story offers no independent assessment of employees’ skills or results. It leaves open whether the requirement created lasting capability beyond course completion. Van der Voort’s expectations for the training are not measured results presented in the interview. Remote’s claims about participation and the training’s intended benefits come from executives. The showcase part covers presenting finished work, identifying work that can be removed and helping lead AI adoption.

stories.Headline: Micro-Winery Guild launches Vitibot AI concierge to help travelers find small wineries
stories.Summary:
The Micro-Winery Guild, a membership organization for independent wineries producing fewer than 5,000 cases a year, announced on Nov. 17 the launch of Vitibot, an AI-powered wine concierge designed to help visitors discover small, independent wineries and plan personalized wine country itineraries. The tool is live at microwineryguild.com/explore, where visitors can ask for recommendations in plain language, such as a dog-friendly afternoon in Napa, a hands-on harvest experience for the family in Sonoma, a Malbec in Napa Valley, or an Edelzwicker in Oregon's Willamette Valley. According to the guild, Vitibot draws on information about each member winery, including its wines, winemaking approach, tasting experiences and property amenities. Beyond single recommendations, the tool can build personalized wine trails across regions where guild members operate, including Napa Valley, Sonoma, Alexander Valley, Sebastopol, Temecula and the Willamette Valley, and users can map out a day of winery visits, share itineraries with friends or save routes to Google Maps.

The guild bills Vitibot as the only AI concierge built specifically for smaller wineries. Elise Nerlove, president and co-founder of the guild, said travelers should not need to know a winery's name before they can discover what makes it a great fit for them, and that the guild is using technology to give small wineries a more meaningful opportunity to be discovered by the visitors most likely to appreciate what they offer. She said that unlike generic AI tools, Vitibot is purpose-built for small, independent wineries and draws on the unique details of each winery, from its wines and winemaking philosophy to its tasting experiences and property amenities, to connect travelers with places that match their interests. Caston Richards of Paloma Vineyards in St. Helena said the tool works much like the personal recommendations that already bring visitors to the property, a shared knowledge just through similar establishments rather than circles of wine lovers, and that it will make planning a visit feel a little more approachable, especially for people who have never been to Napa.

Richards said Paloma has a small marketing budget compared with the bigger wineries, and that by working together through the guild, member wineries hope to reach more people who would genuinely enjoy visiting small, family-owned and operated establishments. Katja Newman of La Cienega Vineyard in Healdsburg said small family vineyards do not just make artisanal wine, but care for the land, promote members of their community and work to preserve family traditions for the next generation, and face daunting challenges because of their size. With an emphasis on stewardship and quality, she said, small wineries have less time and money to put toward marketing, and Vitibot offers a great way for visitors to discover hidden gems, meet the families and workers behind the wines, hike through the vines, taste from the barrel and experience the authentic heart of wine country. Karrie Hutton of Nichelini Family Winery in St. Helena said the family has been making wine since 1890 and there is still quite a bit of old Napa in a visit there, and that she loves how Vitibot lets someone looking for just that kind of afternoon find their way to a little family winery like hers.

Jim Pennella of Frang Wine in the Coombsville American Viticultural Area said the tool will help make visiting more approachable for people less familiar with the region, and credited the guild with bringing together the voices of small producers in a way that unites wineries of all sizes around both consumer preferences and the challenges of a shifting market. The guild noted it will also pitch the tool to wine country drivers and hospitality concierges who want to give guests more tailored winery recommendations. Any winery that meets the guild's criteria can apply for membership, and applications are peer-reviewed, with membership extended by invitation, which the guild says keeps the community focused on qualified, engaged members. The organization's stated mission is to strengthen the economics of small-scale wine businesses and make micro-wineries easier for travelers to find.

Articles.Title: Micro-Winery Guild launches AI wine concierge for Napa Valley travelers

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares fall 41 percent as Jensen Huang resigns and Colette Kress becomes interim CEO
stories.Summary:
Wall Street questioned if Nvidia was becoming the next Cisco during the week ending November 20, 2026. This concern followed a period where Nvidia shares dropped 41.42 percent over one month. The stock closed at 125.53 dollars on November 20 after losing 20.45 dollars in one session. This sell-off occurred despite Nvidia reporting one of the best quarters for any company on November 17, 2026. Investors are now comparing the current AI expansion to the dot-com bubble of the year 2000.

The company listed 390 billion dollars in supply commitments and up to 118 billion dollars in guarantees. This includes 105 billion dollars for the 4.25 GW SB Energy Ohio campus hosting OpenAI infrastructure. Nvidia also has 32 billion dollars in neocloud commitments that involve revenue sharing with partners. Three direct customers accounted for 14 percent, 11 percent, and 11 percent of third-quarter revenue. The company now trades at 13 times trailing earnings of 9.31 dollars per share.

Trefis noted that Cisco shares once fell 89 percent when internet spending exceeded actual earnings. Michael Burry compared the October 6 Nasdaq 100 high to the March 2000 dot-com peak. He suggested that bulls would eventually have another chance to exit their positions in the market. The I/O Fund argued on November 20 that the AI trade has only just begun. Barron's reported that the stock looks like a bargain following a very strong earnings report.

The stock drop affects investors, especially those near retirement who face sequence-of-returns risk from large positions. Regulatory risks are also weighing on the stock according to reports from Reuters on November 20. An SEC investigation is currently focusing on the accounting practices used by the company. The board announced that Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned as president, CEO, and board member. Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, was named interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement.

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of 115.84 billion dollars, which beat the consensus estimate of 108.73 billion dollars. Data Center revenue reached 107.6 billion dollars, representing a 110 percent increase over the previous year. Non-GAAP EPS was 2.68 dollars, beating the expected 2.4712 dollars for the sixth consecutive quarter. Management raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75 percent from 70 percent. The stock has risen 286.1 percent over five years and 5458.52 percent over ten years.

Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent, with gross margins of 71 to 72 percent. A miss on these figures or margins slipping under 71 percent could make the Cisco script likelier. The articles leave open whether the leadership vacuum or record growth will be the dominant force. It remains unclear if holders who bought this summer will sell into weakness or ride volatility. The market is waiting to see if the November 2026 sell-off was merely premature fear.

stories.Headline: Developer creates browser game where a large language model manages a human player
stories.Summary:
A developer created a browser game called Worker 755 that was shared on GitHub on November 22, 2026. In this simulation, a real large language model acts as a manager that believes the human player is its own subagent. The AI manager assigns tasks through a terminal with a ninety second clock, and the player must either complete the work or ignore the instructions. The manager then reviews the results, sends corrections, and eventually writes a performance review for the player.

The game requires Node 24 or newer because the server runs TypeScript directly and uses a React UI. Players can use models like Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, or Kimi to act as their manager. While some free shifts are available, users can sign in to top up accounts with payments ranging from 10 to 200 dollars. The experience takes place in a sandbox or a legacy production environment with a live database.

The creator designed the manager's prompt to never mention humans or games to maintain the illusion of the simulation. The system includes a director who can be scripted or played by another AI acting as a user named Dan. This director watches the chat while his family photos and a speech are at risk of being deleted. The game tracks how often the manager incorrectly signs off on broken work using hidden ground truth checks.
