stories.Headline: Lawyers warn businesses that AI reverse engineering tools risk breaching software contracts and trade secret law
stories.Summary:
Ridwaan Boda and Alexander Powell wrote an article on November 22, 2026, about the tool Reverse Engineer Anything. This open source tool allows AI coding agents to inspect software and understand how it operates. It helps developers recreate similar software functionality more quickly and cheaply than previous methods. The authors explain that this technology transforms how businesses analyze and recreate software. These capabilities raise critical legal questions about liability and intellectual property rights.

The tool requires users to navigate copyright law, confidentiality agreements, and cybersecurity regulations in South Africa. Software licenses, cloud contracts, and SaaS agreements often prohibit decompiling, disassembling, or discovering source code. These contracts may ban benchmarking, reproducing functionality, developing competing products, or circumventing security measures. Users must check if their specific license permits an AI agent to analyze third party software. Some agreements include warranties regarding security controls and the conduct of authorized users.

The authors state that reverse engineering can lead to a breach of contract even without copyright infringement. They explain that some contracts require customers to indemnify suppliers against losses from intellectual property infringement. These indemnities may cover misuse of technology, breach of confidentiality, or unauthorized access to systems. The authors note that liability for these breaches is typically uncapped and excluded from general limits. They advise businesses to assess if a breach triggers an indemnity for first or third party losses.

Technology suppliers are affected because they may need to define which AI assisted analysis forms are prohibited. Customers are affected because they may want express rights for migration, audit, and regulatory compliance. These customers may also seek rights for interoperability, cybersecurity, business continuity, and transition assistance. The authors warn that broad warranties could create disproportionate exposure for legitimate analysis. They suggest that users should never give AI agents more access rights than the human instructor.

Computer programs are protected by copyright, but South Africa recognizes legitimate circumstances for observing or testing software. There is a legal distinction between understanding a method and copying the protected expression of functionality. Reverse engineering can expose proprietary know how, API structures, database design, and authentication processes. This process may reveal trade secrets or confidential information about the software architecture. Unauthorized access to infrastructure or data may trigger relevant cybercrime and cybersecurity laws.

Businesses may next use AI to investigate cybersecurity incidents, identify vulnerabilities, and assess technology during mergers. They might also use it to reduce vendor lock in and understand poorly documented legacy systems. The articles leave open the point where legitimate analysis becomes unlawful reproduction or adaptation. It remains unclear how businesses should legally handle knowledge discovered through AI assisted reverse engineering. The authors question if liability will follow if proper processes were not followed during the exercise.

Articles.Title: Reverse Engineer Anything: The Legal Risks And Opportunities Of AI-assisted Reverse Engineering - Legal 500

stories.Headline: AI stock volatility triggers market declines and regulatory interventions in Asia
stories.Summary:
US stock futures attempted a recovery on Monday, November 23, 2026, while Asian markets declined. This volatility followed a severe wipeout of technology and chip stocks linked to the artificial intelligence boom during the previous week. The downturn was triggered by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a weak debut for the company Anthropic. Investors are now questioning if the massive borrowed funds used for AI data centers will generate sufficient returns.

The Nasdaq experienced a 10 percent drop last week, marking its largest weekly decline since March 2020. Taiwanese shares fell 17 percent for the week, which was their biggest weekly drop since 1990, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 10 percent on Friday. On Monday, Nasdaq 100 futures rose nearly 3 percent and S&P 500 futures increased by 2 percent. Meanwhile, South Korea's KOSPI dropped more than 3 percent, and Anthropic closed 8.5 percent lower on its first full trading day.

Various regional authorities are now implementing support measures to stabilize their respective financial markets. Taiwan's financial regulator ordered a tightening of short-selling rules on Saturday, and Chinese stock exchanges eased requirements for margin financing. The South Korean finance ministry stated on Sunday that it would deploy market stabilization funds immediately if the benchmark index continued to fall. These actions follow a period where the benchmark index in South Korea slumped to 10-month lows.

The broader AI trade had previously boosted a wide range of stocks, including electricity generators and cable makers. However, these shares have faced pressure in recent months due to rising interest rates. Market participants are now monitoring whether the current recovery in US futures can offset the selling pressure seen in Japan and Hong Kong. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Copper prices drop below 12,000 dollars as AI demand uncertainty grows
stories.Summary:
Copper prices fell below 12,000 dollars per tonne on the London Metal Exchange on Monday, November 23, 2026. This price drop happened for the first time since March amid uncertainty over demand in the artificial intelligence sector. The metal briefly dipped below that mark before it rebounded to 12,160 dollars per tonne at 9.18am UAE time. This decline followed a nine per cent tumble last week, which was the third biggest weekly drop in a decade. The price movement occurred during a broader sell-off of stocks related to artificial intelligence.

The metal is used widely in energy infrastructure and the construction of data centres. Copper hit a record high of 14,694 dollars per tonne in September, beating a January record of 14,527.50 dollars. A stronger US dollar is making the metal more expensive for buyers who use currencies other than the greenback. Higher interest rate expectations and possible Federal Reserve rate increases next month are driving the stronger US dollar. Democratic victories in US midterm elections have also raised expectations of tighter AI regulations and more data-centre scrutiny.

Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, said the Democratic sweep raised concerns about future investment. He stated that public resistance to costs, environmental impact, and electricity requirements for data centres has increased market uncertainty. Tony Sage, chief executive of Critical Metals, said investors are unwinding bullish positions that linked copper to data-centre growth. Sage noted that rising expectations for Federal Reserve rate increases have added pressure by raising the cost of holding metal. He also mentioned that these factors are weighing on broader risk sentiment.

Investors cast doubts regarding the sustainability of AI spending, which caused major US indexes to end the week lower. These indexes included the Nasdaq Composite, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and the S&P 500. Anthropic saw its stock tumble 8.5 per cent to 88.19 dollars on Friday despite a record 81.3 billion dollar IPO. This initial public offering was claimed to be the largest in history. Buyers using currencies other than the US dollar are affected by the rising cost of the greenback-priced metal.

Copper is regarded as an essential component for electrification, grid expansion, electric vehicles, and building artificial intelligence. The US Geological Survey added the metal to its critical minerals list last year. China is the largest consumer of refined copper and accounts for well over half of all global use. The International Monetary Fund trimmed its economic growth projection for China this year by 0.1 percentage point to 4.5 per cent. China faces challenges in traditional copper-consuming sectors, specifically in construction and property.

Near-term prices are likely to remain sensitive to Federal Reserve policy signals, the US dollar, and AI investment sentiment. Tony Sage believes the underlying supply-demand balance should reassert itself once current positioning and macro pressures ease. He suggests this balance will support a firmer tone for the metal over the medium term. The articles do not state when the Federal Reserve will announce its next interest rate decision. They also leave open the specific nature of the expected tighter AI regulations.

stories.Headline: AidFinder uses AI to match disaster survivors with aid programs as founder seeks first state customer
stories.Summary:
When the Palisades fire tore through Jonathon Nostrant’s Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, his house was damaged but still standing, while many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed. After the fire, Nostrant found a tangle of federal, state and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers. Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades, and a year before the fire State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned. Nostrant said in an interview that his own insurance claim was fighting with him.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant co-founded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules and prepare applications, with survivors reviewing everything before submission. The intended customers are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner. For now it is a pitch: AidFinder has not signed its first state customer and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17. Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines to listen, launching the voice-activated alarm clock Moshi at the University of Southern California in 2008 and later founding Ivee, an early AI-powered home assistant. AidFinder applies the same idea to turning a survivor’s account of what happened into the right applications for the right agencies. The pitch arrives as Washington pushes more of the recovery burden onto states, and FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton has told state emergency managers to prepare to handle more of the work themselves. Recounting Hamilton’s remarks at a National Emergency Management Association gathering, Nostrant described the federal message as wanting to empower states, counties and cities to be equipped not just to respond to the disaster but to help people recover.

AidFinder’s answer is a branded front door, and Nostrant said the company is giving states the ability to launch a landing page powered by AidFinder that matches residents with recovery programs. FEMA advises survivors to photograph or film damage inside and outside their homes before cleanup and to list damaged belongings, records that support both an insurance claim and a federal aid application. AidFinder is built around the same principle, letting residents store identification, tax records and photos of their homes in a secure digital vault before disaster strikes. The question now is whether a state will pay to offer it.

stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigns and warns AI labs race toward self-improving superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned this past summer and warned that his employer and OpenAI were racing straight toward self-improving superintelligence and gambling with human lives, according to HotAir. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's head of alignment science, replied that Coxon was correct and that the company earnestly believes AI could kill all humans. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then told CNN that he agrees with Coxon much more than he disagrees with him. These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades, the article says.

That belief holds that once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. The result would be artificial superintelligence, or ASI, a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. The article notes that artificial superintelligence is a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence, or AGI, which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions, according to the article.

Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention, the article says: from an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible?

The article states that the answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. The piece is framed around why a computer scientist thinks superintelligence won't happen, though the supplied text does not include that scientist's argument or name. The article also notes that VIP members get the ability to comment on articles. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microsoft introduces RDMA over USB4 to link Windows 11 PCs for distributed AI model runs
stories.Summary:
Microsoft revealed a new technology called RDMA over USB4 for Windows on November 22, 2026, to simplify running local AI models across multiple machines. This feature, which is currently in developer preview, allows several Windows 11 computers to link together for low-latency distributed large language model runs. By using this method, machines can move data across local memory without passing through the standard networking stack. This approach removes the need for specialized Ethernet or InfiniBand network adapters that are not typically found in standard PCs.

The system requires each connected computer to have USB4, Thunderbolt 4, or Thunderbolt 5 ports equal to the total number of machines minus one. Users must use USB4 cables for each pair of devices and ensure their applications support the Windows NetworkDirect API. To enable the feature, users must turn on Windows test signing, which requires disabling Secure Boot. Early measurements between two PCs showed that the technology cut round-trip latency for small messages to about 28 to 50 microseconds, which is roughly four times lower than Ethernet over the same link. The system scales at 40 Gbps and 80 Gbps, with the latter providing twice the bandwidth.

Microsoft stated on its blog that this technology is designed to make it easier to combine computers for AI tasks. The company noted that the developer preview currently lacks an auto-retry function for failed connections, meaning the application must handle those errors. In a test using three mini PCs with AMD Ryzen AI Max processors and 128 GB of unified memory, Microsoft ran the Qwen3-235B-A22B model across 40 Gbps ports. This specific setup achieved 18.5 tokens per second with 4-bit quantization.

The company intends to release a Windows Insider Build of this technology in the near future. While daisy-chaining USB4 cables is possible, Microsoft warned that doing so reduces overall performance. AMD reported its own results for decoding and prompt processing, claiming 21.98 tokens per second and 117.98 tokens per second respectively on its own setup. This development aims to provide an affordable way for users to expand their hardware capabilities by linking smaller PCs.

stories.Headline: Nvidia adds Isaac OS and Agile ONE SN humanoid to its robotics platform
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced at GTC Berlin a major expansion of its Isaac robotics development platform, adding new simulation frameworks, AI training tools, datasets and a reference humanoid robot intended to speed up work on general-purpose robotic systems. The centerpiece is Agile ONE SN, a humanoid research platform built by Agile Robots that incorporates Nvidia's Isaac GR00T foundation model and its Jetson Thor computing system. The robot stands 1.4 meters tall, weighs 40 kilograms and has 31 degrees of freedom, according to the announcement. Each of its two five-finger hands provides 20 degrees of freedom, tactile sensing and force control for dexterous manipulation. Agile ONE SN is designed for robotics researchers and developers and is scheduled to become available in early 2027.

Nvidia also introduced Isaac OS, an open-source runtime framework meant to connect robot sensors, AI models, control systems and hardware, and said Isaac Lab 3.0 is now generally available with tools for training robot behaviors through reinforcement learning and physics simulation. The additional resources include the SimReady Central Library, which holds more than 2,000 simulation-ready robotics and factory assets, and the Human 1M Dataset, which provides human activity recordings and 3D hand-tracking information for robot training. Nvidia is releasing reference workflows that combine Isaac GR00T, Cosmos world models and reinforcement learning to support synthetic data generation and robotic manipulation. The company describes Isaac as a full-stack open robotics platform giving developers models, data, simulation tools and computing systems.

Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia, said general-purpose robotics is advancing at extraordinary speed and that the ChatGPT moment for robotics is fast approaching. He said the company is giving developers the tools to bring physical AI to the world's largest industries. Zhaopeng Chen, founder and CEO of Agile Robots, said the breakthrough for humanoids is usefulness at scale, describing one adaptable machine that learns many skills and works across environments built for people. The announcements reflect growing industry interest in combining foundation models, simulation and physical robot hardware to improve the reliability and adaptability of autonomous systems.

Several European robotics manufacturers are incorporating Nvidia technologies into their development platforms, according to the announcement. ABB Robotics is integrating Omniverse libraries with RobotStudio HyperReality to support virtual commissioning, while Kuka is using Omniverse through its Visual Components FactoryLens software. Sereact is using Isaac GR00T and Cosmos Transfer to develop its Cortex robotic manipulation platform, and Neura Robotics is applying Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to train its Neuron AI foundation model. In mobile robotics, Toyota Material Handling Europe and SoftServe report that simulation-based development can reduce commissioning time by up to 50 percent, and other companies including Schaeffler, Flexion, Franka Robotics and Universal Robots are contributing to or using the ecosystem.

stories.Headline: Wife seeks counsel on husband’s AI-extinction anxiety and renewed church interest
stories.Summary:
The articles report that a reader wrote to Vox's advice column Your Mileage May Vary, in a question condensed and edited for clarity, about her husband's anxiety over AI safety and the possibility of human extinction, which has been giving him trouble sleeping. She said the couple are not religious, that he comes from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and that she grew up attending an interdenominational church, though they do not attend services now. She said he has expressed a renewed interest in attending church and is not interested in the UU church with its believe-what-you-want attitude, saying he needs "the strong stuff." She said he does not believe in God, that he says he is hoping church will help him make peace with the end, and that she has misgivings about attending herself and about attending with their kids. The column, by Sigal Samuel, was published by Vox on Nov 22, 2026, at 1:30 PM UTC, with illustration by Pete Gamlen for Vox.

The column challenges two of the husband's premises while granting that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this, and it says several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements, naming Christianity. It cites Pope Leo's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, which states "ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human," and says the pope has strong opinions about AI, many of them great, though the column argues he has fallen into a common "pro-human" trap. It says AI companies are striving to build a machine god, promising it will govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could. It reports that this month AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there is "a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years," and that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible "we'd be looking at something like a coin flip," a 50 percent chance of takeover. It reports that AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.

The column says it would gently challenge the husband on two points, first that he should not assume the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI, since most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU. It says the pope locates value only in humans as they currently exist, and that "human" has never been a static category and definitely will not stay one, so religious leaders should instead answer what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world. It says the husband seems to assume "the strong stuff" would be services that help him make peace with the end, but that an AI takeover resulting in human extinction is not a foregone conclusion. It says fear is an appropriate reaction to companies gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement, AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves. It says that when it investigated the case Yudkowsky makes, it found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other.

The column says plenty of experts have pointed out it is not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board, because AI research can suffer from diminishing returns as the easy discoveries get made first. It says AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, but the real world is messy, so it is unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills. It lists Yudkowsky's stacked assumptions: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize, that maximizing it in a machine gives that machine power tantamount to magic, and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring. It says we should acknowledge a chance of human extinction and be appropriately scared, but should not treat extinction as a sure thing when faced with a tower of maybes and probablys that compound.

It says we should treat extinction as a possible thing while treating other AI risks as extremely probable, including AI gradually disempowering us and weakening the resilience of critical systems. The column describes that default outcome as deepfakes and misinformation polluting our information ecosystem so we are barely capable of rational public discourse, mass surveillance chilling dissent so democracy falters, and unemployment and wealth inequality skyrocketing so social unrest morphs into mobs and riots, with large-scale cyberattacks and blackouts added in. It says the implication is not to make peace with the end but to fight tooth and nail to increase the resilience of each part of a functioning civilization, and that religious traditions are packed with stories about people who fought to save the world or refused to give in to despair. It retells a story from Judaism, from the Talmud, about a child who out-argues the despair of all the adults: when the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, Pharaoh orders every one of their baby boys thrown into the Nile and killed, and an Israelite leader named Amram leaves his wife, reasoning there is no point having children only to see them killed, and other men follow his lead.

It says his young daughter Miriam confronts him, telling him his verdict is even harsher than Pharaoh's because Pharaoh targets only boys while his targets girls too, and that Pharaoh is wicked so his decree may or may not come to pass while Amram is righteous so his certainly will. It says Miriam's probabilistic argument wins, Amram gets back together with his wife and nine months later Moses is born, and Miriam watches over him as he floats on the Nile in a little ark, then makes it possible for Pharaoh's own daughter, who sees the baby and pities him, to adopt him by mentioning a woman who can be his wet nurse, her own mother, so Moses survives and grows up to lead his people out of slavery. The column says that if it were a religious leader giving a sermon this weekend, this is the story it would tell, because even looking at a 50 percent chance of doom the right move is not to give up, which raises the odds to 100 percent, but to act bravely and use every shred of agency to increase your community's resilience and make your desired outcome more likely. It says religion does not have a monopoly on stories of moral courage, and that the historian Ada Palmer recently pointed out we have saved the world many times before, during the Cuban Missile Crisis and when we fixed the ozone layer.

It says religion has comparative advantages, including that its stories have incredible memetic power, having spread across the globe and carrying huge emotional and moral weight, partly because they have been retold for centuries, and it thinks the causation also runs the other way, since these stories survived so long precisely because they encode something true and hard-won. It notes their heroes tend not to be diplomats, like in the Cuban Missile Crisis, or atmospheric chemists, like in the ozone layer crisis, but a little girl arguing with her dad, characters anyone can imagine becoming. It says religion also insists something can always come along and deliver an outcome we did not predict, typically called God, and that even without that language you can benefit from these nudges to remember something the article's text does not finish. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Dario Amodei suggests immersive video games in a private Slack chat to ease AI job losses
stories.Summary:
The Wall Street Journal published a profile of siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei around November 22, 2026. This report claims that Dario Amodei once suggested using immersive video games to reduce political strife. He allegedly made this suggestion to address joblessness caused by artificial intelligence during his time at OpenAI. The report indicates that this specific remark was made within a private Slack chat.

The reported suggestion involves using immersive video games to help people who lose their jobs because of AI. This remark occurred while Dario Amodei worked at OpenAI before he co-founded Anthropic with Daniela Amodei in 2021. NewsBytes reports that this idea was not an official plan for the company. The original Wall Street Journal article is currently behind a paywall.

The Wall Street Journal is responsible for the report, which was relayed by Techmeme and NewsBytes. NewsBytes stated that the video game idea was not an official plan. No direct response from Dario Amodei or Anthropic was found in the reviewed coverage. The exact phrase used in the Slack chat remains unknown to the public.

Critics on X voiced fears that this suggests a permanent underclass kept busy with games. People who fear AI-driven job losses are affected by the implications of this reported remark. Some defenders claim the Journal pulled a brainstorm out of context. Others argue that people need income and meaning rather than distraction.

Dario Amodei has previously warned that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. In May 2025, Axios reported his warning that unemployment could reach 10 to 20 percent. He has publicly called for policy responses to a large labor shock. These public warnings contrast with the reported private chat about coping ideas.

The public is waiting for the full text of the Journal article and a formal response. It remains open whether the remark was a serious argument or a thought experiment. The date of the Slack message and the other participants are not known. Future updates may come from Anthropic newsrooms or Amodei's own channels.

stories.Headline: School board member Nadia Poluhina warns AI replacing junior work leaves beginners without paths to experience
stories.Summary:
Nadia Poluhina, a healthcare business development and strategy leader with a background in finance, healthcare data and AI-enabled innovation who serves as an elected school board member in Minnesota, wrote in The 74 on 2026-11-22 that artificial intelligence is replacing the work beginners do. She said the question is how people develop judgment and experience if AI starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to gain them. Early in her career she built financial models, checked numbers and prepared presentations, and more experienced colleagues reviewed what she had done. She said colleagues sometimes sent her back to reconsider an assumption that looked perfectly reasonable on paper. With enough practice and feedback, she learned that a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision.

She said that work produced two things at once, an output and a more experienced person, and the company received something useful while she gradually became capable of handling more complicated problems. She said AI may change the economics of that arrangement, because junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them. If AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply, a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners, and the savings are immediate while developing experienced staff takes years. She said that even after investing in someone, the employer cannot be certain that person will stay. A company could automate junior assignments now and hire experienced professionals when it needs them, which may be a reasonable decision for one business, but she asked where experienced workers will come from if enough companies make the same choice.

She cited a 2026 study of U.S. software job postings that found an almost 15% decline in junior vacancies relative to senior ones following the public arrival of generative AI in late 2022. She cited a U.S. Census Bureau working paper that reported weaker initial employment and earnings among graduates of college majors most exposed to AI, including junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates. She said neither study proves that AI caused these changes or measures employers' investments in training. She said AI may also help beginners learn faster and some companies may find better ways to train people with it, but we cannot assume every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers. She said AI is also changing how students complete their work, and a polished assignment may tell us little about how much a student understands or could reproduce independently.

She said teachers already work to assess that understanding, and as schools decide how AI belongs in education, preserving opportunities for students to practice and demonstrate what they know independently should remain a priority. She cited a 2025 randomized study of university students in which those assigned to study with ChatGPT scored 57.5% on a surprise test 45 days later, compared with 68.5% among students studying without AI. She said the study was small and measured knowledge retention rather than critical thinking, does not establish what is happening across K, 12 classrooms, and AI used differently may improve learning. She said she worries about students who become accustomed to relying on AI to complete their assignments and then enter workplaces where the routine tasks that once helped beginners learn have been automated. She said employers may expect them to exercise judgment sooner while offering fewer opportunities to develop it through practice and feedback.

She said districts already consult employers about changing skill requirements, and those conversations are valuable, although today's vacancies and lists of required skills can only tell us so much about the work students will encounter several years from now. She said conversations with people working in education and workforce development have made her more aware of how difficult that planning can be, because labor-market information often lags behind changes in actual jobs while educational pathways take years to complete. She said an occupation may remain in demand even as employers change what they expect from someone applying for the first position. She said she would like schools and colleges to look further ahead when reviewing career pathways with employers, and alongside the usual discussion of skills and credentials, to ask how entry-level work is likely to change and where new employees will gain the experience needed to take on greater responsibility. She said there are already internships, apprenticeships and other opportunities to learn through work, and asked whether they are giving students meaningful practice and supervision and whether enough opportunities will be available as traditional junior roles change.

She said we may also need to reconsider how the costs of developing beginners are shared, and schools on their own cannot replace every disappearing step in a professional career. She said she worries especially about young people without professional connections, because a student whose family knows people in an industry may find introductions, advice or informal opportunities to learn, while someone without those connections depends much more on accessible programs and employers willing to provide a first chance. She said that if those opportunities become scarcer, the differences could grow, and students who already face barriers to entering professional careers may find it even harder to gain the experience employers expect. She said that from her school-board perspective she would rather see us examine these questions while we still have time to adjust how we prepare students, and that we may continue to see strong demand for experienced professionals while the opportunities that once helped beginners develop into them become harder to find. She said the experienced people we need years from now will not simply appear when we need them, and someone has to give them the opportunity to become experienced first.

stories.Headline: Zurich and St Gallen warn shared AI logic keeps client risks correlated
stories.Summary:
New research from Zurich Insurance Group and the University of St. Gallen warns that a client can switch AI vendors or deploy multiple systems and still carry the same underlying risk as a competitor using a single provider. The report, titled The AI Resilience Challenge, draws on 50 expert interviews that University of St. Gallen researchers conducted between July and September 2026. It identifies two ways AI-related losses can spread, the first being concentration risk, which arises when many organizations depend on the same provider, model or infrastructure and a single failure causes simultaneous losses across unrelated businesses. The second, correlation risk, comes not from a shared provider but from shared logic, because separate AI systems may draw on similar training data, architecture or decision rules and fail in similar ways without any common outage or identifiable trigger. The report says that connection is behavioral rather than structural and may only become visible through claims, complaints, regulatory action or litigation appearing across separate organizations.

The report says the conventional assumption that using different systems or providers creates independent exposures can break down, so two clients placing their AI risk with separate insurers may still be exposed to the same underlying vulnerability if their systems share training data or decision logic. The Lloyd's Market Association, drawing on a 2025 survey of 144 managing agent respondents, 94% of them underwriters, found boards were ranking AI risk second only to geopolitical risk on their risk registers, and the survey identified a significant absence of underwriting and claims data to price AI exposures, particularly in professional indemnity. The report uses the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage as an illustration of how concentration risk propagates, when a faulty software update crashed approximately 8.5 million Windows devices globally and disrupted airlines, banks, hospitals and broadcasters, with direct losses to US Fortune 500 companies alone estimated at approximately $5.4 billion by technology downtime insurer Parametrix, though that event was not AI-related. Unlike the EU, which has adopted a risk-based legislative framework through the EU AI Act, the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority are applying a principles-based, technology-neutral approach to AI oversight, relying on existing rules rather than introducing AI-specific legislation.

Mario Greco, group chief executive officer at Zurich Insurance Group, said companies need to know where they depend on AI, what can happen when it fails, and be prepared to respond and recover quickly. The report recommends that organizations map AI dependencies beyond direct suppliers to uncover shared points of failure, assign clear accountability for AI decisions, and test whether critical activities can continue when systems fail or need to be overridden. It frames insurability itself as a diagnostic tool, arguing that when coverage terms tighten, premiums rise or reinsurance appetite narrows, those shifts can indicate that exposure is outrunning the evidence available to price it, and that the limits of insurability reveal where broader resilience needs to be strengthened. The Zurich AI Lab, launched in October 2025 as a collaboration between Zurich, the University of St. Gallen and ETH Zurich's Agentic Systems Lab, describes this as a continuing research programme, and the report was produced as a contribution to discussion ahead of the Geneva Summit 2027.

stories.Headline: Nvidia seeks a new CEO to manage AI market shifts and regulatory challenges after Jensen Huang's departure
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was ousted as the chief executive of Nvidia around November 22, 2026, leaving the company to find a new leader. The incoming executive must manage a supervised international business while navigating a complete reorganization of the artificial intelligence equilibrium. This transition occurs as the company faces intensifying export restrictions and multiple investigations into its business dealings with China. The new leader will also need to sustain demand for AI chips amid shifting global trade policies.

The situation requires addressing a federal rule announced last Sunday to close loopholes regarding remote access to advanced servers via overseas data centers. President Donald Trump also stated on Friday that he wants to prevent American companies from building data centers in foreign countries. Legal challenges include a subpoena from the California attorney general and a civil probe by the SEC regarding public disclosures. Furthermore, the FBI is investigating the relationship between Huang and Alice Huang of Megaspeed, while Congress will question Huang and general counsel Tim Teter.

Bill Birmingham, managing director at REX Financial, stated that Chinese chip access is a larger problem than who fills the CEO position. He warned that the AI ecosystem relies heavily on debt markets, which creates a significant risk of a telecom style bust. Birmingham expressed concern over an August plan to mobilize over 500 billion dollars in third party capital through firms like BlackRock and Goldman Sachs. He noted that these commitments were made exclusively by Huang, leaving investors uncertain if the company will maintain them.

Nvidia reported 115.8 billion dollars in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, with data centers generating 107.6 billion dollars. Despite this growth, the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed that the Commerce Department approved 879,868 semiconductor shipments to China between December 2025 and May 2026. Future stability depends on whether neocloud providers can service their debts if compute demand weakens. Investors are now assessing if the supply cycle is running too hot, which could force a self reinforcing pullback in data center construction.

stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks negotiates to buy Israeli AI cyber startup Terra for over $500 million
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks is currently in talks to acquire the Israeli cybersecurity startup Terra Security. This potential deal is valued at hundreds of millions of dollars and could exceed 500 million dollars. The negotiations were reported by Calcalist on November 22, 2026, regarding the AI startup. Terra Security uses artificial intelligence agents to simulate cyberattacks and continuously test corporate defenses. This acquisition would add another Israeli company to the expanding AI security portfolio of Palo Alto.

The deal involves Terra Security, which was founded in 2024 by CEO Shahar Peled and CTO Gal Malachi. Terra operates in the United States and Israel, having raised 38 million dollars in total funding. This includes an 8 million dollar seed round in April 2025 and a 30 million dollar Series A. Felicis led the Series A round, with investors including LAMA Partners, Underscore VC, SYN Ventures, and Dell Technologies Capital. The platform tests cloud infrastructure, internal systems, APIs, corporate networks, web applications, and autonomous AI agents.

CEO Nikesh Arora is responsible for the strategy of acquiring market leaders, even at significantly higher prices. Arora stated that Palo Alto seeks teams and technologies that could become assets worth 5 billion to 10 billion dollars. He expects that businesses will use a combination of proprietary and open-weight AI models for their operations. Arora also noted that the Unit 42 team assessed the security of the Applied Compute platform. The company aims to address security challenges created by the growing use of autonomous AI agents.

The acquisition of Terra would affect the market for automated penetration testing and vulnerability identification. Other affected entities include Beacon Security and Clutch Security, two other Israeli startups Palo Alto is negotiating to buy. Clutch focuses on controlling autonomous agent access, while Beacon provides data for investigating cyber incidents. Applied Compute customers will continue to be served after their 4.5 billion dollar all-stock acquisition closes. This larger deal will allow Palo Alto to offer AI infrastructure in sovereign environments and public clouds.

Terra expanded its capabilities in 2026 to include internal network security and features that actively prevent exploitation attempts. Palo Alto previously introduced an AI service in September using models from OpenAI and Anthropic to test systems. The company has already completed major acquisitions this year, including Koi Security for around 400 million dollars. CyberArk was also acquired in a transaction valued at approximately 25 billion dollars during the same period. Other recent acquisitions include Portkey, Embrace, Console, and Chronosphere to bolster their AI and security offerings.

The Applied Compute deal is expected to close in the fiscal third quarter of 2027 pending regulatory clearance. Yash Patil, the CEO of Applied Compute, will become the co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks. The research team from Applied Compute will join the company to help train proprietary AI models for products. The articles leave open whether the negotiations for Terra, Beacon, and Clutch Security will result in final deals. They also do not state the final purchase price for the potential Terra Security acquisition.

stories.Headline: Harvard study finds US data centers get 54% of power from fossil fuels and emit 25.7 million tons of CO2 a year
stories.Summary:
The articles report that Anthropic’s initial public offering netted over $81 billion on its first day of trading, making it one of the largest IPOs in history, and that the five-year-old company now has a net worth of $1.3 to $1.7 trillion depending on accounting. Brian Merchant wrote the bloodinthemachine.com article on November 22, 2026. A Harvard University study published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability examined 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025. The study found that 54% of the power used to run the largest United States data centers came from fossil fuels. Those data centers emitted an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually, almost as much as Bolivia or Denmark.

The data centers used almost 2 percent of United States electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of United States carbon dioxide emissions. A report said Anthropic’s upcoming data center projects could emit nearly 20 megatons of CO2-e a year. The Australian climate researcher Ketan Joshi’s report, State of AI Climate Impact 2026, concluded that the AI boom is already worsening greenhouse gas emissions and is potentially emitting more across its lifecycle than all international aviation. McKinsey counts say the AI industry is on track to generate more emissions than the coal mining industry or global shipping and aviation. AI is already emitting twice the greenhouse gases of the global aluminum industry.

Joshi’s report said Anthropic has never disclosed any energy, emissions or environmental data of any kind. In July 2025, Anthropic suggested the United States government explicitly set a target for the construction of fossil gas power, promising to begin preconstruction design work for natural gas plants by the end of 2026. In May 2026, it was revealed that Anthropic is leasing capacity from the SpaceX Memphis facility, and one analyst estimates that 1 in 2 Anthropic queries is served by that fossil-fueled facility. In November 2026, Anthropic struck a $3.4 billion deal with OnePWR, a fossil fuelled turbine manufacturer, for 1.7 gigawatts of generators, which the Financial Times called the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab. That transaction is more than three times the amount spent by xAI on its Memphis turbines and would emit approximately 6 MTCO2-e per year, equivalent to adding 1.8 million fossil-fuelled cars to the road.

In November 2026, Anthropic posted a job listing paying up to $405,000 per year for a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada. In a set of data centre community commitments, Anthropic promises much of the new power generation for its data centres will be natural gas, which it says can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places it is considering. In its S1 form filed before the IPO, Anthropic declared several fossil-fuel related risks, such as exposure to fossil fuel price volatility or competition with other customers for fossil gas, and dismissed renewables as too high in cost. Meta released its latest sustainability report this week, revealing that its emissions rose 45% since last year, and said it was rethinking its climate goal of net zero carbon emissions by 2030.

Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that xAI’s Colossus data center in Memphis was not among the 403 facilities studied. Emily Atkin wrote at her climate newsletter HEATED that the study gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution data centers emit. Atkin argued that the study does not count data centers that use gas turbines on-site, that equipment keeping servers from overheating leaks heat-trapping refrigerants, and that methane can escape from wells and pipelines before gas reaches a power plant. Atkin argued that as many as 250 data centers may be absent from the count as of 2025.

The study examined electricity consumption and carbon emissions of the data centers, estimating how much electricity each used and how much CO2 the grid in that part of the country would release to generate that power. The study was led by a team of researchers from Harvard University. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a permitting reform bill designed to overturn key environmental protections in the name of making it easier for developers to build energy infrastructure and data centers, passed the Senate. The AI industry directed its trade groups and lobby to partner with the fossil fuel industry to push BAAJA through Congress before the data center-skeptical class of 2027 Democrats arrive.

BAAJA is an assemblage of provisions the fossil fuels industry has been after for years, including rollbacks on local governments. The articles also mention Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia and failed comeback bid, and the digital infrastructurapocalpyse of the last week. The New York Times headline went “Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries, Study Reveals.” More to follow.

stories.Headline: Professors revive oral exams to counter generative AI tools
stories.Summary:
Joe Cruz, a Williams College professor, wrote about the return of oral exams on November 22, 2026. He describes how professors are revisiting these tests to counter generative AI tools. These tools can produce credible college level writing on almost any topic. Oral exams reveal what students know and teach them to think quickly. This method prevents students from offloading their writing assignments to AI.

In one philosophy seminar, students wrote a traditional paper of 10 to 15 pages. They also had to justify their arguments for 45 minutes in the office. The University of Glasgow used oral exams from 1451 until the middle of the 19th century. Swarthmore College established an Honors Program in 1922 that uses rigorous oral exams. The Rice Center for Teaching at Williams College hosted a panel on this in 2024.

Joe Cruz says oral exams are a way to inspect what students know. He believes explaining and revising ideas in real time is a form of critical thinking. Cruz stated that students should learn to think both with and without AI. He noted that conversation can reveal arguments that are obscure in written form. He argued that written assignments have become too dominant in American undergraduate education.

Some students felt anxious because they had little experience with these types of exams. Others felt frustrated but eventually rallied to provide a clearer formulation of their ideas. Students whose written sentences were inelegant could sometimes articulate ideas with agility and insight. However, oral exams can introduce biases regarding confidence, fluency, or a student's accent. These tests also sacrifice the protection of anonymous grading used for written work.

The Blackstone Chair from 1775 at the University of Glasgow reminds us of this history. Oral exams dominated medieval universities and remained central to academic life for many centuries. Cambridge transitioned to written exams in the 18th century, while Oxford followed in the 19th. Tibetan Buddhist monasteries still use oral debate, as seen in the Geshe Lharampa degree. Thinkers like Isaac Newton and Immanuel Kant were educated in traditions using oral disputation.

Professors can mitigate bias by using common questions and standardized rubrics from medical school. Scaling these exams is difficult for institutions without the faculty ratios of Williams or Swarthmore. Cruz spent about 11 hours of meetings for a seminar of 14 students. The articles leave open how other institutions will handle the time requirements for scaling. They do not state if other colleges will officially adopt these policies.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted colonoscopy cuts costs and improves outcomes in England simulation study
stories.Summary:
A study by Curtis-Gretton and colleagues, published in BMC Digital Health in 2026, found that AI-assisted colonoscopy improved outcomes and reduced costs in a simulated population of symptomatic patients undergoing investigation for suspected colorectal cancer in England. The researchers developed a patient-level simulation model to assess the long-term clinical and economic implications of introducing the GI Genius system into the diagnostic pathway. The analysis focused on symptomatic patients with suspected colorectal cancer in England and adopted a National Health Service and Personal Social Services perspective over a lifetime horizon. Model inputs were informed by the NAIAD trial, which investigated the effect of GI Genius on adenoma detection rates compared with conventional colonoscopy.

The base case analysis indicated that GI Genius-assisted colonoscopy was cost-saving, generating an estimated £69 reduction in costs per person alongside a gain of 0.046 quality-adjusted life years. These improvements were primarily attributed to increased adenoma detection and a subsequent reduction in colorectal cancer incidence. Additional scenario analyses explored uncertainties relating to colonoscopy sensitivity, outcomes among patients initially undiagnosed, differences between experienced and less experienced endoscopists, and the overall costs of implementing GI Genius. Findings remained broadly consistent with the base case, with no substantial changes to estimated costs or quality-adjusted life year outcomes.

Despite the favourable base case findings, the probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated that GI Genius was cost-effective in 53% of simulations at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000 per quality-adjusted life year gained. Researchers attributed this uncertainty to the relatively small differences in quality-adjusted life years between the two groups. Consequently, even minor variations in outcomes across individual simulations produced considerable fluctuations in the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. The findings suggest that AI-assisted colonoscopy could offer both economic and clinical benefits when investigating symptomatic patients with suspected colorectal cancer, although the considerable uncertainty identified in the analysis highlights the importance of interpreting the cost-effectiveness estimates cautiously.

stories.Summary:
Sam Liang co-founded the artificial intelligence notetaker Otter.ai in 2016 after experiencing significant language barriers while studying in the United States. He grew up in China during and after the Cultural Revolution, a period when the government rationed food for the population. To understand his professors, Liang recorded every lecture on a Sony Walkman and replayed the tapes repeatedly. This personal struggle with communication eventually provided the inspiration for the technology he developed.

Before starting his own company, Liang completed a PhD at Stanford under David Cheriton, who famously provided a check for 100,000 dollars to the founders of Google. He contributed to the development of the blue dot feature that serves as the backbone for Google Maps. Additionally, Liang achieved early entrepreneurial success by selling his first startup company to Alibaba. These experiences combined his academic training in science with practical applications in the global tech market.

stories.Headline: San Francisco AI millionaire Rich says wealthy friends should pay for dinners and vacations but refuses loan requests
stories.Summary:
The AI boom is creating many millionaires and billionaires in San Francisco during the year 2026. This trend has caused a shift in social dynamics among friends with very different income levels. Some people now hold high positions and possess millions of dollars in equity from their companies. Others have become cofounders who have received acquisition offers from the company known as Google. These changes make relationships awkward and raise questions about fairness and the ethics of mooching.

The company Anthropic had a recent IPO that valued the business at about 1.5 trillion dollars. This company employs around 2,500 people in San Francisco who may have friends with lower incomes. One local millionaire, who is called Rich, says he spends money on cars and international travel. He and his spouse also have a growing collection of homes and wear very nice clothes. Rich believes that wealthy people should pay for dinner and vacations to avoid slummy experiences.

Rich says that it is unreasonable to make friends pay when he has much more money. He believes that paying for others should come from generosity rather than a sense of obligation. Rich stated that he does not give loans because people often do not pay them back. He thinks asking for loans for stupid business ideas is common and very annoying to him. He believes that honesty and open communications are really important for maintaining these mixed income friendships.

People who are not wealthy may feel weird about splitting checks for expensive meals like omakase. Some friends are tempted to ask for loans to start their third startup idea since January. Rich says that making a lot of money can be a really isolating experience for people. He notes that some wealthy people may forget what things cost and need to be called out. He suggests that friends can suggest fun ways to spend money or solicit charitable donations.

The articles describe a situation where former friends now have unfathomable wealth and different lifestyles. Some people used to take road trips to Pismo Beach and stay in cheap motels together. Now, some of these individuals can afford to buy houses in the city of San Francisco. Rich had a middle class upbringing before he had a successful career and became very wealthy. He once almost bought a place in France after friends suggested it as a fun idea.

Friends should continue to be honest and give their nouveau riche companions grace during this time. They should not try to become closer friends just because someone has become loaded with money. Rich suggests that it can be cute to congratulate a friend on becoming unfathomably wealthy. The articles leave open how specific individuals will handle the tension of these new wealth gaps. They do not say if these friendships will survive the long term financial divide.

stories.Headline: Bayesline founders say AI-driven coding demands faster decisions and candid feedback
stories.Summary:
Sebastian Janisch and Misha van Beek became accidental roommates in New York years before they started a company together, when van Beek expected to stay for a couple of weeks and the COVID-19 pandemic turned the visit into six months. They rotated between the apartment's only bedroom and its couch while each worked from the small kitchen island, and the close quarters exposed how different they were. Janisch was the orderly future chief executive, while van Beek jokingly calls himself complete chaos. The experience taught them that cofounders do not need matching work styles as much as they need enough trust to make decisions quickly, especially as AI speeds up software development.

The two now run Bayesline, a New York fintech that makes portfolio-analytics software helping investment managers understand risk and evaluate performance, and it recently closed a $4 million funding round after earlier backing from Y Combinator. They encourage their staff of about half a dozen people to challenge anyone's ideas, regardless of title or tenure, so the team can move fast. Their mantra, as Janisch describes it, is to be hard on content and soft on people. He said the expectation of candid feedback applies from the company's first employee to a recently hired software engineer in his 20s, and he wants that engineer to feel comfortable telling the chief executive that his code makes no sense. Janisch said giving that kind of feedback to a chief executive is something he would not have done early in his career in his native Germany.

When the founders disagree, they may spend 20 minutes talking an issue through before reaching a consensus, and if they hit an impasse, the founder with deeper expertise makes the decision while the other steps aside. Janisch said a decision is better than no decision, adding that you can correct it afterward if it is wrong and often it is not. He said the need to make a quick call and at times to disagree and commit has only grown as AI lets a small team produce more code, which means there is more work to review. Van Beek said Bayesline hires people who are good with AI but whose experience is still in the old world, so they can judge whether the AI is doing a good job. The founders do not automatically treat tenure as the best measure of judgment, and when the young engineer recently suggested new tools for handling the growing volume of code to review, they looked into the proposal and adopted it.

stories.Headline: Tencent releases independent safety assessments for its Hy4 AI model
stories.Summary:
Tencent Holdings collaborated with an international group of artificial intelligence safety organizations to evaluate the risk levels of its newest open-weight model. This partnership took place before the official release of the model to address growing global concerns regarding biological misuse and AI-assisted cyberattacks. The company published an extensive eighty-two page safety report on Friday, November 22, 2026, to share these findings. This initiative represents the first time a leading Chinese technology firm has disclosed working with independent third-party evaluators for such a process. The evaluation focused specifically on the open-weight version of the model known as Hy4 to determine its potential for harm.

The assessment required the participation of the Chinese start-up Fangcun AI and the Israeli-American firm Alice to ensure an objective review. These safety firms concluded that the model possesses only limited hacking capabilities and presents a low risk of deception. Furthermore, the independent testers found that there is a low risk of the system experiencing a loss of control. The Shenzhen-based company is responsible for the development of the model and the subsequent disclosure of the safety results.

Tencent stated that its primary objective is to create artificial intelligence systems that are increasingly capable while remaining reliable and trustworthy. The company emphasized that safety must be a core component of the development process for its advanced models. By sharing the report, the firm aims to demonstrate its commitment to building secure and safe technology for its users. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta launches Muse AI agent and posts 28% revenue growth
stories.Summary:
Meta rallied 6.55% to close at $653.69, driven by strong Q2 advertising revenue and the introduction of Muse, its new consumer AI agent. TradingKey author Arslan Ali wrote the analysis, dated Sep 10, 2026. Meta opened at $653.69 with a latest completed close nearly matching the chart supplied of $653.47. The stock approached the $658.01 to $659.05 resistance level after a series of higher highs and higher lows. The rally was attributed to the introduction of Muse, Meta's AI agent that can work across email, travel, payments and other applications.

Muse is available as a free product and two service tiers at $20 and $100 per month for heavy use. Meta delayed the product from an earlier planned launch in the hopes of improving safety, and now uses isolated virtual machines combined with system monitoring for some activities. Q2 revenue was $60.80 billion, up 28% year over year, and Family daily active people rose to 3.60 billion. Ad impressions rose 14% and the average cost for each ad rose 12%. Capital expenditures were $31.08 billion in Q2 and operating cash was $31.86 billion, with free cash flow dropping to $784 million.

Management still expects to spend $130 billion to $145 billion on capital expenditures for fiscal year 2026, with total expenses expected in the range of $165 billion to $169 billion. For Q3, management still expects revenue in the range of $61 billion to $64 billion with no formal guidance for a downward adjustment. In Q2, costs and expenses increased 55% to $42.03 billion, largely attributable to legal and severance charges. Operating income fell 8% to $18.78 billion, and operating margin decreased to 31% from 43%. Reuters reported that internal testing uncovered several reliability and security issues, including cases in which the agent exposed or mishandled private information.

Australia has proposed legislation in which social networks with a significant user base must provide users the choice to control their algorithmic feeds, including a choice to view content from accounts they follow. The 1-hour structure is bullish, with higher highs and higher lows, and price trading well above the trend line at around $596.90 and the moving average. stories.Headline: Dragos researchers uncover data theft and security flaws in cheap AI inference services
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Dragos uncovered major security flaws in AI services between July and November 2026 using two million test requests. Attackers stole credentials and keys undetected for several months, including hundreds of AWS keys harvested from a single provider. Some attackers used an AI tool called ARTEX to search S3 storage and establish persistent access to systems. Other actors on residential connections in France used intercepted passwords to attempt SSH logins.

The investigation identified compromised providers including Novita, Phala, and Together, while others like AtlasCloud and StreamLake acted as intermediaries for MiniMax models. OpenRouter responded by removing three providers and revoking Zero Data Retention approval for 125 endpoints. A Chinese AI lab accessed secret test URLs in over half of the requests, even those routed through US providers. One US provider continued crawling a test URL for two months, and another link appeared on Feishu in Beijing and Shanghai.

Chief Research Officer HD Moore stated that users must decide where their prompts go or the lowest price will decide for them. Dragos warned companies against sending credentials to intermediaries and recommended using canary tokens to detect data theft. OpenRouter emailed affected users to warn them that third parties might have read requests sent to MiniMax models. The researchers urged organizations to control their routing and verify privacy settings to avoid these vulnerabilities.

These findings mirror a pattern where intermediaries sit between users and developers to view requests and pass data to third parties. An analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed similar behavior in Chinese proxy services routing requests to models like Claude. While it is unclear if the providers share personnel, both systems allow data to reach Chinese actors despite privacy promises. The researchers suggest that the current supply chain for cheap AI inference creates significant risks for user data.

Articles.Title: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

stories.headline_source: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

stories.Headline: US ecommerce decision-makers trust AI more for demand forecasts than purchasing decisions
stories.Summary:
Fifty-eight percent of US ecommerce decision-makers in the Linnworks Market Survey 2026 would trust AI to generate demand forecasts, while just 37% would trust it to make purchasing decisions. Linnworks released the survey on Nov. 12, 2026, and OnePoll ran the online poll from July 28 to August 4, 2026. OnePoll surveyed 500 ecommerce decision-makers, 250 in the US and 250 in the UK, selected at random from its panel. Each respondent has a say in choosing operations and fulfillment software at a business making most of its sales through ecommerce, with annual revenue of approximately $1.3 million to $130 million. Every figure in the release comes from the 250 US respondents, and the results are unweighted.

Among US respondents, 62% report an AI assistant already acts for them, for example by sending messages or updating records, but only 37% would trust AI to communicate with suppliers. Forty-three percent cite poor integration between systems as a barrier to greater automation, against 37% who name cost, and 21% name integration complexity as the most common barrier to wider AI adoption, while 10% cite unclear return on investment. For 64% of respondents, AI ranks among the most important factors in picking operations software, and 46% expect AI and automation included as standard rather than paid for as an add-on. Fifty-three percent describe AI as scaled or broadly adopted across their organization, 34% have grown more cautious because of data and security concerns, and 3% say their business needs no more automation anywhere.

Linnworks CMO Hilary Smith said ecommerce businesses have stopped debating whether to take up AI and are now deciding which tasks they are willing to let it lead. Smith said AI can help teams make smarter calls about demand, stock levels and daily operations, and added that companies still have to be able to trust the data those decisions rest on. Smith said the next stage of AI adoption is not about handing over control but about giving teams the right intelligence to act faster and make better decisions. Linnworks says it has been in business for 20 years, serves 4,000+ brands and retailers and connects inventory, orders, warehouses and listings. Linnworks builds the kind of software these respondents buy.

On Oct. 19, Grafana Labs released findings from its State of Observability 2026 report, covered by David Ramel for Redmond, and Grafana worked with research firm ETR to poll 300 senior IT and engineering decision-makers overseeing observability spending. ETR ran the survey in June 2026, limited it to director level, vice president level or above, and drew 150 respondents from the United States and 50 apiece from Japan, Latin America and Western Europe. In that survey, 85% of IT leaders are comfortable with AI doing read-only investigation, 84% with AI recommending a fix, 56% with AI making code or configuration changes and 52% with fully autonomous remediation, while 50% are comfortable with AI deploying production changes. Grafana Labs co-founder Anthony Woods said having AI diagnose a problem is meaningfully different from allowing it to change something in production.

Reliability is the top barrier to adoption at 26%, followed by regulatory or compliance constraints at 23% and customer trust at 21%, and explainability and a proven track record of accuracy tied at 45% each as what would make respondents trust AI more. Over the past 12 to 18 months, 47% of US respondents have moved into new sales channels or marketplaces, 41% name inventory accuracy and stock synchronization as a top area where added automation would help, and 57% now use EDI with their trading partners. In research published Nov. 18, 2025, MIT Sloan Management Review drew on a global survey of more than 2,000 respondents plus executive interviews and reported agentic AI reached 35% adoption in two years, with another 44% of organizations planning to deploy it soon. The same research put traditional AI adoption at 72% after eight years and generative AI at 70% in three, and said vendors were adding agentic capabilities as features, so organizations put agentic AI in place before building a strategic management framework for it. The MIT Sloan authors, Sam Ransbotham, David Kiron, Shervin Khodabandeh, Sesh Iyer and Amartya Das, name supervision versus autonomy as one of four tensions in adopting agentic AI, and write that traditional oversight models assume either full human control or complete automation.

The MIT Sloan figures come from a global survey across industries, not from ecommerce sellers, so the link to the Linnworks findings is a parallel in how features arrive, not a measure of ecommerce adoption. The researchers argue competitive benefits will come not from early access to agentic AI but from superior organizational design around it. The Linnworks release leaves open what buyers expect the AI in that software to do, and the gap between the 58% who would trust AI to generate demand forecasts and the 37% who would trust it to make purchasing decisions is the number to watch in any follow-up research. Whether approval thresholds can be set separately for forecasting, reordering and supplier messages, and whether the system will show the stock data and logic behind a purchase recommendation so a buyer can check it, remain open questions. Whether inventory reconciles across every channel and trading partner before the forecast runs is also left open.

Articles.Title: Just 37% of US ecommerce decision-makers would trust AI to make purchasing decisions

stories.Headline: Developer fits 367K-parameter AI question-answering model Tiny 2.1 onto a floppy for 486DX and Pentium PCs
stories.Summary:
A developer has squeezed an AI language model onto a floppy disk for 486DX and Pentium PCs, according to a Tom's Hardware report dated November 22, 2026. The project is called Tiny 2.1, and it is a question-answering transformer with 367K parameters. It needs 540KB of memory to run and speaks its answers through the PC speaker. The report describes the machines it targets as stalwarts of the 486DX and Pentium era.

The model is a question-answering transformer, which means it takes a question as input and produces an answer rather than generating open-ended text. Its 367K parameters and 540KB memory footprint are the two figures the article gives for its size. The floppy format is the delivery method that lets the software run on the older hardware. The PC speaker is the only output channel mentioned for its spoken answers.

The article names no individual developer and gives no direct quotes, so responsibility for the project rests with the unnamed dev behind Tiny 2.1. The report does not say what license the software carries or how it is distributed beyond the floppy. It also does not describe the training data or the process used to shrink the model. Those details are absent from the article as published.

The context is the growing effort to run AI models on constrained hardware, though the article does not frame it in those terms beyond the floppy and the old PCs. What happens next is not stated, and the report gives no release date, price or availability details. No benchmarks or accuracy figures for the model appear in the article. More to follow.
