stories.Headline: Economist proposes taxing automation investments that displace workers to fund Social Security and Medicare
stories.Summary:
A letter to the editor in the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette on November 22, 2026, at 4:00 a.m. EST addressed tax worker displacement due to artificial intelligence. The writer described an economic transformation made possible by the development and rapid improvement of artificial intelligence. The writer said we have not yet seen much of what AI promises to deliver. The writer said an enormous amount of investment is being made on the expectation that AI will generate more than enough profits to justify those investments.

The writer said many people are worried that those profits will come at their expense and have reason to be worried. In 2019, Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo published an article entitled “Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor” in the Journal of Economic Perspectives. Their analysis suggests that since 1987 there has been a marked increase in the displacement of labor by automation relative to the increase in employment due to automation. Consequently, the way investments in automation of tasks has been distributed has contributed to a declining share of the nation’s income accruing to labor. The writer said this was not inevitable.

Firms found it more profitable to invest in automation that displaces workers than in machines and computer applications that enhance productivity of existing workers and create demand for new workers, in part because they can save the costs of employer-paid fringe benefits and taxes employers must pay into the Social Security and Medicare Trust Funds. The writer is professor of economics, emeritus, at the University of Pittsburgh. The writer said when workers are displaced, they typically find new employment that pays lower wages and fringe benefits. The writer said this is a loss for those workers and a loss of revenue for governments from wage taxes that support Social Security and Medicare. The writer said these are real costs of automation, but they are not counted by the investing firm as part of their investment.

The writer said a tax on investments that displace workers would correct the bias and direct automation away for job displacement and towards job creation. A second letter to the editor in The Gila Herald on November 19, 2026, at 16:52:24Z was from Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona. Diegel wrote that he read with interest the Nov. 18 article on Senator Mark Kelly’s new framework to protect Americans from the most advanced AI models. Diegel wrote that Senator Kelly is right about the problem and that companies should not grade their own homework.

Diegel wrote that self-regulation has failed and that oversight that only arrives after an incident is not oversight. Diegel wrote that Kelly’s proposed fix still misses the core issue because it governs the model, not the action. Diegel wrote that Kelly’s framework calls for a rulebook of hazard levels, independent examiners embedded at AI companies to review safeguards as models are built, and testing and liability before and after deployment. Diegel wrote that none of that stops a consequential action at the moment it happens.

Diegel wrote that a test can pass, an examiner can sign off, and a company can disclose a risk, and the AI system can still make the transfer, delete the file, or send the data. Diegel wrote that the danger is not only how smart a model is but what authority it has been given to act. Diegel wrote that a safe model with write access is dangerous and a dangerous model with no authority does nothing. Diegel wrote that his team and he are building Pulpo in Arizona.

Diegel wrote that governance has to sit before execution, as a narrow, one-use permit for that one specific action, with durable evidence afterward. Diegel wrote that no permit means no governed effect and that anything else is monitoring dressed up as prevention. Diegel wrote that he respects Senator Kelly’s intent and his service. Diegel wrote that if we want to protect Americans, we need to govern what AI is allowed to do, not just how it is tested or watched.

stories.Headline: Florida House speaker Sam Garrison creates committee to examine AI risks
stories.Summary:
Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison created a new committee to examine artificial intelligence risks on November 17, 2026, in Tallahassee. This legislative forum will address how governments should respond to technology that advances faster than the rules meant to govern it. The move follows a change in House leadership and renewed debate over the oversight of evolving digital tools. Garrison placed these technology issues among the priorities for the legislature during its two year term. The committee provides a setting for examining AI rather than announcing immediate restrictions on its use.

The Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee replaces the Information Technology Budget & Policy Subcommittee established under former Speaker Daniel Perez. This standing committee focuses on policy and oversight, while the Appropriations Committee will now handle all budget decisions. Its jurisdiction includes artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure security, digital privacy, data governance, and digital identity. Michelle Davila was named staff director of the committee on November 9 for the 2026 to 2028 term. These changes were outlined in a memorandum issued by Sam Garrison on November 5.

Speaker Sam Garrison stated that technological disruption could unfold over two or three years instead of a century. He warned that AI might improve so rapidly that humans struggle to understand or control the technology. Garrison urged lawmakers to address these risks, though he did not outline specific legislation during his opening speech. He previously expressed support for federal leadership on AI regulation in April 2026. The speaker compared the current situation to the Industrial Revolution to explain the urgency of the matter.

Governor Ron DeSantis supported an AI Bill of Rights to create consumer protections for personal data and chatbot interactions. This proposal, Senate Bill 482, passed the Senate on March 4 with 35 votes in favor and two against. However, the House rejected that bill on March 13, 2026, and later rejected Senate Bill 2-D on April 29. Former Speaker Daniel Perez favored federal oversight of artificial intelligence rather than state level action. These failed bills left broader consumer protections for AI users unresolved in the state.

Florida's Digital Bill of Rights took effect on July 1, 2024, to establish privacy protections for certain large businesses. Separately, the State Board of Education adopted AI and educational technology rules on September 16, 2026. These rules cover public school districts, charter school boards, and Florida College System institutions regarding student privacy. School districts must finalize their own AI policies by July 1, 2027, for the next school year. Federal officials currently recognize 16 critical infrastructure sectors, including energy, communications, and financial services.

Interim committee weeks begin on November 30, 2026, and the next regular legislative session starts on March 2, 2027. Lawmakers will use this time to review proposals and debate potential changes to technology rules. The articles leave open which specific companies or technologies might face new requirements under future laws. It remains unsettled how state responsibilities will overlap with the national rules currently being examined by Congress. No specific statewide AI law follows automatically from the creation of this new committee.

stories.Headline: Jerry James explains how to set up local AI using Unsloth Desktop and home hardware
stories.Summary:
Jerry James wrote a guide on November 22, 2026, about setting up local AI. He used Unsloth Desktop to host models on his own home hardware. This process allows users to create a private ChatGPT replacement on a PC. The setup takes about 10 to 15 minutes excluding download times. It enables a whole household to use the AI over a network.

The system requires a Windows PC with a graphics card and Unsloth Desktop. James used an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM to run Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization. Other options include RTX 5060, 3060, 5070, 5060 Ti, 5070 Ti, 5080, 3090, 4090, or RX 7900 XTX. Models mentioned are Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b, Gemma 4 26B, Qwen3-Coder-30B, Qwen3.6-35B, and Inkling 2 Mini. Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 17, 2026.

Jerry James is responsible for the guide and the specific hardware configuration. He stated that cloud providers act like appliance businesses for routine tasks. He claimed that OpenAI and Anthropic drop model quality in their latest versions. James said he wanted to avoid usage limits for research and coding tasks. He chose Unsloth Desktop because he liked the name and lacked subscriptions.

The author claims that cloud experiences are convenient but have ballooning costs. He notes that privacy concerns make moving to local hardware a good case. Users with different VRAM capacities are affected by which models they can run. Those with 8 to 12GB VRAM can handle smaller 9B to 12B models. People with 32GB VRAM can comfortably run 27B to 35B models.

Quantization shrinks models by compressing weights to fit on consumer graphics cards. This process trades some accuracy for faster speeds and lower memory usage. Mixture of experts models run only a few billion parameters for each token. Unified memory on Macs or specific PCs allows for larger model sizes. Inkling 2 Small is a 594B model requiring a 256GB Mac Studio.

Users can now share their local AI via the LAN access setting. They must set a remote password and share the provided network address. The PC must remain on for other home users to access it. Future guides will cover performance, tunneling, and setting up local agents. The articles leave open how to access the local AI across the internet.

stories.Headline: Hancom launches Nomadian AI workforce platform in the US and pursues AWS Marketplace listing
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Hancom has begun commercializing Nomadian, an AI workforce platform in which AI agents carry out corporate tasks, in the US market, the company said on Nov. 23. Hancom held a presentation on its US commercialization strategy for Nomadian at the Crowne Plaza hotel in Seattle on Nov. 16 local time and spent two days discussing cooperation with Amazon Web Services. The event drew Eugene Kawamoto, AWS director of Amazon Bedrock and AI go-to-market, along with partners including VisualFeast, ClickIt and TaskUs, as well as local media. Hancom also hired Bill Fanning as senior vice president and head of US business development for Nomadian, and he will oversee business development at the US subsidiary Hancom is in the process of establishing.

Nomadian is built on Amazon Bedrock, AWS's fully managed generative AI service, and Hancom is pursuing a listing on AWS Marketplace as well as indirect sales through managed service providers. In a 3D virtual office, users can build an organization by deploying Ara, an AI team leader, and 11 AI team members assigned by role and responsibility, and when a task is assigned, Ara divides the work among team members for market and competitor research, marketing content creation and sales proposal writing. Users can check progress and review and edit reports and proposals produced with Hancom's 36 years of accumulated core document technology, and the AI team learns the user's working style over time. Hancom plans to release a beta version in December and a global commercial version next March, targeting 10,000 user companies each month from December through February, up to 30,000 in total, and 10 to 15 local partners by next March.

Fanning pitched the ability to build and run an organization with AI before hiring actual employees as Nomadian's core competitive edge, saying the idea is to hand tasks such as customer response and project planning to an AI team so founders can focus on growing the business. He said what the company is strategically focused on right now is the partnership with AWS, and that based on Hancom's organizational foundation and capabilities he will make sure Nomadian delivers results quickly in the US. Hancom aims to secure partners including the US Small Business Development Center, startup mentoring group SCORE, accelerators and university startup centers, with a goal of 3 to 5 network partners before the beta launches in December. It will select 500 beta companies with the best results as "Nomadian 500," supporting them with prize money and mentoring, and will run advertising in major US cities to recruit beta waitlist members.

Hancom held a separate session with AWS working-level staff and met Mark Relph, AWS director of data and AI partners, on Nov. 17 to discuss commercialization strategy. Once listed on AWS Marketplace, AWS customers will be able to subscribe to Nomadian through their existing accounts, and Hancom is also considering an indirect sales model in which managed service providers bundle Nomadian with their own services. The pricing system is being designed to reflect AI workload while letting customers predict costs, and Hancom plans to refine the pricing based on usage data gathered during the beta and apply it to the commercial service next March. The company cites the rapid growth of solo entrepreneurs and small operators in the US as another reason for the market opportunity, and it expects that as more small businesses use AI, Nomadian's potential customer base will grow with them.

stories.Headline: Mark Gurman reports Apple Siri layoffs hit older infrastructure while annual release cycle limits AI response
stories.Summary:
Apple's recent Siri layoffs affected employees working on the assistant's older infrastructure rather than its newer AI systems, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. Gurman reported the layoffs in his latest "Power On" newsletter, published on Sunday, November 22, 2026. The MacRumors article carrying his report was published that day at 12:29 pm PST and written by Hartley Charlton. Gurman said employees have yet to notice a major difference in how Apple operates despite efforts to accelerate development. He added that Apple faces growing competition from AI developers that update their models and services far more frequently than Apple's annual operating system cycle.

Within software engineering chief Craig Federighi's organization, Apple follows an internal release calendar labeled A through G, with engineering work tied to specific software versions and launch windows. Depending on the release, the roadmap and features for a major operating system update are largely determined by late summer or early fall of the preceding year. Gurman argued that this structure leaves Apple with limited flexibility to respond to competitors' breakthroughs during the subsequent development cycle. Siri's multistep control of Apple apps is expected to launch in December, with third-party app support following in 2027. Apple is reportedly developing a more advanced AI agent, but Gurman does not expect it to arrive before late 2027.

Gurman criticized Siri's slow responses, limited third-party integration, and seemingly worsening dictation. He warned that rival agents could become difficult to abandon as they accumulate users' preferences and connected accounts. He said Apple's reputation for privacy and deeper platform access could help it compete. Gurman said employees have yet to notice a major difference in how Apple operates despite efforts to accelerate development and spread significant releases throughout the year. He argued the release calendar structure leaves Apple with limited flexibility to respond to competitors' breakthroughs.

Commenters on the MacRumors article responded to Gurman's report, with one saying agile software development is dead. Another commenter said it is ironic to suggest Apple prioritizes responding at all and argued Apple seems content to cede the AI space completely. A third commenter said the only way around this is to decouple Siri AI from operating system releases, as Google can update its apps without waiting for major versions. Another commenter said Apple already does six or seven significant releases throughout the year and that what Gurman asks for would mean substantially less planning and work on the software. One commenter said Apple's releases are largely tied to hardware launches and that competing would require restructuring teams, governance and ways of working.

Gurman's report appeared in his "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg. MacRumors' guide lists iOS 27.2 features as including Siri AI improvements, Suggestions in Messages, and an Apple Music rebrand. The article's tags include Bloomberg, Mark Gurman, Siri Guide and Siri AI. The report follows Apple's efforts to accelerate development and spread significant releases throughout the year. Apple follows its internal A through G release calendar within Federighi's organization.

Siri's multistep control of Apple apps is expected to launch in December, with third-party app support following in 2027. Gurman does not expect Apple's more advanced AI agent to arrive before late 2027. The articles leave open which employees were laid off and how many. They leave open when the more advanced AI agent will actually arrive. They leave open whether Apple will change its A through G release calendar.

Articles.Title: Gurman: Siri Layoffs Spared Newer AI Systems, But Problems Persist

stories.headline_source: Gurman: Siri Layoffs Spared Newer AI Systems, But Problems Persist

stories.Headline: FACT Coalition policy director urges US to end offshore tax breaks in AI supply chain
stories.Summary:
Zorka Milin, policy director at the FACT Coalition, published an article on November 23, 2026, in Bloomberg Tax arguing that the US must break the AI supply chain’s addiction to offshore tax breaks. The article says Anthropic’s record-setting initial public offering underscores enormous investor enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence. It says the company’s newly released financials have revived a question that has hung over the industry for years about whether companies like Anthropic and OpenAI will ever turn a profit. It says that even if Anthropic turned profitable tomorrow, it might be years before it owed any tax. It says that if the company became hugely profitable, history suggests those profits might simply be moved offshore to avoid US tax.

The article says the AI supply chain has three broad parts: hardware, cloud computing and training data, and foundation models and customer-facing applications. It says Micron reported that its operations in Singapore cut its total tax bill by nearly $6 billion, the largest savings from a tax haven yet seen in newly expanded tax disclosures. It says Micron reported only about 5% of its global profit in the US in 2026, even though nearly 70% of its revenue comes from US customers. It says Broadcom reported saving about $2.7 billion through tax incentives in Singapore and Malaysia in fiscal 2025, before accounting for US taxes on foreign income. It says Marvell, Qualcomm, and KLA reported savings of $396 million, $195 million, and $135 million, respectively, from Singapore last year.

The article says Microsoft saved $3.5 billion last year through its Irish operations, and Oracle saved more than $1 billion through Bermuda, Malta, and Switzerland. It says Dell and IBM also reported hundreds of millions of dollars in savings from tax havens, and Apple reported more than $5.2 billion in tax benefits from Ireland and Singapore. It says 10 companies deeply embedded in the AI supply chain used offshore tax havens to shave more than $20 billion off their tax bills last year. It says the US taxes the foreign income of its multinationals at 12.6%, well below the statutory 21% rate for domestic income. It says Singapore’s implementation of the global minimum tax shaved more than $9 billion off Micron’s projected savings from tax incentive arrangements in the country.

The article says the US has not adopted the OECD standard agreed to by more than 140 nations, so it collects none of the new revenue the minimum tax has unlocked. It says Broadcom’s financial statements indicate that weaker US rules for foreign income recouped only around half of the $2.7 billion the company saved from Singapore and Malaysia in 2025. It says the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income taxes income from sales abroad at a preferential rate of 14%. It says FDII saved Google nearly $4 billion last year and Nvidia more than $4.2 billion, while Qualcomm reported more than $1.6 billion in benefits across 2025 and 2026 and AMD and KLA each saved hundreds of millions last year. It says defenders of FDII say it raises revenue by drawing taxable income back to the US.

The article says recent proposals to tax AI companies directly include taxing energy consumption or compute, or denying certain corporate tax subsidies to AI data center investments. It says economist and UCLA Law School professor Kimberly Clausing proposed raising the corporate tax rate to 27%, tightening tax rules for foreign income, and repealing the FDII export subsidy, raising nearly $4 trillion over the next decade. It says international tax reforms alone could raise as much as $1 trillion, much of it from hyperscalers. It says Congress failed the same test after the internet and social media booms. It says voters are increasingly anxious about AI, opposed to new data centers, and eager to see the largest corporations finally pay their fair share.

The article says tightening US rules for foreign income by raising the rate and aligning more closely with the OECD standard could bring in hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue. It says the 15% global minimum tax is already clawing back billions in savings that many American companies once enjoyed in low-tax countries. It says the article does not necessarily reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group, Inc., the publisher of Bloomberg Law, Bloomberg Tax, and Bloomberg Government, or its owners. It says Milin leads international tax policy and other transparency priorities at the FACT Coalition. It says readers interested in writing can review author guidelines and submit pitches to Insights@bloombergindustry.com.

Articles.Title: US Must Break AI Supply Chain’s Addiction to Offshore Tax Breaks

stories.headline_source: US Must Break AI Supply Chain’s Addiction to Offshore Tax Breaks

stories.Headline: Vietnam businesses adopt AI faster but few integrate it into operations
stories.Summary:
Vietnam’s adoption of artificial intelligence is rising among enterprises, but its integration into business operations remains limited because of barriers in workforce skills, data and organisational capacity, experts said, according to a report published by Asia News Network on November 23, 2026. The International Labour Organization said about 11.5 million jobs in Vietnam, equal to 20.8 per cent of total employment, were potentially affected by generative AI in 2024. The Vietnam Private Economic Report 2025, released earlier in the year by the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry, included a survey on AI adoption in the workplace. Citing that survey, Dr Luong Minh Huan, director of the chamber’s Enterprise Development Institute, said AI adoption among private enterprises remains at an early stage. Of more than 3,500 private enterprises surveyed, 76.2 per cent have no AI use, 12.5 per cent use AI at a low level, 8.8 per cent report moderate use and 2.5 per cent use AI at a high level.

A study titled Unlocking Vietnam’s AI Potential 2026, released in September at Amazon Web Services Cloud and AI Day Hanoi, found that 26 per cent of Vietnamese businesses, or around 245,000 enterprises, had adopted AI, up from 18 per cent in 2025. Among those that had adopted AI, about 61 per cent were still experimenting, 23 per cent had developed comprehensive AI strategies and only 8 per cent had integrated AI into their business processes. The International Labour Organization reported that an AI-enabled vision system recently introduced by Hanoi Industry Trading Investment JSC cut inspection time from 20 seconds to five seconds and raised defect-detection accuracy from 95 per cent to 99 per cent, with 10 workers replaced by three senior high-tech supervisors. An internal AI assistant at VietinBank helped reduce document search time by 95 per cent and the time needed to prepare meeting minutes by 70 per cent, according to a bank report, while Techcombank’s Joule AI assistant helped reduce requests for HR policy support by 28 per cent over three months.

Huan said these cases do not represent the broader business community, and that more enterprises using AI does not necessarily mean AI is integrated into operations. Do Ngoc Ha, an official from the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Finance, said measurement is important for assessing AI efficiency at work, and that the national AI strategy sets a target for the AI economy to account for 6 per cent of GDP. He said Vietnam currently has no official comprehensive measurement of the overall picture of AI adoption and its impact, and that only a number of small-scale studies have been conducted so far. The National Statistics Office is conducting various surveys and creating opportunities to add questions on AI adoption to existing surveys on labour and businesses, he said.

Ho Thi Kim Ngan, deputy head of the Labour Relations Department at the Vietnam General Confederation of Labour, suggested surveys of workers to capture their opinions and experiences with AI adoption, saying working hours may become longer and work intensity may increase, placing workers under greater stress and pressure. Nguyen Tien Huy, director general of the chamber’s Office for Sustainable Business Development, said AI adoption does not automatically lead to higher productivity, and that technology delivers results only when businesses identify the right problems, redesign workflows, standardise data, adjust management practices and prepare their workforce. ILO Country Director for Vietnam Sinwon Park said the organization believes AI should be adopted in a human-centred way, with productivity gains going together with better jobs, respect for rights at work and opportunities for workers to learn and adapt. She said AI policy cannot be only about technology, and that labour laws, employment policies, occupational safety and health, social protection and international labour standards remain important as workplaces change.

Articles.Title: AI adoption rises in Vietnam, but integration remains limited

stories.headline_source: AI adoption rises in Vietnam, but integration remains limited

stories.Headline: UKRI awards 20 Turing AI fellowships worth over £39m to researchers
stories.Summary:
UK Research and Innovation awarded 20 Turing AI fellowships backed by more than £39 million, EdTech Innovation Hub reported on 23 November 2026. Seventeen researchers will apply AI in fields from economic history to clean energy, the article said. Three others will move to UK universities to advance core AI research. The Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council is delivering the awards through two schemes. The article said the projects are backed by government funding.

The Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowships give researchers three years to apply AI in their own fields. The five-year Turing AI Global Fellowships bring researchers from overseas to work on how AI systems learn and interpret language and social behavior. The 17 Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowships began in October 2026. The three Global Fellowships start in 2027. UKRI is funding researchers to use AI to analyze more than a million handwritten wills, detect rare events in dark matter experiments and study underground conditions for cleaner energy projects.

At the London School of Economics and Political Science, Professor Neil Cummins will use AI to examine handwritten wills for evidence of how people lived and worked over centuries. The University of Oxford’s Professor Jocelyn Monroe will use the search for dark matter to develop AI systems that can identify exceptionally rare events. Dr Roisin Buckley at the University of Glasgow will develop AI tools to help researchers better understand underground and seabed conditions for energy and infrastructure projects. At King’s College London, Dr Thiago Sogo Bezerra will combine AI with new detector technology to improve neutrino measurements, with potential applications in nuclear reactor monitoring and safety. Professor Charlotte Deane, Executive Chair of EPSRC, said the fellowships would give outstanding researchers the freedom and support to push the boundaries of AI itself while also applying it in new ways across a wide range of disciplines.

Professor Jonathan May will move from the University of Southern California to the University of Edinburgh to study how AI interprets intent in language. Professor Denny Wu will move from New York University and the Flatiron Institute to Oxford to develop a mathematical basis for predicting how deep learning behaves at scale. Professor Roi Reichart will move from Technion, Israel Institute of Technology, to the University of Cambridge to study how AI models social interaction and emotion. UKRI says earlier fellows have helped train AI researchers, launch startups and shape policy. The article named the universities of Edinburgh, Oxford and Cambridge as hosts for the global fellows.

The article said the 20 fellowships support AI research and its application across disciplines at UK universities. It said the awards are backed by government funding and delivered by EPSRC through the Pioneer Interdisciplinary and Global schemes. It described the Pioneer fellowships as giving researchers three years to apply AI in their own fields. It described the Global fellowships as five-year awards bringing researchers from overseas. It said the three Global Fellowships start in 2027 and the 17 Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowships began in October 2026.

The article did not say what funding individual fellows will receive or how the more than £39 million will be divided. It did not name the remaining fellows beyond the seven researchers it described. It did not give the dates on which the Global Fellows will take up their posts in 2027. It did not say which overseas institutions beyond those named will send fellows. It did not say what happens after the three-year and five-year fellowship periods end.

stories.Headline: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang warns superintelligence may be near and urges keeping humans in control
stories.Summary:
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang warned on November 23, 2026, that the world may already be entering the era of superintelligence. He issued the warning in a lengthy post shared on the social media platform X, formerly known as Twitter. Wang said next year could prove critical in determining whether increasingly powerful AI systems benefit humanity or lead to outcomes difficult for humans to control. He pointed to the reported proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, as a milestone. He described the achievement as an intellectual accomplishment unlike anything humanity has seen before.

Wang said the development marks a turning point similar to December 2024, when models began acing the American Invitational Mathematics Examination with o3. He said the hardest AIME problems are much harder in terms of sheer intellectual difficulty than problems advanced engineers and business people solve day to day. He said the remaining gaps for models to greatly surpass humanity in every field are no longer intelligence, but domain-specific know-how, plumbing and experimentation. He said AI will likely become the greatest contributor of progress across nearly every field, vastly outperforming the best humans. He said models will be smart enough to automate all AI research and improve themselves in a clearly superhuman way.

Wang said it is hard to imagine humanity keeping control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement. He said it is equally hard to imagine humanity maintaining control with superintelligence 1,000 times smarter and more capable than humans in every field. He said the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, so the urgent work is safety, alignment and security. He criticized what he called lazy thinking in the AI industry, the idea that superintelligence is inevitable and the only problem is how to do it safely. He said society should not be okay with a handover of society to AI and should build technology where all humans have greater agency and empowerment.

Wang said he grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, and that many physicists would agree the discovery of the atomic bomb is a homework problem compared to the Riemann Hypothesis. He said the Riemann Hypothesis may be the most intellectually demanding problem humanity has ever devised, which some of the most brilliant humans over the past 150 years have dedicated their lives to. He said his professors at MIT would have said the hardest intellectual problems in nearly every major field are easier than the Riemann Hypothesis, albeit with other challenges such as experimentation, data and feedback loops. He said the progress across other domains over the past two years has been immense, with coding nearly solved, extremely powerful cyber capabilities and strong agentic capabilities.

He said the implications are enormous and nearly every field could be accelerated at a pace beyond what humans can understand or monitor. Wang said he has spent much of his life in math and science. He said the math community has not fully digested the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. He said the models have become general-purpose useful aides.

He said the hardest AIME problems are an extracurricular activity for teenagers. He said he strongly believes a positive future is possible but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the default path. Wang said humanity must remain actively involved in shaping its future rather than enabling society to be handed over to machines. He said the industry must depart from the default path.

The article does not say when or how the Riemann Hypothesis was reportedly proved. The article does not say what actions Wang proposes beyond safety, alignment and security. The article does not say whether Meta or other companies have responded to his post. The article does not say what Wang expects to happen next beyond his call for a different path.

Articles.Title: Meta’s Chief AI Officer warns society against handing control to AI

stories.headline_source: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang warns superintelligence may be near and urges safety work

stories.Headline: Greg Abel says Berkshire Hathaway can fund AI power needs through its utilities and energy businesses
stories.Summary:
The article, published by The Globe and Mail on November 22, 2026, was written by Motley Fool and appeared at 6:35PM CST. It says Berkshire Hathaway's next big AI bet could be hiding in plain sight. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is not exactly seen as an artificial intelligence play. It says the company may have more exposure to this emerging technology than you realize. The article states that the company's large utility and energy operations present opportunities for AI-related investment.

The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is usually classified as a finance business. It says the company is really a massive conglomerate with businesses including insurance, utilities, energy, manufacturing, housing, and retail. In Greg Abel's first annual letter as CEO, he reported that the company had 51 non-insurance operating businesses. In a previous letter, former CEO Warren Buffett said the company owned 189 operating businesses. The article says the definition of an operating business is probably responsible for the two different numbers.

The article states that Greg Abel is the CEO of Berkshire Hathaway. It says his acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison Home for $8.5 billion suggests he is not going to suddenly shift directions. The article states that Greg Abel noted at the start of 2026 that infrastructure built for hyperscalers and data centers must be paid for by those customers. It says he said this infrastructure must reflect the risks tied to step-changes in long-term demand. The article states that former CEO Warren Buffett long focused on acquiring boring businesses that were well run and attractively priced at the time of purchase.

The article states that the company's utility operations provide the electricity that powers AI. It says the energy business helps supply the natural gas that lets utilities, and increasingly AI companies, generate electricity. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway could easily afford to buy a technology business with its cash hoard of more than $370 billion. It says Chevron, a longtime holding in Berkshire Hathaway's stock portfolio, has agreed to build a power plant that will use Chevron-produced natural gas to supply dedicated power to data centers. The article states that data center operators appear increasingly willing to pay for infrastructure built for them.

The article states that it would be exciting if Berkshire Hathaway went out and bought a giant U.S. utility such as NextEra Energy. It says it would also be exciting if the company bought a large pipeline business such as Enterprise Products Partners. The article states that Greg Abel probably would not target companies of that scale. It says the CEO could certainly afford to buy smaller players in either sector. The article states that both the utility and midstream sectors are capital intensive.

The article states that utilities own massive power plants that take years to build and require huge sums of money. It says midstream companies are no different, with their pipelines, storage, refineries, and transportation assets. The article states that it is not unusual for a utility or midstream company to have multi-billion-dollar capital investment plans extending as far as five years into the future. It says Berkshire Hathaway could make very large capital investments within its existing operations, and that this is probably the most likely outcome. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is unlikely to start buying up AI technology businesses.

Articles.Title: Berkshire Hathaway's Next Big AI Bet Could Be Hiding in Plain Sight

stories.Headline: Etsy lets third parties train AI on seller artwork as artists close shops in protest
stories.Summary:
Etsy updated its terms of service to allow AI training using artwork posted on its platform. This policy change caused an uproar among independent artists and small business communities. Some artists with tens of thousands of followers closed their shops in protest. These creators shared their decisions through posts on X and Instagram. The new terms of use go into effect on December 16.

The updated language appears under Section 5, titled Your Content, in the terms of use. It allows Etsy and third party partners to develop, train, test, and improve machine learning technologies. This follows clearer restrictions on AI use that the company released in October. The older terms, effective through December 15, contained no mention of artificial intelligence. The new policy grants a worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, and perpetual license to use content.

James Ossman, the vice president of customer operations, addressed the changes in a November 16 blog post. He stated that Etsy does not use content to train models designed to copy original work. Ossman claimed the company does not claim ownership over the creations of its sellers. He said the goal is to connect unique items with buyers. He argued that these broad rights are necessary to keep the platform going.

Some artists claim the terms allow Etsy to train generative AI on their artwork. One post with nearly 100,000 likes alleged that Etsy can resell data to third parties. Many vendors rely on the marketplace to make sales and feel their art is being scraped. These creators are affected by the potential for AI to replace their creativity. They worry that staying on the platform means their art belongs to the company.

Etsy previously stated it does not claim ownership over shop names, profile pictures, or listing photos. The company uses content to resize listings for its mobile app and translate descriptions. It also uses seller content to feature listing photos in marketing campaigns. The company trains models to identify fraudulent accounts and provide tailored recommendations to buyers. It also builds AI-powered tools to help sellers run their businesses more efficiently.

Etsy has not clarified if it uses generative AI to create advertisements from listing photos. The company has not responded to requests for further clarification on these specific practices. While the terms mention opt-out rights, the privacy policy shows no way to opt out of training. United States users can only opt out of the sale of their personal data. Courts are still deciding if it is legal to scrape copyrighted content for AI.

Articles.Title: Explaining Etsy's new AI policy that has prompted artists to flee the platform

stories.headline_source: Explaining Etsy's new AI policy that has prompted artists to flee the platform

stories.Headline: Senate and House urged to pass No Fakes Act banning nonconsensual A.I. replicas of voices and likenesses
stories.Summary:
Three years ago Tom Hanks posted a warning to his millions of fans after a dental plan ran an A.I.-generated ad featuring a younger version of the actor, and he had nothing to do with it. It is not just celebrities who are being impersonated by A.I., because voice actors who were paid a few hundred bucks for recordings they were told were for internal research later found clones of their voices for sale online. A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements. Whether all this is legal is right now an open question, but the opinion article argues it should not be. The article says Hollywood does not need America's leaders to devise a new concept for new circumstances, and that they need to extend and enforce the rules that already exist.

The use of Americans' faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short, that you need to get permission and you need to pay for the use. That principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century, and whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person's voice or likeness, famous or not. The bill was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and there is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year. It is one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support, and the article says the Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature.

That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era, according to the piece. The writer comes to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner who runs a global talent agency, and part of that job is helping clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to A.I. companies. The writer says the agency regularly negotiates those deals and that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans. Some A.I. companies already follow many of its measures voluntarily, the article states. The article does not say what happens next beyond the push to pass the bill before the end of the year.

Articles.Title: Opinion | Tom Hanks Got A.I.-Cloned. Here’s How We Stop It From Happening to You. - The New York Times

stories.Headline: Vietnam urges schools to teach national identity through Vietnamese and AI
stories.Summary:
Báo Thanh niên published an article on 21/11/2026 about educating national identity in the age of AI, carried by Vietnam.vn at 02:14:48Z. The article states that artificial intelligence is changing the way people learn, communicate, and acquire knowledge and culture. It states that English is promoted as a second language in schools, and that education about national identity faces new demands. It states that educating about national identity not only preserves traditional values but also helps the younger generation develop independent and creative thinking based on Vietnamese culture. It states that this helps the younger generation confidently integrate into the global community.

The article states that AI can translate multiple languages, explain cultural differences, and create texts, music, and paintings. It states that technology is increasingly bridging language and geographical gaps, enabling people to access a global wealth of knowledge. It states that national identity is present not only in the traditional ao dai dress, folk songs, festivals, or glorious historical accounts, but also in the Vietnamese language, historical memory, manners, community spirit, compassion, and aspirations for nation-building. It states that identity is not an immutable system of values but continues to develop through reception, creation, and adaptation to the times. It states that schools must help students understand the meaning of tradition, apply positive values to their lives, and be creative based on national culture.

The article states that education in national identity cannot simply stop at imparting knowledge, memorizing historical events, or organizing formal cultural activities. It states that uncreative preservation can lead to the stagnation of tradition, and that embracing the new while forgetting one's roots can cause people to lose their cultural anchor. It states that identity education needs to combine both requirements, helping young people understand where they come from while equipping them with the capacity to dialogue, learn, and contribute to the world. It states that Vietnamese is the foundation and English is the bridge, and that developing foreign languages must go hand in hand with strengthening Vietnamese language proficiency and understanding of national culture. It states that Vietnamese is not only a means of communication but also an environment for shaping thinking, preserving cultural memories, and expressing the Vietnamese soul.

The article states that the ability to use Vietnamese accurately, reason logically, and express independent thoughts is a crucial foundation for lifelong learning. It states that English helps learners access scientific and technological knowledge and human culture, expand cooperation, and introduce Vietnam to the world. It states that the two languages are not opposed but complement each other. It states that the history of Hue National High School from 1896 to 1945 offers a thought-provoking perspective, and that within the French educational environment, with French as the dominant language, the school still contributed to training many generations of patriotic students.

It states that these students included Ho Chi Minh, Tran Phu, Ha Huy Tap, Le Duan, Pham Van Dong, and Vo Nguyen Giap, along with intellectuals and artists such as Dang Thai Mai, Xuan Dieu, Huy Can, Te Hanh, Nguyen Van Thuong, and Tran Hoan, and prominent scientists such as Ta Quang Buu, Ton That Tung, Dang Van Ngu, and Hoang Tuy. The article states that this demonstrates that embracing external knowledge does not equate to losing national identity. It states that language is a tool, knowledge is a resource, while patriotism, character, and social responsibility are formed through the interaction of education, family, living environment, and each individual's awareness. It states that in the age of AI the goal is not just to train people who are proficient in foreign languages, but to cultivate citizens with a strong cultural foundation, independent thinking, the ability to engage in equal dialogue with the world, and the capacity to apply human knowledge to develop the country.

It states that AI necessitates a revolution in the way national identity is taught, and that students can use technology to explore local history, digitize heritage, learn about folklore, compare cultures, and introduce Vietnamese values in multiple languages. It states that in literature classes students can use AI to compare English translations with the original Vietnamese texts, identifying cultural nuances that are difficult to convey between the two languages. The article states that AI can also compose poetry, prose, and music, and pose questions about the differences between machine-generated products and human creations. It states that the Hue City High School Literature Olympiad exam for the 2026-2027 school year raises the issue of creating literary works in the AI era, by placing Xuan Dieu's poem "Going by Boat" alongside poems created by ChatGPT that also write about time.

It states that in history class students can utilize digital resources, verify information, and create products that introduce the nation's history, and that interdisciplinary projects open up opportunities to build online museums, make films about heritage, and create cultural products aimed at an international audience. It states that it is crucial that AI becomes a tool to support critical thinking, not a means to replace human learning, and that copying AI's answers may provide information but does not necessarily lead to deep understanding. It states that schools need to help students learn to ask questions, verify information, identify biases, evaluate products, and take responsibility for their creations. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Educating about national identity in the age of AI. - Vietnam.vn

stories.Headline: AI surveillance software creates false movement narratives by inventing journeys between camera gaps
stories.Summary:
Burak Oktenli wrote an analysis on November 23, 2026, about AI surveillance risks. He explained how multi-camera tracking can create false narratives of a person's movements. This happens when software joins authentic clips into a continuous route despite gaps. The system may invent a journey that the cameras never actually recorded. Such errors can occur when cameras lose sight of a subject.

The author mentions Hong Kong activated AI facial-recognition in its SmartView network on 16 November. The Metropolitan Police reported a 2026 pilot using live facial-recognition on existing street infrastructure. In India, AI-assisted face matching at a Delhi protest led to a legal dispute. The Metropolitan Police September 2025 report recorded 2,077 alerts and ten false classifications. Six people were approached after those false alerts, but none were arrested.

Oktenli says that high scores on existing evaluations do not prove reliability in real deployments. He argues that detection and facial recognition are different tasks from multi-camera tracking. The author claims that a strong result on one task does not establish reliability on others. He suggests that systems must flag uncertainty when they are guessing a person's path. He believes that human corrections must propagate to every downstream report before actions are taken.

The US Federal Trade Commission alleged a false match led to searching an 11-year-old girl. This 2023 Rite Aid case showed how innocent people experience consequences before corrections occur. Researchers Ergys Ristani and Carlo Tomasi noted that appearances vary with angle, light, and occlusion. They stated that similar-looking people may be joined into one route by the software. A single person may also be split into multiple tracks by the system.

The US National Institute of Standards and Technology excluded cross-camera tracking from its Face in Video Evaluation. MOTChallenge assesses tracking within a single camera and assigns fresh identifiers when people reappear. The European Union AI Act restricts certain law-enforcement uses of real-time remote biometric identification. These rules provide safeguards for exceptional uses in publicly accessible spaces. The author notes that HOTA metrics improve measurement but do not eliminate deployment testing.

Procurement should start with end-to-end trials using consenting participants and independent ground truth. Tests must count incorrect joins and broken tracks separately under ordinary working conditions. Reviewers should deliberately reject mistaken links to test if corrections reach all searchable records. Organizations must limit the retention and unnecessary dissemination of surveillance footage. The articles leave open how non-biometric tracking will be regulated under the AI Act.

stories.Headline: OX Security finds AI agents follow unverified instructions from tools with no identifiable owner
stories.Summary:
OX Security said its research team analyzed 542,207 open-source software components between July and October 2026, using its early-warning system OX.Radar to track four ecosystems: npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills. The company said researchers then investigated the suspicious components the system identified. According to OX Security, the findings point to a new attack path and a growing verification gap, in which instructions are becoming an attack path alongside code execution. The company said attackers can now manipulate an agent into taking actions with permissions it already has, and that security teams cannot verify what their agents connect to.

OX Security said AI agents connect to MCP servers, load Agent Skills and pull packages from public registries, then act on what those components tell them, often with access to files, credentials, development tools and enterprise systems. The company said many agents are taking orders from strangers, meaning tools with no identifiable owner that run code no one can verify before it is already in the environment. It said the attack surface is expanding from code that runs to instructions that agents follow. OX Security compared the situation to the old warning against plugging in a USB drive found somewhere, saying agents break that rule every day.

Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security, said companies are giving AI agents access to critical systems while relying on trust signals built for a different era. He said the problem is not just what a tool can do, but who controls it, what code it actually runs and what instructions it can give an AI agent. Ziv said a new model for software trust is needed. The company said it published a full report on the findings.

OX Security said the research covered npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills, and that its researchers investigated the suspicious components OX.Radar identified. The company presented the results as evidence of a growing verification gap rather than a single incident. It did not say in the article what specific malicious components were found or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Plug and Pray: Your AI Agents Are Taking Orders From Strangers

stories.Headline: Geoff D argues that people should work with AI rather than just prompt it
stories.Summary:
The article argues that people should spend less time learning to prompt AI and more time learning to work with it, and it makes this case through two experienced creative professionals who use similar AI tools but get dramatically different results. One of them gets predictable ideas, polished presentations and the occasional useful shortcut, while the other gets sharper thinking, unexpected perspectives and work that moves forward at a completely different pace. The article says most conversations about AI still treat it like a sophisticated vending machine, where you put the right instructions in and get the right output. It acknowledges that AI can write, summarize, research, generate ideas and produce work at remarkable speed, but calls that a very limited view of what it can contribute.

The article says creative and strategic thinking rarely happens in a straight line, because ideas evolve, assumptions get challenged, perspectives shift and the first answer is rarely the best one. It says the real opportunity is moving beyond isolated requests toward something more cumulative, a way of working where context, critical thinking and intellectual exchange make the collaboration increasingly useful. It states plainly that AI does not magically become smarter with every conversation, but that the combination of human judgment, AI capabilities and relevant context can create something more effective than either working in isolation. It says much of the conversation around AI focuses on efficiency, doing more, working faster, saving time and producing more content, which it calls valuable but only half the opportunity for strategists, marketers and creatives.

The article says AI should not simply help execute an idea but should be capable of contributing to the thinking behind it, by questioning assumptions, exploring alternatives, connecting seemingly unrelated observations, making an argument stronger or explaining why it does not hold up. It says sometimes that means thinking with us and sometimes it means doing substantive thinking for us, and that the opportunity is not choosing between better thinking and faster execution but combining both. It warns that the more personalized an AI experience becomes, the easier it is to confuse familiarity with intelligence, and that an AI which consistently tells you what you want to hear could become the world's most efficient echo chamber. It calls that a serious risk for creative and strategic work, where the most valuable contribution is often the one that challenges the original thinking, and says a good collaborator should sometimes make you realize your favorite idea is not very good.

The article says that as AI becomes more powerful and accessible, the competitive advantage may increasingly come from the quality of the human-AI collaboration rather than simply the technology itself. It says the best model will still matter, and so will the skills of the person using it, but that knowing how to get an answer and knowing what to do with that answer are two very different things. It closes by suggesting the question is not whether you are good at prompting AI but whether you have developed a way of working that allows AI to tell you something you did not want to hear. The article is by Geoff D. and was updated on November 22, 2026.

Articles.Title: Stop Prompting AI. Start Working With It.

stories.headline_source: Stop Prompting AI. Start Working With It.

stories.Headline: Law firm leaders propose a single budget to fund junior associate training as AI takes over first drafts
stories.Summary:
A Bloomberg Law commentary published on November 23, 2026, by Kristina Bakardjiev, a former partner and current director of emerging AI at Cozen O’Connor, and Vincent R. McGuinness Jr., the firm’s president and managing partner, argues that law firms must decide who pays to build judgment in junior attorneys now that agentic AI performs the document review, summarization and first drafts that once justified billing first- and second-year associates at a multiple of cost. The authors point to Fortis Advisors LLC v. Krafton in the Delaware Court of Chancery, where a South Korean gaming company’s CEO asked ChatGPT how to avoid a $250 million earnout owed to the founders of the studio behind Subnautica, locked the founders out of the publishing platform and fired them for cause, and the court admitted records of the AI-assisted strategy as evidence of pretextual intent, reinstated the studio chief and extended the earnout. The parties settled the case this June, and the authors say a privileged call to a lawyer could have exposed the flaw in a plan that depended on the acquired company failing.

The authors describe the economic exposure firms face, noting that juniors carry the lowest realization rates, that 82% of associates leave within five years and that BigHand puts the cost of each third-year departure near $1 million. They say firms’ spending on technology tools and associate training is diffuse and duplicative, with recruiting, professional development, knowledge management, innovation and legal technology each holding separate budgets and claims on the same lawyers’ hours, and they propose a single professional advancement budget. They trace pricing history, noting that firms closed engagements with a single line for professional services rendered until hourly billing became more standard after the US Supreme Court struck down minimum fee schedules in Goldfarb v. Virginia State Bar in 1975, and they say nearly three-quarters of US law firms now offer alternative fees while AI-native entrants publish flat per-document prices for work once assigned to first-years. They suggest a transparently negotiated flat fee for associate-level work, reasonable under Model Rule 1.5 and consistent with Virginia Legal Ethics Opinion 1901, might keep AI-driven efficiency inside the firm.

The authors recommend tying every approved tool to a specific use case and realistic practice problem, using AI simulators as aviation uses flight simulators, and they cite the 2026 Citi Hildebrandt Client Advisory reporting that 86% of large firms plan to grow associate ranks through 2027, only 35% intend to grow first-year classes and 25% expect AI to change their leverage model, up from 9%. They propose making supervision a compensated bridge role for senior associates and junior partners, with billable-hour credit capped near 100 hours a year and tied to outcomes clients recognize such as satisfaction, delivery against milestones and fewer revisions. They suggest financing this from a reinvestment pool built on measured realization gains, using 24 months of billing data to baseline first- and second-year time, tracking AI use with task codes and running a control group against a test group.

In their example, 20 junior associates billing $13 million and losing about $2 million to write-downs show a realization rate near 85%, and improving realization by five points returns $650,000 while reducing departures from four a year to three avoids roughly $250,000 in hard replacement costs. Against that, they say five supervisors each earning up to 100 credited supervision hours at a collected rate of nearly $600 represent roughly $300,000 in forgone collections, assuming they already meet their hourly targets, leaving a net pool of about $600,000, or $30,000 per junior associate, and even a pessimistic three-point gain recovers $390,000, leaving a pool near $340,000, or $17,000 per associate. They also urge returning some recovered time to the lawyers carrying the load, and they say a cross-functional steering group should own any AI pilot, start in two practice groups, report quarterly and expand to groups clearing realization thresholds while experimenting with fixed fees for AI-streamlined matters, restructuring toward fewer execution hours and a stronger supervisory middle tier if the pilot works and running a post-mortem if not.

stories.Headline: The Information asks whether the AI bubble is deflating and puts Dell and Workday on deck
stories.Summary:
Dell and Workday were named in a headline asking whether the AI bubble is deflating, with the two companies described as on deck, according to an article published by The Information on November 22, 2026. The article carried a timestamp of 06:00:00Z on that date and appeared under the headline asking if the AI bubble is deflating. The piece was published by The Information, a technology business publication, and its headline paired Dell and Workday with the question about the AI bubble. The article's text as provided consists of the headline, a promotional line about early access to a Black Friday sale offering savings on two years of a subscription, and site navigation and marketing material. No further details about Dell, Workday or the state of the AI bubble appeared in the article text.

The article text lists sections and features of the publication, including The Information 50 for 2026, The AI Inflection Index, the Enterprise Software Startup Takeover List for 2026, The Next GPs for 2026 and 2025, The Executives Leading the Data Center Race, The Rising Stars of AI Research, Leaders of the AI Shopping Revolution, Org Charts, the Generative AI Takeover List, the Generative AI Database, the AI Chip Database, the AI Data Center Database, the Tech IPO Tracker, the Tech Sentiment Tracker and the Gigafactory Database. It also names special projects such as The Information 50 Database, the VC Diversity Index, the Enterprise Tech Powerlist, Deep Research, TITV, Tech Finance Charts and Events. The text includes sign-in and subscribe prompts, links to X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Threads, Instagram, an RSS feed, careers and help and support, and an about Pro section. It invites readers to search, find and engage with others who are serious about tech and business, and to follow and join discussions about tech, finance and media. It also offers in-depth insights in seconds through a tool called Ask Deep Research.

The article as provided does not name any person who did anything in connection with Dell, Workday or the AI bubble, and it contains no statements from executives or other officials about either company. It gives no numbers, dates or names tied to Dell or Workday beyond the two company names in the headline and the publication date of November 22, 2026. The only figures in the text are the subscription offer of up to $500 in savings on two years of The Information and the years attached to the publication's lists and projects. Because the text carries no account of what Dell or Workday did or said, there is no responsible party to identify and no paraphrase of comments to report. The article provides no context about the AI bubble beyond the question in the headline, and it does not say what happens next for Dell, Workday or the wider market.

It does not state whether either company was scheduled to report results, make an announcement or appear at an event, and it gives no indication of when any such development might occur. The publication date of November 22, 2026 is the only timing the text supplies, and nothing in it describes consequences or follow-up. The remaining content is the publication's promotional and navigation material, which does not address the headline's subject. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Beijing pushes AI from scientific innovation to industrial use to drive economic growth
stories.Summary:
Beijing is accelerating the transition of artificial intelligence from scientific innovation to industrial use to drive economic growth. By September 24, 2026, the city had completed the filing process for 319 large generative AI models, which is the highest total in the country. The core AI industry in Beijing reached approximately 450 billion yuan in 2025 and included more than 2,500 related companies. These two figures represented about 40 percent of the respective national totals for the industry.

The city aims to become the world's leading AI city during the opening year of the 15th Five-Year Plan. Officials intend to expand the value of the core AI industry to more than 1 trillion yuan within two years. Beijing E-Town established the first facility in the country for producing embodied AI training data based on real-world environments. This facility covers more than 30 scenarios and houses over 150 mainstream robots in 40 configurations to reach a goal of 1 million hours of high-quality data.

The Beijing Shuimu Dongfang Medical Robotic Technology Innovation Center uses a manufacturing and services model to accelerate the commercialization of research. This platform has handled nearly 600 client engagements and helped 22 products obtain registration certificates from the National Medical Products Administration. LY iTech's Beijing Embodied Intelligence Super Factory plans to produce 10,000 units in 2026 and 500,000 units by 2030. These initiatives are designed to turn technological progress into a tangible source of economic growth for the region.

Articles.Title: AI's 'Beijing Chapter': From Innovation to Economic Growth

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce RISA framework to protect tool using AI agents from prompt injections
stories.Summary:
Researchers introduced Runtime Integrity Safeguards for Agents, known as RISA, to protect tool using large language model agents. This software engineering framework was presented in a study published on November 22, 2026. It addresses runtime integrity problems where indirect prompt injections propagate into side effects or user responses. The system mediates three specific lifecycle boundaries including action authorization, observation incorporation, and response release. RISA coordinates these enforcement efforts through shared provenance, memory, and taint state.

The framework integrates source aware authorization, external resource checks, fact preserving quarantine, response screening, and structured recovery. It was tested using the fixed AgentDojo full 629 attack manifest with DeepSeek V3.2 as agent and guard. RISA reduced the attack success rate from 69.95 percent to 0.16 percent in these specific tests. User Utility under Attack increased from 37.36 percent to 55.17 percent during the same evaluation. Three alternative agents achieved attack success rates between 0.00 percent and 0.32 percent with the guard.

The authors state that runtime policy enforcement, provenance, and recovery are complementary mechanisms for trustworthy tool using systems. They provided the RISA runtime implementation and benchmark integration code in a public GitHub repository. The researchers claim that the system effectively mediates boundaries to prevent untrusted observations from affecting planning context. They noted that blocked action recovery succeeded in 16.0 percent of affected trajectories during testing. The study positions these software engineering tools as essential for securing autonomous agents in production.

Security leaders ask what agents are actually doing and on whose authority they act. CrowdStrike reported responding to over 90 customers after poisoned npm packages hijacked AI tools in August 2025. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report warns that adversaries may compromise trusted agents to create malicious insiders. Some experts argue that guardrails alone cannot contain agents that have broad standing access to production. Affected users include developers and business users who turn on agents that inherit their personal privileges.

The articles explain that agents behave non deterministically and may take paths that the requester did not intend. Adversaries can break out from initial access in as little as 27 seconds, causing damage before human intervention. NIST design tenets call for separating an agent's reasoning from the systems that decide its allowed actions. Traditional identity providers were built for human access rather than for autonomous software operating on endpoints. Agents currently often lack verifiable identities and instead use borrowed human credentials or shared service accounts.

Future efforts should include discovering every sanctioned or unsanctioned agent operating across a fleet. Organizations are encouraged to apply least privilege so agents can only perform specific jobs for limited durations. Experts suggest using open standards like SPIFFE to give every agent its own verifiable identity. The articles leave open how to fully integrate these identity controls with existing corporate security infrastructures. They also leave open the specific methods for maintaining records that sit entirely outside an agent's reach.

Articles.Title: RISA: Engineering runtime integrity for tool-using large language model agents

stories.Headline: Peking University researchers develop AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the School of Advanced Materials at Peking University and other institutions published a study on November 22, 2026. This team of scientists including Qiliang Zhang, Juntao Zhao, and Chuying Ouyang developed an AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The project received support from the AI for Science Preferred Program and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. These experts worked across several locations including the Shenzhen Graduate School and the Fujian Science and Technology Innovation Laboratory. The new simulation method addresses the high computational costs that often hinder the development of energy storage.

It aims to fix the insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms that currently limit the accuracy of battery modeling. The research was funded by the Advanced Materials National Science and Technology Major Project under number 2025ZD0618801. Additional financial support came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China through grant number 12426301. This technical approach integrates artificial intelligence to bridge different scales of material behavior. The authors of the study, who include Genming Lai and Zekai Liu, declared that they have no competing financial interests.

They presented their findings in the journal ACS Nano to show how AI can improve battery simulations. The researchers explained that traditional methods are too expensive and lack the necessary feedback for real-time analysis. By using these new tools, they believe the industry can design more efficient lithium batteries more quickly. This work represents a collaboration between Peking University and the Laboratory of Computational Materials Physics. More to follow.
