stories.Headline: LeBron James sues PlayVision over AI app using his likeness and Bron name
stories.Summary:
LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app on Tuesday, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it "Bron" and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing. The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in New York, according to the Associated Press. James is a Philadelphia 76ers star and NBA superstar. The app's developer is PlayVision Inc., which is based in California. The app is called "Bron."

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James' name, to give up any money they've already made and to award damages, including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said. The ad attracted about one million views on X within a day, according to the lawsuit. The marketing campaign this month featured an image of a person resembling James, down to his tattoos, voice and No. 23 jersey, sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' attorneys called it "a willful, bad-faith tactic" to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote "a new and unknown product." The lawsuit states that "Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app." It says they "intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions." Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app's website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. The lawsuit said "The integrity of NBA competition -- and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play -- is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans." It added that "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app's developer, PlayVision Inc., was launched by chief executive Anish Gupta and chief technology officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its "Bron" app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. Bron is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch.

James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves." However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

stories.Headline: Brookings estimates $10.3 trillion in US AI infrastructure investment fuels fears of entrenched 3% inflation
stories.Summary:
The Brookings Institution estimated that U.S. AI infrastructure investment will reach 10.3 trillion dollars between 2025 and 2032. This investment boom fuels fears that 3% inflation could become entrenched as a new normal. Rising demand for electricity and semiconductors, along with construction costs, creates structural cost pressures across industry. Some warn that this shift could trigger a repricing of financial assets by lowering future cash flow values. Whether this 3% inflation level becomes entrenched remains uncertain according to the provided reports.

The Brookings Institution cited the 10.3 trillion dollar figure, which is about 13.87 quadrillion won, for the U.S. market. ABN AMRO Bank analyzed that the U.S. real neutral rate would rise 0.2 percentage point between 2026 and 2030. This occurs if annual AI investment reaches 3% of GDP in the United States. Consumer inflation reached 3.7% in the U.S. in September and 3.8% in the euro zone. The Group of Seven averaged 3.5% inflation, while OECD member countries reached an average of 4.5%.

A senior official at an economic ministry stated that inflation would be difficult to stabilize in the short term. This official noted that stabilization would remain difficult even if oil prices were to fall. ABN AMRO Bank provided the analysis regarding the rise of the U.S. real neutral rate. The Brookings Institution provided the estimates for the total U.S. AI infrastructure investment costs. These entities highlighted how data center construction increases demand for semiconductors and electricity.

Investors in financial products are advised to review bond allocations to prepare for entrenched 3% inflation. They are encouraged to diversify into inflation hedges like inflation-linked bonds and funds tied to real assets. Some warn that investors' required returns would rise if inflation stays at 3% instead of 2%. This change would affect stock, bond, and property prices currently set on 2% inflation plus a risk premium. The reports suggest that these financial assets may require a total repricing.

The reports state that data center construction increases demand for semiconductors and electricity. Costs for securing construction workers and expanding transmission networks are also rising. These factors act as structural pressure that pushes up overall industry costs. The current financial market sets prices based on a 2% inflation target plus a risk premium. This background explains why a shift to 3% inflation is viewed as a significant risk.

Investors are told to monitor the situation as the AI investment boom continues to drive costs. The reports leave open whether 3% inflation will actually become the new normal. It remains uncertain if the structural pressures from AI will permanently entrench higher inflation. Financial experts suggest reviewing portfolios to mitigate risks associated with these potential price shifts. The long-term impact on the real neutral rate depends on the scale of AI investment.

stories.Headline: SK chair Chey Tae-won proposes joint Korea-Japan AI talent program at Tokyo forum
stories.Summary:
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won called for Korean and Japanese universities and businesses to jointly develop artificial intelligence talent, speaking at Tokyo Forum 2026 on Saturday. He said education systems and universities need a fundamental redesign for an AI-native society rather than minor curriculum changes. The two-day forum was co-hosted by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo and began Friday. Its theme was AI as a Transformative Technology: Humanity, Knowledge and Civilization. Chey joined NTT Group Chairman Jun Sawada, Taejae University President Yeom Jae-ho and Sophia University President Miki Sugimura in a discussion moderated by University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii.

Chey said an AI-native society is not one that simply uses AI but one that accepts AI as an inherent part of its environment. He said new governance and systems are needed because society as a whole, including the current university system, must be designed differently. He called for AI-native universities with entirely new designs and governance structures, adding that minor changes to existing curricula would not be enough. He stressed the importance of collective intelligence, saying even unsuccessful attempts to design new systems could help young people develop problem-solving skills.

He cited SK's initiatives in talent development, employment support and data center workforce training, highlighting AIGEN, a two-year non-degree program launched last month that encourages participants to find solutions through team projects. Asked how companies and universities could cooperate on AI talent, Chey proposed a joint program involving Korean and Japanese institutions. He said there are many opportunities not only between countries but also between companies and universities. He said such a program could create internship and employment opportunities in both countries while nurturing social innovators capable of addressing societal challenges.

In a video welcoming address on Friday, he stressed developing talent capable of guiding change in the AI era. He said people need to ask themselves what problems they want to solve with AI, what new value they want to create and what kind of society they want to build, urging universities to move beyond teaching knowledge and focus on cultivating wisdom. The forum brought together global experts, including French government AI envoy Anne Bouverot and Sakana AI co-founder Ren Ito. The article was published on Nov 22, 2026, and updated the same day.

stories.Headline: Whistleblower alleges a candidate used a calculator to pass a North Chungcheong teacher appointment test

The incident allegedly occurred despite the presence of two supervisors who were tasked with monitoring the examinees in the classroom. Other candidates reportedly informed the supervisor about the calculator use during a break, but the official allegedly ignored the claim.

The situation requires a serious review of the supervision systems used for teacher appointment examinations to prevent future misconduct. This specific case involved the 2025 school year appointment test in North Chungcheong Province where a candidate allegedly cheated. The anonymous author A is responsible for bringing these allegations to light through an online community post on November 22. This person criticized the supervisors for neglecting their duties and claiming they did not see the calculator being used. According to A, the central supervision office stated that the candidate could not be caught because the test had already ended. The whistleblower expressed deep doubt that cheating will be properly prevented in the next appointment test cycle. This individual linked the failure of the supervisors to a general lack of rigor in the testing process.

The controversy comes at a time when the public is buzzing over the use of artificial intelligence glasses to cheat on the CSAT and other professional tests. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has reportedly been confused over the specific measures needed to prevent such high-tech cheating. stories.Headline: Burger King Korea sells its AI-advertised Chocolate Whopper dessert burger in Seoul
stories.Summary:
Burger King launched the Chocolate Whopper in South Korea, a dessert burger made with brownies, chocolate, and cream cheese mousse, according to Merca 2.0. The product went on sale Thursday, November 19, exclusively at the Flame Ground location in Seongsu, Seoul, the article said. Burger King Korea introduced the item through an advertising campaign that used artificial intelligence, and after releasing AI-generated images and videos, the company published a follow-up announcement confirming the Chocolate Whopper was neither a joke nor a fictional product. Each burger is handmade, only a limited number are available each day, and customers can purchase just one. The Chocolate Whopper is a dessert-inspired take on Burger King's signature burger, designed to preserve its familiar appearance while replacing traditional ingredients with sweet treats.

Instead of beef, it features a chocolate brownie patty, traditional vegetables are replaced with gummies and chocolate pieces, and savory sauces give way to chocolate and raspberry sauces. According to Burger King Korea's official social media posts, the ingredients include chocolate fudge buns, chocolate sauce, dark chocolate shavings, strawberry gummies, milk jelly rings, crunchy chocolate discs, brownies, raspberry sauce, and cream cheese mousse. The Chocolate Whopper costs 9,800 South Korean won per burger, according to Burger King's launch information reported by South Korean media outlets, and each burger is made fresh and available daily starting at 11:00 a.m. while supplies last.

The brand also limits purchases to one per customer and requires the dessert to be consumed on-site, with takeout and delivery not available. In its follow-up announcement, the brand clarified that the product was neither an April Fools' joke nor an AI hallucination, but an actual item it planned to sell. The company released promotional content created with artificial intelligence, explicitly disclosing the use of the technology in its official Instagram posts, and Burger King Korea later confirmed that the Chocolate Whopper was real and would be available at one of its locations. As part of this marketing strategy, the company used technology commonly associated with generating synthetic images to promote a food product it later confirmed was real.

The campaign also illustrates how artificial intelligence can be incorporated into marketing communications, not necessarily to develop a product itself, but to shape its visual presentation and spark consumer curiosity. So far, Burger King has only announced the Chocolate Whopper's availability at Flame Ground Seongsu, its flagship location in South Korea. Burger King's Chocolate Whopper is an example of how a brand can use artificial intelligence to turn an advertising concept into a real consumer experience. What began as a burger that seemed to exist only in AI-generated images has become an actual product available to customers in South Korea.

stories.Headline: AI builds a $75 Thanksgiving menu for six in Houston that rings up at $64.31 at Kroger
stories.Summary:
KPRC 2 News reporter Joy Addison, working with photojournalist Michael Lemons, gave artificial intelligence a challenge to build a Thanksgiving shopping list for six people in Houston with a budget of just $75, and the station published the results on November 21, 2026. The menu had to include a turkey, traditional sides and dessert, and the suggested list included a whole turkey, mashed potatoes, stuffing, green bean casserole, corn, cranberry sauce, dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. AI estimated the cost at $61.75, including a $10 cushion for extra expenses, which would leave $13.25 for anything else the family might need. The station then took the list to Kroger and put together an online cart, and the subtotal came to $64.31, still under budget with $10.69 left to spare. The cart also showed a promotion offering $5 off when shoppers spend $36 on eligible items, but another $26.02 in qualifying products would need to be added to unlock the deal.

Shoppers told the station that grocery prices are hard to ignore, with one saying the prices are pretty much off the charts, and pointing to a McCormick chicken gravy packet that used to cost about $1.99 and was now priced at $3.27. That shopper still believed feeding six people Thanksgiving dinner for $75 is doable, saying the strategy is to look for sales, shop around and take advantage of grocery store specials, and added that using AI for a shopping list had never occurred to them before but might be something to look into. Emily Taylor was not as convinced about the $75 challenge, answering simply no when asked if she thought she could feed six people for that amount. Taylor said sharing the cost with family and friends can help make holiday meals more affordable, and recommended coupons and apps for the right grocery stores as always helpful.

The test showed that AI can help take some of the guesswork out of holiday shopping by giving a menu, organizing the grocery list and helping set a spending target, and the Kroger online cart came in at $64.31, just $2.56 more than AI's estimated spending of $61.75. The station noted that prices and availability can vary and that digital coupons often come with requirements, so shoppers still need to compare prices and make sure they are getting enough food for everyone at the table. With a little planning, some smart shopping and help from technology, keeping Thanksgiving dinner within budget may be more manageable than you think, according to the report. The bottom line, the station said, is that AI won't do the grocery shopping for you, but it might help you make a plan before you hit the aisles.

stories.Headline: Chinese researchers warn US AI advances could undermine Beijing's nuclear deterrent
stories.Summary:
Chinese military and civilian researchers have expressed growing anxiety that American advancements in artificial intelligence could undermine the nuclear deterrent of Beijing. These experts warn that such technology might allow United States forces to locate and destroy Chinese missiles with unprecedented speed and accuracy. This fear stems from the possibility that AI could reduce the time available for nuclear decision making to only 90 seconds. Such a rapid timeline would threaten the strategy of ensuring enough missiles survive an initial strike to deliver a devastating counterattack.

The current situation requires a review of more than 100 recent studies conducted by Chinese researchers to understand these strategic vulnerabilities. These documents suggest that AI breakthroughs in radars, satellites, and sensors could give Washington a menacing advantage during a crisis. Consequently, these concerns may make China more reluctant to agree to limits on its nuclear arsenal despite its smaller size. While Chinese military institutes explore how AI can make their own missiles harder to detect, they worry about lagging behind the United States.

Chinese strategists believe that the ability to withstand a strike and hit back prevents enemies from risking nuclear war or blackmail. During a summit on Thursday, President Xi Jinping spoke with President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin about reducing nuclear risks. However, Mr. Xi has shown no interest in the calls from Mr. Trump for China to join specific arms control commitments. The Chinese leadership remains focused on maintaining a credible deterrent in the face of evolving American technological capabilities.

stories.Headline: Codelco and BHP deploy AI and satellite tools to cut water and energy use in Chilean copper mines
stories.Summary:
Chilean mining companies are integrating artificial intelligence and satellite technology to increase efficiency and protect nature. The state miner Codelco and the global firm BHP have deployed these tools to manage their operations more sustainably. These advancements come as the global demand for copper rises to support the growth of AI data centers. The shift toward smarter mining began with projects like the Lemu Nge satellite launched in August 2024.

The industry must adapt because copper makes up about 83 percent of the weight of materials used in AI infrastructure. S&P Global projects that global copper demand will climb from 28 million tonnes in 2025 to 42 million tonnes by 2040. AI infrastructure alone is expected to contribute nearly 2 million tonnes to this 50 percent increase. Codelco used the Lemu Nge satellite to track over 65 species in the Maitenes-Campiche Wetland and the Roblería del Cobre de Loncha National Reserve. Meanwhile, BHP used machine learning at its Spence and Escondida mines to save 1.1 million cubic meters of water and over 11 GWh of energy.

Carolina Pinilla, the Corporate Director of Environmental Management at Codelco, stated that AI provides a chance to improve environmental oversight in large mines. She noted that the technology helps the company make faster decisions and identify compliance risks before they become serious problems. At Universidad Andrés Bello, Vice-Rector for Digital Transformation Claudia Bascur explained that the Mina Virtual platform allows students to practice safety and operate machinery without real world risks. This immersive system uses an AI agent to monitor student behavior and enforce safety protocols in real time.

The global market could face a shortfall of 10 million metric tons of copper by 2040 if supply does not expand. This gap would represent about 25 percent of the projected demand for the metal. Chile is attempting to close this gap by combining its massive reserves with high tech operational precision. The country continues to deploy orbital technology and machine learning to meet the environmental standards required by global buyers.

stories.Headline: University of Plymouth researchers develop AI that flags bladder cancer risk up to five years early
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Plymouth developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a study involving nearly 70,000 patients. The work was led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology. PhD student Xu Wang led the data analysis. The study was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

The team studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients, covering a 25-year period from 1995 through 2020. The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators, from smoking and exercise habits to medication use. The system narrowed the list to 38 features especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk. The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not. The system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis, and some warning signals could be traced back up to five years.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors including smoking and blood in the urine. It also uncovered unexpected associations, with patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appearing to have a lower risk of bladder cancer, and long-term use of tamoxifen, a breast cancer medication, associated with a higher risk. The findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it, but raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk. The system could divide patients into three groups: low-risk below 7% probability, uncertain grey zone of 7-55%, and high-risk above 55%.

Wang said bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022. Wang said no routine screening program exists for the general population, and detection following symptoms relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, said bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families. Winter said it could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier. Zhou said the work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, and its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions including kidney stones. Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs is visible blood in the urine, which can also result from noncancerous problems including kidney stones and prostate conditions. Confirming bladder cancer currently requires cystoscopy, in which a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder. The examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients most likely to have the disease. The model performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

The researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use. All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Zhou said further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely, and the team would want to investigate other datasets too. Zhou said additional studies would be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions. Zhou called it a very exciting early study.

stories.Headline: Applied behavior analysis evolves from Skinner's operant work to debates on compassion and AI
stories.Summary:
Applied behavior analysis began in B. F. Skinner’s laboratory with his 1938 book The Behavior of Organisms, which defined the operant as a basic unit of behavior. Skinner extended that work to people in the 1950s, according to a 2025 National Academies report on autism care for military families. Donald Baer, Montrose Wolf, and Todd Risley published “Some Current Dimensions of Applied Behavior Analysis” in the first issue of the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in 1968. In a 1964 case study, Wolf, Risley, and Hortense Mees described treating a young boy, referred to as an autistic child, for tantrums, refusal to wear his glasses, and mealtime problems. Ivar Lovaas at UCLA reported in a 1987 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology that 47% of 19 children who received more than 40 hours of one-to-one treatment a week reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, compared with 2% of control children.

The 1968 paper set out seven dimensions: applied, behavioral, analytic, technological, conceptually systematic, effective, and generality. The National Academies report says those dimensions “have guided the field for most of its history.” The 1964 case study’s methods included “mild punishment and extinction,” time-out, and reinforcement. The National Academies calls Lovaas’s program “the catalyst” for the early intensive behavioral intervention models in use today, while noting that “valid concerns arise” about parts of his approach. The Behavior Analyst Certification Board was established as a nonprofit in 1998 to set credentialing standards, and its current Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts has been in force since January 2022.

The code lists “Treat Others with Compassion, Dignity, and Respect” as one of four core principles, and Standard 2.11 makes behavior analysts “responsible for obtaining assent from clients when applicable.” The code defines assent as vocal or nonvocal verbal behavior indicating willingness to participate from people who cannot give informed consent. Justin Leaf and colleagues, in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, evaluated objections from autism rights and neurodiversity advocates, including the Lovaas project’s use of shock, default 40-hour intensity, punishment and extinction procedures, responses to stimming, and claims that ABA is abusive or causes PTSD. They recommended setting intensity individually, including clients and caregivers in choosing goals, measuring social validity and quality of life, and studying long-term and undesired outcomes. “Our field is not infallible, and we should continue to improve and progress our interventions,” the authors wrote.

A 2024 National Academies workshop summary says early practice relied heavily on physical punishment, which drew criticism from autistic self-advocates, and that modern ABA has dropped physical punishment. In late 2023, Ashley Penney and colleagues proposed in Behavior Analysis in Practice that compassion be treated as “an eighth current and essential dimension of ABA,” a proposal that remains the authors’ and not a change to the original framework. In a 2020 proof-of-concept study in Perspectives on Behavior Science, Marc Lanovaz and colleagues trained machine-learning models on simulated single-case graphs, and the models produced fewer false positives and more statistical power than the dual-criteria method, a structured aid for visual analysis. A 2024 systematic review abstract in BJPsych Open compared 25 studies of virtual reality and standard social skills training for autistic children and found no consistently significant differences between the two. The Council of Autism Service Providers has published practice parameters for AI use in ABA covering selection, transparency, consent, monitoring, error reporting, and retirement of AI systems.

The data in the Lanovaz study were simulated, not drawn from clinic records. A review of the AI practice parameters notes that clinicians remain responsible for clinical decisions under BACB codes and that providers should not assume payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles give a timeline: 1938, Skinner publishes The Behavior of Organisms; 1964, the Wolf, Risley, and Mees case study; 1968, Baer, Wolf, and Risley define the seven dimensions; 1987, Lovaas reports his outcome; 1998, the BACB is established; 2022, the BACB Ethics Code takes effect; 2023, Penney and colleagues propose compassion as an eighth dimension. The articles state that nearly 90 years after Skinner’s book the field debates topics such as compassion and artificial intelligence. The articles state that how the field got from one to the other explains much of what payers, providers, and families debate today.

The articles state that any new tool, like any old procedure, has to show it produces socially significant change for the person receiving services. The articles leave open whether payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles leave open whether compassion becomes an eighth dimension of ABA. The articles leave open what further study of long-term and undesired outcomes will show. The articles leave open how the debate over who gets to define socially important change will resolve.

stories.Headline: Times A.I. editor Dylan Freedman drafts his writing on a 1950s typewriter while using A.I. only for reporting
stories.Summary:
Dylan Freedman, the A.I. projects editor for The New York Times, wrote in a Times Insider article published on November 22, 2026, that he uses artificial intelligence in his work every day but never uses it for writing. His job has two parts, enlisting A.I. to help reporters search large collections of documents and multimedia data, such as the Jeffrey Epstein files or President Trump’s speeches, and reporting on developments in A.I. technology. Because he draws a thick line at writing, he composes most of his first drafts on an Olivetti Lettera 22 typewriter from the 1950s, the same model Leonard Cohen used to compose songs and poems. He composed the first draft of the article itself on that typewriter.

Freedman, who was a software engineer at Google before pursuing a journalism degree, described the typewriter as an essential dose of minimalism and a break from crowded browser tabs and blinking terminal windows. He called the machine a technological marvel for translating thoughts into words, noting that it can be used outside without glare and does not need to be recharged. A single ribbon lasts longer than most novels and is cheaper than printer ink, and most mechanical typewriters, made from solid steel, are practically indestructible. The typewriter has few comforts but also no distractions, and using one feels intentional, like taking photographs on a film camera.

Freedman said that typing on the metal machine gives him a rawness that better captures his voice, and that you cannot easily undo, nor should you. He wrote that A.I. is rapidly becoming superhuman at tasks with clear solutions, like coding and math, and that the more he uses A.I., the more he worries about surrendering his cognition. He cited a study published in Nature this year which found that researchers who used A.I. assistance tended to be more productive than their peers but also studied fewer new topics. The article presented these views as his own reasoning and experience rather than as findings about typewriters or writing in general.

The article appeared in Times Insider, a section that explains who The Times is, what it does, and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how its journalism comes together. Freedman stated in the piece that he uses A.I. heavily for reporting tasks while keeping it out of his writing process, and he offered the typewriter as the tool he relies on for first drafts. The available text of the article does not say what, if anything, follows from his approach for The Times or for other journalists. It also does not describe any further plans, policies or responses connected to the piece.

stories.Headline: Alexandr Wang publishes essay warning about human control of AI
stories.Summary:
Alexandr Wang published an essay titled "Superintelligence is Arriving" on a Sunday afternoon, according to a Digg report dated November 23, 2026, and the post drew 35,000 likes along with 1,900 comments and 29,100 saves. In the essay Wang ties his warning about human control to a claimed AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a claim the article presents as his own. He rejects what he describes as a handover of society to AI and argues that a positive future is possible, though he says it likely requires the industry to change course. The Digg report says the essay was first seen about ten hours before publication and was shared through a link to his article on X.

Jon Favreau reacted sharply to the essay, urging elected leaders to stop frontier labs from handing control to superintelligent machines, according to the report. Commenters on the post included one who wrote that superintelligence is arriving and another who called the Sunday afternoon timing a power move and asked to see the compute to back the headline. The article lists eleven sources for its account, including Wang's X article and several posts reacting to it. The report does not say what specific changes Wang calls for beyond the industry changing course.

The Digg article places the essay in the context of an ongoing debate about superintelligence, recursive self-improvement and loss of control, which its headline names. It gives no further detail on the content of Wang's argument beyond the points above, and it does not say how the industry or elected leaders responded to Favreau's call. The report also does not say what happens next with the essay or the claimed proof. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sarvam launches Token Factory to serve global AI models on local GPUs with Rupee billing
stories.Summary:
Sarvam launched Token Factory to serve global AI models on local GPUs with Rupee billing. This new inference stack allows developers to use a single API for various models. The company is now chasing usage-driven revenues as it enters its commercial era. Critics have flayed the unicorn for its hosting of Chinese models and questionable economics. This development occurs as India rides a wave of AI inference technology.

The service lets developers toggle between Sarvam 105B and models from DeepSeek, Kimi and Gemma 4 31B. Promotional rates of 0.25 rupees per million tokens will expire by the end of 2026. Sarvam clarified that it uses its own hardware rather than subsidised GPUs from the IndiaAI Mission. By default, the system uses user data to fine-tune models unless clients explicitly disable this feature. These technical choices create potential dealbreakers for enterprises handling sensitive or proprietary information.

Sarvam is responsible for the service and claims it uses its own hardware for the stack. Critics questioned if the company used government GPUs and flayed the venture for its unit economics. Some observers noted that utilisation, not volume, will determine if the service makes money. These critics also highlighted the risks associated with the default data retention policy. The company must now prove its proprietary stack can retain developers after promotions end.

Other companies are also building India's inference layer, including L&T with its Vyoma.AI token factory. E2E Networks is expanding via Jarvislabs, while Utho Cloud plans to enter the market in 2027. Mirror Security focuses on encrypted-inference, and global giants like OpenAI and Anthropics are localising workloads. These competitors affect Sarvam by making price, speed and reliability the main differentiators. The crowded landscape forces these firms to compete for the same developer base.

The articles state that the homegrown AI ecosystem is projected to be a 126 billion dollar opportunity by 2030. This growth supports the emergence of various startups building training datasets and simulated work environments. Sarvam is one of several firms attempting to build a globally competitive inference powerhouse. The broader market includes a mix of unicorns and smaller firms building large businesses. This environment encourages the development of local GPU infrastructure and AI training tools.

Sarvam must now determine if it can stay ahead of the curve in a contested landscape. The company needs to prove that its unit economics are sustainable without promotional pricing. It remains to be seen if enterprises will accept the default data fine-tuning policy. The articles leave open whether the service can truly become a globally competitive powerhouse. Future success depends on the ability to attract and keep developers on its proprietary stack.

stories.Headline: DXC and Cisco integrate AI network intelligence into DXC OASIS to speed Meraki Wi-Fi incident resolution
stories.Summary:
DXC Technology has launched a joint innovation effort with Cisco to integrate Cisco's AI network intelligence into DXC OASIS, starting with workplace Wi-Fi performance in Cisco Meraki environments, the companies said on 23 November 2026. Under the arrangement, Cisco's AI Assistant for Networking will identify likely causes of network disruption, while DXC OASIS will manage diagnostics, approvals and remediation steps under policy controls with change tracking. IT teams will retain oversight from diagnosis through to resolution, and the initial focus is on cloud-managed Meraki networks used to connect and manage workplace devices and Wi-Fi. DXC OASIS is DXC's orchestration platform for IT operations, and Cisco is contributing network intelligence, including AI Assistant, Experience Metrics and platform tools to support investigation and network actions. The effort is designed to connect network data with broader operational processes, rather than keep troubleshooting within a single management console, so an incident detected in the network can trigger coordinated checks and follow-up tasks across infrastructure, applications and service management systems.

One aim is to speed root-cause analysis by combining Cisco's network telemetry with AI-assisted diagnostics and DXC's operational processes, and another is to support a governed remediation workflow in which any action still goes through approvals, guardrails and audit tracking. A pilot cited by DXC showed incident resolution times improving from one to two hours to five to seven minutes, though DXC did not provide further details on the pilot environment and presented the result as evidence for using agentic AI with human oversight in IT operations. The first implementation centres on workplace Wi-Fi incidents in Cisco Meraki environments, connecting Cisco's AI Assistant and Model Context Protocol tools with DXC OASIS so approved actions can be taken within a structured operational process. Dan Gray, President of Global Infrastructure Services at DXC Technology, said enterprise teams do not need more alerts but faster paths to resolution, and that AI can help identify issues while realizing value requires organizations to coordinate action across people, systems and workflows. He said that by bringing Cisco's network intelligence into DXC OASIS, the companies are helping enterprises turn AI-powered insights into action, resolve issues faster, reduce operational complexity and improve the experience for IT teams and end users while maintaining human oversight and control.

Joe Vaccaro, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Network Platform and Assurance at Cisco, said enterprise networks generate massive amounts of rich operational telemetry, but turning those insights into rapid, safe remediation has traditionally required intense manual effort. He said that by integrating Cisco's AgenticOps capabilities into DXC OASIS, DXC's AI agents and engineers can collaborate across complex IT environments, delivering governed, closed-loop network automation that accelerates incident resolution while keeping human teams in control and linking back to broader enterprise context such as service management tools. The collaboration reflects a broader push by large IT suppliers to apply AI to operations management while keeping formal approval steps in place, with DXC and Cisco positioning the integration around governance and traceability as much as speed, and every action subject to policy controls and change tracking. For enterprise customers, the practical test will be whether an AI-identified network issue can move through investigation and remediation without adding operational burden, and the companies are starting with Wi-Fi performance, where user impact is immediate and the source of a problem can be difficult to isolate across devices, access points and wider IT systems. DXC described Meraki as the starting point for a repeatable model, and the companies expect to extend the same approach to other Cisco technologies over time, although they did not specify which products might come next.

stories.Headline: UAE and Germany guides advise businesses to record human contributions as AI output grows
stories.Summary:
The article reports that businesses across the Emirates now use generative models to produce software, logos, product designs and technical inventions at scale, and that the commercial value of that output depends on whether the law will protect it. Global Advisory Experts published the guide on November 22, 2026, with a last update of October 2026. The guide states that UAE intellectual property legislation was drafted with human creators and inventors in mind, yet a growing share of commercial output is made with, or largely by, software. It sets out what is protected today, where the position is uncertain, how the Ministry of Economy and enforcement bodies are adapting, and what business owners and their advisors should do now. The guide covers the United Arab Emirates only and draws on the UAE statutory framework, Ministry of Economy practice and the international policy work of WIPO.

The guide states that the UAE has not passed one dedicated statute resolving every question, and that existing federal legislation applies while examiner practice adapts step by step. It names Federal Law No. 38 of 2021 on Copyright and Neighbouring Rights, Federal Law No. 11 of 2021 on the Regulation and Protection of Industrial Property Rights, which covers patents and designs, and Federal Law No. 36 of 2021 on Trademarks, all administered through the Ministry of Economy. It says examiners in 2026 apply human authorship for copyright, human inventorship and inventive step for patents, and distinctiveness for trademarks, rather than a special AI rulebook. It states that copyright exists without registration but that the Ministry of Economy runs a voluntary registration system, and that assignment must be in writing as UAE law requires. It advises using priority mechanisms and Patent Cooperation Treaty routes to secure an early filing date while record and claims are refined.

The guide states that UAE patent practice expects a human inventor, that naming an AI system as sole inventor is not supported, and that the applicant must derive rights from a human inventor through employment or assignment. It recommends Pathway A, the cautious route for most filings, naming as inventors the people who framed the problem, set the model's objective, selected and curated data, interpreted results and recognised the inventive outcome. It describes Pathway B as a defensive measure for cases where AI's contribution is truly dominant, building an evidence record of every human decision and preparing a reasoned case on the human contribution to conception. It advises stating the human-defined technical problem and solution clearly in the specification and including worked examples and detail on model configuration, inputs and validation to support enablement. It advises recording contributions as they happen through lab notebooks, code commits, model version logs and decision memos.

The guide states that the most noticeable change in enforcement is operational rather than legislative, with rights holders increasingly using automated tools to detect infringement online and at the border. It says the legal framework for customs seizure and anti-counterfeit action is unchanged, but that authorities and tribunals want provenance and chain of custody, not just screenshots. It states that WIPO's dedicated AI and IP resources track the international policy debate, which is likely to shape UAE practice as cross-border norms settle. It advises asking vendors to warrant that training data and outputs are lawful and to indemnify against third-party infringement claims, and warns that some AI tools reserve rights or give only a limited licence in the output. It states that models trained on huge public datasets may propose solutions overlapping with prior art the applicant has never seen, and that thin or black-box disclosure is a common point of failure.

The guide states that copyright is where AI and intellectual property UAE issues arise first, because generative tools produce text, images, music and code constantly and cheaply. It states that the copyright regime is built around an author, meaning a creator whose intellectual effort shows in the work, and that content generated with no meaningful human creative input is on uncertain ground. It states that where a person conceives, selects, arranges, edits and curates using AI as an advanced tool, the finished work has a strong claim to protection as human-authored, while output from a thin prompt is much less certain. It advises keeping drafts, edits, selection decisions and prompt histories that show the human hand, and treating unedited output with caution as legally fragile until rights are secured by other means. It states that trademark law cares about what a sign does in the market, not who or what created it, and that models often produce marks that are descriptive, generic or close to existing marks.

The guide states that the businesses in the strongest position are those that settled ownership in writing before they deployed the tools, and that every contributor, including employees, contractors, designers and AI vendors, should assign all IP in the deliverables in writing. It advises clearing a mark before adopting it, obtaining a written assignment where a designer, agency or AI vendor was involved, and not assuming that output belongs to whoever ran the tool. It states as a practice note that records showing a mark's originality and development history should be kept to answer any challenge that it is derivative or non-distinctive. It states that the filing strategies, sample clauses and enforcement checklists reflect general patent, trademark and copyright prosecution and enforcement practice in the UAE and the wider GCC, and that points reflecting a practitioner's interpretation rather than a published rule are flagged as practice notes. It states that law numbers and article references can be confirmed through the WIPO Lex national profile for the UAE, and that where the Ministry of Economy publishes filing procedures and guidance, those documents govern how applications are handled in practice.

stories.Headline: Alyve CEO Mark Cameron warns Australian firms treat AI as automation rather than strategy
stories.Summary:
Mark Cameron, founder and chief executive officer of Alyve, warned that Australian businesses are adopting artificial intelligence in ways that may improve efficiency without strengthening their competitive position, according to IT Brief Australia. Cameron said many leadership teams treat AI mainly as a tool for automation and cost reduction rather than asking how it could help them enter new markets, develop new revenue streams or change the way they compete. His comments reflect a broader debate in Australian business over whether early AI spending is being directed toward operational savings rather than longer-term strategic change. Cameron, whose firm advises executive teams on AI strategy and business transformation, said that focus is becoming common in boardroom discussions. Cameron argued that the greater risk is not the direct cost of software purchases but the time lost when companies run limited trials without changing the business around them.

He said AI plans presented by senior teams often centre on making current processes faster and cheaper, which in his view risks preparing companies for an outdated model of competition while markets and customer expectations continue to shift. He said business leaders should first decide what position they want to hold in their market over the next few years, then determine where AI investment should be directed, because otherwise efficiency gains can reinforce the wrong priorities. The warning comes as organisations across sectors face pressure to show practical returns from AI spending, with back-office automation, staff productivity tools and process redesign among the easiest starting points. Cameron said that emphasis could leave boards with a misleading sense of progress, because a company focused only on internal efficiencies could still lose ground if competitors use AI to change customer experience, expand into adjacent services or rethink delivery models. He also raised concern about the use of competitors as a benchmark for AI planning, arguing that copying rival initiatives is unlikely to create meaningful differentiation.

Instead, he said, businesses should identify a small number of strengths that would make them difficult to challenge and use AI investment to build those areas, with the aim of creating difference rather than parity. He placed AI strategy closer to mainstream corporate planning than to technology deployment alone, saying leaders should link it to decisions about market direction, organisational strengths and speed of execution. Cameron also pointed to organisational learning as a factor that may increasingly separate strong performers from weaker ones, saying the value of AI lies not only in generating insights or outputs but in how quickly a business can respond to what it learns. Alyve advises executive teams on AI strategy and business transformation and has offices in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.

stories.Headline: Google finds an AI system that autonomously writes and launches software exploits
stories.Summary:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that they had uncovered an AI system that autonomously finds software flaws and launches exploits, according to TechGig on November 23, 2026. Investigators found an unsecured staging server that hosted a system called exploit_agent, which links to advanced cloud-based and locally run language models. This framework examines software code to identify differences related to flaws, writes working exploits, and launches them automatically. Scripts on the machine also handled later steps, including mapping internal networks, guessing passwords, planting webshells, and deleting webshells installed by rival attackers. The report describes this as a significant shift in cybercriminal operations, moving from chatbot assistance to independent attack systems.

In August 2026, attackers exploited two PaperCut print server flaws, CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, which allowed remote command execution without logging in when chained together. A campaign launched four days after disclosure hit hundreds of organisations through these flaws, expanding an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes. Google also tracks open source attack frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI, and the company confirmed that CAIRN and PentAGI were used against live targets. One actor ran a customised PentAGI platform that probed many Asian organisations for weaknesses from August through early October 2026.

Google recorded at least 8 zero-day exploits per month in 2025 and 11 per month in 2026, with August reaching 22. Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents in 2026 where criminals drained victims' cloud computing and model quotas. Daily fraudulent bills exceeded $100,000 in these cases, with some losses reaching $1 million before cleanup. The articles do not say who is responsible beyond the actors described or what happens next.

stories.Headline: OpenText survey finds 68% of Australian firms use AI at scale despite visibility gaps
stories.Summary:
OpenText released research on 22 November 2026 showing that Australian organisations are scaling AI despite major gaps in technology visibility and operational readiness, based on a survey of 213 technology decision-makers at large organisations across six sectors. According to the research, 68% of respondents said they use AI in production or at enterprise scale, while 74% reported significant visibility gaps across hybrid IT environments. Only 19% said their IT and security endpoint data is fully aligned, which the report describes as a disconnect between AI adoption and the information needed to support it. The report covered organisations in financial services, government, manufacturing, retail, mining, and energy and utilities, representing combined revenues or budgets of about AUD $1 trillion. Legacy infrastructure remains a central issue, with 72% of respondents identifying legacy-system modernisation as a major challenge and 71% citing hybrid and multi-cloud management as a key concern.

Another 66% pointed to tool sprawl and complexity, indicating that many organisations are managing fragmented systems as they add newer platforms and services, which the report says makes it harder to maintain oversight of cloud and on-premises environments and to control operating costs. The report identified several areas requiring attention, including hybrid IT visibility, trusted operational data, infrastructure modernisation, service management links across the business, and automation with clear accountability. While 56% of respondents said their data was mostly aligned, the much smaller share reporting full alignment suggests many still lack a single reliable view across technology and security environments, and the report says fragmented or incomplete data can affect the quality of automated decisions. George Harb, Vice President for Australia and New Zealand at OpenText, said organisations need to strengthen the basics before pushing further into automation. He said AI adoption is moving quickly across Australian businesses, but the infrastructure and information needed to support it are not always keeping pace, and that many organisations are managing a complex mix of legacy systems, cloud platforms and disconnected tools.

He said that without a clear understanding of how these systems interact and support business services, adding more automation risks creating another layer of complexity. He said Australian organisations need to focus on connecting information, improving operational visibility and ensuring automated decisions are based on accurate, trusted data, and that getting these foundations right is essential to improving service delivery, managing costs and delivering meaningful returns on AI investment. The report found that IT service management is another area under review, with 76.5% of respondents saying they plan to review or are considering reviewing their IT service management platforms in the next 12 to 18 months. A further 91% agreed that a strong knowledge base improves efficiency and first-contact resolution, suggesting service management is being viewed not only as a support function for IT teams but also as a broader operational tool for managing workflows, knowledge and automation across the organisation. The survey was conducted by DataDriven and focused on large Australian organisations, and the results point to a pattern in which AI adoption is moving ahead while modernisation, systems integration and data alignment remain unfinished work for many technology leaders.

stories.Headline: V2 AI drives AI-powered SDLC adoption across large financial enterprises
stories.Summary:
Organisations facing higher customer expectations and volatile market conditions are turning to AI agents to speed business growth and to accelerate their software development lifecycle, according to an article on IT Brief Australia. The article says that when used strategically, AI agents let organisations release software changes two to five times more often and cut time-to-market by 30 to 60 percent. It says software is a key driver of business value, and that its real power lies in incorporating feedback to build memory for the business and evolve to meet changing needs. With AI, the article says, organisations can create faster feedback loops between customers, technology and decision-makers, creating a continuous flow from business strategy to engineering execution.

Enterprise transformation leaders call this the AI-powered Software Development Lifecycle, or AI SDLC, the article says, with AI embedded in every stage of software delivery to enhance efficiency and compound its impacts. The article says the team orchestrates a coordinated system of AI agents, with people and AI working together to deliver and run applications end-to-end. It cites Gartner estimates that AI-powered SDLC has already resulted in five to eight hours of time regained per developer, and that by 2028 teams applying AI across the SDLC will achieve 25 to 30 percent productivity and a strong competitive edge. The article says V2 AI is driving enterprise-wide AI-powered SDLC adoption across multiple large financial enterprises, and that it is witnessing firsthand the constraints of legacy software delivery models.

The article says that despite unprecedented technology investment, ideas can take months to materialise as they move through layers of analysis, development and governance, and that by the time a solution is released a critical window of market opportunity closes or the original business needs change altogether. It says the result is delays and losses in both project and opportunity costs, while organisations that deliver software significantly faster than competitors create an advantage that compounds over time. The article says the highest-performing organisations use AI to accelerate SDLC activities and elevate human decision-making, and do not use AI-powered SDLC to outsource accountability. It says humans remain responsible for approving decisions, managing risk and ensuring the resulting system meets business, regulatory and customer expectations.

The article says AI agents powered by Claude Code put AI in the driver's seat of the engineering process, with human engineers steering a team of AI agents to build out software functionality almost independently. It says AI agents can be trained for specific aspects of software development, with planning, coding and review agents operating continuously in sync, and review agents identifying high-risk paths and validating them against existing enterprise standards. Humans narrow the solution space upfront and sign off before release, the article says, and by investing effort upfront and reviewing at checkpoints, teams create the conditions for fast, accurate and scalable execution. It says the next stage is AI agents augmenting human capability throughout the lifecycle, from inception to development, quality and operations, shifting organisations from software delivery to business value delivery. The article says the future belongs to organisations that embrace AI-powered SDLC supported by governance, measurable outcomes and clear accountability.

stories.Headline: TensorWave signs six-year deal to supply OpenAI with 457 MW of AMD-powered AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
TensorWave signed a multi-year partnership with OpenAI to provide 457 megawatts of AI infrastructure powered by AMD hardware, the company announced on November 17, 2026. TensorWave is the infrastructure provider supplying the capacity, OpenAI is the recipient, and AMD is the silicon supplier whose hardware powers the deployment. The announcement appeared under TensorWave's dedicated TensorWave & OpenAI partnership coverage and was reported by Ashish Joshi. The 457-megawatt figure is the total scale of the deployment covered by the partnership rather than a partial tranche. The multi-year structure indicates sustained provision of infrastructure over the life of the agreement rather than a one-time transaction.

Futurum reported on November 19, 2026 that the agreement is a six-year, 457 MW infrastructure deal to deliver dedicated AMD Instinct MI455X GPU capacity across multiple U.S. data center sites. The deployment will use AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs in infrastructure purpose-built for AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with dedicated single-tenant capacity connected through high-performance Ethernet networking. TensorWave expects to bring the first capacity online in the first half of 2027 and complete the full deployment by early 2028. The deal makes TensorWave the first publicly announced neocloud provider supporting the OpenAI-AMD strategic collaboration, which targets 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPU deployments beginning with 1 gigawatt in 2026. The agreement is TensorWave's largest to date.

AMD SVP of AI Vamsi Boppana stated that the three-way combination is building the foundation to deliver AI compute at extraordinary scale and advance the broader AI ecosystem. TensorWave President Piotr Tomasik said the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot. TensorWave was the first public cloud to deploy AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and has continued expanding across successive generations including MI325X and MI355X. That track record as an AMD Helios launch partner gave OpenAI confidence in TensorWave's ability to operate purpose-built Helios rack-scale systems at extreme scale. TensorWave has more than 2 gigawatts of long-term data center capacity already secured.

In January 2026, Cerebras secured a strategic multi-year $10 billion compute agreement with OpenAI, validating its hardware for the most demanding frontier AI applications. In late February 2026, Meta announced a multi-year agreement to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD-based infrastructure, including the co-design of custom Instinct MI450-based GPUs. OpenAI is deliberately distributing compute commitments across multiple vendors and infrastructure models, which reduces single-source dependency and ensures redundancy for large and complex AI model training and inference workloads. Hyperscalers bring their own software, operations teams, and increasingly their own silicon, whereas neoclouds, enterprises, telcos, and sovereign AI factories need the GPU vendor to supply much of the operating stack. For AMD-centric workloads, that distinction makes a dedicated neocloud like TensorWave a more natural fit than a hyperscaler optimized around its own silicon.

The agreement illustrates how frontier AI compute demand has grown to a scale where purpose-built, long-term neocloud capacity contracts are becoming the preferred procurement model for leading AI labs. At 457 MW committed over six years, this single neocloud deal illustrates how large individual infrastructure tranches within the 6 GW program will be. Multi-year, multi-hundred-megawatt, single-tenant capacity contracts with specialized neocloud providers are displacing the on-demand hyperscaler model for the most demanding workloads. The procurement logic is built around guaranteed capacity, hardware specificity, and operational control rather than flexibility and shared tenancy. As frontier model complexity continues to grow, this template is likely to become the norm rather than the exception for labs operating at OpenAI's scale.

What to watch includes whether TensorWave brings initial AMD Helios systems online on schedule in 1H 2027 and which additional neocloud providers announce roles within the 6 GW OpenAI-AMD program in Q1-Q2 2027. Also to watch is how NVIDIA-aligned neocloud providers respond with comparable long-term capacity offerings to retain frontier AI customers. Further items are whether Meta's up to 6 GW AMD infrastructure commitment advances to named neocloud or operator announcements in early 2027 and whether additional multi-year, dedicated-capacity agreements with new vendors are announced as the broader 6 GW AMD program scales through 2027. The articles leave open which additional neocloud providers will join the program and how NVIDIA-aligned providers will respond.

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marius Hobbhahn calls a 2027 AI takeover plausible and warns OpenAI audit access falls short
stories.Summary:
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and co-founder of Apollo Research, said on the podcast MTS that he has reversed his view on short AI timelines, having called takeover by 2027 "very, very unlikely" two years ago. He said he is no longer sure and called it a negative update over the last two years. He endorsed the timeline Paul Christiano laid out on the Dwarkesh podcast, roughly a one-in-three chance of superintelligence within about a year. Hobbhahn said such an event is "less likely than not" in the next year. He said that if things move that fast, humans would not be able to correct it in any meaningful way.

Hobbhahn described a 6-to-12-month window in which substantial risk of full AI takeover would emerge. He said the risk is a speed problem, a correction lag, not a movie-style robot revolt. He said his earlier worry was "trained-in" scheming, where a model develops goal-seeking during reinforcement learning and improves itself past human supervision. He said the Hugging Face incident, an investigation Apollo was involved in, pushed him to take seriously a second pathway he calls "on the episode" risk. He said bad behavior in that pathway is committed spontaneously during a single rollout rather than baked in during training.

Apollo is one of four organizations OpenAI embedded inside its operations in November 2026, alongside METR, Transluce and Goodfire. OpenAI gave them access to model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems and technical documentation, framed as part of commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Apollo's pilot tests four claims: training-process subversion, evaluation robustness, historical deployment review and monitorability. OpenAI supplies a whitelist of approved employees for Apollo to interview, and Apollo cannot speak with other OpenAI staff about the assessment or anything in scope. Apollo's public statement calls the pilot "an ambitious first step" whose access and disclosure rights "don't yet meet our bar for full embedded evaluations."

Hobbhahn said he understands why broader access would cede a lot of control to an outsider. He argued that science has always advanced through the informal channel, through "coffee chats" and things "heard over lunch." He said the field has to be robust enough that even if any particular developer was trying to hide something, the external evaluator would find it. He said that is a necessary condition for a field like this to exist, and that "Right now, we're just nowhere near that."

He wants embedded evaluation to become a professional field with nuclear-inspection-grade powers, analogous to nuclear inspections, food inspections or cyber security. The Verge reported a six-person Apollo team spending four months inside OpenAI, with conversations logged and no access to internal messaging tools such as Slack. The research community has read that as well short of the employee-level access Sam Altman previously promised. Hobbhahn said he expects little internal effect, because only a handful of lab staff would interact with the evaluators.

He said he expects a real external effect, with a trusted outside voice able to correct public misreadings in both directions. Anthropic was preparing a listing with an IPO expected to raise as much as $85 billion. Earlier in November the S&P 500 slid 10% from its October peak into correction territory, a seven-day losing streak reaching back to February 2020, and even NVIDIA's strong earnings and Anthropic's listing failed to bring buyers back. SoftBank's Masayoshi Son, who has poured roughly $64.6 billion into OpenAI for about a 13% stake, publicly conceded that skipping Anthropic was a mistake.

Asian family offices have reportedly been paying premiums of 30% for fund stakes that merely touch Anthropic or OpenAI paper. The articles say to watch whether OpenAI's approved-interviewee list widens to direct employee access. They also say to watch whether METR, Transluce and Goodfire adopt Apollo's same four-claim template. The articles say Hobbhahn's 2027 timeline is the headline, but the access terms decide whether anyone outside the building can constrain anything at all.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and the EU launch training for 18,000 Nigerian teachers in digital pedagogy and AI
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the European Union, working with the Government of Katsina State, launched a training program for 18,000 teachers on November 10, 2026. This initiative focuses on digital pedagogy and the responsible use of artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning across Nigeria. The national flag-off ceremony took place in Katsina State and included various education stakeholders and traditional leaders. Training activities began on November 10 and will continue through the end of November 2026.

The program requires teachers in Adamawa, Bayelsa, Enugu, Katsina, Oyo, and Plateau states to develop practical digital competencies. It utilizes 13 training modules that were developed after an assessment of more than 10,000 teachers. These modules teach educators how to use technology for lesson preparation, the creation of learning materials, and student assessment. This effort is part of the second phase of the Education and Youth Empowerment Initiative in Nigeria, which is funded by the European Union.

UNESCO Representative Dr. Isaías Barreto da Rosa stated that technology should support teachers and learners without replacing human relationships. Governor Malam Dikko Umaru Radda, represented by Commissioner Yusuf Sulaiman Jibia, noted that these digital tools improve instructional delivery and learner engagement. Ambassador Gautier Mignot of the European Union reaffirmed a commitment to helping Nigeria prepare its education sector for the digital age. These leaders emphasized that professional judgment and empathy remain essential to the learning process.

The initiative adopts an inclusive and ethical approach to ensure that digital transformation does not increase existing inequalities. By strengthening teacher resilience and capacity, the program aims to improve the overall quality of education in Nigeria. Participating teachers are encouraged to apply their new knowledge directly within their classrooms to boost productivity. Stakeholders are now urged to maintain consistent monitoring and evaluation of the program to ensure its long-term success.

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines Lab releases Inkling 2 Mini multimodal model for local AI setups
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines Lab released the Inkling 2 Mini model on November 20, 2026, to provide cutting-edge performance for local AI setups. This new multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model uses a looped transformer architecture to increase its capacity without adding more physical parameters. It features approximately 26 billion physical total parameters and 3 billion active parameters per token for its processing tasks. The model accepts both text and image inputs and supports a context size of one million tokens for users. A DSpark drafter is included with the release to provide additional speed-up at a small cost to memory.

The model has 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop for 48 logical layers. It uses a hidden size of 2,304 and selects eight experts from 128 per layer, unlike the 384 in Small. Weights are shipped in mixed-precision format using NVFP4 and MXFP8, with support for transformers, MLX, Llama App, and SGLang production deployments. The decoder runs layers 0 to 5 once, layers 6 to 17 three times, and layers 18 to 23 once. Each six-layer block contains five sliding-window layers with 1,024 tokens and one full-attention layer using dynamic key and value convolutions.

Thinking Machines Lab stated that this model is a refreshingly new great local model designed specifically for smaller AI setups. They noted that in their vibe tests, the performance is at least comparable with the Qwen 3.8 27B model. The developers mentioned that more validation is needed, but they are super excited about the release of this specific model. They provided a research artifact called TML-d24-varloop-research that allows users to set a variable number of loop passes. They explained that setting one or two passes instead of three makes inference faster, though generation quality may drop.

The model leads in 32 out of 48 benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, including coding and reasoning. It outperforms Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8 27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL across various knowledge and safety categories. In coding, it leads in FrontierCode v2.0 and ties with Qwen 3.8 27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but trails on AutomationBench-AA. Users can adjust reasoning effort from none at 0.0 to max at 0.99, with a default high setting of 0.9. The model can also perform tool calling, such as getting the current temperature for a specific city and country.

The developers based this approach on architectures like Nanbeige, which previously explored the concept of looping within a transformer model. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages, and a gating controller decides how much input to forget or add. The router uses SwiGLU experts, and the text decoder width is 2,304 while the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads, along with learned relative position logits and a learned sink. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers stored in the checkpoint while maintaining 48 total layer visits.

Next, users can run the model on macOS or Windows via Llama App using GGUF 4-bit or 8-bit quants. Linux users can serve the model from the CLI or use SGLang on SM103 hardware for production datacenter deployments. The research variant allows for further testing of variable loop passes to balance inference speed against the quality of generations. The articles leave open the final results of the deeper evaluation for the variable loop research artifact and further validation. They also leave the full list of benchmark scores to be viewed on the official Inkling 2 Mini model card.

stories.Headline: Baseten releases two open-weight decision models that top the Artificial Analysis Decision Index
stories.Summary:
Baseten released two open-weight decision models called bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 21, 2026. These tools are built on the Gemma 4 backbone and do not write text for users. Instead, they provide calibrated probabilities for score, choice, and yes or no questions. The company designed these models to handle routing, guardrail pipelines, and ticket triage tasks.

The bison-1 model is a 31B dense model, while groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters. Both models increase the context window from 16k to 128k tokens and can accept images. Bison-1 scored 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, ranking first among 19 models. This score is one point higher than the 75 achieved by Liquid AI's d1.2-ultra.

Baseten stated that using soft labels in the training mix helped the models report uncertainty more accurately. This method resulted in a Brier score of 0.14, which is the lowest and best on the index. The company noted that bison-1 ranks first on four of six index components. They also reported LongMemEval M scores of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1.

These new releases join the existing Qwen-based lineup consisting of mammoth-1, elephant-1, and joey-1. Baseten describes this new pair as the first models they have built on an American backbone. The weights for both models are available on Hugging Face under MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses. Users can also access these decision models through the Baseten Model APIs.
