stories.Headline: AI helps uncover a Ghostscript flaw that exposes Google and Zoom to attack
stories.Summary:
A series of major technology failures across the United States over the past two weeks slowed banking transactions, interrupted Microsoft and Apple services, disabled a classified National Security Agency network and temporarily grounded commercial air traffic nationwide, the New York Times reported on Saturday. U.S. officials said they had no evidence the incidents were caused by malicious cyberattacks. Instead, they attributed several of the disruptions to software patches intended to strengthen systems against newly discovered vulnerabilities. The disruptions came as confirmed cyberattacks on systems in the U.S. and Europe underscored the growing vulnerability of interconnected networks. Hackers had already targeted American municipal water systems and European refrigeration infrastructure.

The Times reported that Iranian hackers targeted scores of municipal water systems in the United States this summer, exploiting weak or default passwords on computers controlling operations. Recent cyberattacks against refrigeration systems in Europe showed how even relatively unsophisticated hackers can disrupt equipment essential to commercial operations. Cybersecurity researcher Paulos Yibelo, founder of PWN AI, discovered a serious software vulnerability called Upload2Shell using artificial intelligence to examine file-upload processes. The flaw involved Ghostscript, decades-old software widely used to process documents and images, and could potentially have allowed attackers to compromise systems at major companies including Google and Zoom by uploading a specially crafted file. Yibelo reported the discovery to the software developer and affected companies, which issued patches.

Microsoft reportedly released more than 1,400 security patches in October, roughly 10 times its historical baseline. The NSA experienced a days-long outage of a classified network after installing faulty updates designed to address vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, which officials cited by the Times said had been identified with the assistance of artificial intelligence. Retired Gen. Paul Nakasone, the former director of the NSA and U.S. Cyber Command, said at a Washington conference hosted by Vanderbilt University's Institute of National Security that the past week is "the new normal." Nakasone, who also serves on OpenAI's board, called artificial intelligence "the most disruptive technology" in history and said, "We are in an era where we've got to think differently about how we're going to be more resilient."

He said industries and agencies are trying to rapidly modernize and at the same time defend themselves, and that "A.I. is driving all of this, the opportunities and the challenges." Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., warned the White House that existing cybersecurity defenses were struggling to keep pace, writing that "A.I. is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace." Michael Yeh, Microsoft's vice president of customer security and trust, said some of the most frequently exploited vulnerabilities were discovered years ago and that "None of those are A.I.-driven attacks," adding that "These are people exploiting existing legacy vulnerabilities" that can be decades old. Rob Joyce, a former senior NSA cybersecurity official, said at Cyberwarcon on Friday that AI was not "inventing brand new ways to hack" but was intensifying pressure to repair existing weaknesses, comparing the situation to a forest fire in which "All that tech that's on fire and going to burn down" while "all the little things that are down in the forest floor" will grow stronger and more capable.

The disruptions affected consumers who suddenly could not access banking services, businesses experiencing interrupted operations, and travelers stranded by computer failures. Experts disagree about whether artificial intelligence will ultimately make the internet safer or produce an endless cycle of newly discovered vulnerabilities and emergency repairs. Repeated disruptions affecting financial transactions, communications, transportation and national security systems risk undermining confidence in the institutions responsible for protecting them. Public skepticism does not prove that officials are concealing cyberattacks, yet the combination of confirmed intrusions, aging infrastructure and increasingly frequent outages creates a difficult credibility problem, especially when technical explanations are not accompanied by detailed public findings.

The distinction between a failed software update and a deliberate cyberattack is increasingly difficult for ordinary Americans to assess, particularly when the consequences can look nearly identical. The incident illustrates a growing dilemma in which security teams must respond quickly to newly discovered weaknesses, but rushing to install protective updates can itself trigger serious disruptions. The incident also illustrates how AI is dramatically accelerating the discovery of security flaws in technology that businesses and government agencies have relied upon for decades. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fed governor Barr warns AI threatens trading, bank runs and cyber stability
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr on Monday laid out a range of perils that AI could bring to trading, cybersecurity and consumer and investor protection. He built on a central bank report issued the previous Friday that showed a surge in concern about the risks the new technology poses to financial stability. Barr spoke in prepared remarks for delivery in Milan, Italy. His remarks came hours before Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was to open a conference at the San Francisco Fed. AI developers, business leaders and academics were expected at that conference to discuss the implications of the new technology for productivity, jobs and the economy more broadly.

Some 87% of contacts surveyed for the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, issued on Friday, cited AI as a salient risk to the financial system. They pointed to worries about cyberattacks, complex AI-related financing, and the possibility of an AI earnings slowdown spurring broad stock market declines. Barr expanded on some of those concerns and added several more. He cited the potential that increased reliance on AI models in trading could lead to herd-like behavior that could disrupt markets. He cited the possibility that self-learning algorithms could manipulate and destabilize markets.

Barr said banks may be unable to confirm whether an AI agent attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts is actually authorized by the customer to do so. He said even legitimate AI agents acting at lightning speed on behalf of retail banking customers could accelerate bank runs and overwhelm traditional safeguards. He pointed to cyber risks from AI-enabled cyberattackers or even rogue AI agents exploiting vulnerabilities in the financial system. He said AI developers struggle with ensuring their models are well controlled, numerically and legally precise, explainable, and replicable. He said the risk needs to be reduced that AI reinforces biases in consumer lending.

Barr said there is also a need to guard against risks that could result from the use of AI in financial markets, including collusion, market manipulation, or trading strategies that result in significant market volatility or even systemic risk. He did not comment in his prepared remarks on the outlook for monetary policy or the economy. A new Federal Reserve review of the best available evidence suggests the emerging AI revolution is still in its early days when it comes to seeing a return on AI investment. The Fed economists find that the data show AI adoption is high and growing. AI-adopting firms tend to apply it in only a couple of business areas at a time, such as IT and HR, or marketing and strategy, rather than across the entire organization.

Research and development, a business area where AI might provide a particularly significant boost to more fundamental innovation and productivity gains, has relatively low uptake, according to the Fed economists. Business areas like IT, marketing, finance, and strategy seem to be the most common AI applications, with less use in HR and actual production. More dramatic changes, such as using AI as part of a firm's core production process, engaging in wholesale reorganization, or fully automating some tasks, might be necessary to sustain any productivity boost over the long term. The establishment of new AI-centered businesses could also be an important channel for longer-run productivity improvements. Demand for new AI products has resulted in AI adoption growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all.

A report from METR, an AI research nonprofit, finds that Anthropic's internal use of AI has helped the company roughly double the pace at which its models improve on tasks that can be clearly measured. AI pundit and podcaster Dwarkesh Patel said he has come to the view that the world is only a couple years away and possibly only a couple months away from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. Anthropic's S-1 public offering document offers a bunch of underwhelming case studies of how customers are using its models. As the company puts it, it believes enterprises are still in early phases of deployment, and it believes most knowledge workers have yet to fully experience what frontier AI can help them accomplish. The Fed paper concludes that AI is not yet playing much of a role, if any, in the recent upturn in US productivity growth.

The Fed paper's conclusion leaves open when AI will play a role in US productivity growth. Barr's remarks leave open what the Fed will do about the risks he listed. The articles do not say what the Milan remarks or the San Francisco Fed conference will lead to. The articles do not say how the Fed's review or the Financial Stability Report will change policy. The articles do not say what Anthropic's public offering will result in.

stories.Headline: Egyptian firms boost AI and fintech investment to drive growth and regional expansion
stories.Summary:
Egyptian companies are increasing their investments in artificial intelligence and fintech as drivers of growth and competitiveness amid rapid shifts in global markets, according to discussions by experts at the fourth edition of the Executive Education Summit organized by ESLSCA University on November 21 and 22, 2026. During a session titled "From Chaos to Sustainable Growth," representatives from technology, financial services, and education companies said that building flexible business models and investing in technology and human resources are critical to turning economic challenges into opportunities for growth and regional expansion. Malak El Baba, Vice President and General Manager of Visa in Egypt, Libya, and Sudan, said artificial intelligence is reshaping commerce and digital payments, citing the "Stay Secure" study showing that 91% of consumers in Egypt use artificial intelligence in shopping and 88% trust its role in fraud protection. She added that more than 83% of Egyptian companies plan to invest in agentic commerce over the next two years, and she stressed the importance of integrating payment and financing solutions into the purchasing experience as commerce grows across social media platforms and digital gaming.

Ahmed Nader, CEO of Geidea, said the company grew over five years from a team of 3 to 4 individuals to nearly 1,200 employees, with the number of merchants it serves reaching approximately 100,000. He said Geidea broadened its services from point-of-sale solutions to e-commerce, restaurant, and retail services, up to lending and embedded finance powered by artificial intelligence, and he affirmed that digital payment solutions and faster financial inclusion drive corporate growth, particularly for small and medium enterprises. Mohamed Tawfik, Managing Director of TP in Egypt and Chief Operating Officer for English-speaking African markets, said investment in technology and specialized talent helps companies operating in Egypt compete regionally and export services to global markets. He noted that attracting talent in computer science and medical sectors is one of the most prominent expansion challenges while serving clients in the United States and Europe, and he said the company cooperates with the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Information Technology Industry Development Agency (ITIDA) to address the repercussions of regional tensions and ensure business continuity.

Karim El Hennawy, CEO and Secretary-General of ESLSCA University, said rapid technological evolution forces organizations to retrain leaders and employees and to develop strategic thinking and crisis management skills. He explained that the COVID-19 pandemic and remote work accelerated shifts expected by 2030 and 2040 into a reality within three to four years, reinforcing the importance of practical skills and adaptability to labor market changes. Omar El Shenity, Founder and CEO of Qaf Education, said organizations need to move from reactive management to flexible operating models based on data and proactive planning amid continuous changes in labor market needs and its trend toward specialized disciplines. The summit was held with more than 1,200 participants, 60 speakers, and 50 partners, under the auspices of the Ministries of Industry, Higher Education and Scientific Research, Communications and Information Technology, and Health and Population, and it discussed the future of leadership, management, and organizational development amid technological and economic transformations.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT predicts XRP reaches $5 by the end of 2029
stories.Summary:
ChatGPT predicted on November 21, 2026 that XRP could reach $5 by December 31, 2029, about 460% above the forecast's 89-cent starting price. The prediction was published by Sam Daodu, editor of the Crypto Desk at 24/7 Wall St., in an article dated November 21, 2026. XRP was trading around 90 cents, having fallen 22.4% over the past two weeks and 32.1% in the last 30 days. Its close of nearly 91 cents on November 20 was its lowest close of the past year, far below its January 5 high of $2.35. ChatGPT's $5 target is far below Standard Chartered's forecast of $19.60 for 2029.

ChatGPT assigns a 55% weight to the $5 base scenario, a 30% weight to a $1.50 low scenario and a 15% weight to a $15 high scenario. The low scenario of $1.50 is about 66% higher than XRP's current price, and the scenarios imply market values of about $112 billion, $373 billion and $1.12 trillion. These values assume 74.6 billion XRP in circulation by the end of 2029, starting from the current 63.5 billion and adding 300 million new coins each month for 37 months, mainly from Ripple's escrow. XRP reached its all-time high of $3.65 in July 2025 with fewer coins in circulation, and its market value stands at about $57.2 billion, ranking sixth among all cryptocurrencies. The base scenario needs market value to grow about 6.5 times, and the high scenario of $15 could match Bitcoin's current market value of around $1.17 trillion.

ChatGPT forecasts XRP finishing 2026 at 85 cents, a 6% drop from current levels, then rising to $1.55 in 2027, $2.75 in 2028 and $5 in 2029. The model says XRP must stay above $1 consistently in the second quarter of 2027, hit $2 in the first quarter of 2028, exceed $3 in the third quarter of 2028, surpass the all-time high of $3.65 in the second quarter of 2029, about a 310% increase from 89 cents, and reach above $5 in the fourth quarter of 2029. The first hurdle is $1, about 11% above current prices, and XRP must reclaim its 20-day moving average of $1.08 and its 200-day average of $1.24, about 20% and 38% higher. ChatGPT estimates a 12% chance of XRP reaching Standard Chartered's $19.60 target by December 2029, a level implying a market value of around $1.46 trillion. The model gives a 25% chance for a $10 target and a 15% chance for $15.

Standard Chartered anticipates XRP could hit $12.60 in 2028, $19.60 in 2029 and $28 in 2030, and its 2028 forecast is higher than any other major prediction in the comparison. ChatGPT connects the $19.60 target to steady inflows pushing US spot XRP funds into the $15 billion to $20 billion range, with the Bitwise XRP ETF (NYSEARCA:XRP) as a notable example. According to SoSoValue data, total net assets in these funds dropped to $989.6 million as of November 20, down approximately 35% from $1.51 billion on October 28. Investors pulled out $10.4 million on November 9 and around $5 million on November 20, with no net inflows so far in November.

The second condition is that banks and payment companies would have to use XRP as the bridge currency for cross-border transfers. The article says the possibility of XRP reaching $5 by the end of 2029 seems less likely than ChatGPT's 55% weight implies, because ETF outflows and Bitcoin's slide could push prices lower. Bitcoin is trading around $58,084, below its June 30 closing low of about $58,566, and XRP has tended to follow Bitcoin's downward movements. After past declines of 70%, XRP continued to fall to 92% and 95% below its peak, and it already trades about 75% below its all-time high.

A major U.S. bank or payment network using XRP for cross-border transactions at scale could raise the price prediction to as high as $15. If Bitcoin falls below $40,000, the forecast for XRP could drop to around $1.50, which the article calls a reasonable basis for anyone trying to gauge the value of 3,000 XRP. An encouraging sign that $5 remains possible would be total assets in XRP funds climbing back above $1.51 billion. To maintain ChatGPT's optimistic outlook, XRP needs to stay above $1 by mid-2027, then break through $2 and surpass its all-time high of $3.65.

The article leaves open whether ETF outflows and Bitcoin's slide will push prices lower than the forecast assumes. It also leaves open whether a major U.S. bank or payment network will start using XRP for cross-border transactions at scale. The article does not say when XRP funds might return above $1.51 billion. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Homelabber uses two RTX 3090s and a RAM drive to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi AI model
stories.Summary:
A homelabber detailed improvements to a second generation Optane AI build on Reddit. This person used two RTX 3090 GPUs to run a large AI model. The project was reported by Shane Downing on 21 November 2026. The build runs the 2.8 trillion parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model. It achieves a generation speed of 3.11 tokens per second.

The system uses 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, on a RAM drive. This setup uses Linux tmpfs and DAX for the Optane portion. The model file is a Q2_K version that shrinks the size to 865 GB. Two RTX 3090 GPUs provide 48 GB of total VRAM for the build. The model is a mixture of experts with 896 experts and 104B active parameters.

The builder stated that the persistent Optane memory gets very hot. Because of this heat, the builder says the Optane sticks still need fans. The builder also noted that DRAM is faster than the Optane memory. This distribution of the workload allows the model to avoid slower memory reads. The builder used llama.cpp to measure the performance of the hardware.

The RAM drive boosted generation speed by 41 percent and prompt evaluation by 26 percent. Prompt evaluation reached 16.8 tokens per second compared to 13.3 tokens per second without the drive. Without the RAM drive, generation speed dropped to 2.20 tokens per second. The GPUs handle attention, shared experts, the KV cache, and the current conversation context. These components are used on every token to maintain high memory bandwidth.

The original build was designed to save money by using Optane instead of DRAM. The model is a mixture of experts where only a few experts run per token. Sixteen routed experts and two shared experts are chosen for any given token. A 16 bit precision version of the model would take about 5.6 TB. Moonshot released a 4 bit MXFP4 format version that is about 1.56 TB.

The GPUs manage the dense feed forward network layer that is not split into experts. The routed expert tensors stay on the CPU side in Optane and the RAM drive. The RAM drive is volatile but appears to the system as a disk. Not every enthusiast has enough free system memory to create such a drive. The articles do not state if the builder will add more GPUs.

stories.Headline: Brevo offers AI email tools that generate content and personalize campaigns
stories.Summary:
Brevo, an all-in-one customer relationship management and marketing platform, offers AI-powered email marketing tools that help businesses create, manage and optimize email campaigns more efficiently, according to an article by Jason Will published on vocal.media on 21 November 2026. The platform combines artificial intelligence with marketing automation so that businesses can generate email content, personalize customer experiences, analyze campaign performance and improve engagement. Brevo says its tools suit any company, whether a small startup, an online store or an established organization. The article describes the offering as a way for marketers to reach the right audience with the right message.

The features include AI-assisted content creation that helps marketers generate email copy, improve subject lines and develop promotional messages, which the article says saves time. Brevo also allows businesses to customize emails using customer information, preferences and behavior, and it provides automation tools that send emails based on customer actions and predefined conditions, such as welcome emails for new subscribers, abandoned-cart reminders and follow-up messages after purchases. Campaign analytics and reporting tools let marketers monitor metrics including open rates, click-through rates and conversions, while smart audience segmentation divides contact lists into specific groups based on customer details and engagement. The article lists the benefits as saving time, improving personalization, increasing engagement, supporting business growth, providing valuable insights and simplifying marketing management.

The article names no individual responsible for the platform and carries no statement from Brevo or its representatives, attributing the described capabilities to the platform itself. It advises that AI-generated content should always be reviewed to ensure accuracy, brand consistency and a natural communication style. Businesses across industries can use the tools, the article says, with e-commerce stores recovering abandoned carts and recommending products, educational institutions sharing course updates, newsletters and admission announcements, and service-based businesses sending appointment reminders, promotional offers and customer follow-ups. Small businesses can also maintain regular communication with customers without requiring a large marketing team.

The article presents Brevo as an alternative to traditional email marketing, which it says often involves manually creating messages, organizing subscriber lists and monitoring campaign results at a cost of time and resources. By combining automation, personalization, customer management and AI-assisted tools, Brevo lets marketers streamline their campaigns and focus on developing better marketing strategies, according to the article. It concludes that as artificial intelligence continues to transform digital marketing, platforms like Brevo make it easier for businesses of all sizes to create customer experiences, strengthen relationships and support long-term growth. The article gives no release date, pricing or independent performance data for the platform.

stories.Headline: EU researchers find most high-automation farm tools rely on offline rule-based software
stories.Summary:
The articles report that researchers on the European Union-funded Horizon Europe OpenAgri project published an inventory of open-source agricultural digital solutions in the journal Smart Agricultural Technology. The inventory mapped 191 digital software and hardware technologies designed for modern agricultural production. The researchers found that tools delivering the highest levels of direct farm automation depend predominantly on deterministic rule-based algorithms and offline edge computing rather than cloud-based deep learning systems. Candidate solutions were identified between 2024 and June 2026 through consortium expertise, targeted keyword queries across GitHub, and specialized community resources. The articles were published on bioengineer.org on 2026-11-21T06:00:00Z.

Of the 191 qualifying solutions, software platforms constituted approximately four-fifths of the catalog and the remaining entries were open-hardware implementations. Farm management information systems made up roughly one-quarter of the database, followed by systems for precision irrigation, livestock monitoring, chemical fertilization, and crop disease diagnosis. Using the European Commission's nine-level Technology Readiness Level framework, 114 solutions, or roughly 60 percent, fell in levels four through six, 62 solutions, or 32 percent, reached levels seven through nine, and 15 entries, or 8 percent, sat in levels one through three. Among the 160 GitHub-hosted solutions, the median repository recorded 17 community stars, six forks, two contributing developers, and zero commits over the preceding twelve months, while 42 percent showed active code modifications in the preceding year and nearly one-fifth logged more than 100 recent commits. Only 28 of the 191 solutions, or approximately 15 percent, had corresponding peer-reviewed scientific publications.

The researchers constructed a standardized empirical baseline to categorize software maturity, deployment architectures, connectivity demands, and legal licensing terms. They implemented a systematic mapping review that treated public code repositories, developer manuals, and hardware schematics as primary evidentiary records, and extracted GitHub metrics on a fixed reference date of August 31, 2026, using the platform's REST application programming interface. They emphasized that publicly accessible source code does not automatically constitute open-source software under copyright law. They observed that advanced neural networks remain a distinct minority within agricultural open source. They noted that autonomous operational intervention does not require advanced machine learning or high-speed cloud infrastructure.

The study cited an independent audit from the European Court of Auditors showing that publicly funded digital tools and decision-support platforms frequently disappear from public access once consortium grant agreements expire. The authors observed that publicly accessible agricultural source code has historically failed to translate into proportional real-world adoption or systematic software reuse. They highlighted a persistent structural divide in which digital assets remain scattered across GitHub, GitLab, institutional servers, and individual project websites without uniform metadata or centralized discovery mechanisms. They cited limited digital literacy among farming demographics, infrastructural gaps in rural telecommunications, and concerns about technical complexity and data governance.

Prospective adopters are forced to navigate inconsistent documentation and unclear technical specifications. The investigation found that 51 solutions, or 26.7 percent of the catalog, published accessible source code without any formal software license. Among licensed projects, developers used frameworks ranging from the MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses to the GNU General Public License and the European Union Public Licence, while hardware repositories used the CERN Open Hardware Licence or Creative Commons terms. On connectivity, 44 tools, nearly one-quarter of the inventory, operate entirely offline after installation, 66 technologies, or 34 percent, require only minimal connectivity, and cloud-native architectures demanding continuous maximum connectivity represented 21 percent of the catalog.

Exactly half of the surveyed solutions, or 95 projects, incorporated no artificial intelligence, 53 relied on deterministic agronomic rules, mathematical threshold models, or simulation logic, 27 used machine learning models, and 16 used advanced deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural networks and YOLO object detectors. Of the nine solutions classified as delivering very high operational intervention, eight functioned using classical control-theory mathematics and rule-based software logic, including autonomous tractor autosteering, and only one employed advanced deep learning, while 23 fully offline solutions delivered high operational intervention. Representative solutions ranged from farm records platforms like farmOS, autonomous tractor guidance packages like AgOpenGPS, and smart robotic platforms like FarmBot, to optical spot-spraying weed locators and drone-based pest detection models. The survey also cataloged cross-domain communication tools including the Zenoh protocol.

Niche agricultural applications and localized farm tools were typically sustained by single developers or small research teams, whereas domain-agnostic communications frameworks, databases, and middleware engaged broad international communities exceeding 50 active contributors. The articles state that 73 percent of open-hardware designs operated completely offline or with minimal connectivity, whereas software platforms were more evenly split across cloud-dependent SaaS infrastructures and local on-premise execution environments. The articles do not state what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: A Brooklyn family makes a personal readiness plan as AI and cyber warnings raise outage risks
stories.Summary:
The warnings are coming thick and fast, according to a New York Times article published on November 21, 2026, which reports that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said the Iranian government has its sights on U.S. energy, water and financial services systems. Senior executives at A.I. companies say their tools could act on their own and wreak similar havoc, or human hackers could deploy A.I. against the same kinds of targets. The article asks readers to imagine a nationwide power outage, or a municipal water system that turns off or becomes unsafe, or the internet stopping for a while. It notes that a lot of important things people are used to accessing on the fly, such as Waze for a teen driver to get home or Venmo to pay a caregiver, would suddenly be unavailable.

The article says there is no way to know the odds of any of this happening, but they are probably higher than they were a year ago. It cites an Anthropic security executive who recently described a vulnerability tsunami headed our way, and it concludes that some preparation seems prudent right about now. Millions of people who are familiar with extreme weather already know the basic outlines of personal readiness, while the rest of us probably do not. That included the article's author and his underprepared family of four, in their midsize Brooklyn apartment building, until they made their own plans in recent weeks.

The article does not name a single official responsible for personal readiness beyond the author himself, who describes his own household as underprepared before it made plans. It paraphrases Mullin's warning about Iranian intentions toward U.S. energy, water and financial services systems, and it relays what senior A.I. company executives say about their tools acting on their own. The Anthropic security executive is quoted only for the phrase vulnerability tsunami, with no further statement attributed to that person. No other named person is given a direct comment in the available text.

The context the article offers is that the warnings are arriving quickly and that the risk is probably greater than a year ago, though it states plainly that the odds cannot be known. It frames the problem around everyday dependence on services like navigation and payment apps that would fail in a wider outage. The available text ends before the article's own planning guidance, so what specific steps the author and his family took is not described here. What happens next, in the article's account, is simply that some preparation seems prudent right about now.

stories.Headline: Researcher Tommy He releases tufazip, an AI tool that losslessly compresses one gigabyte of Wikipedia to 105.39MB
stories.Summary:
Researcher Tommy He built a tool called tufazip that losslessly compressed one gigabyte of Wikipedia data. This achievement was announced in a research post on November 19, 2026. The system reduced the text to 105.39MB using a self-learning AI transformer model. It does not use any hand-built models to achieve this specific result. The process relies on a neural network as its only predictor.

The system requires two Nvidia B200 GPUs and two Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPUs. Compression takes 631,548 seconds, while decompression takes 645,748 seconds, which is about a week. The full package includes a quantized 4.33MB pre-trained starter model with 34 million parameters. The full model is a 12-layer Transformer containing 163 million parameters. Total memory use peaked at 68,525 MiB for compression and 73,748 MiB for decompression.

Tufa Labs is responsible for the project and the resulting research. They stated that tufazip is the best entry on the Large Text Compression Benchmark using only a neural network. The company noted that other entries mix transformers with hand-built models. They explained that the predictor updates must be fully deterministic to ensure no data is lost. Tufa Labs also clarified that the tool is for research purposes and not a product.

The Large Text Compression Benchmark is the primary metric affected by this new entry. As of November 19, the 105.39MB version of tufazip ranked 13th on this list. Twelve other hybrid compressors currently beat its score by mixing different model types. The benchmark is strictly for text, meaning it does not apply to media files. Users would need massive hardware resources to actually run the current version.

The tool uses a self-contained language model that learns on the fly rather than using a cloud. Training occurs in two stages, starting with an offline phase for the starter model. The full model then learns online by predicting and training on each token. The unpacking side repeats these steps to rebuild the model alongside the text. This method allows the model to be rebuilt without storing the full trained version.

The first online-only version of the tool ranked second when submitted in early September. That earlier version resulted in a file size of 105.98MB. It required 647,595 seconds to compress and 630,136 seconds to decompress the data. The GPUs for that version peaked at 43.37 GiB of VRAM between them. The articles leave open whether this research will ever become a commercial product.

stories.Headline: Alaska-led consortium uses AI and microbes to recover rare earths from coal waste
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, the National Science Foundation awarded a six million dollar grant to an Alaska-led consortium. This group will use microbes and artificial intelligence to extract rare-earth elements from domestic coal refuse. The project is a four-year Focused EPSCoR Collaborations research grant. It aims to develop microbial biotechnology and AI models for mineral recovery. The initiative is titled Transformative Bioprocessing and AI-Driven Frameworks for Sustainable Critical Mineral Recovery.

The project runs through August 31, 2030, and is part of a 39.9 million dollar national infrastructure portfolio. The University of Alaska Anchorage leads the effort, with Dr. Brandon Briggs as lead principal investigator. Dr. Subhabrata Dev, Dr. Masoumeh Heidari Kapourchali, and Dr. Mohammad Heidari Kapourchali also lead the Anchorage team. The University of Alaska Fairbanks receives 913,000 dollars under Dr. Srijan Aggarwal. Partners include the University of Wyoming with Tyler Brown and Montana Technological University with Dr. Robin Bullock and Dr. Courtney Young.

Dr. Brandon Briggs said the project is the result of ten years of research to create a viable multi-state enterprise. He believes biological processing can condense traditional mineral recovery into four or five streamlined operations. Dr. Srijan Aggarwal stated that no single institution could provide the necessary breadth of skills alone. He noted that combining engineering, microbiology, and machine learning creates a holistic platform for resource recovery. Tyler Brown explained that the goal is establishing commercial viability for extracting resources from industrial waste.

The project affects domestic manufacturing, which currently imports over 70 percent of processed rare earths from foreign suppliers. These minerals are essential for defense avionics, wind turbines, electric vehicle motors, and telecommunications. Researchers noted that the regional partnership bridges the gap between basic discovery and industrial deployment. The work targets coal waste in Alaska, Appalachian basins, and the Powder River Basin in Wyoming. This process helps remediate legacy industrial waste sites while generating high-value domestic feedstocks.

Traditional rare-earth production relies on open-pit mining, energy-intensive roasting, and aggressive acid leaching. These methods use concentrated acids and generate large volumes of hazardous wastewater. The consortium uses bacteria, including Shewanella oneidensis and extremophilic strains from Alaskan glacial environments. AI models using reinforcement learning and deep neural networks will control bioreactors by tracking pH and metal ions. This approach replaces corrosive chemical pathways with environmentally benign geomicrobiological reactions.

The first 18 months involve cataloging coal refuse samples and performing metagenomic sequencing of bacterial communities. Through 2028, researchers will build continuous-flow benchtop bioreactors coupled with edge-computing AI models. The final two years will focus on assembling a modular biorefinery demonstration unit for multi-kilogram batches. This unit will generate techno-economic lifecycle assessments for energy utility and commercial mining partners. The articles leave open the specific results of the pilot materials engineering and downstream precipitation tests.

stories.Headline: Li, Shao and Nan report agentic AI systems advancing oncology research and discovery
stories.Summary:
Cancer researchers are moving from standalone artificial intelligence models toward integrated, agentic systems across oncology, according to updates presented at the 2026 American Association for Cancer Research Annual Meeting and reported in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. The researchers highlighted platforms such as Synapse, which coordinate large-scale research data to establish interoperable and reproducible scientific workflows. Building on that coordination foundation, conversational and multi-agent tools including DrBioRight, GP CoPilot, and the Isabl AI Agent allow natural language interaction with multimodal cancer data. By letting scientists explore complex datasets conversationally, these systems lower technical barriers for investigators working directly with multimodal oncology records.

Agentic frameworks have also advanced the transformation of real-world oncology data, carrying out clinical document abstraction, patient cohort extraction, and analysis of social determinants of health with documented high accuracy and scalability. The implementation of self-critical systems significantly improves overall reliability during data transformation tasks, according to the report. In clinical application, artificial intelligence shows expanding impact through validated imaging biomarkers, enhanced clinical trial matching, and scalable cohort identification across populations. These validated tools support clinical environments by refining patient identification processes and establishing reliable imaging markers for therapeutic assessments. At the same time, multi-agent computing systems are accelerating therapeutic discovery efforts, particularly in CAR-T development and immunotherapy target identification.

The work was reported by Li, Shao, and Nan in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology, volume 19, issue 1, Article 50, with DOI 10.1186/s13045-026-01823-5, and the bioengineer.org item was credited to Nathaniel Bowman on November 21, 2026. The article does not record direct statements from the authors beyond its description of the advances. Collectively, the report says, these technological advances position artificial intelligence as an active, collaborative partner alongside researchers in cancer research and precision oncology initiatives. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: UN-backed talks in Switzerland end without consensus on rules for deadly autonomous weapons
stories.Summary:
UN diplomats met in Switzerland this week to discuss the use of artificial intelligence in war, and the talks ended Saturday with nations agreeing to further discussion but without a consensus on firm rules for deadly autonomous weapons. A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Gara, a multifunctional unmanned aerial vehicle equipped with artificial intelligence elements, before flying it over positions of Russian troops near the frontline in Ukraine's Donetsk region in May. The UN-backed talks this week on regulating AI in warfare ended Saturday without a consensus on developing firm rules on how to rein in deadly autonomous weapons. Nations at the Switzerland meeting agreed to further discussion on regulating AI in warfare.

The talks were UN-backed and held in Switzerland this week, and they ended Saturday. Nations agreed to further discussion but reached no consensus on developing firm rules on how to rein in deadly autonomous weapons. The Gara is a multifunctional unmanned aerial vehicle equipped with artificial intelligence elements. A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Gara before flying it over positions of Russian troops near the frontline in Ukraine's Donetsk region in May.

The articles give no named officials, no statements from negotiators and no attributed remarks from any government or delegation. They report only that nations agreed to further discussion and that there was no consensus on firm rules for deadly autonomous weapons. No responsible official is named and no one is quoted, so no position can be paraphrased. The only named place is Switzerland, and the only named region is Ukraine's Donetsk region.

The articles name no other countries, groups or individuals affected beyond the nations at the Switzerland talks and the Ukrainian serviceman preparing the Gara. They give no statements from others and no named affected parties. The serviceman is described only as preparing the Gara before flying it over Russian troop positions near the frontline in Donetsk region in May. No casualty figures, no numbers of weapons and no number of participating nations are given.

The articles give no background beyond the May episode in Donetsk region and the Switzerland talks this week. They do not say when the talks began, how many nations attended or what earlier rules existed. They do not describe the Gara's manufacturer, capabilities or combat record. They do not say what the further discussion will cover or when it would happen.

The articles say only that nations agreed to further discussion, with no date, venue or format given. They leave open whether firm rules on deadly autonomous weapons will ever be agreed. They leave open what the further discussion will cover and who will take part. They leave open the Gara's role and the outcome of its use over Russian positions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Yan Li's DRPG-AI framework outperforms twelve audit baselines on AI risk detection
stories.Summary:
A computational framework called DRPG-AI, developed by researcher Yan Li and published in the Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences, outperformed twelve mainstream audit and fairness baselines on gold-standard tabular benchmarks. The framework transforms machine learning lineage records into a learnable substrate for automated risk reasoning and regulatory governance. It replaces manual retrospective checklists with proactive, compliance-by-construction optimization. Evaluations ran on the UCI Adult and COMPAS datasets. The work was reported on November 21, 2026.

DRPG-AI attained an overall risk-detection F1-score of 0.8763, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.9180, and a regulatory compliance coverage rate of 0.9561. Over the strongest composite baseline, Themis coupled with W3C PROV, it showed a 6.13 percent improvement in detection F1-score, a 5.02 percent gain in discrimination area, and a 14.31 percent increase in compliance coverage. The framework formalizes pipeline execution as a heterogeneous, directed provenance graph with five distinct node classes and six admissible edge relations. The node classes are data, transformation, model, prediction, and policy nodes, and the edge types are restricted to derived_from, used_by, trained_on, produces, governed_by, and audited_by. The risk engine uses four edge-typed message-passing layers with eight attention heads and a hidden dimension of 128, plus three causal dilated convolutional layers with kernel width three and dilation factors of one, two, and four.

Li's framework computes an attribute provenance set for each graph node using a recursive closure formulation and learns relation-consistent semantic embeddings through a self-supervised provenance reconstruction loss grounded in negative triple sampling. Ground-truth labels were generated deterministically: bias was assigned when statistical parity difference exceeded 0.10 on any protected attribute, drift when Kullback-Leibler divergence exceeded 0.05, membership-inference leakage when shadow-model confidence gaps exceeded 0.15, and adversarial contamination when Fast Gradient Sign Method perturbations flipped labels in five percent or more of samples. The remaining 75 percent of graph entities served as negative class observations. A temperature-scaling calibration head reduced Expected Calibration Error from 0.1455 to 0.0380, a 3.84-fold improvement, and calibrated scores propagated along ancestor chains with a mixing parameter of 0.62. The planner maps defects to seven actions, namely sanitization, re-annotation, re-training, quarantine, auditing, reporting, and no-operation, scored against twenty articles of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and seven articles of the General Data Protection Regulation, with hard weights of 1.0 for mandatory commands and 0.5 for discretionary recommendations.

The total loss balances focal risk classification loss, self-supervised provenance reconstruction loss, calibration loss, structural weight regularization, and a differentiable compliance reward term with weighting coefficients of 1.0, 0.5, 0.3, 1e-5, and 0.2. Because argmax operations and indicator functions are non-differentiable, the authors used a straight-through gradient estimator alongside a parameterized sigmoid relaxation during backpropagation. The UCI Adult dataset contains 48,842 instances with a 3.15-to-1 class imbalance and a 3.40 percent label noise rate, while the COMPAS recidivism dataset comprises 7,214 records with a 1.20-to-1 balance and a 6.80 percent noise rate. Statistical significance was confirmed using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across forty paired observations generated from twenty stratified splits per dataset, with Bonferroni correction applied. The baselines spanned provenance tools like MLflow and ProvCheck, fairness toolkits such as Fairlearn and Aequitas, and hybrid systems.

The articles state that modern artificial intelligence systems increasingly mediate high-stakes determinations spanning judicial recidivism assessments, consumer credit scoring, clinical diagnostics, and organizational hiring. Defective data inputs or uncalibrated transformations can induce discriminatory treatment, utility degradation, and non-compliance with binding legal instruments like the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the General Data Protection Regulation. Remediation costs escalate exponentially when failures remain undetected until after model deployment, often exceeding the cost of pre-training intervention by an order of magnitude. Existing governance paradigms treat data provenance as static historical documentation rather than an active mathematical structure capable of inference. Conventional toolkits report aggregate demographic disparities without tracing the precise upstream transformations responsible for the bias, enforce compliance through uncoupled audit spreadsheets, and treat data lineage, operational risk metrics, and statutory compliance artifacts as isolated institutional silos.

At test time, the hard mathematical operations are reinstated to preserve rigorous operational bounds, terminating with the generation of structured governance artifacts including annotated graph files, remediation plans, and audit logs. The framework applies Integrated Gradients in the embedding space against type-conditioned class centroids to isolate the exact feature dimensions responsible for flagged anomalies. The articles do not state what deployment, adoption, or regulatory review follows the published evaluation. The articles do not name the twelve baselines beyond MLflow, ProvCheck, Fairlearn, Aequitas, and Themis coupled with W3C PROV. The articles do not give the full results of the Bonferroni-corrected significance testing.

Articles.Title: Heterogeneous Provenance Graphs Enable Compliance by Construction in Artificial Intelligence Systems

stories.Headline: Historians of technology call recent US tech outages routine failures in innovation cycles
stories.Summary:
A nationwide ground stop halted all flights across the United States, customers found themselves unable to conduct transactions at America’s largest bank, Microsoft Outlook went down, Apple services became inaccessible, and even the National Security Agency’s classified email system went offline, according to a New York Times report published on November 21, 2026. The article, written by William J. Broad, describes a spate of recent tech outages that annoyed and puzzled many people across the country. Some officials linked the failures to routine tech upgrades, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested that a cause might be the global rush to build defenses against A.I. hackers. No public evidence suggested that cyberattacks had caused any of the failures, the report stated.

Historians of technology call such mishaps mundane, arguing that disasters in complex systems are inevitable parts of innovation’s boom-bust cycles. In ages past, the report says, advancements often came with the loss of thousands of lives, citing steamboat explosions at the dawn of the industrial age, the Hindenburg disaster in the early years of commercial flight, and the Apollo 1 fire near the start of the space age. From this view, the recent outages are simply part of the learning curve and are blessedly bloodless. Because inventors tend to work at the cutting edge of physics, materials science and human understanding, significant failures and trial and error are the main way they uncover the hidden flaws behind their bright ideas, according to the article.

Historians tend to agree that cycles of progress and failure have been part and parcel in the creation of steam power, electrical grids, airplanes, chemicals, medicine, rocketry and computers, the report states. The article presents this pattern as a paradox of advancement, in which the same drive that produces new tools also produces the failures that reveal their hidden flaws. The piece was published under a headline asking whether a new era of A.I.-driven chaos might just be progress, and it frames the recent outages within that longer history. The report does not say what specific fixes or changes, if any, followed the ground stop, the bank outage, the Outlook disruption, the Apple service failure or the NSA email outage.

The article names William J. Broad as the author and gives November 21, 2026, as the publication date, and it attributes the historical view to historians of technology rather than to any single named expert. It records Marco Rubio’s suggestion about defenses against A.I. hackers while noting that no public evidence tied the failures to cyberattacks. The report does not identify the largest bank, the operators of the affected services, or any agency response beyond the NSA system going offline. It ends its available text with the historians’ broad agreement on cycles of progress and failure, and it offers no further account of what happens next.

stories.Headline: Researchers link hospital support and job crafting to positive AI attitudes in nurses
stories.Summary:
Xuan Cui, Haihong Li, Min Shi, and Ting Zhao conducted a cross-sectional investigation among clinical nurses in China. The researchers published their findings in Frontiers in Medicine by November 21, 2026. They studied how hospital backing and self-initiated professional modifications connect with technology reception. The team analyzed responses from 305 clinical nurses at a tertiary grade A general hospital. Their work focused on the link between organizational support, job crafting, and artificial intelligence attitudes.

The study required data from 305 nurses at a Chinese tertiary grade A general hospital between April and June 2026. It used the Perceived Organizational Support Scale revised by Li, the Nurse Job Crafting Scale translated by Cao, and the Attitudes towards AI Application at Work scale. The researchers followed Institutional Review Board approval reference LW-20260402001-01 and used the Wenjuanxing digital survey platform. Participants included 280 females and 25 males, with 135 nurses aged 30 to under 40 years. Educational levels ranged from one doctoral credential to 255 bachelor degrees and 36 technical college diplomas.

The authors stated that proactive job crafting accounts for 60.8 percent of the association between organizational support and positive AI attitudes. They explained that organizational support theory suggests employees reciprocate employer value with constructive attitudes and innovative behaviors. The researchers noted that job crafting involves task, relational, and cognitive modifications to optimize job demands and resources. They emphasized that their cross-sectional design reflects statistical associations rather than proven causal effects. The team argued that identifying workplace conditions can alleviate anxieties and encourage proactive technological adoption.

A systematic review of 37 studies with 10,000 participants showed nurses feel guarded optimism and unease regarding algorithmic transparency. A qualitative synthesis across five nations identified concerns about professional displacement, clinical autonomy, and workloads from poorly integrated interfaces. Nurses are affected because they are the largest cadre of direct patient care providers and critical to implementation. These professionals expressed fears regarding ethical liability, deskilling, and the loss of patient-centered human connection. Many nurses reported ambivalence and cautious sentiment across the healthcare workforce.

AI is expanding through clinical inpatient and outpatient settings for decision support, documentation, risk warning, shift scheduling, and patient education. A meta-analysis of 23,451 nurses across 18 countries linked perceived support to lower burnout and reduced resignation intentions. A study of 472 Jordanian nurses connected structural organizational backing to sustained electronic health record utilization. Earlier Chinese investigations identified job crafting as a conduit between institutional backing and innovative behaviors or well-being. The authors observed that scholarship rarely examined job crafting as an explicit mediator for artificial intelligence acceptance.

The researchers suggest that longitudinal follow-up trials are necessary to prove causal effects. Future efforts may focus on the 75.7 percent of nurses who have not attended formal training. The articles leave open how to improve the 45.9 percent institutional device availability rate. They do not specify how to resolve the identified fears of professional displacement or ethical liability. The text does not detail specific policy changes needed to increase organizational support.

stories.Headline: Ava DuVernay releases 14th documentary on Netflix and defends AI animation of archival photos
stories.Summary:
Ava DuVernay has made a new Netflix documentary called “14th,” which examines the Reconstruction-era amendment that defined American citizenship and promised every person equal protection of the laws, and it opens in select U.S. and U.K. theaters on Friday, Nov. 27, before streaming globally on Netflix on Dec. 4. The film grew out of a fight that reached the Supreme Court, after President Donald Trump’s January 2025 executive order sought to end automatic citizenship for children born to parents in the country illegally or temporarily. On June 30, the justices struck down that order in a 6-3 decision, ruling that the Constitution guarantees citizenship to virtually all children born in the United States. DuVernay told The Guardian she had not planned a follow-up to “13th,” and for about a year she believed she was making a film about birthright citizenship alone before her research widened the project to cover all five sections of the amendment. Ratified in 1868, the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to people born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction, overturned the Supreme Court’s 1857 Dred Scott decision, and barred states from denying any person due process or equal protection.

DuVernay conducted more than 50 interviews for the film, and the lineup crosses party lines, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., and former Sen. Jeff Flake, R-Ariz., along with conservative author Donald T. Critchlow, voting rights advocate Stacey Abrams, law professor Robert Chang and historians Eric Foner and David Blight. Civil rights attorney Sherrilyn Ifill, who led the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund for nearly a decade and in 2025 founded Howard University’s 14th Amendment Center for Law and Democracy, is among the film’s central voices, and DuVernay called her “the Meryl Streep of 14th.” The film premiered Oct. 9 as the closing-night selection of the 64th New York Film Festival, a decade after “13th” became the first documentary to open that festival, and its international premiere followed at the BFI London Film Festival. It was produced through DuVernay’s company, ARRAY, with DuVernay, Spencer Averick, Tammy Garnes and Paul Garnes as producers.

Critics have split on the film, with Time Out awarding it five stars and calling it a must-see, while TheWrap critic Siddhant Adlakha found it scattered and short on its director’s usual rigor, though he still credited it as educational and important, and Jourdain Searles argued at RogerEbert.com that a careless presentation undercuts the film’s good intentions. Much of the conversation has centered on DuVernay’s use of artificial intelligence to add motion to black-and-white archival photographs, a technique that drew criticism online after the premiere and that Adlakha called manipulative. DuVernay has defended the approach, telling The Hollywood Reporter in late October that the production did not use it to fabricate a person or make an avatar of a person and that it animated photographs in the public domain, and she said filmmakers need to think soberly about how far the technology has spread into their work. At the New York premiere, she compared the effect to looking through a stereoscope, the 3D photo viewer popular in the Civil War era. When Netflix announced the project in July, DuVernay said in a statement that if “13th” asked who gets caged, then “14th” asks who gets counted.

stories.Headline: Roberto Riggio models distributed AI pipelines with a dual plane orchestration framework
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Roberto Riggio formulated a mathematical model and algorithmic framework to orchestrate distributed artificial intelligence workloads across converged connect-compute networks. The work was published in the Journal of Network and Systems Management by researcher Roberto Riggio. The investigation addresses deployment of complex multi-stage machine learning pipelines across heterogeneous physical substrates spanning end-user devices, near-edge servers, far-edge clusters, and centralized clouds. The central architectural contribution formalizes Artificial Intelligence Functions as modular and independently deployable software components encapsulating individual stages of a machine learning workflow. The framework establishes an explicit functional split separating an inference-focused data plane from a parameter-focused control plane.

The architecture treats Artificial Intelligence Functions as first-class orchestratable building blocks, each encapsulating an individual pipeline stage from lightweight sensor filtering and video anonymization to neural network inference and federated averaging. Every unit exposes four operational interfaces, with the northbound interface if1 providing an application-level configuration entry point for runtime parameters such as loaded model architectures, inference batch sizes, and telemetry reporting intervals. The westbound mechanisms divide into the if3 interface for the machine learning data plane and the if2 interface for the machine learning control plane, which exchanges model parameters, gradient updates, distilled representations, and distribution statistics. The data plane carries ordered, high-bandwidth, latency-critical inference traffic demanding strict sub-hundred-millisecond latencies with strictly acyclic dependency flow. The control plane carries episodic bulk transmissions of model state dispatched at intervals ranging from seconds to hours, accommodating latencies up to several seconds, often forming cyclic or hub-and-spoke topologies.

The author notes that split inference, wherein intermediate activations of a single partitioned model are transmitted between nodes, is classified under the data plane because intermediate activations represent continuous request-specific payloads that strictly gate execution progress. The paper formalizes the global mapping challenge as an Integer Linear Programming model aimed at minimizing cumulative placement cost while satisfying capacity, mapping uniqueness, semantic anchoring, latency, and multi-commodity flow conservation constraints. The formulation ensures each virtual function is mapped to exactly one substrate node, each physical node hosts at most one function from a given request, and cumulative resource demands never exceed available physical capacities. Hardware acceleration constraints enforce that functions requiring graphical processing units are mapped exclusively to acceleration-equipped substrate nodes, while anchoring constraints bind specific functions to fixed physical endpoints such as physical cameras or localized radio controllers. The author developed a two-phase greedy heuristic termed AIFG-H that decouples node placement from link routing, sorting functions in topological order along the acyclic data plane graph and mapping data plane links along latency-shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm while routing control plane links along hop-shortest paths.

Experimental evaluations across multiple substrate topologies demonstrated that the greedy heuristic achieves near-optimal resource placement costs while decreasing algorithmic computation times by three to four orders of magnitude compared to standard integer linear programming solutions. The evaluation framework benchmarked the algorithms across nine experimental scenarios combining three Waxman random substrate sizes, small with 20 nodes, medium with 50 nodes, and large with 100 nodes, with three request complexity tiers ranging from simple graphs of three to five functions to complex graphs of eight to twelve functions. Experiments evaluated 500 problem instances per scenario on server hardware equipped with an Intel Xeon Gold processor and 256 gigabytes of memory. The greedy heuristic was compared against exact solutions computed with IBM CPLEX version 22.1 under a 3600-second execution limit, as well as three comparative baseline algorithms: an acceleration-extended service function chaining heuristic designated SFC-ACC, a node-ranking virtual network embedding algorithm termed VNE-NR, and an adapted composite edge application algorithm known as CEA.

To isolate the specific impact of the control and data plane split, an ablated heuristic variant termed AIFG-H-uni was evaluated, wherein link differentiation was disabled. The study positions its technical motivation within the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence workloads across sectors such as automated mobility, healthcare, industrial automation, and immersive entertainment. These emerging applications integrate interdependent functional stages encompassing data acquisition, feature extraction, real-time inference, and centralized model consolidation. While fifth-generation mobile networks provide programmable connectivity fabrics through features like network slicing, multi-access edge computing, and disaggregated radio access, orchestrating non-monolithic machine learning pipelines across these fabrics remains challenging.

Traditional orchestration architectures rooted in virtual network function and service function chain placement fail to capture the dual nature of modern artificial intelligence tasks, typically modeling service requests as chains or directed acyclic graphs carrying a single class of uniform inter-component traffic. Consequently, standard frameworks cannot effectively reconcile the latency-critical streaming demands of live inference execution with the high-bandwidth, latency-tolerant bulk transfers required for centralized retraining, federated model parameter aggregation, drift-triggered updates, or canary rollouts. The publication details two representative industrial use cases, the first examining a pedestrian crossing warning system designed to detect approaching vehicles and trigger acoustic or visual alarms in real time. The corresponding application graph connects five functions: a camera-anchored video ingestion unit, an obfuscation component that blurs faces and license plates for privacy compliance, a hardware-accelerated feature extraction unit running object detection, an actuation interface controlling physical crossing signals, and a cloud-hosted consolidation engine managing federated learning updates.

The second use case targets adaptive video streaming using the MPEG Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP protocol, in which telemetry functions interface with an Open Radio Access Network Near-Real-Time Radio Access Network Intelligent Controller via the A1 interface to monitor physical channel conditions. Co-located bitrate prediction models process radio measurements to forecast client throughput, directing proactive chunk selection at a central media server while cloud-based update functions push revised model weights downstream over control plane links. The framework represents application requirements as an Artificial Intelligence Forwarding Graph, defined as a directed multigraph where vertices denote individual functions and edges represent typed virtual links constructed over typed triples to accommodate parallel edges connecting the same pair of functions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Rep. Nathaniel Moran co-founds House AI caucus to balance safety and innovation
stories.Summary:
Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas co-founded a new House AI caucus on November 21, 2026. This legislative group aims to address the rapid growth of artificial intelligence within the United States government. The representative believes that Congress must act quickly to manage the evolving landscape of this technology. He intends to lead efforts that balance safety with the need for technical progress.

The initiative requires the creation of specific safeguards to mitigate the potential risks associated with artificial intelligence. These measures must be carefully designed so they do not stifle innovation or slow down domestic development. Representative Moran argues that overly strict regulations could allow China to gain a significant competitive advantage. He believes the United States must maintain its leadership in the global technology sector.

Representative Moran is responsible for championing this balanced approach to legislative oversight of artificial intelligence. He stated that the government should protect the public without hindering the growth of new tools. The congressman emphasized that the goal is to secure the nation while fostering a pro-innovation environment. He believes that strategic oversight will prevent risks without sacrificing the speed of American discovery.

stories.Headline: DARPA awards New Mexico State University $600,000 to develop verified AI reasoning architectures
stories.Summary:
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency awarded a research grant to New Mexico State University on November 20, 2026. This funding supports the development of verified neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence architectures for safety-critical defense engineering. The agency provided 600,000 dollars for this specific research effort over a two-year period. Computer scientists at the university will pair machine learning pattern recognition with formal logical proofs. This work falls under the Compositional Learning-And-Reasoning for Automated Complex Systems Engineering program.

The project, called Project SPARTA, involves New Mexico State University, Arizona State University, and the University of Nebraska at Omaha. Professor Son Tran and Assistant Professor Stylianos Vasileiou lead the effort at New Mexico State University. Professor Chitta Baral directs the Arizona State University group, while Professors Yuliana Lierler and Jorge Fandinno lead the Nebraska team. The program requires native algorithmic compositionality instead of using post-hoc validation filters on large models. It utilizes splitting-based logic programming, polynomially-bounded automated reasoning, and tensorized adaptation interfaces.

Principal investigator Son Tran stated that integrating these AI branches provides machine learning speed with verifiability. He noted that reasoning proofs offer strong logical explainability and computational tractability for practical engineering. Tran emphasized that computational tractability is the make-or-break criterion for real-time deployment in industrial systems. The goal is to replace unverified statistical guesses with rigorous logical guarantees. This approach ensures that mathematical proofs execute within deterministic processing budgets.

Superpower Daily reported that this initiative represents fundamental basic science rather than a commercial product. The outlet noted the challenge of scaling formal verification across complex systems beyond laboratory benchmarks. Defense contractors building unmanned aerial systems or radar signal processors are affected by these outputs. These contractors could eventually integrate reusable verification libraries into safety-critical firmware. University research offices must also manage subawards and export controls like ITAR and EAR.

Deep neural networks rely on correlation rather than deduction, which creates vulnerabilities in safety-critical domains. Failures can occur in flight control software, aerospace trajectory synthesis, autonomous naval navigation, and power grid automation. DARPA's Defense Sciences Office identified the current serial configuration of AI safety as fundamentally brittle. The CLARA program was solicited as a Disruption Opportunity to fast-track high-risk basic research. McAllister and Quinn noted that these opportunities challenge prevailing commercial assumptions.

During the first twelve months, teams will establish theoretical formalisms and engineer prototype mapping modules. The second year involves integrating algorithms into a unified open-source toolchain for rigorous benchmarking. Researchers will measure verification runtime, proof validity, and model generalization using DARPA-supplied engineering challenges. The articles leave open whether formal verification can remain scalable across arbitrary complex systems. They do not state if the project will meet all its technical milestones.

stories.Headline: Researchers find data infrastructure gaps limit AI use in ESG financial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers Miehleketo Mathebula, Abiodun Modupe, Vukosi Marivate, and Elda Du Toit conducted a systematic literature review. They published their investigation in the journal Discover Artificial Intelligence by November 21, 2026. The study assessed how artificial intelligence is applied across environmental, social, and governance financial intelligence. They examined 70 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2017 and 2025. The authors wanted to find the cause of operational limitations in sustainable finance analytics.

The review requires moving past proprietary data dependencies and incompatible metadata schemas. It identifies gaps in unstandardised disclosure environments across the Global Reporting Initiative and Sustainability Accounting Standards Board. The Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures also creates inconsistent reporting structures. Researchers used IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and MDPI databases starting January 7, 2026. They analyzed 1,623 candidate records before narrowing the final corpus to 70 articles.

The authors stated that computational model architectures have significantly outpaced the required data infrastructures. They argued that principal constraints arise from institutional disparities rather than algorithmic complexity. The researchers urged the community to stop treating commercial ESG ratings as objective ground-truth labels. They also said that post-hoc explainability cannot compensate for unverified data provenance. They claimed technological interventions cannot fix absent semantic crosswalks.

The study affects the research community and those using high-stakes financial environments. It notes that African institutions contributed only eight studies compared to larger volumes from Asia, Europe, and North America. South Africa produced 11 documents but showed very low global integration. The review found that most tasks were executed in isolation on curated benchmark corpora. These tasks rarely demonstrated integration with live compliance verification or supervisory auditing pipelines.

The background shows a shift from traditional machine learning to generative language modeling. Traditional machine learning appeared 40 times, while deep learning appeared 36 times. Natural language processing had 26 implementations, and general large language models had 15. The review used a six-criterion appraisal framework to score studies up to ten points. This process involved two independent reviewers who achieved a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.82.

Next, the authors propose a conceptual architecture for preprocessing, semantic standardisation, and governance oversight. They illustrated this using a South African report prepared under the King IV governance code. The articles leave this architecture as an unvalidated design blueprint rather than a deployed solution. Future progress requires concerted global investments in open-access benchmark datasets. The researchers leave the actual deployment of these software solutions open.
